glossary.pardon vs reprieve vs respite vs remissi: The distinct clemency tools available to the Governor under Article 161 — a pardon (complete absolution), reprieve (temporary stay of execution of sentence), respite (postponement, often on special grounds like pregnancy or illness), remission (reduction of sentence duration without changing its nature), and commutation (substituting a lighter form of punishment for a harsher one).
glossary.extent of State executive power (Article: The Article 162 rule that a State's executive power extends to matters over which the State Legislature can make laws, mirroring the President's coextensive Union executive power under Article 73, subject to the Constitution and to the Concurrent List proviso favouring Union executive power.
glossary.coextensiveness of State executive and l: The general principle underlying Article 162 that a State's executive competence tracks its legislative competence — the State executive can act wherever the State Legislature could validly legislate, absent some other constitutional qualification.
glossary.Concurrent List executive-power subordin: The proviso to Article 162 providing that, on Concurrent List subjects (where both Parliament and State Legislatures can legislate), the State's executive power is subject to and limited by any executive power the Constitution or Parliamentary law expressly confers on the Union or its authorities.
glossary.Council of Ministers headed by Chief Min: The Article 163(1) constitutional body — the Council of Ministers with the Chief Minister at its head — that aids and advises the Governor in exercising his functions, establishing the State-level parliamentary system of responsible government mirroring Article 74's Union-level design.
glossary.Governor's discretionary functions carve: The Article 163(1) exception under which the Governor may act in his own discretion, without ministerial aid and advice, only in the specific situations where the Constitution itself requires such discretionary action — a narrow exception to the default rule of acting on ministerial advice.
glossary.finality of Governor's discretion determ: The Article 163(2) rule making the Governor's own decision about whether a matter falls within his discretionary zone final, and shielding the validity of his action from challenge merely on the ground that he ought or ought not to have exercised discretion — though not an absolute bar to judicial review for mala fides or wholly extraneous considerations.
glossary.ministerial advice immunity from judicia: The Article 163(3) rule barring any court from inquiring into whether, and if so what, advice Ministers tendered to the Governor — protecting the confidentiality of Cabinet-level communications from judicial scrutiny.
glossary.tribal welfare Minister proviso (Article: The proviso to Article 164(1) constitutionally mandating that Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh, and Odisha each have a Minister specifically in charge of tribal welfare, who may additionally handle Scheduled Castes/backward classes welfare or other assigned work — recognising these States' significant Scheduled Tribe populations.
glossary.15% cap and 12-minimum Council of Minist: The Article 164(1A) rule, inserted by the Ninety-first Amendment Act, 2003, capping a State's total Council of Ministers (including the Chief Minister) at 15% of the Legislative Assembly's total membership, subject to a proviso guaranteeing a floor of at least 12 Ministers regardless of Assembly size — aimed at curbing oversized Councils used for political accommodation.
glossary.Tenth Schedule disqualification bar on b: The Article 164(1B) rule, also inserted by the Ninety-first Amendment, 2003, barring a Legislature member disqualified under the Tenth Schedule's anti-defection paragraph 2 from Ministerial appointment for a period tied to the disqualification's duration or until a fresh election, whichever is earlier — closing a loophole where defectors could otherwise be rewarded with ministerial office.
glossary.collective responsibility to Legislative: The Article 164(2) foundational responsible-government principle making the State Council of Ministers, as a body, collectively answerable to the Legislative Assembly for the government's actions and decisions — the Assembly (not the Governor or Legislative Council) can remove the government via a no-confidence vote.
glossary.Minister's oath of office and secrecy (S: The Article 164(3) requirement that a State Minister take the oaths of office and of secrecy, in the Third Schedule's prescribed forms, administered by the Governor before the Minister enters upon office — paralleling the Union-level Ministerial oath under Article 75(4).
glossary.six-consecutive-month non-membership ces: The Article 164(4) rule automatically terminating a Minister's office if he remains outside the State Legislature (neither House) for six consecutive months — ensuring Ministers are, with only a brief grace period, accountable, elected or nominated members of the Legislature.
glossary.Advocate-General for the State: The Article 165 constitutional office — a Governor-appointed chief legal adviser to the State Government, qualified to be a High Court Judge, who advises on legal matters, performs assigned legal-character duties, and discharges functions conferred by the Constitution or other law, holding office during the Governor's pleasure.
glossary.executive action expressed in Governor's: The Article 166(1) formal rule that all executive action of a State Government is legally expressed as taken in the Governor's name, even though real decision-making in practice rests with the Council of Ministers — preserving the formal constitutional unity of the State executive.
glossary.authentication of orders/instruments (Go: The Article 166(2) mechanism under which orders and instruments issued in the Governor's name are authenticated per Governor-made rules, with the resulting order's validity shielded from challenge merely on the ground that the Governor did not personally make or execute it — enabling practical government functioning through delegated authentication.
glossary.Governor's rules for business transactio: The Article 166(3) power letting the Governor make 'rules of business' governing how State government business is conveniently transacted and allocated among Ministers, excluding matters within the Governor's own constitutionally-required discretionary zone under Article 163.
glossary.Chief Minister's duty to communicate Cou: The Article 167(a) duty requiring the Chief Minister to proactively communicate to the Governor all Council of Ministers decisions relating to State administration and legislative proposals, without needing to be asked.
glossary.Governor's power to call for information: The Article 167(b) power letting the Governor call for and receive from the Chief Minister any information relating to the administration of State affairs or legislative proposals — the State-level counterpart to the President's Article 78(b) power.
glossary.Governor's power to require full-Council: The Article 167(c) power letting the Governor require the Chief Minister to submit, for the full Council of Ministers' consideration, any matter an individual Minister decided on his own that the Council as a body has not yet reviewed — a mechanism for ensuring collective Cabinet oversight of individually-taken decisions.
glossary.bicameral vs unicameral State Legislatur: The Article 168(1) classification of State Legislatures as either bicameral (Governor plus a Legislative Council and a Legislative Assembly, currently a specific named list of States) or unicameral (Governor plus a Legislative Assembly alone, for all other States).
glossary.Legislative Council and Legislative Asse: The Article 168(2) naming convention for a bicameral State Legislature's two Houses — the upper House is the Legislative Council, the lower (and, in unicameral States, sole) House is always the Legislative Assembly.
glossary.Governor as constituent part of State Le: The Article 168(1) structural rule making the Governor a formal constituent part of the State Legislature (alongside the House or Houses), exactly paralleling the President's constituent role in Parliament under Article 79 — the Governor is not a House member but is nonetheless part of the Legislature as an institution.
glossary.State-initiated request for Council abol: The Article 169(1) precondition that a State's Legislative Assembly must itself pass a special resolution before Parliament may abolish an existing Legislative Council or create a new one for that State — the State's own Assembly, not Parliament unilaterally, initiates the process.
glossary.special State Assembly resolution majori: The dual-majority threshold an Article 169(1) resolution must clear in the State Legislative Assembly — a majority of the Assembly's total membership, and a majority of not less than two-thirds of members present and voting — a deliberately high bar for a structurally significant decision.
glossary.deemed non-amendment under Article 368 (: The Article 169(3) rule that a Parliamentary law abolishing or creating a State Legislative Council, even though it may amend constitutional text (e.g., Article 168's bicameral-States list), is not deemed an amendment for Article 368 purposes — so it can be passed by ordinary Parliamentary majority without Article 368's special procedure.
glossary.Legislative Assembly size range (60-500): The Article 170(1) numerical bounds on a State Legislative Assembly's membership — not more than 500 and not less than 60 members, all directly elected — mirroring the Lok Sabha's Article 81 size-range structure at the State level.
glossary.direct election from territorial constit: The Article 170(1) rule that all Legislative Assembly members are chosen by direct election from single-member territorial constituencies within the State, the same electoral method used for the Lok Sabha.
glossary.one-vote-one-value ratio principle (Stat: The Article 170(2) delimitation principle requiring that, so far as practicable, the population-to-seat ratio be uniform across all territorial constituencies within a State — preventing some constituencies' votes from carrying disproportionately more or less weight than others.
glossary.delimitation freeze tied to 2026 census: The Article 170(3) proviso mechanism (mirroring Article 82's identical Lok Sabha freeze) pegging State Assembly seat totals to the 1971 census and constituency boundaries to the 2001-census-based delimitation, until the first census taken after 2026 is published — a policy freeze extended multiple times by constitutional amendment.
glossary.Legislative Council size cap (one-third: The Article 171(1) rule capping a State Legislative Council's total membership at one-third of that State's Legislative Assembly membership, subject to a proviso guaranteeing an absolute floor of 40 members.
glossary.five-fold composition of Legislative Cou: The default five-category composition formula for a State Legislative Council under Article 171(3), absent a different Parliamentary law: local-authorities' electorate (~1/3), graduates' electorate (~1/12), teachers' electorate (~1/12), MLA-elected non-MLA members (~1/3), and Governor-nominated members (the remainder).
glossary.local authorities' constituency (Legisla: The Article 171(3)(a) electorate category — roughly one-third of Council seats elected by members of municipalities, district boards, and other local authorities Parliament specifies by law — representing local self-government bodies' interests in the upper House.
glossary.graduates' constituency (Legislative Cou: The Article 171(3)(b) electorate category — roughly one-twelfth of Council seats elected by persons who have been university graduates (or holders of an equivalent qualification) for at least three years and reside in the State.
glossary.teachers' constituency (Legislative Coun: The Article 171(3)(c) electorate category — roughly one-twelfth of Council seats elected by persons who have taught for at least three years in educational institutions within the State not lower in standard than a secondary school.
glossary.MLA-elected Council seats (Article 171(3: The Article 171(3)(d) electorate category — roughly one-third of Council seats elected by the State's Legislative Assembly members themselves, but only from among candidates who are not already Assembly members.
glossary.Governor's nominated Council members — s: The Article 171(3)(e) and 171(5) category — the remaining Council seats, filled by Governor's nominees possessing special knowledge or practical experience in literature, science, art, the co-operative movement, or social service, a closed list of five qualifying fields.
glossary.proportional representation by single tr: The Article 171(4) electoral method used for all elected Legislative Council seats (sub-clauses (a) through (d)) — proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote, rather than the first-past-the-post system used for directly-elected Assembly and Lok Sabha seats.
glossary.five-year Legislative Assembly term (Sta: The Article 172(1) default tenure of a State Legislative Assembly — five years from the date appointed for its first meeting, with automatic dissolution upon expiry unless the Assembly is dissolved sooner — mirroring the Lok Sabha's Article 83(2) term.
glossary.Emergency extension of Assembly term (St: The proviso to Article 172(1) letting Parliament extend a State Legislative Assembly's term by law, one year at a time, while a Proclamation of Emergency is in operation, subject to a hard cap of six months after the Emergency ends — the State-level counterpart to the Lok Sabha's Article 83(2) Emergency-extension proviso.
glossary.Legislative Council permanence with one-: The Article 172(2) rule that a State Legislative Council, unlike the Assembly, is never dissolved as a body — instead, roughly one-third of its members retire every second year per Parliament-made rules, producing staggered, continuous membership exactly like the Rajya Sabha under Article 83(1).
glossary.Indian citizenship requirement (State Le: The Article 173(a) baseline eligibility rule requiring a candidate for a State Legislature seat to be an Indian citizen — the first of several cumulative qualification requirements.
glossary.pre-candidacy oath before Election-Commi: The Article 173(a) requirement that a State Legislature candidate make and subscribe the Third Schedule oath or affirmation before a person the Election Commission has authorised for that purpose, as a precondition to being chosen for the seat — distinct from the separate post-election oath a member later takes under Article 188 before actually sitting.
glossary.minimum age 25 (Assembly) / 30 (Council): The Article 173(b) minimum-age eligibility thresholds for State Legislature membership — 25 years for a Legislative Assembly seat and 30 years for a Legislative Council seat — mirroring the Lok Sabha (25) and Rajya Sabha (30) age differential under Article 84(b).
glossary.further qualifications by Parliamentary: The Article 173(c) residual category letting Parliament prescribe additional qualifications for State Legislature membership by law, principally exercised through the Representation of the People Act, 1951.
glossary.Governor's summoning power (State Legisl: The Article 174(1) power letting the Governor summon the House or each House of a State Legislature to meet at a time and place of his choosing, subject to the mandatory maximum six-month gap between sessions.
glossary.six-month maximum gap between sessions (: The Article 174(1) rule guaranteeing a State Legislature meets at least twice a year, by prohibiting more than six months from elapsing between one session's last sitting and the next session's first sitting — the State-level mirror of Article 85(1)'s identical rule for Parliament.
glossary.Governor's prorogation power (State Legi: The Article 174(2)(a) power letting the Governor prorogue (formally end the sitting of) the House or either House of a State Legislature without dissolving it — ending a session while the House's membership and life continue.
glossary.Governor's dissolution power (Legislativ: The Article 174(2)(b) power letting the Governor dissolve the Legislative Assembly specifically — a power that, per Article 172(2), can never be exercised against a Legislative Council, which is constitutionally immune from dissolution.
glossary.Governor's power to address the House(s): The Article 175(1) power letting the Governor personally address the Legislative Assembly, either House (in a bicameral State), or both Houses assembled together, and require members' attendance for that purpose — a general-purpose, any-time communication tool mirroring the President's Article 86(1) power.
glossary.Governor's power to send messages to the: The Article 175(2) power letting the Governor send written messages to the State Legislature's House or Houses on any matter, pending Bill or otherwise, obliging the receiving House to consider the message's subject with all convenient despatch — the State-level mirror of Article 86(2).
glossary.Special Address at each year's first ses: The Article 176(1) mandatory obligation requiring the Governor to address the Assembly (or both Houses together) at the start of the first session after each general election and at the start of each calendar year's first session, informing the Legislature of the causes of its summons — functionally a government policy statement, mirroring the President's Article 87(1) duty.
glossary.allotted-time debate on Governor's Speci: The Article 176(2) requirement that State Legislature procedural rules set aside dedicated time for discussing the matters raised in the Governor's Special Address — ensuring the address triggers substantive legislative scrutiny.
glossary.Ministers' and Advocate-General's floor: The Article 177 rule giving every State Minister and the Advocate-General the right to speak and participate in the Assembly's, both Houses', and any Legislature committee's proceedings regardless of their own House membership, but expressly without conferring any right to vote — voting remains tied to actual membership of the relevant House.
glossary.Speaker and Deputy Speaker of Legislativ: The Article 178 requirement that every State Legislative Assembly elect two of its own members as Speaker and Deputy Speaker, refilling either office by fresh election whenever vacant — mirroring the Lok Sabha's Article 93 arrangement.
glossary.automatic vacation on ceasing Assembly m: The Article 179(a) rule that a State Assembly's Speaker or Deputy Speaker automatically vacates that office the moment he ceases to be an Assembly member — the presiding office cannot exist independently of membership.
glossary.resignation of Speaker/Deputy Speaker in: The Article 179(b) mechanism letting the Speaker or Deputy Speaker resign at will via a signed writing addressed to the counterpart officer (Speaker to Deputy Speaker, or vice versa).
glossary.removal by absolute-majority Assembly re: The Article 179(c) removal mechanism for a State Assembly's Speaker or Deputy Speaker — a resolution passed by a majority of all then Assembly members (not merely those present and voting), which cannot even be moved without at least fourteen days' prior notice of intent.
glossary.Speaker's continuation in office through: The second proviso to Article 179 ensuring a State Assembly's Speaker (specifically, not the Deputy Speaker) continues in office through the Assembly's dissolution, vacating only immediately before the newly-constituted Assembly's first meeting — preventing any leaderless gap.
glossary.Deputy Speaker filling a vacant Speaker': The Article 180(1) rule that, while the Speaker's office itself is vacant, the Deputy Speaker performs the Speaker's duties — the first-line continuity mechanism for a State Assembly.
glossary.Governor-appointed member filling both o: The Article 180(1) last-resort mechanism letting the Governor appoint an Assembly member to perform the Speaker's duties, but only where both the Speaker's and Deputy Speaker's offices are simultaneously vacant.
glossary.acting Speaker for a single sitting's ab: The Article 180(2) cascading fallback for a State Assembly sitting where the Speaker (whose office is not vacant) is merely absent that day — the Deputy Speaker acts first, then a rules-designated person, then someone the Assembly itself determines for that sitting.
glossary.disqualification from presiding during o: The Article 181(1) natural-justice rule barring a State Assembly's Speaker or Deputy Speaker from presiding over the sitting considering his own removal, even if physically present, with Article 180(2)'s absence-fallback rules applying as if he were absent.
glossary.Speaker's first-instance-only voting rig: The Article 181(2) carve-out letting the Speaker vote in the first instance on his own removal resolution or any other matter during such proceedings — departing from his ordinary Article 189 no-vote-except-tie-breaking rule — while still denying him the tie-breaking casting vote.
glossary.Chairman and Deputy Chairman of Legislat: The Article 182 requirement that a bicameral State's Legislative Council elect two of its own members as Chairman and Deputy Chairman, refilling either office whenever vacant — structurally closer to the Speaker-selection model of Article 178 than to the Rajya Sabha's ex officio Vice-President-as-Chairman arrangement.
glossary.automatic vacation on ceasing Council me: The Article 183(a) rule that a Legislative Council's Chairman or Deputy Chairman automatically vacates office upon ceasing to be a Council member — the Council-level mirror of Article 179(a).
glossary.resignation of Chairman/Deputy Chairman: The Article 183(b) mechanism letting the Chairman or Deputy Chairman of a Legislative Council resign at will via signed writing addressed to the counterpart officer.
glossary.removal of Chairman/Deputy Chairman by a: The Article 183(c) removal mechanism for a Legislative Council's Chairman or Deputy Chairman — an absolute-majority resolution of all then Council members, requiring at least fourteen days' advance notice before it can even be moved, with no dissolution-continuity proviso needed since the Council itself is never dissolved.
glossary.Deputy Chairman filling a vacant Chairma: The Article 184(1) rule that, while the Chairman's office of a State Legislative Council is vacant, the Deputy Chairman performs the Chairman's duties — the Council-level mirror of Article 180(1)'s Speaker/Deputy Speaker rule.
glossary.Governor-appointed Council member fillin: The Article 184(1) last-resort mechanism letting the Governor appoint a Legislative Council member to perform the Chairman's duties, but only where both the Chairman's and Deputy Chairman's offices are simultaneously vacant.
glossary.acting Chairman for a single sitting's a: The Article 184(2) cascading fallback for a Legislative Council sitting where the Chairman (office not vacant) is merely absent — Deputy Chairman acts first, then a rules-designated person, then someone the Council itself determines for that sitting.
glossary.disqualification from presiding during o: The Article 185(1) natural-justice rule barring a Legislative Council's Chairman or Deputy Chairman from presiding over the sitting considering his own removal, even if physically present — the Council-level mirror of Article 181(1).
glossary.Chairman's first-instance-only voting ri: The Article 185(2) carve-out letting the Chairman vote in the first instance on his own removal resolution or any other matter during such proceedings, departing from Article 189's ordinary rule, while still being denied the tie-breaking casting vote.
glossary.salaries and allowances of presiding off: The Article 186 guarantee that the Speaker, Deputy Speaker, Chairman, and Deputy Chairman of a State Legislature receive salaries and allowances fixed by State legislative law, defaulting to Second Schedule figures absent such law.
glossary.Second Schedule default (State presiding: The Article 186 fallback mechanism applying Second Schedule salary/allowance figures to the State Legislature's four presiding/deputy-presiding officers until the State Legislature enacts its own law on the subject.
glossary.separate secretarial staff per House (St: The Article 187(1) rule guaranteeing each House of a State Legislature its own secretarial staff, subject to a proviso permitting common posts across both Houses in bicameral States.
glossary.common posts across both Houses proviso: The proviso to Article 187(1) permitting a bicameral State's Legislature to create secretarial posts common to both the Assembly and the Council, avoiding unnecessary staffing duplication while still guaranteeing each House its own dedicated staff.
glossary.State law regulating Legislature secreta: The Article 187(2) power letting a State Legislature regulate, by law, the recruitment and conditions of service of persons appointed to its House(s)' secretarial staff — the primary, preferred regulatory mechanism.
glossary.Governor's interim rules for Secretariat: The Article 187(3) interim rule-making power letting the Governor regulate Secretariat staff recruitment and service conditions absent a State law on the subject, but only after consulting the Speaker (Assembly staff) or Chairman (Council staff), with such rules yielding to any later State law.
glossary.member's oath before taking seat (State: The Article 188 requirement that every State Legislature member — Assembly or Council — make and subscribe the Third Schedule oath or affirmation before the Governor (or his delegate) before actually taking his seat, distinct from the earlier Article 173(a) pre-candidacy oath.
glossary.ordinary-majority voting rule (State Leg: The Article 189(1) default rule that all questions in either House of a State Legislature are decided by a majority of members present and voting (excluding the presiding officer), other than matters for which the Constitution prescribes a special majority.
glossary.Speaker/Chairman's no-vote-except-castin: The Article 189(1) proviso barring the Speaker, Chairman, or person acting as such from voting in the first instance, while giving him a casting vote in the case of an equality of votes — the Council/Assembly-level mirror of Article 100(1)'s Union rule.
glossary.House's power to act despite vacancies/i: The Article 189(2) validity-preserving rule that proceedings of a State House remain valid despite an unfilled vacancy or the participation of a person later found not entitled to sit/vote, ensuring legislative business isn't retroactively invalidated.
glossary.quorum: 10 members or one-tenth, whichev: The Article 189(3) quorum rule for a State Legislature House — the greater of ten members or one-tenth of the total membership — and the linked duty of the presiding officer to adjourn or suspend the sitting if quorum is not met.
glossary.bar on dual-House membership within one: The Article 190(1) rule that no person may simultaneously be a member of both the Legislative Assembly and Legislative Council of the same State; State law prescribes how the seat in one House is vacated upon election/nomination to the other.
glossary.bar on membership across multiple States: The Article 190(1)/Article 190(2) rule barring simultaneous membership in the Legislatures of two or more States, with Parliament empowered to make the specifying law; a person elected to Legislatures of two or more States must vacate his seat in all but one within the prescribed time or his seat in every House becomes automatically vacant.
glossary.seat vacation on Article 191 disqualific: The Article 190(3) rule that a State Legislature member's seat becomes vacant if he becomes subject to any Article 191 disqualification, or if he resigns in writing addressed to the Speaker/Chairman and the resignation is accepted.
glossary.genuineness-of-resignation inquiry by Sp: The Article 190(3) proviso (inserted by the Thirty-third Amendment, 1974) requiring the Speaker or Chairman, before accepting a resignation, to satisfy himself that it is voluntary and genuine, with a discretion to withhold acceptance if not so satisfied — a safeguard against coerced or fraudulent resignations.
glossary.sixty-day unauthorised absence seat forf: The Article 190(4) rule letting a State House declare a member's seat vacant if he is absent from all its sittings for sixty days without its permission, excluding periods of prorogation or adjournment for more than four consecutive days when computing the sixty days.
glossary.office of profit disqualification (State: The Article 191(1)(a) disqualification barring a person from being chosen as, or being, a State Legislature member if he holds an office of profit under the Union or State Government (other than an office Parliamentary/State law declares not to disqualify) — the State-level mirror of Article 102(1)(a).
glossary.unsound mind disqualification (State Leg: The Article 191(1)(b) disqualification for a person of unsound mind so declared by a competent court, mirroring Article 102(1)(b) at Union level.
glossary.undischarged insolvent disqualification: The Article 191(1)(c) disqualification for an undischarged insolvent, mirroring Article 102(1)(c) at Union level.
glossary.citizenship/foreign allegiance disqualif: The Article 191(1)(d) disqualification for a person not an Indian citizen, or who has voluntarily acquired foreign citizenship, or is under any acknowledgement of allegiance/adherence to a foreign State, mirroring Article 102(1)(d).
glossary.Parliamentary-law disqualification groun: The Article 191(1)(e) residual disqualification ground for grounds made by or under any law enacted by Parliament, mirroring Article 102(1)(e); Parliament, not the State Legislature, holds this residual law-making power.
glossary.Minister exemption from office-of-profit: The Explanation to Article 191(1) clarifying that a person is not disqualified merely for being a Minister of the Union or a State — the office-of-profit bar does not reach a Minister's own ministerial office.
glossary.Tenth Schedule anti-defection disqualifi: The Article 191(2) disqualification (added by the Fifty-second Amendment, 1985) for defection under the Tenth Schedule, applying to State Legislature members exactly as Article 102(2) applies it to Parliament members.
glossary.Governor as adjudicator of Article 191(1: The Article 192(1) rule that questions on whether a sitting State Legislature member has become subject to any Article 191(1) disqualification are decided by the Governor, whose decision is final — the State-level mirror of the President's role under Article 103, but confined to Article 191(1) grounds only (Tenth Schedule defection questions go to the Speaker/Chairman instead).
glossary.mandatory, binding Election Commission o: The Article 192(2) requirement that before deciding any Article 191(1) disqualification question, the Governor must obtain the Election Commission's opinion and act according to it — making the Governor's 'final' decision substantively an Election-Commission-driven determination.
glossary.per-day penalty for sitting/voting witho: The Article 193 penalty of five hundred rupees for each day a person sits or votes as a State Legislature member before making the Article 188 oath, or while knowing he is not qualified or is disqualified, or while knowing a Parliamentary law forbids it.
glossary.penalty recovered as a debt due to the S: The Article 193 enforcement mechanism specifying that the per-day penalty for improper sitting/voting is recovered as an ordinary civil debt owed to the State Government, not through a separate criminal or contempt process.
glossary.freedom of speech in State Legislature: The Article 194(1) guarantee of freedom of speech within a State Legislature, subject to the Constitution and to the House's own rules and standing orders — the State-level mirror of Article 105(1)'s Parliamentary freedom of speech.
glossary.immunity from court proceedings for legi: The Article 194(2) absolute immunity shielding a State Legislature member from any court proceeding over anything said or any vote given in the House or its committees, and shielding authorised publication of House reports/papers/proceedings from liability.
glossary.State-law-defined residual powers/privil: The Article 194(3) rule that beyond the specific speech/vote immunities, a State House's other powers, privileges, and immunities are whatever the State Legislature defines by law.
glossary.pre-44th-Amendment default privileges (S: The Article 194(3) fallback rule that, absent State legislative law defining privileges, a State House's powers/privileges/immunities default to whatever applied immediately before the 44th Amendment Act, 1978's section 26 came into force (20-6-1979) — not automatically equated with UK House of Commons privileges.
glossary.privileges extended to non-member floor-: The Article 194(4) rule extending clauses (1)-(3)'s speech/vote/privilege protections to any person who, though not a member, has a constitutional right to speak and participate in a State House's proceedings (e.g., a Minister or the Advocate-General under Article 177).
glossary.salaries and allowances of ordinary memb: The Article 195 guarantee that ordinary members of a State's Legislative Assembly and Legislative Council — as distinct from the four presiding officers covered by Article 186 — receive salaries and allowances fixed by State legislative law.
glossary.pre-Constitution Provincial Assembly rat: The Article 195 fallback rule that, absent State legislative law on member salaries/allowances, the rates and conditions applicable immediately before the Constitution's commencement to the corresponding pre-Constitution Province's Legislative Assembly members apply instead.
glossary.either-House origination for ordinary Bi: The Article 196(1) rule that an ordinary (non-Money, non-financial) Bill may originate in either House of a bicameral State's Legislature, subject to Articles 198 and 207's Money/financial Bill restrictions.
glossary.both-Houses agreement requirement (bicam: The Article 196(2) rule that a Bill is deemed passed by a bicameral State's Legislature only once both Houses agree to it (with or without mutually accepted amendments), subject to Article 197's override mechanism for Council disagreement.
glossary.non-lapse of pending Bills on prorogatio: The Article 196(3) rule that a Bill pending in either House of a State Legislature does not lapse merely because that House is prorogued.
glossary.non-lapse of Council-pending Bills on As: The Article 196(4) rule that a Bill pending only in the Legislative Council — one the Assembly has not yet passed — survives an Assembly dissolution, since it was never the Assembly's interrupted business.
glossary.lapse of Assembly-pending/Assembly-passe: The Article 196(5) rule that a Bill still pending in the Legislative Assembly, or already passed by the Assembly and awaiting the Council, lapses automatically when the Assembly is dissolved.
glossary.Legislative Council's suspensive (delayi: The structural characterisation, confirmed by Article 197, that a State Legislative Council can only delay and recommend changes to ordinary Bills, never permanently block them — the Assembly's second passage overrides any Council objection.
glossary.three-month Council delay threshold (fir: The Article 197(1)(b) rule letting the Assembly invoke its override procedure if more than three months elapse after an ordinary Bill is laid before the Council without the Council passing it.
glossary.one-month Council delay threshold (secon: The Article 197(2)(b) rule letting a Bill be deemed passed if, after the Assembly's second passage, more than one month elapses without the Council passing it.
glossary.Assembly's deemed-passage override on se: The Article 197(2) rule that after the Assembly passes an ordinary Bill a second time and transmits it to the Council, the Bill is deemed passed by the Legislature in the Assembly's second-passage form regardless of the Council's rejection, delay, or unaccepted amendments.
glossary.Money Bill introduction restricted to As: The Article 198(1) rule barring a Money Bill from being introduced in a State's Legislative Council — it must originate in the Legislative Assembly.
glossary.fourteen-day Council recommendation wind: The Article 198(2) time limit within which a State Legislative Council must return a Money Bill to the Assembly with its recommendations, mirroring the Rajya Sabha's identical fourteen-day window under Article 109(2).
glossary.Assembly's absolute accept/reject discre: The Article 198(3)-(4) rule that the Legislative Assembly may accept or reject, wholly or partly and at its own discretion, any Money Bill recommendation from the Council, with the Bill deemed passed in whatever form results from the Assembly's decision.
glossary.deemed passage on Council silence past f: The Article 198(5) rule that if the Council does not return a Money Bill within fourteen days, the Bill is deemed passed by both Houses in the form the Assembly originally passed it.
glossary.seven-category exhaustive Money Bill def: The Article 199(1) exhaustive list of seven subject-matter categories — taxation, State borrowing/guarantees, Consolidated/Contingency Fund custody and flows, appropriation, charged expenditure, and incidental matters — that alone can make a State Bill a Money Bill; a Bill containing other subject matter falls outside this definition even if it also touches these topics.
glossary.fines/fees/local-tax carve-out from Mone: The Article 199(2) exclusion providing that a Bill is not a Money Bill merely because it imposes fines or pecuniary penalties, licence or service fees, or because it lets a local authority impose/alter taxes for local purposes.
glossary.Speaker's final certification of Money B: The Article 199(3) rule making the Legislative Assembly Speaker's decision on whether a State Bill is a Money Bill conclusive and final, foreclosing further dispute over its classification in ordinary practice.
glossary.mandatory Speaker's certificate endorsem: The Article 199(4) requirement that the Speaker sign and endorse a certificate on every Money Bill both when it is transmitted to the Legislative Council and when it is presented to the Governor for assent, giving downstream actors conclusive documentary proof of its status.
glossary.Governor's three options on a passed Bil: The Article 200 rule that a Governor presented with a duly passed State Bill must choose one of three responses: assent to it, withhold assent, or reserve it for the President's consideration.
glossary.Governor's non-Money-Bill return-for-rec: The Article 200 first proviso letting the Governor, for non-Money Bills only, return a Bill once with a message suggesting reconsideration or specific amendments before deciding on assent.
glossary.mandatory assent on Bill's reconsidered: The Article 200 first-proviso rule that once a State Legislature re-passes a Governor-returned Bill (with or without amendment), the Governor is constitutionally bound to assent and cannot withhold assent on that second presentation.
glossary.mandatory reservation for High-Court-end: The Article 200 second proviso requiring a Governor to reserve — never directly assent to — any Bill that in his opinion would, if enacted, so derogate from a High Court's powers as to endanger the position the Constitution designed it to fill; a State-specific judicial-independence safeguard with no Union-level parallel.
glossary.President's binary assent/withhold choic: The Article 201 rule that once a Governor reserves a State Bill for Presidential consideration, the President's own choice is limited to assent or withholding — no further reservation is available at this final stage.
glossary.President's non-Money-Bill return-for-re: The Article 201 proviso letting the President, for non-Money Bills only, direct the Governor to return a reserved Bill to the State Legislature with a reconsideration message paralleling Article 200's first proviso.
glossary.six-month reconsideration window (Presid: The Article 201 proviso's mandatory time limit — six months from receipt of the President's return message — within which a State Legislature must reconsider a returned Bill; re-passage (with or without amendment) sends it back to the President for renewed, still-discretionary consideration.
glossary.annual financial statement (State budget: The Article 202(1) term for the State budget — the Governor's yearly statement of estimated receipts and expenditure laid before the State Legislature, mirroring the Union's Article 112 annual financial statement.
glossary.charged-versus-votable expenditure split: The Article 202(2) requirement that estimated State expenditure be shown separately as expenditure charged on the Consolidated Fund of the State (immune from an Assembly vote) versus other, votable expenditure.
glossary.expenditure charged on Consolidated Fund: The Article 202(3) list of six automatically charged expenditure categories — Governor's emoluments/office expenses, presiding officers' salaries, State debt charges, High Court Judges' salaries, court/arbitral award satisfaction, and any other law-declared charged expenditure — insulated from the ordinary vote-of-confidence budget process.
glossary.no-vote-but-discussable rule for charged: The Article 203(1) rule that charged expenditure estimates cannot be put to an Assembly vote for approval or rejection, but remain fully open to legislative discussion and scrutiny.
glossary.demands for grants (votable State expend: The Article 203(2) mechanism by which non-charged (votable) State expenditure estimates are presented to the Legislative Assembly as individual demands for grants, each subject to Assembly assent, reduction, or refusal.
glossary.Assembly's power to reduce or refuse a g: The Article 203(2) power letting the Legislative Assembly assent to, reduce the amount of, or wholly refuse any demand for a grant — the Assembly's role is to scrutinise and cut proposed votable expenditure, not to originate it.
glossary.Governor's recommendation precondition f: The Article 203(3) rule that no demand for a grant may be made in the Legislative Assembly except on the Governor's recommendation, reserving the power to originate spending proposals to the executive.
glossary.Appropriation Bill combining Assembly gr: The Article 204(1) Bill introduced after the Assembly makes its grants, appropriating from the Consolidated Fund of the State all money needed to meet both the Assembly-approved grants and the fixed charged-expenditure amounts (capped at the previously laid statement's figures).
glossary.amendment bar on grant amount/destinatio: The Article 204(2) rule barring any Appropriation Bill amendment that would vary a grant's amount or destination, or vary the amount of charged expenditure — the underlying figures, once fixed by the grants process, cannot be reopened at the appropriation stage.
glossary.presiding officer's final ruling on amen: The Article 204(2) rule making the presiding officer's decision on whether a proposed Appropriation Bill amendment is inadmissible under the amendment bar final and unchallengeable.
glossary.legal-appropriation precondition for wit: The Article 204(3) rule that no money may be withdrawn from a State's Consolidated Fund except under an appropriation made by law passed under this Article, subject only to the special mechanisms in Articles 205 and 206.
glossary.supplementary/additional expenditure sta: The Article 205(1)(a) mechanism requiring the Governor to lay a further statement before the State Legislature when an originally sanctioned amount proves insufficient mid-year, or when an entirely new, unbudgeted service needs funding during the current financial year.
glossary.excess-expenditure demand (already-spent: The Article 205(1)(b) mechanism requiring a demand to be presented to the Legislative Assembly when money has already been spent on a service beyond the amount originally granted for it — a retrospective regularisation demand.
glossary.full Article 202-204 procedure applied t: The Article 205(2) rule that the entire ordinary budget procedure — annual financial statement mechanics (202), demands-for-grants discussion (203), and Appropriation Bill requirements (204) — applies in full to supplementary, additional, or excess grants exactly as it does to the original annual budget.
glossary.vote on account (interim advance grant): The Article 206(1)(a) power letting the Legislative Assembly grant an advance for part of a financial year's estimated expenditure while the full Article 203-204 budget procedure is still underway — the mechanism that funds government operations before the annual budget is finally passed.
glossary.vote of credit (indefinite/unforeseeable: The Article 206(1)(b) power letting the Legislative Assembly grant funds for an unexpected demand on State resources too large or indefinite in character to itemise with the detail an ordinary annual financial statement requires.
glossary.exceptional grant (outside current-year: The Article 206(1)(c) power letting the Legislative Assembly make a grant for something that forms no part of any current financial year's ordinary service.
glossary.Assembly-only power for all three specia: The Article 206 characterisation that votes on account, votes of credit, and exceptional grants are all powers of the Legislative Assembly specifically, usable notwithstanding the ordinary provisions' timing constraints, though still routed through Articles 203 and 204's discussion/appropriation requirements.
glossary.Governor's recommendation precondition f: The Article 207(1) rule requiring the Governor's prior recommendation before a Bill or amendment touching any Article 199(1)(a)-(f) financial subject matter can be introduced or moved, and barring such Bills from originating in the Legislative Council.
glossary.tax-reduction/abolition amendment exempt: The Article 207(1) proviso exempting amendments that would reduce or abolish a tax from needing the Governor's prior recommendation — the gatekeeping exists to control new or increased financial burdens, not to block relief.
glossary.fines/fees/local-tax carve-out (financia: The Article 207(2) rule, mirroring Article 199(2), that a Bill or amendment is not treated as touching Article 199(1)(a)-(f) financial subject matter merely because it imposes fines/penalties, licence/service fees, or lets a local authority tax for local purposes.
glossary.Governor's recommendation precondition f: The Article 207(3) rule that any Bill which, once enacted, would involve expenditure from the State's Consolidated Fund cannot be passed by a House unless the Governor has recommended that House consider the Bill — broader than clause (1)'s specific subject-matter list and operative at the passage stage.
glossary.House's own rule-making power for proced: The Article 208(1) power letting each House of a State Legislature make its own rules regulating its procedure and conduct of business, subject to the Constitution's other provisions.
glossary.pre-Constitution Provincial rules defaul: The Article 208(2) fallback rule that, until a House makes its own procedural rules, the corresponding pre-Constitution Province's rules and standing orders apply, as modified by the Speaker or Chairman as appropriate.
glossary.Governor's inter-House communication pro: The Article 208(3) power letting the Governor of a bicameral State, after consulting both the Speaker and the Chairman, make rules specifically governing communication procedure between the Assembly and the Council.
glossary.State law regulating financial-business: The Article 209 power letting a State Legislature enact law regulating the procedure and conduct of financial business (including appropriation Bills) for the purpose of its timely completion.
glossary.financial-business law's priority over A: The Article 209 rule that a State financial-business procedure law prevails over any inconsistent Article 208 procedural rule or standing order.
glossary.State-official-language/Hindi/English bu: The Article 210(1) rule that State Legislature business must be transacted in the State's official language(s), Hindi, or English, overriding Part XVII but subject to Article 348's separate regime for courts and authoritative legal texts.
glossary.Speaker/Chairman's mother-tongue accommo: The Article 210(1) proviso letting the Speaker or Chairman permit a member who cannot adequately express himself in the State's official language(s), Hindi, or English to address the House in his mother-tongue.
glossary.fifteen-year sunset on English (extendab: The Article 210(2) default rule that English ceases to be an available language for State Legislature business fifteen years after the Constitution's commencement (1950), unless the State Legislature itself extends it by law — in practice, most States have so extended it.
glossary.extended sunset periods for specified St: The two provisos to Article 210(2) granting specially extended default sunset periods — twenty-five years for Himachal Pradesh, Manipur, Meghalaya, and Tripura; forty years for Arunachal Pradesh, Goa, and Mizoram — reflecting those States' distinct linguistic landscapes at the time of their reorganisation/statehood.
glossary.bar on Legislature discussion of Judge's: The Article 211 rule barring any discussion in a State Legislature of a Supreme Court or High Court Judge's conduct in discharging his judicial duties, protecting judicial independence and channelling conduct concerns into the Constitution's dedicated removal process instead.
glossary.procedural-irregularity immunity for Leg: The Article 212(1) rule that a State Legislature's proceedings cannot be invalidated in court merely on the ground of an alleged procedural irregularity — though substantive constitutional violations remain open to challenge.
glossary.immunity for officers exercising procedu: The Article 212(2) rule shielding any officer or member (e.g., the Speaker or Chairman) exercising constitutionally vested powers over procedure, business conduct, or order-maintenance in a State Legislature from court jurisdiction over that specific exercise of power.
glossary.Governor's Ordinance-promulgation power: The Article 213(1) power letting a Governor promulgate Ordinances with full force of State law when the Legislative Assembly (or, in bicameral States, either House) is not in session and the Governor is satisfied immediate action is necessary.
glossary.President's-instructions precondition fo: The proviso to Article 213(1) barring the Governor from promulgating an Ordinance, without the President's instructions, on any matter that would have needed prior Presidential sanction to introduce as a Bill, mandatory Presidential reservation, or Presidential assent after reservation to become valid State law.
glossary.six-week automatic-lapse rule from Legis: The Article 213(2)(a) rule that a State Ordinance automatically ceases to operate six weeks after the Legislature reassembles, unless earlier disapproved or already withdrawn — in bicameral States with staggered reassembly dates, the six weeks run from the later date.
glossary.House disapproval resolution ending an O: The Article 213(2)(a) mechanism letting a State Ordinance be ended before the six-week lapse period via a disapproval resolution passed by the Assembly and (in bicameral States) agreed to by the Council.
glossary.Governor's power to withdraw an Ordinanc: The Article 213(2)(b) power letting the Governor withdraw a promulgated Ordinance at any time, independent of the automatic lapse or disapproval mechanisms.
glossary.Ordinance's substantive validity limits: The Article 213(3) rule that a State Ordinance is void to the extent its content would be invalid if enacted as an ordinary State Legislature Act assented to by the Governor — an Ordinance cannot achieve through emergency power what an ordinary Act could not validly achieve.
glossary.President-instructed Ordinance treated a: The proviso to Article 213(3) deeming a President-instructed Ordinance to be a State Act that was reserved for and assented to by the President, specifically for determining whether it validly prevails over an inconsistent Union/existing law on a Concurrent List matter.
glossary.one High Court per State (as originally: The Article 214 baseline guarantee that every State has its own High Court — simplified by the Seventh Amendment (1956) to a single-sentence guarantee, with the possibility of a shared common High Court for multiple States separately addressed by Article 231.
glossary.High Court as a court of record: The Article 215 status making every High Court's proceedings and judgments authoritatively recorded, self-proving without further evidence, and precedentially binding within its jurisdiction — the High Court-level mirror of Article 129's Supreme Court status.
glossary.High Court's contempt-of-itself punishme: The Article 215 power, inherent in a High Court's court-of-record status, letting it punish for contempt of itself without needing separate statutory conferral — procedurally regulated in practice by the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971.
glossary.Chief Justice plus President-determined: The Article 216 rule that every High Court consists of a Chief Justice plus as many other Judges as the President, from time to time, deems necessary to appoint — a flexible, executively adjustable strength unlike the Supreme Court's Parliamentary-law-fixed strength.
glossary.High Court Judge's appointment by Presid: The Article 217(1) appointment mechanism: a Presidential warrant issued after consultation with the Chief Justice of India, the State Governor, and (for puisne Judges) the High Court's own Chief Justice — the process the 2014 NJAC amendment attempted to replace before being struck down in 2015.
glossary.sixty-two-year retirement age (High Cour: The Article 217(1) mandatory retirement age for a regular (non-additional, non-acting) High Court Judge, raised from sixty to sixty-two years by the Fifteenth Amendment Act, 1963.
glossary.Judge's voluntary resignation by writing: The Article 217(1) proviso (a) mechanism letting a High Court Judge resign at will via signed writing addressed to the President.
glossary.removal via Article 124(4) impeachment p: The Article 217(1) proviso (b) rule applying the identical Article 124(4) Supreme-Court-Judge impeachment procedure — proved misbehaviour/incapacity plus a special Parliamentary majority — to the removal of a High Court Judge.
glossary.office vacation on Supreme Court elevati: The Article 217(1) proviso (c) rule that a High Court Judge's office is automatically vacated upon his appointment as a Supreme Court Judge or his transfer by the President to another High Court within India.
glossary.ten-year judicial office or ten-year Hig: The Article 217(2) alternative eligibility tracks for High Court Judge appointment — at least ten years holding judicial office in India, or at least ten years as an advocate of one or more High Courts — open only to Indian citizens.
glossary.Explanation-inclusive service-period com: The Article 217(2) Explanation clauses (a), (aa), and (b) crediting mixed judicial/advocate/tribunal/special-legal-knowledge service, and pre-15-August-1947 comparable service, toward the ten-year eligibility thresholds for High Court Judge appointment.
glossary.President's final age-dispute determinat: The Article 217(3) mechanism resolving any dispute over a sitting High Court Judge's age — decided by the President after consulting the Chief Justice of India, with the President's decision being final.
glossary.NJAC amendment struck down — collegium c: The 2014 Ninety-ninth Amendment's substitution of a National Judicial Appointments Commission for the consultative appointment process under Article 217(1), which the Supreme Court struck down as unconstitutional in Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v. Union of India (2015), restoring the pre-amendment collegium-based consultative practice despite the amended text formally remaining on the books.
glossary.Article 124(4)/(5) removal procedure ext: The Article 218 cross-reference importing Article 124(4)'s special-majority Parliamentary address removal procedure and Article 124(5)'s Parliamentary power to regulate proof/investigation procedure, substituting 'High Court' for 'Supreme Court' throughout — the textual mechanism that operationalises Article 217(1) proviso (b)'s removal cross-reference.
glossary.Judge's oath before Governor per Third S: The Article 219 requirement that every newly appointed High Court Judge make and subscribe an oath or affirmation, in the Third Schedule's prescribed form, before the State Governor (or the Governor's appointee) before entering upon office — the High Court-level counterpart to Article 124(6)'s Presidential-oath requirement for Supreme Court Judges.
glossary.post-retirement practice ban on former p: The Article 220 lifelong restriction barring a person who has held office as a permanent Judge of a High Court from pleading or acting in any court or authority in India except the Supreme Court and the other High Courts — a High-Court-specific integrity safeguard with no Supreme Court parallel.
glossary.Part-B-State High Court exclusion from A: The Article 220 Explanation excluding, for that Article's purposes only, a High Court for a State specified in Part B of the pre-Seventh-Amendment First Schedule — a now largely historical carve-out tied to the pre-1956 Part A/Part B/Part C State classification abolished by the States Reorganisation Act.
glossary.Parliament-law-determined High Court Jud: The Article 221(1) rule that High Court Judges' salaries are fixed by Parliamentary law (as substituted by the Fifty-fourth Amendment, 1986), defaulting to the figures specified in the Second Schedule absent such law.
glossary.no-disadvantage protection for Judge's a: The Article 221(2) proviso barring any disadvantageous variation of a High Court Judge's allowances or leave-of-absence/pension rights after his appointment — textually silent on salary itself, unlike the allowances/leave/pension protection.
glossary.President's power to transfer a Judge be: The Article 222(1) power letting the President transfer a sitting Judge from one High Court to any other High Court — originally exercised after CJI consultation, textually replaced by NJAC recommendation in 2014 but restored to CJI-consultation practice by the NJAC's 2015 strike-down.
glossary.compensatory allowance for transferred J: The Article 222(2) entitlement, inserted by the Fifteenth Amendment (1963), giving a transferred Judge a compensatory allowance in addition to ordinary salary, determined by Parliament by law or, absent such law, fixed by Presidential order.
glossary.President's appointment of acting Chief: The Article 223 power letting the President appoint one of a High Court's other Judges to perform the Chief Justice's duties when that office is vacant or the sitting Chief Justice is temporarily unable to act — the High Court-level counterpart to Article 126.
glossary.additional Judges for temporary High Cou: The Article 224(1) mechanism letting the President appoint additional Judges, for a fixed term not exceeding two years, to address a temporary increase in business or arrears of work — distinct from a permanent expansion of the Court's sanctioned strength under Article 216.
glossary.acting Judge appointment during Chief Ju: The Article 224(2) mechanism letting the President appoint an acting Judge to substitute for a specific Judge (other than the Chief Justice) who is temporarily unable to act, or who is himself acting temporarily as Chief Justice, serving until the permanent Judge resumes duties.
glossary.sixty-two-year cap for additional/acting: The Article 224(3) rule applying the same sixty-two-year retirement age ceiling used for regular High Court Judges under Article 217(1) to additional and acting Judges appointed under this Article, regardless of their appointment term.
glossary.recall of retired Judges to sit and act: The Article 224A mechanism, inserted by the Fifteenth Amendment (1963), letting a retired Judge of that High Court or any other High Court be requested to sit and act again, with full jurisdiction/powers/privileges of a regular Judge while sitting, but without being otherwise deemed a Judge of that Court.
glossary.retired Judge's consent precondition for: The proviso to Article 224A making a retired Judge's recall to sit and act entirely voluntary — nothing in the Article can compel him to accept the request, an absolute safeguard for post-retirement autonomy.
glossary.continuity of existing High Court jurisd: The Article 225 rule carrying forward an existing High Court's jurisdiction, administered law, and Judges' administrative/rule-making powers unchanged from immediately before the Constitution's commencement, subject to the Constitution itself and to competent subsequent legislation.
glossary.removal of pre-Constitution revenue-juri: The Article 225 proviso abolishing, from the Constitution's commencement onward, any pre-existing restriction on a High Court's original jurisdiction over revenue matters or revenue-collection acts — the one substantive change layered on top of Article 225's otherwise continuity-preserving baseline.
glossary.High Court's writ jurisdiction under Art: The Article 226(1) power letting every High Court issue directions, orders, or the five prerogative writs (habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto, certiorari) to any person, authority, or Government within its territory, both to enforce Part III Fundamental Rights and for any other legal purpose.
glossary.Article 226 writs for 'any other purpose: The Article 226(1) phrase extending High Court writ jurisdiction beyond Fundamental Rights enforcement to any other legal purpose (e.g., correcting jurisdictional/legal errors affecting ordinary legal rights) — a scope textually wider than Article 32's Fundamental-Rights-only Supreme Court writ jurisdiction.
glossary.cause-of-action-based territorial writ j: The Article 226(2) rule letting a High Court exercise its writ power based on where the cause of action wholly or partly arises, even if the respondent Government/authority/person's seat or residence lies outside that High Court's territory — an access-to-justice-expanding territorial rule.
glossary.two-week interim-order vacation hearing: The Article 226(3) rule, inserted by the Forty-fourth Amendment (1978), requiring a High Court to dispose of an application to vacate an ex parte interim order within two weeks (or the next working day if the Court is closed), failing which the interim order automatically stands vacated — a post-Emergency-era safeguard against indefinite unchallenged interim relief.
glossary.Article 226 not in derogation of Supreme: The Article 226(4) confirmation that High Court writ jurisdiction operates concurrently with, and does not diminish, the Supreme Court's own parallel writ power under Article 32(2).
glossary.High Court's power of superintendence ov: The Article 227(1) general grant of administrative and judicial superintendence to every High Court over all courts and tribunals within its territorial jurisdiction — the true source of authority, with clause (2)'s specific powers being merely illustrative of it.
glossary.Governor's previous-approval requirement: The proviso to Article 227(3) requiring any rules, forms, or fee tables made by a High Court under clauses (2)-(3) to be consistent with existing law and to receive the Governor's previous approval before taking effect.
glossary.Armed Forces tribunal exclusion from HC: The Article 227(4) carve-out entirely excluding courts or tribunals constituted by or under any law relating to the Armed Forces from a High Court's superintendence power under this Article.
glossary.mandatory case withdrawal for substantia: The Article 228 rule mandating a High Court to withdraw a subordinate-court case once satisfied it involves a substantial constitutional-interpretation question necessary for disposal — after which the High Court may either decide the whole case itself or determine only the constitutional question and remit the rest back to the subordinate court.
glossary.Chief Justice's power to appoint High Co: The Article 229(1) power letting the Chief Justice (or a delegated Judge/officer) appoint a High Court's own officers and servants, subject to a Governor's rule requiring State Public Service Commission consultation for specified outside appointments.
glossary.Governor's rule-making for State Public: The proviso to Article 229(1) letting the Governor make a rule requiring, for specified cases, that no person not already attached to the Court be appointed to a Court office save after consultation with the State Public Service Commission.
glossary.Governor's approval requirement for HC s: The proviso to Article 229(2) requiring Governor approval specifically for Chief-Justice-made rules on High Court officers'/servants' salaries, allowances, leave, or pensions, even though other service-condition rules need no such approval.
glossary.High Court administrative expenses charg: The Article 229(3) guarantee that a High Court's administrative expenses (including officer/servant salaries, allowances, and pensions) are charged directly upon the State's Consolidated Fund — non-votable expenditure insulated from the ordinary annual appropriation-vote process, paralleling Article 202(3)(d)'s charged-expenditure list.
glossary.Parliament's power to extend/exclude HC: The Article 230(1) power letting Parliament, by law, extend a State High Court's jurisdiction to, or exclude it from, a Union territory — the mechanism by which Union territories lacking a dedicated High Court are brought within an existing State High Court's jurisdiction.
glossary.State Legislature's inability to alter H: The Article 230(2)(a) rule barring the State Legislature from increasing, restricting, or abolishing a State High Court's jurisdiction over a Union territory once Parliament has extended it — that jurisdiction remains exclusively within Parliament's control.
glossary.President substituted for Governor in Un: The Article 230(2)(b) rule reading Article 227's 'Governor' reference as 'the President' specifically for rules/forms/tables governing subordinate courts situated within a Union territory to which a State High Court's jurisdiction has been extended.
glossary.Parliament's power to establish a common: The Article 231(1) power letting Parliament, by law, establish a single common High Court serving two or more States (or States plus a Union territory), notwithstanding the Chapter's otherwise State-specific default — the express exception promised by Article 214, exemplified by the Punjab and Haryana High Court.
glossary.principal-seat State substitution for Ar: The Article 231(2)(c) rule reading Articles 219's (oath) and 229's (officers/expenses) 'the State' references, for a common High Court, as the single State where that High Court has its principal seat.
glossary.Union-territory principal-seat substitut: The proviso to Article 231(2) substituting President, Union Public Service Commission, Parliament, and Consolidated Fund of India for the Article 219/229 references to Governor, Public Service Commission, Legislature, and State Consolidated Fund respectively, where a common High Court's principal seat is itself located in a Union territory.
glossary.Governor's district judge appointment po: The Article 233(1) power letting the Governor appoint, post, and promote district judges only in mandatory consultation with the High Court exercising jurisdiction over that State — the district-judiciary-level counterpart to the judiciary-executive collaborative appointment model seen in Article 217.
glossary.seven-year advocate/pleader eligibility: The Article 233(2) direct-entry eligibility gateway letting a person not already in Union or State service be appointed a district judge only with at least seven years' standing as an advocate or pleader, and only on the High Court's own recommendation.
glossary.retrospective validation of pre-1966 dis: The Article 233A curative provision, inserted by the Twentieth Amendment Act, 1966 in direct response to the Supreme Court's Chandra Mohan v. State of Uttar Pradesh ruling, retrospectively validating pre-1966 district judge appointments/postings/promotions/transfers made without strict Article 233/235 compliance, plus every judicial act those judges performed before that cutoff.
glossary.Governor's judicial service recruitment: The Article 234 power letting the Governor recruit persons other than district judges into the State judicial service via rules made after consulting both the State Public Service Commission and the relevant High Court — the entry-level counterpart to Article 233's district-judge-specific appointment process.
glossary.High Court's control over subordinate ju: The Article 235 vesting of comprehensive administrative control — including posting, promotion, and leave — over district courts and all courts subordinate to them, and over judicial officers below district judge rank, in the High Court rather than the State executive; the cornerstone subordinate-judiciary independence guarantee.
glossary.subordinate judicial officer's service-l: The Article 235 concluding safeguard preventing the High Court's control power from stripping a judicial officer of any service-law appeal right, or from authorising treatment inconsistent with his prescribed conditions of service.
glossary.'district judge' definitional scope (Cha: The Article 236(a) expansive definition of 'district judge' covering city civil court judges, additional/joint/assistant district judges, small cause court chief judges, presidency magistrates, and sessions judges at various levels — ensuring Chapter VI applies uniformly across this functionally equivalent cluster of senior subordinate judicial posts.
glossary.'judicial service' definitional scope (C: The Article 236(b) definition confining 'judicial service' to a service consisting exclusively of persons intended for district-judge-and-below civil judicial posts — deliberately excluding criminal-side magistracy, which is why Article 237's separate extension mechanism is needed.
glossary.Governor's power to extend Chapter VI to: The Article 237 power letting the Governor, by public notification, extend Chapter VI's entire framework (recruitment, High Court control, etc.) to specified classes of magistrates — the mechanism that completed the separation of the criminal-side subordinate judiciary from executive administration under Article 50's Directive Principle.
glossary.President's administration of Union terr: The Article 239(1) default rule making every Union territory administered by the President — in practice the Union Council of Ministers — acting through an appointed administrator of the President's chosen designation, unless Parliament has by law provided a different arrangement (e.g., under Articles 239A or 239AA).
glossary.Governor as ex officio Union territory a: The Article 239(2) power letting the President appoint a State's Governor as administrator of an adjoining Union territory, with the Governor required to exercise that administrator role independently of his own State's Council of Ministers — keeping the dual capacities constitutionally separate.
glossary.Parliament's power to create local Legis: The Article 239A(1) power letting Parliament, by ordinary law, create an elected or partly-elected local Legislature, a Council of Ministers, or both, for the Union territory of Puducherry (and, by separate statutory extension, Jammu and Kashmir) — with the law itself defining that body's constitution, powers, and functions.
glossary.Article 239A law exempted from Article 3: The Article 239A(2) rule deeming any law creating a local Legislature/Council of Ministers under clause (1) not to be a constitutional amendment for Article 368 purposes, letting Parliament use its ordinary law-making majority rather than Article 368's special procedure.
glossary.National Capital Territory of Delhi and: The Article 239AA(1) renaming of the Union territory of Delhi as the National Capital Territory of Delhi, with its Article 239 administrator redesignated the Lieutenant Governor, effective from the Sixty-ninth Amendment Act, 1991's commencement.
glossary.Delhi Legislative Assembly's State List/: The Article 239AA(3)(a) grant of law-making power to the Delhi Legislative Assembly over State List and Concurrent List matters applicable to Union territories, subject to the Entries 1/2/18 carve-out and to Parliament's overriding power under clause (3)(b).
glossary.Entries 1, 2, and 18 State List carve-ou: The Article 239AA(3)(a) exclusion of Public Order (Entry 1), Police (Entry 2), and Land (Entry 18) — plus related Entries 64, 65, 66 insofar as they touch those three — from the Delhi Legislative Assembly's law-making competence, keeping these sensitive subjects under Union control given Delhi's status as the national capital; the single most litigated feature of Delhi's governance framework.
glossary.repugnancy rule between Delhi Legislativ: The Article 239AA(3)(c) rule that a Parliament law prevails over a repugnant Delhi Legislative Assembly law on the same matter (subject to a Presidential-assent saving proviso for reserved Assembly laws), while Parliament always retains power to legislate over or amend the Assembly's law regardless.
glossary.Lieutenant Governor's reference-to-Presi: The proviso to Article 239AA(4) requiring the Lieutenant Governor to refer any difference of opinion with his Ministers to the President for decision and act accordingly, while permitting the LG to take urgent interim action pending that decision if he judges it necessary.
glossary.Delhi Council of Ministers collectively: The Article 239AA(6) rule making the Delhi Council of Ministers, headed by the Chief Minister, collectively answerable to the Legislative Assembly — the responsible-government feature distinguishing Delhi's Council of Ministers from an ordinary Union territory's administrator-only model.
glossary.President's power to suspend Article 239: The Article 239AB power letting the President, satisfied either that Delhi's Article 239AA machinery has broken down or simply that suspension is necessary/expedient for proper administration, suspend some or all of Article 239AA's operation (or laws made under it) and revert Delhi to direct Article 239 administration — Delhi's functional (though textually thinner, unratified-by-Parliament) analogue to Article 356 President's Rule.
glossary.administrator's Ordinance-making power d: The Article 239B(1) power letting the administrator of a Union territory with an Article 239A Legislature (currently Puducherry, and cross-applied to Delhi's Lieutenant Governor by Article 239AA(8)) promulgate Ordinances with law-making force when that Legislature is not in session and immediate action is necessary — modelled on, but more constrained than, a Governor's Article 213 power.
glossary.mandatory President's-instructions preco: The proviso to Article 239B(1) requiring the administrator to obtain the President's instructions before promulgating any Ordinance — a mandatory precondition with no equivalent constraint on a Governor's ordinary Article 213 Ordinance-making power, reflecting the administrator's subordinate constitutional position.
glossary.six-week Ordinance expiry from Legislatu: The Article 239B(2)(a) rule that an administrator's Ordinance must be laid before the territorial Legislature and automatically ceases to operate six weeks after the Legislature's reassembly, or earlier if the Legislature passes a resolution disapproving it — paralleling Article 213(2)(a)'s identical rule for Governors' Ordinances.
glossary.President's regulation-making power for: The Article 240(1) power letting the President make regulations for the peace, progress, and good government of a closed list of smaller Union territories (currently the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Lakshadweep, Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu, and conditionally Puducherry) that generally lack their own functioning Legislature.
glossary.regulation's Act-of-Parliament-equivalen: The Article 240(2) rule giving a Presidential regulation under this Article the same force and effect as an Act of Parliament applicable to that territory, including the power to repeal or amend any existing Parliament-made or other law applicable there — a stronger law-making force than an Article 239B administrator's Ordinance.
glossary.regulation-making power's automatic paus: The provisos to Article 240(1) switching off the President's Puducherry regulation-making power from the date its Article 239A Legislature first meets, while automatically restoring that power for any period the Legislature is later dissolved or its functioning suspended — ensuring the territory is never left without a source of law-making authority.
glossary.Parliament's power to constitute a dedic: The Article 241(1) power letting Parliament, by law, either constitute an entirely new High Court dedicated to a Union territory (as with the Delhi High Court) or declare an existing court within that territory to be a High Court for constitutional purposes — the alternative route to Article 230's extension of an existing State High Court's jurisdiction.
glossary.Chapter V (Article 214 onward) applied t: The Article 241(2) rule applying Part VI Chapter V's entire High Court framework (court-of-record status, Judge appointment, tenure, writ jurisdiction, superintendence, etc.) to a High Court constituted for a Union territory exactly as it applies to a State High Court under Article 214, except to whatever extent Parliament by law modifies or excepts specific provisions.
glossary.continuity of pre-1956 Union-territory H: The Article 241(3) savings rule continuing, after the Seventh Amendment Act, 1956's commencement, the jurisdiction that any High Court was already exercising over a Union territory immediately before that commencement, subject to the Constitution and competent subsequent legislation.
glossary.Gram Sabha definition (village-level ele: The Article 243(b) definition of 'Gram Sabha' as the complete body of persons registered in the electoral rolls of a village within a village-level Panchayat area — the whole village electorate, distinct from the smaller elected Panchayat that governs that area.
glossary.Panchayat definition (self-government in: The Article 243(d) definition of 'Panchayat' as an institution of rural local self-government, by whatever local name called, constituted under Article 243B.
glossary.'population' defined by last published c: The Article 243(f) definition anchoring 'population' throughout Part IX to the figures of the last preceding census that have been published — the fixed baseline for every proportionality and reservation calculation in this Part.
glossary.Gram Sabha's State-law-determined powers: The Article 243A rule leaving the actual powers and functions a Gram Sabha exercises at the village level entirely to State legislation, giving the Gram Sabha constitutional standing without prescribing any minimum substantive content.
