glossary.mandatory three-tier Panchayat structure: The Article 243B(1) requirement that every State constitute Panchayats at all three levels — village, intermediate, and district — converting what were previously optional, State-discretion structures into a uniform constitutional floor.
glossary.twenty-lakh population exemption from in: The Article 243B(2) exception letting a State with a population not exceeding twenty lakhs skip constituting an intermediate-level Panchayat, recognising that tier as disproportionate administrative overhead for very small States.
glossary.population-proportionate territorial con: The Article 243C(1) proviso and (2) rule requiring that, so far as practicable, the ratio of population to elected seats be uniform across a State's Panchayats at a given level, and across constituencies within a single Panchayat area.
glossary.mandatory direct election for all Pancha: The Article 243C(2) rule that every Panchayat seat must be filled by direct election from territorial constituencies within the Panchayat area — no Panchayat seat may be indirectly elected or nominated.
glossary.representation of MPs/MLAs/MLCs and lowe: The Article 243C(3) optional State-law provision letting village-level Chairpersons sit in intermediate/district Panchayats, intermediate-level Chairpersons sit in district Panchayats, and MPs/MLAs/MLCs whose constituencies overlap a Panchayat area be represented in that Panchayat.
glossary.indirect Chairperson election for interm: The Article 243C(5)(b) mandatory rule that an intermediate- or district-level Panchayat's Chairperson be elected by, and from among, that Panchayat's own elected members — contrasted with a village-level Chairperson, whose election method is left to State law under clause (5)(a).
glossary.population-proportionate SC/ST seat rese: The Article 243D(1) rule reserving Panchayat seats for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in proportion to their population share within that specific Panchayat area, with reserved seats rotated among different constituencies.
glossary.one-third women sub-reservation within S: The Article 243D(2) rule requiring at least one-third of the SC/ST-reserved seats under clause (1) to be further reserved specifically for SC/ST women.
glossary.one-third overall women seat reservation: The Article 243D(3) rule reserving at least one-third of all directly elected Panchayat seats for women generally — a figure that already includes, rather than adds to, the SC/ST women counted under clause (2) — and which, unlike SC/ST reservation, does not sunset under Article 334.
glossary.Chairperson office reservation for SC/ST: The Article 243D(4) rule mirroring the seat-reservation scheme for the office of Chairperson at every Panchayat level — State-population-proportionate SC/ST reservation plus a minimum one-third women's reservation, both allotted by rotation among different Panchayats at each level.
glossary.Article 334 sunset clause on SC/ST Panch: The Article 243D(5) rule automatically terminating SC/ST seat and Chairperson-office reservation under clauses (1), (2), and (4) when the period specified in Article 334 expires — a sunset that expressly does not apply to the separate one-third women's reservation.
glossary.State-law backward class reservation ena: The Article 243D(6) permissive (non-mandatory) provision letting a State Legislature additionally reserve Panchayat seats or Chairperson offices for backward classes of citizens, subject to the general constitutional constraints on reservation (aggregate cap, quantifiable-data justification) developed in the Court's reservation jurisprudence.
glossary.fixed five-year Panchayat term: The Article 243E(1) rule fixing every Panchayat's term at exactly five years from the date of its first meeting, 'and no longer,' subject only to earlier dissolution under existing law.
glossary.protection against legislative dissoluti: The Article 243E(2) rule preventing a mere legislative amendment from itself dissolving a Panchayat that is already functioning — such a Panchayat continues until its full five-year term (or a lawful dissolution under separately existing law) runs out.
glossary.mandatory six-month re-election deadline: The Article 243E(3) rule requiring fresh Panchayat elections to be completed within six months of an earlier dissolution (subject to a de minimis exception where under six months of the term would have remained anyway), with clause (4) confirming the reconstituted Panchayat serves only the remainder of its predecessor's original term.
glossary.State-Legislature-election disqualificat: The Article 243F(1)(a) default rule disqualifying a person from Panchayat membership if he is disqualified under the law governing elections to that State's own Legislature, subject to the Article's own age-floor proviso.
glossary.twenty-one-year minimum age floor for Pa: The proviso to Article 243F(1)(a) ensuring no person is disqualified for Panchayat membership merely for being under twenty-five, provided he has attained twenty-one — lowering the usual State Legislature candidacy age specifically for Panchayat purposes.
glossary.State-law-designated authority for Panch: The Article 243F(2) rule leaving the adjudicating authority and procedure for Panchayat member disqualification disputes entirely to State legislation, unlike Article 192's constitutionally fixed Governor-plus-Election-Commission mechanism for State Legislature members.
glossary.State-law devolution of self-government: The Article 243G enabling provision letting a State Legislature, by law, endow Panchayats with powers and authority necessary to function as genuine institutions of self-government, including devolving responsibility for economic-development/social-justice planning and scheme implementation.
glossary.Eleventh Schedule as the illustrative su: The Article 243G(b) cross-reference to the Eleventh Schedule's twenty-nine subject-matter entries as illustrative areas in which economic-development/social-justice schemes may be entrusted to Panchayats — the Schedule itself does not transfer legislative authority away from the State; actual devolution still requires specific State legislation.
glossary.Panchayat's own tax/toll/fee levy author: The Article 243H(a) enabling provision letting State law authorise a Panchayat to levy, collect, and appropriate its own taxes, duties, tolls, and fees, subject to State-specified procedure and limits — a Panchayat's own-source revenue tool.
glossary.State-collected tax assignment to Pancha: The Article 243H(b) enabling provision letting State law assign to Panchayats specific taxes/duties/tolls/fees that the State Government itself levies and collects, subject to specified purposes, conditions, and limits — a revenue-sharing rather than independent-taxation mechanism.
glossary.Consolidated Fund of the State grants-in: The Article 243H(c) enabling provision letting State law provide for grants-in-aid to Panchayats from the State's Consolidated Fund — in practice the primary revenue source for most Panchayats given limited own-source taxation potential.
glossary.State-law-constituted Panchayat Funds fo: The Article 243H(d) enabling provision letting State law constitute dedicated Funds for crediting all moneys received by or on behalf of Panchayats and governing withdrawals from those Funds — the accounting infrastructure underlying Panchayat finance.
glossary.periodic State Finance Commission for Pa: The Article 243I(1) requirement that the Governor constitute a Finance Commission within one year of the Seventy-third Amendment's 1992 commencement, and thereafter every five years, to review Panchayat financial position and recommend on inter-governmental revenue distribution, tax assignment, and grants-in-aid — the State-tier structural mirror of Article 280's Union Finance Commission.
glossary.State-Panchayat revenue distribution rec: The Article 243I(1)(a) mandate directing the State Finance Commission to recommend on principles governing the division of State tax/duty/toll/fee proceeds between the State and Panchayats, the allocation of the Panchayats' share across tiers, which levies to assign to Panchayats, and appropriate grants-in-aid.
glossary.Governor's mandatory laying of Finance C: The Article 243I(4) requirement that the Governor cause every State Finance Commission recommendation, together with an explanatory memorandum on action taken, to be laid before the State Legislature — a transparency and legislative-oversight obligation, though the recommendations themselves are not textually made binding.
glossary.State-law Panchayat account-maintenance: The Article 243J enabling provision leaving the entire framework for Panchayat account maintenance and auditing to State legislation, without constitutionally designating any specific auditing authority (unlike Article 148's entrenched Comptroller and Auditor-General).
glossary.State Election Commission for Panchayat: The Article 243K(1) body — a single State Election Commissioner appointed by the Governor — vested with superintendence, direction, and control of Panchayat electoral-roll preparation and election conduct, later extended to Municipal elections by Article 243ZA.
glossary.High-Court-Judge-equivalent removal prot: The proviso to Article 243K(2) barring removal of the State Election Commissioner except in like manner and on like grounds as a High Court Judge, and barring disadvantageous variation of service conditions after appointment — insulating Panchayat election administration from executive control, mirroring Article 324(5)'s protection for the Chief Election Commissioner.
glossary.Union-territory extension of Part IX wit: The Article 243L mechanism extending the entire Panchayat Part to Union territories by textually substituting 'Administrator appointed under article 239' for 'Governor' and a Union territory's own Legislative Assembly for 'State Legislature,' subject to Presidential exceptions/modifications by public notification.
glossary.blanket carve-out of Fifth/Sixth Schedul: The Article 243M(1)-(3A) default exclusion of Fifth Schedule Scheduled Areas, Sixth Schedule tribal areas, Nagaland/Meghalaya/Mizoram, Manipur's District-Council hill areas, Darjeeling's district-level Panchayat tier, and (for SC reservation only) Arunachal Pradesh from Part IX's ordinary Panchayat scheme, because these areas run on separate constitutional local-government tracks.
glossary.special-majority State-Assembly resoluti: The Article 243M(4)(a) mechanism letting Nagaland, Meghalaya, or Mizoram's own Legislative Assembly extend Part IX to that State by a resolution passed with both a majority of total membership and a two-thirds majority of members present and voting.
glossary.PESA extension route for Scheduled/triba: The Article 243M(4)(b) mechanism letting Parliament extend Part IX to Fifth Schedule Scheduled Areas and Sixth Schedule tribal areas by ordinary law with tailored exceptions and modifications (not an Article 368 amendment) — the constitutional basis for the Provisions of the Panchayats (Extension to the Scheduled Areas) Act, 1996 (PESA).
glossary.one-year transitional continuance of pre: The Article 243N rule letting State Panchayat laws inconsistent with Part IX continue in force for up to one year after the Seventy-third Amendment's 1992-93 commencement (or until sooner amended/repealed), while separately protecting already-sitting Panchayats' existing terms absent an affirmative Legislative Assembly dissolution resolution — a now largely spent, purely transitional provision.
glossary.delimitation-law judicial-review bar for: The Article 243-O(a) absolute bar preventing any court from questioning the validity of delimitation or seat-allotment laws made under Article 243K — mirroring Article 329(a)'s identical bar for Parliamentary/State Legislature delimitation laws.
glossary.election-petition-only channel for chall: The Article 243-O(b) rule confining every challenge to a Panchayat election's validity to an election petition presented under State-enacted procedure, ousting ordinary writ or civil litigation over election validity — mirroring Article 329(b)'s identical channeling rule for Parliamentary/State Legislature elections.
glossary.Metropolitan area definition (ten-lakh p: The Article 243P(c) definition of 'Metropolitan area' as a Governor-notified area of ten lakh or more population, spanning one or more districts and comprising two or more Municipalities, Panchayats, or other contiguous areas — the planning-unit concept underlying Article 243ZE's Metropolitan Planning Committee.
glossary.Municipality definition (self-government: The Article 243P(e) definition of 'Municipality' as an institution of urban local self-government constituted under Article 243Q — the Part IXA counterpart to Article 243(d)'s Panchayat definition.
glossary.three-tier Municipality structure (Nagar: The Article 243Q(1) requirement that every State constitute a Nagar Panchayat for transitional (rural-to-urban) areas, a Municipal Council for smaller urban areas, and a Municipal Corporation for larger urban areas — the urban three-tier structure paralleling Article 243B's rural village/intermediate/district Panchayat tiers.
glossary.industrial-township exemption from Munic: The proviso to Article 243Q(1) letting the Governor notify an urban area as an 'industrial township' (based on size and municipal services already provided by an industrial establishment) and thereby exempt it from having a constituted Municipality at all.
glossary.ward-based direct election as the defaul: The Article 243R(1) default rule that every Municipality seat is filled by direct election from wards (territorial constituencies into which the Municipal area is divided) — the urban counterpart to Article 243C(2)'s mandatory direct election for Panchayat seats.
glossary.non-voting expert-member representation: The Article 243R(2)(a)(i) optional State-law provision letting persons with special municipal-administration knowledge or experience sit in a Municipality, subject to the proviso denying them any right to vote in Municipality meetings — ensuring unelected experts cannot outvote directly elected ward members.
glossary.mandatory Wards Committee for three-lakh: The Article 243S(1) requirement that every Municipality with a population of three lakhs or more constitute Wards Committees (each covering one or more wards) as a sub-Municipal representative tier, with elected ward members automatically sitting on the corresponding Committee under clause (3).
glossary.population-proportionate SC/ST seat rese: The Article 243T(1) rule reserving Municipality seats for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in proportion to their population share within that specific Municipal area, with reserved seats rotated among constituencies — the urban counterpart to Article 243D(1)'s Panchayat rule.
glossary.one-third overall women reservation in M: The Article 243T(3) rule reserving at least one-third of all directly elected Municipality seats for women generally, inclusive of the SC/ST women already counted under clause (2), and — unlike SC/ST reservation — not subject to the Article 334 sunset under clause (5).
glossary.fixed five-year Municipality term with h: The Article 243U(1) rule fixing every Municipality's term at exactly five years from its first meeting, 'and no longer,' coupled with a proviso guaranteeing the Municipality a reasonable opportunity of being heard before dissolution — the urban counterpart to Article 243E(1), with an added explicit hearing right not textually present in the Panchayat provision.
glossary.State-Legislature-election disqualificat: The Article 243V(1)(a) default rule disqualifying a person from Municipality membership if he is disqualified under the law governing elections to that State's own Legislature, subject to the Article's own age-floor proviso — the urban mirror of Article 243F(1)(a).
glossary.twenty-one-year minimum age floor for Mu: The proviso to Article 243V(1)(a) ensuring no person is disqualified for Municipality membership merely for being under twenty-five, provided he has attained twenty-one — identical in substance to Article 243F(1)(a)'s proviso for Panchayats.
glossary.State-law devolution of self-government: The Article 243W enabling provision letting a State Legislature, by law, endow Municipalities and Article 243S Committees with powers and authority necessary to function as institutions of self-government, including devolving economic-development/social-justice planning and scheme implementation — the urban mirror of Article 243G.
glossary.Twelfth Schedule as the illustrative sub: The Article 243W(a)(ii)/(b) cross-reference to the Twelfth Schedule's subject-matter entries (urban planning, public health, slum upgradation, fire services, etc.) as illustrative areas for Municipal/Committee devolution — the Schedule itself does not transfer legislative authority; actual devolution still requires specific State legislation.
glossary.Municipality's own tax/toll/fee levy aut: The Article 243X(a) enabling provision letting State law authorise a Municipality to levy, collect, and appropriate its own taxes, duties, tolls, and fees, subject to State-specified procedure and limits — the urban mirror of Article 243H(a).
glossary.State-collected tax assignment to Munici: The Article 243X(b) enabling provision letting State law assign to Municipalities specific taxes/duties/tolls/fees that the State Government itself levies and collects — a revenue-sharing mechanism mirroring Article 243H(b).
glossary.single Finance Commission reviewing both: The Article 243Y(1) rule extending the same Article 243-I State Finance Commission's mandate to also review Municipal financial position and recommend on State-Municipality revenue distribution, tax assignment, and grants-in-aid — confirming there is no separate Municipal Finance Commission, only a single unified body covering both rural and urban local government.
glossary.State-law Municipal account-maintenance: The Article 243Z enabling provision leaving the entire framework for Municipal account maintenance and auditing to State legislation, without constitutionally designating any specific auditing authority — the urban mirror of Article 243J.
glossary.shared State Election Commission for Mun: The Article 243ZA(1) rule placing Municipal elections under the same Article 243K State Election Commission that administers Panchayat elections, confirming a single Commission covers both rural and urban local-body elections in a State.
glossary.Union-territory extension of Part IXA wi: The Article 243ZB mechanism extending the entire Municipalities Part to Union territories by textually substituting 'Administrator appointed under article 239' for 'Governor' and a Union territory's own Legislative Assembly for 'State Legislature,' subject to Presidential exceptions/modifications by public notification — the urban mirror of Article 243L.
glossary.Scheduled/tribal-area and Darjeeling Gor: The Article 243ZC exclusion of Fifth Schedule Scheduled Areas and Sixth Schedule tribal areas from Part IXA by default, protection of the Darjeeling Gorkha Hill Council's functions and powers, and the Parliamentary ordinary-law extension route for Scheduled/tribal areas — a shorter, urban-tailored version of Article 243M lacking that Article's Northeast-hill-State-specific clauses.
glossary.mandatory District Planning Committee co: The Article 243ZD(1) requirement that every State constitute, at the district level, a District Planning Committee to consolidate Panchayat and Municipality plans into a single draft district development plan — the structural bridge connecting Part IX (Panchayats) and Part IXA (Municipalities).
glossary.four-fifths rural/urban-elected-member c: The proviso to Article 243ZD(2)(b) requiring at least four-fifths of a District Planning Committee's members be elected members of the district Panchayat and district Municipalities, apportioned by rural/urban population ratio — an unusually high elected-member floor signalling strong preference for local, elected-body-driven district planning.
glossary.mandatory Metropolitan Planning Committe: The Article 243ZE(1) requirement that every Article 243P(c) Metropolitan area (population ten lakh or more, spanning multiple Municipalities/Panchayats) have its own Metropolitan Planning Committee to prepare an integrated draft development plan for the area as a whole.
glossary.two-thirds elected-member composition fl: The proviso to Article 243ZE(2)(b) requiring at least two-thirds of a Metropolitan Planning Committee's members be elected Municipality members and Panchayat Chairpersons in the Metropolitan area, proportionate to Municipal/Panchayat population ratio — lower than the four-fifths floor for District Planning Committees, reflecting Metropolitan Committees' additional institutional and Union-Government representation.
glossary.one-year transitional continuance of pre: The Article 243ZF rule letting State Municipal laws inconsistent with Part IXA continue in force for up to one year after the Seventy-fourth Amendment's 1992-93 commencement (or until sooner amended/repealed), while separately protecting already-sitting Municipalities' existing terms — a now largely spent transitional provision, the urban mirror of Article 243N.
glossary.delimitation-law judicial-review bar for: The Article 243ZG(a) absolute bar preventing any court from questioning the validity of delimitation or seat-allotment laws made under Article 243ZA — the urban mirror of Article 243-O(a) and Article 329(a).
glossary.election-petition-only channel for chall: The Article 243ZG(b) rule confining every challenge to a Municipal election's validity to an election petition presented under State-enacted procedure — the urban mirror of Article 243-O(b) and Article 329(b).
glossary.multi-State co-operative society definit: The Article 243ZH(d) definition of a co-operative society whose objects are not confined to one State, registered under law relating to multi-State co-operatives — a category to which Part IXB applies with the Article 243ZR Parliament/Central-Act/Central-Government substitution.
glossary.dual Central/State Registrar definition: The Article 243ZH(f) definition of 'Registrar' as either the Central Registrar (appointed by the Central Government for multi-State co-operative societies) or the State-appointed Registrar (for ordinary State-registered co-operative societies) — reflecting Part IXB's dual Union/State jurisdictional structure.
glossary.four co-operative principles constitutio: The Article 243ZI requirement that State legislation on co-operative society incorporation, regulation, and winding up be based on the internationally recognized co-operative principles of voluntary formation, democratic member-control, member-economic participation, and autonomous functioning — Part IXB's foundational values clause.
glossary.twenty-one-director maximum board-size c: The first proviso to Article 243ZJ(1) constitutionally fixing the maximum number of directors on a co-operative society's board at twenty-one, regardless of State law.
glossary.mandatory SC/ST and women board-seat res: The second proviso to Article 243ZJ(1) requiring State law to reserve one board seat for Scheduled Castes or Scheduled Tribes and two board seats for women, on every individual-membership co-operative society with members from those categories.
glossary.five-year board term with casual-vacancy: The Article 243ZJ(2) rule fixing a co-operative board's (and its office bearers') term at five years from election, with casual vacancies fillable by nomination from the same member class only if less than half the original term remains.
glossary.non-voting co-opted expert directors on: The Article 243ZJ(3) mandatory State-law mechanism for co-opting up to two additional directors with banking/management/finance/specialised-field experience onto a co-operative board, denied voting rights and office-bearer eligibility — mirroring Article 243R(2)(a)(i)'s non-voting Municipal expert-member design.
glossary.seamless board-transition election-timin: The Article 243ZK(1) overriding rule requiring co-operative board elections to be completed before the outgoing board's term expires, so the newly elected board assumes office immediately with no administrative gap.
glossary.State-law-designated election authority: The Article 243ZK(2) rule leaving the identity of the authority or body superintending co-operative society elections entirely to State law — a deliberate departure from Article 243K/243ZA's constitutionally fixed State Election Commission for Panchayat/Municipal elections.
glossary.six-month maximum board supersession/sus: The Article 243ZL(1) overriding rule capping any co-operative board's supersession or suspension at six months (extended to one year for non-multi-State banking co-operatives under the fourth proviso), regardless of contrary State law.
glossary.five enumerated statutory grounds for co: The first proviso to Article 243ZL(1)'s closed list of permissible supersession/suspension grounds: persistent default, negligence in duties, acts prejudicial to the society or members, constitutional/functional stalemate, or the election authority's failure to conduct elections as required.
glossary.no-Government-stake immunity from board: The second proviso to Article 243ZL(1) completely barring supersession or suspension of a co-operative board where the Government holds no shareholding, loan, financial assistance, or guarantee in that society — a strong constitutional autonomy protection implementing Article 243ZI's autonomous-functioning principle.
glossary.one-year supersession cap for non-multi-: The fourth proviso to Article 243ZL(1) substituting 'one year' for the general 'six months' supersession/suspension cap specifically for banking co-operative societies that are not multi-State co-operative societies.
glossary.mandatory annual audit with prescribed a: The Article 243ZM(1)-(3) scheme requiring at least annual auditing of every co-operative society, State-law-prescribed minimum auditor/auditing-firm qualifications, and general-body (not board) appointment of the auditor from a State-Government-approved panel — a markedly more prescriptive audit regime than Article 243J's or 243Z's single-sentence Panchayat/Municipal audit clauses.
glossary.six-month post-financial-year audit comp: The Article 243ZM(4) rule requiring every co-operative society's accounts to be audited within six months of the close of the financial year to which they relate.
glossary.apex co-operative society audit report l: The Article 243ZM(5) requirement that an apex co-operative society's (as defined by State Act) audit report be laid before the State Legislature in the State-law-prescribed manner — paralleling the Article 243I(4)/243Y(2) Finance Commission report-laying obligations.
glossary.six-month annual general body meeting de: The Article 243ZN enabling provision letting State law require every co-operative society's annual general body meeting to be convened within six months of financial-year close — timed to align with the Article 243ZM(4) audit deadline so audited accounts can be reviewed at that meeting.
glossary.member's right of access to the co-opera: The Article 243ZO(1) enabling provision letting State law give every co-operative society member access to the books, information, and accounts relating to that member's own regular transactions with the society — narrower than a general right to all society records.
glossary.minimum-participation requirement for co: The Article 243ZO(2) enabling provision letting State law impose minimum meeting-attendance and minimum service-utilisation requirements on co-operative society members, reciprocally balancing the Article 243ZO(1) information-access right with an engagement obligation.
glossary.six-item mandatory annual return to Stat: The Article 243ZP direct constitutional mandate requiring every co-operative society to file, within six months of financial-year close, a six-item annual return (activity report, audited accounts, surplus-disposal plan, bye-law amendments, election/meeting-timing declaration, and any other Registrar-required information) with the State-Government-designated authority.
glossary.five mandatory minimum offence categorie: The Article 243ZQ(2) constitutional floor requiring every State's co-operative penal law to criminalise at least: false returns/information, disobedience of lawful orders, an employer's failure to remit deducted employee contributions within fourteen days, an officer/custodian's wilful failure to hand over society property, and electoral corrupt practices — States remain free to add further offences beyond this floor.
glossary.authorised person under Article 243ZQ: The Article 243ZH(a)-defined term for the person to whom an officer or custodian of a co-operative society must hand over the society's books, accounts, documents, records, cash, security, and other property under Article 243ZQ(2)(d)'s offence provision.
glossary.Parliament/Central-Act/Central-Governmen: The Article 243ZR mechanism extending every Part IXB provision to multi-State co-operative societies by substituting 'Parliament' for 'Legislature of a State,' 'Central Act' for 'State Act,' and 'the Central Government' for 'State Government' throughout the Part.
glossary.Union-territory extension of Part IXB wi: The Article 243ZS mechanism extending Part IXB to Union territories by substituting the Article 239 administrator (for territories without a Legislative Assembly) or the territory's own Legislative Assembly (where one exists) for 'Legislature of a State.'
glossary.Presidential opt-out (rather than opt-in: The proviso to Article 243ZS letting the President direct, by Official Gazette notification, that Part IXB shall NOT apply to a specified Union territory or part thereof — a binary disapplication power, textually distinct from Article 243L's and Article 243ZB's opt-in 'exceptions and modifications' tailoring power for Parts IX and IXA.
glossary.one-year transitional continuance of pre: The Article 243ZT rule letting State co-operative-society laws inconsistent with Part IXB continue in force for up to one year after the Ninety-seventh Amendment's 15 February 2012 commencement (or until sooner amended/repealed) — a now largely spent transitional provision, completing the trio alongside Article 243N and Article 243ZF.
glossary.Fifth Schedule Scheduled Area administra: The Article 244(1) rule applying the Fifth Schedule's Governor-and-Tribes-Advisory-Council-centered administrative scheme to Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes in every State other than Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, and Mizoram.
glossary.Sixth Schedule tribal area administratio: The Article 244(2) rule applying the Sixth Schedule's elected-Autonomous-District/Regional-Council administrative scheme specifically to tribal areas in the States of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, and Mizoram, distinct from the Fifth Schedule model used elsewhere.
glossary.Parliament's power to carve an autonomou: The Article 244A(1) power letting Parliament, by ordinary law and 'notwithstanding anything in this Constitution,' form an autonomous State from all or part of the tribal areas specified in Part I of the table appended to paragraph 20 of the Sixth Schedule within Assam, equipping it with a Legislature and/or Council of Ministers.
glossary.two-thirds Parliamentary-majority entren: The Article 244A(3) rule requiring that any amendment to the clause (2)(a)/(b) provisions allocating the Assam autonomous State's legislative and executive powers be passed in each House of Parliament by not less than two-thirds of members present and voting — a middle path between ordinary-law amendment and full Article 368 rigidity.
glossary.autonomous-State law expressly excluded: The Article 244A(4) rule declaring that a law forming the Assam autonomous State under this Article is not to be deemed a constitutional amendment for Article 368 purposes, even though it may have the effect of amending the Constitution.
glossary.territorial extent of Parliamentary law: The Article 245(1) grant letting Parliament make laws for the whole or any part of India's territory, subject to the Constitution's other provisions — the threshold territorial-competence question, distinct from Article 246's subject-matter-competence question.
glossary.territorial extent of State legislative: The Article 245(1) grant letting a State Legislature make laws for the whole or any part of that State — the State-level counterpart to Parliament's India-wide territorial competence.
glossary.extra-territorial operation of Parliamen: The Article 245(2) rule immunizing Parliamentary laws from invalidity merely because they have extra-territorial operation (effects beyond India's territory) — an immunity that applies only to Parliament, not State Legislatures.
glossary.Seventh Schedule three-List distribution: The Article 246 scheme dividing all legislative subject-matter among the Seventh Schedule's Union List (List I, Parliament's exclusive domain), State List (List II, State Legislatures' exclusive domain), and Concurrent List (List III, both Parliament and States, with Parliament prevailing on conflict).
glossary.Union List exclusive Parliamentary compe: The Article 246(1) grant of exclusive Parliamentary law-making power over every matter enumerated in List I (Union List) of the Seventh Schedule, expressly overriding clauses (2) and (3) of the same Article.
glossary.Concurrent List shared Parliament/State: The Article 246(2) grant of law-making power to both Parliament and State Legislatures over List III (Concurrent List) matters, itself subject to Union List priority under clause (1) and Parliamentary-law priority under Article 254's repugnancy rule.
glossary.State List exclusive State competence: The Article 246(3) grant of exclusive State-Legislature law-making power over List II (State List) matters for that State or any part of it, subject to Union List and Concurrent List priority under clauses (1) and (2).
glossary.Parliament's residual power over non-Sta: The Article 246(4) grant letting Parliament legislate on any matter — including State List subjects — for territory not included in any State (i.e., Union territories), since such territory otherwise lacks a State Legislature of its own.
glossary.GST concurrent Union/State legislative p: The Article 246A(1) scheme (inserted by the 101st Amendment, 2016) giving both Parliament and every State Legislature concurrent power to legislate on goods and services tax, expressly overriding the ordinary Article 246 List-distribution and Article 254 repugnancy rules.
glossary.Parliament's exclusive GST power over in: The Article 246A(2) rule reserving GST legislative competence exclusively to Parliament where the supply of goods or services (or both) takes place in the course of inter-State trade or commerce — the constitutional basis for Integrated GST (IGST) under Article 269A.
glossary.GST Council-recommended commencement dat: The Article 246A Explanation deferring the article's application, in respect of goods and services tax referred to in Article 279A(5) (certain petroleum products), until a commencement date recommended by the GST Council.
glossary.Parliament's power to establish addition: The Article 247 power letting Parliament, by ordinary law and notwithstanding the rest of Chapter I's competence rules, establish additional courts for the better administration of Parliamentary laws or existing laws on Union List matters.
glossary.Parliament's exclusive residuary legisla: The Article 248(1) grant of exclusive Parliamentary competence over any legislative subject-matter not enumerated in the State List or Concurrent List, now expressly subject to Article 246A's GST scheme — India's residuary power defaults to the Union, not the States.
glossary.residuary taxation power: The Article 248(2) rule confirming Parliament's residuary legislative power under clause (1) includes the power to impose any tax not mentioned in the State List or Concurrent List.
glossary.Rajya Sabha two-thirds national-interest: The Article 249(1) mechanism letting the Council of States (Rajya Sabha) alone, by a two-thirds-present-and-voting resolution declaring it necessary in the national interest, temporarily authorize Parliament to legislate on a specified State List matter (or GST) for the whole or part of India.
glossary.one-year renewable duration of Article 2: The Article 249(2) rule capping each national-interest resolution's duration at one year, while allowing indefinite renewal through successive approving resolutions passed the same way.
glossary.sunset of Article 249 law six months aft: The Article 249(3) rule providing that a law enabled solely by an Article 249 resolution loses effect, to the extent of the incompetency, six months after the resolution ceases to be in force, except as to things already done or omitted under it.
glossary.Parliament's full State-List legislative: The Article 250(1) rule automatically conferring on Parliament, for as long as an Article 352 Proclamation of Emergency is in operation, full power to legislate on any State List matter (or GST) for the whole or any part of India — no separate resolution needed, unlike Article 249.
glossary.six-month sunset of Emergency-enabled la: The Article 250(2) rule providing that a law Parliament could only make because of an Emergency Proclamation loses effect, to the extent of the incompetency, six months after the Proclamation ceases to operate, except as to things already done or omitted under it.
glossary.State Legislature's law-making power pre: The Article 251 rule confirming that Articles 249 and 250 do not strip a State Legislature of its own ordinary law-making power on the same subjects — the State's competence continues undisturbed except where actual repugnancy with the Parliamentary law arises.
glossary.Parliamentary-law priority on repugnancy: The Article 251 rule that where a State law actually conflicts with a Parliamentary law made under Article 249 or 250, the Parliamentary law prevails regardless of enactment order.
glossary.State law temporarily (not permanently): The Article 251 doctrine that a repugnant State law (vis-à-vis an Article 249/250 Parliamentary law) is inoperative only to the extent of the repugnancy and only so long as the Parliamentary law continues to have effect — reviving automatically once the Parliamentary law lapses, unlike the permanent voidness under Article 254(1).
glossary.State-consent mechanism for Parliamentar: The Article 252(1) voluntary mechanism letting two or more States, via resolutions passed by all Houses of their Legislatures, request Parliament to legislate uniformly on a State List matter otherwise outside Parliament's ordinary competence.
glossary.later adoption by other States via resol: The Article 252(1) provision letting any State not originally party to a consenting resolution later adopt a Parliament-enacted Article 252 Act for itself, by passing its own resolution to that effect.
glossary.State Legislatures barred from amending/: The Article 252(2) rule that once a State has consented to or adopted a Parliament-enacted Article 252 Act, only Parliament — never that State's own Legislature — may subsequently amend or repeal the Act as it applies to that State.
glossary.Parliament's treaty-implementation legis: The Article 253 power letting Parliament legislate on any subject-matter, including State List matters, for the purpose of implementing a treaty, agreement, or convention with another country, or any decision of an international conference, association, or body — overriding the ordinary Article 245-252 distribution of powers.
glossary.general Concurrent List repugnancy rule: The Article 254(1) default rule that where a State law on a Concurrent List matter is repugnant to a Parliamentary law (or existing law) Parliament is competent to enact, the Parliamentary/existing law prevails and the State law is void to the extent of the repugnancy — regardless of which law was enacted first.
glossary.Presidential-assent exception letting re: The Article 254(2) exception letting a State law on a Concurrent List matter, if reserved for the President's consideration under Article 200 and assented to by the President, prevail within that State despite conflicting with an earlier Parliamentary or existing law.
glossary.Parliament's continuing power to overrid: The Article 254(2) proviso confirming that even a President-assented, otherwise-prevailing State law remains subject to Parliament's unrestricted power to later enact a fresh law on the same matter, including one adding to, amending, varying, or repealing that State law.
glossary.procedural (not fatal) treatment of miss: The Article 255 rule that an Act of Parliament or a State Legislature is not invalidated merely because a constitutionally required prior recommendation or previous sanction was not obtained, so long as the relevant authority's assent to the Act was ultimately given — treating such requirements as procedural rather than as fatal conditions precedent.
glossary.curative effect of subsequent assent: The Article 255 principle that a missing Governor's, Rajpramukh's, or President's prior recommendation/sanction for an Act is cured once assent to that Act is given by the specified authority (or, for Governor/Rajpramukh cases, alternatively by the President).
glossary.State's obligation to ensure compliance: The Article 256 rule requiring every State to exercise its executive power so as to ensure compliance with laws made by Parliament and any existing laws applicable in that State.
glossary.Union's directive power to secure that c: The Article 256 corresponding power letting the Union's executive give directions to a State wherever the Government of India considers it necessary to secure the State's compliance with Parliamentary/existing laws.
glossary.State obligation not to impede Union exe: The Article 257(1) rule requiring every State to exercise its executive power so as not to impede or prejudice the exercise of the Union's executive power, backed by a Union power to issue directions to secure that.
glossary.Union directions on nationally/militaril: The Article 257(2) power letting the Union direct a State on construction/maintenance of communications the Union itself declares to be of national or military importance, without restricting Parliament's separate national-highway/waterway powers.
glossary.Union directions on railway protection m: The Article 257(3) power letting the Union direct a State as to measures to be taken for the protection of railways within that State.
glossary.Union's obligation to reimburse States': The Article 257(4) (and mirrored in Article 258(3)) guarantee that the Government of India pays a State for costs incurred in excess of its normal-duty costs when complying with Union directions, by agreement or, failing agreement, via an arbitrator appointed by the Chief Justice of India.
glossary.Presidential entrustment of Union execut: The Article 258(1) power letting the President, with a State Government's consent, entrust Union executive functions (conditionally or unconditionally) to that State Government or its officers.
glossary.Parliament's power to confer State-imple: The Article 258(2) power letting a Parliamentary law applicable in a State confer powers or impose duties on that State or its officers/authorities, even regarding matters outside the State Legislature's own law-making competence, without requiring separate State consent.
glossary.Union's reimbursement obligation for ext: The Article 258(3) guarantee that the Government of India pays a State for extra administrative costs incurred in exercising powers/duties conferred under Article 258, using the same agreement-or-Chief-Justice-arbitrator mechanism as Article 257(4).
glossary.Gubernatorial entrustment of State execu: The Article 258A power letting a State's Governor, with the Union Government's consent, entrust State executive functions (conditionally or unconditionally) to the Government of India or its officers — the mirror image of Article 258(1).
glossary.Union's power to undertake executive/leg: The Article 260 power letting the Government of India, by agreement with a foreign territory's government, undertake executive, legislative, or judicial functions vested in that territory's government, subject to prevailing foreign-jurisdiction law.
glossary.full faith and credit for public acts/re: The Article 261(1) guarantee that public acts, records, and judicial proceedings of the Union and every State receive full faith and credit throughout India's territory, ensuring pan-India legal recognition.
glossary.Parliament's power to prescribe proof/ef: The Article 261(2) delegation letting Parliament legislate on the manner and conditions for proving public acts/records/judicial proceedings under clause (1) and determining their legal effect.
glossary.pan-India executability of civil court f: The Article 261(3) guarantee that final civil-court judgments/orders passed anywhere in India are capable of execution anywhere else in India according to law — the constitutional root of the CPC's decree-execution-transfer provisions.
glossary.Parliament's power to legislate inter-St: The Article 262(1) power letting Parliament legislate for adjudicating disputes/complaints over the use, distribution, or control of inter-State river or river-valley waters, exercised principally through the Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956.
glossary.Parliament's power to oust Supreme Court: The Article 262(2) power letting Parliament, 'notwithstanding anything in this Constitution,' bar the Supreme Court and every other court from exercising jurisdiction over inter-State river water disputes — one of the very few express constitutional authorizations to exclude Supreme Court jurisdiction.
glossary.Presidential power to establish an Inter: The Article 263 discretionary power letting the President, whenever public interest would be served, establish an Inter-State Council by order and define its duties, organisation, and procedure.
glossary.Inter-State Council's three-fold advisor: The Article 263(a)-(c) functions an Inter-State Council may be charged with: inquiring into and advising on inter-State disputes, investigating/discussing subjects of common Union-State or inter-State interest, and making policy-coordination recommendations on such subjects.
glossary.Finance Commission defined for Part XII: The Article 264 interpretive definition confirming that 'Finance Commission' wherever used in Part XII means the Finance Commission constituted under Article 280.
glossary.no taxation without law — constitutional: The Article 265 principle that no tax shall be levied or collected except by authority of law — meaning a validly enacted, competent statute must authorize both the imposition and the collection of every tax in India.
glossary.Consolidated Fund of India: The Article 266(1) fund pooling all revenues received by the Government of India, all loans it raises via treasury bills/loans/ways-and-means advances, and all loan-repayment receipts — withdrawable only in accordance with law per Article 266(3).
glossary.Consolidated Fund of a State: The Article 266(1) State-level counterpart to the Consolidated Fund of India, pooling the analogous categories of State revenue, loan, and repayment receipts, withdrawable only in accordance with law.
glossary.public account of India/State: The Article 266(2) catch-all fund for public moneys received by or on behalf of the Union or State Government that are not part of the Consolidated Fund — e.g., moneys held in a fiduciary/trust capacity — not subject to the same appropriation-by-law requirement as the Consolidated Fund.
glossary.no appropriation from Consolidated Fund: The Article 266(3) rule that no moneys may be withdrawn from the Consolidated Fund of India or of a State except in accordance with law and for purposes/in a manner this Constitution provides — the constitutional basis for the mandatory annual Appropriation Act.
glossary.Contingency Fund of India: The Article 267(1) imprest fund Parliament may establish by law, placed at the President's disposal, to enable advances meeting genuinely unforeseen expenditure pending formal Parliamentary authorisation under Article 115 or 116.
glossary.Contingency Fund of a State: The Article 267(2) imprest fund a State Legislature may establish by law, placed at the Governor's disposal, to enable advances meeting genuinely unforeseen expenditure pending formal State Legislature authorisation under Article 205 or 206.
glossary.imprest advances for unforeseen expendit: The core Article 267 mechanism: a Contingency Fund advance bridges the gap between an urgent, unforeseen spending need and the time it takes to secure formal legislative authorisation, with the advanced amount later recouped from the Consolidated Fund once that authorisation (supplementary/additional grant) is secured.
glossary.Union-List stamp duties levied by Union,: The Article 268 revenue-sharing model for Union List stamp duties: the Union levies (imposes) the duty, collection is bifurcated between the Union (Union territories) and respective States, and all proceeds collected within a State are assigned entirely to that State, bypassing the Consolidated Fund of India.
glossary.inter-State sale/purchase and consignmen: The Article 269(1)-(2) model where the Union both levies and collects taxes on inter-State sale/purchase and consignment of goods (except what Article 269A now covers), but the full net proceeds (minus the Union-territory-attributable share) are assigned to the States where leviable, per Parliament-formulated distribution principles.
glossary.Parliament's power to formulate inter-St: The Article 269(3) power letting Parliament formulate, by law, the principles for determining when a sale, purchase, or consignment of goods takes place in the course of inter-State trade or commerce — historically implemented via the Central Sales Tax Act, 1956.
glossary.Integrated GST (IGST) levied by Union, a: The Article 269A(1) mechanism (inserted by the 101st Amendment, 2016) under which the Union levies and collects GST on inter-State supplies of goods or services, then apportions it between the Union and the States per Parliament-made law following the GST Council's recommendations.
glossary.imports deemed inter-State supply for IG: The Article 269A Explanation deeming any supply of goods or services (or both) in the course of import into India's territory to be an inter-State supply, thereby bringing imports within the IGST apportionment mechanism.
glossary.cross-utilisation of IGST/State-GST amou: The Article 269A(2)-(4) technical accounting rules ensuring that amounts apportioned to a State, and amounts cross-utilised between IGST and State-GST liability via input-tax-credit mechanisms, are not counted as part of the Consolidated Fund of India or of a State — preventing double-counting or fiscal misallocation.
glossary.Parliament's power to formulate place-of: The Article 269A(5) power letting Parliament formulate, by law, the principles for determining the place of supply and when a supply of goods or services (or both) takes place in the course of inter-State trade or commerce — the GST-era successor to Article 269(3)'s older situs principles, implemented via the IGST Act, 2017.
glossary.general Union-List tax/duty pool shared: The Article 270(1)-(2) residual/general revenue-sharing rule: Union List taxes/duties not otherwise specifically allocated (excluding Articles 268/269/269A items, Article 271 surcharges, and Parliament-law-specific cesses) are levied and collected by the Union but a President-prescribed percentage of net proceeds is distributed to the States.
glossary.Union's own-GST and IGST-derived amounts: The Article 270(1A)-(1B) extension (added by the 101st Amendment) bringing the Union's own CGST collections and certain IGST-derived amounts into the same Article 270(2) sharing formula as traditional Union List taxes.
glossary.'prescribed' percentage set by President: The Article 270(3) definition of 'prescribed': before any Finance Commission exists, the President alone prescribes the sharing percentage by order; afterward, the President must prescribe it only after considering the Finance Commission's recommendations.
glossary.Parliament's surcharge power on Article: The Article 271 power letting Parliament, notwithstanding Articles 269 and 270, increase any duty/tax referred to in those Articles by a surcharge for Union purposes, with the whole surcharge proceeds forming part of the Consolidated Fund of India exclusively — bypassing the States' share entirely.
glossary.GST expressly excluded from the surcharg: The Article 271 proviso (added by the 101st Amendment) excluding goods and services tax under Article 246A from Parliament's surcharge power, since GST already has its own dedicated apportionment mechanism under Articles 269A/279A.
glossary.jute-export-duty compensatory grants to: The Article 273(1) grants-in-aid charged annually on the Consolidated Fund of India for Assam, Bihar, Odisha, and West Bengal, in lieu of assigning those States any share of net jute/jute-products export duty proceeds.
glossary.ten-year-or-earlier sunset tied to conti: The Article 273(2) sunset rule: the jute-export-duty compensatory grants continue only as long as the Government of India keeps levying export duty on jute/jute products, or until ten years from the Constitution's commencement, whichever occurs first — now a spent, historical provision.
glossary.Presidential-recommendation precondition: The Article 274(1) procedural gatekeeping rule barring introduction or moving of any Bill/amendment imposing or varying a tax/duty in which States are interested (or redefining 'agricultural income,' affecting Chapter I distribution principles, or imposing an Article 271 surcharge) in either House of Parliament without the President's prior recommendation.
glossary.'tax or duty in which States are interes: The Article 274(2) definition: a tax/duty whose net proceeds (whole or part) are assigned to any State, or by reference to whose net proceeds sums are payable out of the Consolidated Fund of India to any State.
glossary.'agricultural income' definitional-chang: The Article 274(1) rule extending the Presidential-recommendation precondition to any Bill varying the meaning of 'agricultural income' as defined for Indian income-tax purposes, because that definition affects the Union/State taxing-field boundary even though agricultural income tax itself is a State List subject.
glossary.general need-based Union grants-in-aid t: The Article 275(1) main-body discretionary mechanism: Parliament charges sums on the Consolidated Fund of India each year as grants-in-aid for States it determines need assistance, with different sums fixable for different States — the needs-based counterpart to Article 270's formula-based tax-sharing.
glossary.mandatory Scheduled Tribes/Scheduled Are: The Article 275(1) first proviso making it mandatory (not discretionary) to pay capital/recurring grants-in-aid enabling a State to fund Scheduled Tribes welfare schemes or raise Scheduled Areas administration to the level of the State's other areas.
glossary.Assam Sixth Schedule tribal-area special: The Article 275(1) second proviso mandating specific capital/recurring grants to Assam covering both a historical pre-Constitution administration-expenditure-over-revenue deficit and ongoing development-scheme costs for the Sixth Schedule Part I tribal areas.
glossary.Article 244A autonomous State grant appo: The Article 275(1A) rule (added with Article 244A by the 22nd Amendment) governing how the Assam Sixth-Schedule-tribal-area grants under Article 275(1)'s second proviso get paid to or apportioned between Assam and an autonomous State once one is formed under Article 244A.
glossary.President's stand-in power pending Parli: The Article 275(2) mechanism letting the President exercise Parliament's Article 275(1) grant-determination power by order until Parliament legislates, with any such order after a Finance Commission's constitution requiring prior consideration of that Commission's recommendations.
glossary.State/local-authority profession tax val: The Article 276(1) rule that, notwithstanding Article 246, a State or local-authority law taxing professions, trades, callings, or employments is not invalid merely because it relates to a tax on income (a Union List subject) — resolving the State List Entry 60/Union List Entry 82 overlap.
glossary.₹2,500 per annum aggregate profession-ta: The Article 276(2) hard ceiling (raised from ₹250 to ₹2,500 by the Constitution (Sixtieth Amendment) Act, 1988) on the total amount any one person can be charged across all State/local-authority profession, trade, calling, and employment taxes combined in a year.
glossary.Parliament's income-tax power over profe: The Article 276(3) savings clause confirming that a State's power to tax professions/trades/callings/employments does not in any way limit Parliament's separate, Union List power to tax income arising from those same professions/trades/callings/employments.
glossary.transitional savings for pre-Constitutio: The Article 277 grandfather clause protecting taxes, duties, cesses, or fees lawfully levied by a State or local authority immediately before the Constitution's commencement from invalidation merely because the Union List now covers the same subject, letting them continue until Parliament legislates to the contrary.
glossary.\"net proceeds\" defined as gross procee: The Article 279(1) definition applicable throughout Part XII Chapter I: 'net proceeds' of any tax or duty means the gross proceeds thereof reduced by the cost of collection.
glossary.CAG's certification of net proceeds is f: The Article 279(1) rule that the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India ascertains and certifies the net proceeds of any tax/duty (or part thereof) attributable to any area, and that certificate is expressly made final — a narrower, more consequential CAG function than the general Article 148 audit role since it directly drives inter-governmental revenue flows.
glossary.Parliament/Presidential order power over: The Article 279(2) delegation letting Parliament (or the President by order, pending Parliamentary law) fill in the detailed mechanics of how assigned tax/duty proceeds are calculated, when/how payments are made, and how inter-year adjustments and other incidental matters are handled.
glossary.GST Council composition — Union Finance: The Article 279A(2)-(3) membership structure: the Union Finance Minister chairs the GST Council, joined by the Union Minister of State for Revenue/Finance and one nominated Finance/Taxation Minister from each State, who together elect a Vice-Chairperson from among themselves.
glossary.GST Council's broad recommendatory manda: The Article 279A(4) list of matters the GST Council recommends to the Union and States: what taxes/cesses get subsumed into GST, goods/services taxed or exempted, model GST laws and apportionment/place-of-supply principles, turnover exemption thresholds, rates and floor-rate bands, special calamity-relief rates, special provisions for listed hill/border States, and any other GST-related matter.
glossary.weighted voting formula — Centre 1/3, St: The Article 279A(9) decision-making rule: every GST Council decision requires at least a three-fourths weighted-majority vote of members present and voting, where the Central Government's vote carries one-third weight and all State Governments' votes combined carry two-thirds weight.
glossary.GST Council's mandatory inter-government: The Article 279A(11) requirement that the GST Council establish a mechanism to adjudicate disputes between the Union and one or more States, or among States, arising from the Council's recommendations or their implementation — a mandate that, notably, has not been formally implemented as of the mid-2020s.
glossary.quinquennial (or earlier) Finance Commis: The Article 280(1) requirement that the President constitute a Finance Commission (Chairman plus four members) within two years of the Constitution's commencement and thereafter every five years, or earlier if the President considers it necessary.
glossary.Finance Commission's core mandate — tax-: The Article 280(3)(a)-(b) founding-era functions: recommending how net tax proceeds divisible under Part XII Chapter I should be split between Union and States (and among States), and what principles should govern Article 275 grants-in-aid to States.
glossary.Panchayat/Municipality resource-augmenta: The Article 280(3)(bb)-(c) functions (added by the 73rd/74th Amendments) tasking the national Finance Commission with recommending measures to augment a State's Consolidated Fund to support Panchayats and Municipalities, based on that State's own State Finance Commission's recommendations under Articles 243-I/243-Y.
glossary.Finance Commission's self-determined pro: The Article 280(4) rule letting the Finance Commission determine its own working procedure, while Parliament may by law confer additional powers on it in performing its functions.
glossary.mandatory Parliamentary tabling of Finan: The Article 281 obligation requiring the President to lay every Finance Commission recommendation before both Houses of Parliament together with an explanatory memorandum on the action taken on it — the accountability mechanism ensuring departures from non-binding recommendations are publicly disclosed.
glossary.Union/State power to fund any public pur: The Article 282 power letting the Union or a State make grants for any public purpose even outside their own Union/State/Concurrent List legislative competence — the broad residual executive spending power underlying most Centrally Sponsored Schemes.
glossary.Parliament/State-Legislature law (or Pre: The Article 283 rule assigning custody, payment-in, and withdrawal mechanics for the Consolidated Fund, Contingency Fund, and public account to Parliament's law at the Union level (President's rules pending such law) and the State Legislature's law at the State level (Governor's rules pending such law).
glossary.mandatory routing of officer-held/court-: The Article 284 rule requiring non-revenue moneys held by a Union/State officer in official capacity, or moneys any court holds to the credit of a cause/matter/account/person (e.g., suitors' deposits), to be paid into the public account of India or of the State.
glossary.general Union-property exemption from St: The Article 285(1) default rule exempting all Union property from State/local-authority taxation, which only Parliament (not the Union executive) may waive by law.
glossary.pre-Constitution-liability grandfather e: The Article 285(2) transitional carve-out letting a local tax already validly levied on particular Union property immediately before the Constitution's commencement continue, until Parliament legislates otherwise.
glossary.State GST/sales-tax barred on extra-terr: The Article 286(1) bar preventing any State law from taxing a supply of goods or services taking place outside that State, or in the course of import into or export out of India's territory.
glossary.Parliament's power to formulate situs pr: The Article 286(2) delegation letting Parliament formulate, by law, the principles for determining when a supply of goods/services falls into the outside-the-State, import, or export categories barred to State taxation under clause (1).
glossary.State electricity-tax exemption for Unio: The Article 287 default exemption barring State taxation of electricity consumed by the Government of India or consumed in constructing/maintaining/operating any railway, unless Parliament by law otherwise provides.
glossary.pass-through price-reduction guarantee e: The Article 287 anti-evasion mechanism requiring that, where a State does tax electricity sales generally, the price charged to the Government of India or a railway company for exempted consumption must be reduced by exactly the tax amount compared to ordinary large consumers' prices.
glossary.default exemption of inter-State river/r: The Article 288(1) default rule exempting water/electricity stored, generated, consumed, distributed, or sold by an inter-State river/river-valley regulatory authority from pre-Constitution State tax laws, unless the President orders otherwise.
glossary.State Legislature's power to newly impos: The Article 288(2) rule letting a State Legislature impose a fresh tax on inter-State river/river-valley authorities' water/electricity operations, but only via a law reserved for and receiving the President's assent, with any subordinate rate-fixing rules also needing the President's prior consent.
glossary.general State-property/income exemption: The Article 289(1) default rule exempting a State's property and income from Union taxation — the mirror image of Article 285's Union-property exemption from State taxation.
glossary.Parliament's power to tax State governme: The Article 289(2) carve-out letting Parliament by law tax a State Government's trade or business operations (and connected property/income), to whatever extent Parliament chooses to legislate.
glossary.'ordinary functions of Government' carve: The Article 289(3) further carve-back letting Parliament declare specific State trade/business activities (or classes of them) to be incidental to the ordinary functions of Government, removing them entirely from Article 289(2)'s taxing scope.
glossary.cross-reimbursement of shared court/Comm: The Article 290 rule requiring a government whose Consolidated Fund is not charged with a court's/Commission's expenses or a person's pension, but which nonetheless benefits from that court/Commission's service or that person's service, to contribute its fair share to the government whose Fund is charged.
glossary.agreement-or-Chief-Justice-appointed-arb: The recurring Article 257(4)/258(3)/290 dispute-resolution formula: the contribution/reimbursement amount is fixed by agreement between the governments concerned, or, failing agreement, by an arbitrator appointed by the Chief Justice of India.
glossary.fixed annual Devaswom Fund payments char: The Article 290A charged-expenditure obligation requiring Kerala's Consolidated Fund to pay ₹46,50,000 annually to the Travancore Devaswom Fund, and Tamil Nadu's Consolidated Fund to pay ₹13,50,000 annually to its corresponding Devaswom Fund, for temple/shrine maintenance in former Travancore-Cochin territories transferred in the 1956 States Reorganisation.
glossary.general Union-property exemption from St: The Article 285(1) default rule exempting all Union property from State/local-authority taxation, which only Parliament (not the Union executive) may waive by law.
glossary.Union executive borrowing power secured: The Article 292 power letting the Union executive borrow money and give guarantees on the security of the Consolidated Fund of India, without a fresh Parliamentary vote for each loan.
glossary.Parliament's power to fix borrowing/guar: The Article 292 delegation letting Parliament fix, by law, the limits (if any) on the Union's borrowing and guarantee-giving power — exercised in modern practice via the FRBM Act, 2003.
glossary.State executive borrowing power secured: The Article 293(1) power letting a State's executive borrow within India's territory on the security of its own Consolidated Fund, within limits its own Legislature fixes by law.
glossary.Union's power to lend to States or guara: The Article 293(2) power letting the Government of India make loans to any State, or guarantee State-raised loans (within Article 292 limits), with loan funds charged on the Consolidated Fund of India.
glossary.State's borrowing restricted (Union cons: The Article 293(3)-(4) rule barring a State from raising any new loan without the Union Government's consent while any part of a prior Union loan or Union-guaranteed loan to that State remains outstanding, with the Union free to attach conditions to that consent.
glossary.automatic Crown-to-Union/State successio: The Article 294 transitional rule automatically vesting Crown-held property/assets and Dominion-of-India/Governor's-Province rights, liabilities, and obligations in the Union and corresponding States respectively from the Constitution's commencement.
glossary.adjustments carved out for Partition-rel: The Article 294 qualifier making the automatic Crown-to-Union/State succession subject to adjustments needed because of the pre-Constitution creation of the Dominion of Pakistan and the split Provinces of West/East Bengal and West/East Punjab.
glossary.purpose-based Union-vs-Part-B-State succ: The Article 295(1) rule vesting former princely-State (Part B State) property/assets/rights/liabilities in the Union specifically where their purpose would thereafter relate to a Union List matter, subject to any Government-of-India agreement with that State.
glossary.residual/default succession to the corre: The Article 295(2) residual rule making the corresponding Part B State the general successor of a former princely State's government for all property, assets, rights, liabilities, and obligations not caught by the Union List purpose-test in clause (1).
glossary.escheat/lapse/bona vacantia property ves: The Article 296 general rule that ownerless property which would formerly have escheated/lapsed to the Crown or a princely Ruler now vests in the State where it is situated, or in the Union if not situated in any State.
glossary.possession-and-purpose-based proviso ove: The Article 296 proviso making property already in a government's possession/control for a specific purpose at the relevant date vest according to that purpose (Union or State), overriding the general situs-based escheat/bona-vacantia rule.
glossary.Union ownership of undersea lands/minera: The Article 297(1)-(2) rule vesting all undersea lands, minerals, other things of value, and all other resources within India's territorial waters, continental shelf, and exclusive economic zone exclusively in the Union.
glossary.Parliament's power to specify maritime-z: The Article 297(3) delegation letting Parliament specify, by law, the limits of India's territorial waters, continental shelf, exclusive economic zone, and other maritime zones — implemented via the Territorial Waters, Continental Shelf, Exclusive Economic Zone and other Maritime Zones Act, 1976.
glossary.executive power to trade, acquire/hold/d: The Article 298 grant of broad executive power to both the Union and every State to carry on trade/business, acquire/hold/dispose of property, and make contracts for any purpose.
glossary.reciprocal subjection to the other level: The Article 298 provisos making the Union's Article 298 executive power (within a State) subject to that State's legislation, and a State's Article 298 executive power subject to Parliament's legislation, wherever the underlying trade/business/purpose falls outside the acting government's own legislative-list competence.
glossary.mandatory 'expressed to be made by the P: The Article 299(1) requirement that every contract made in exercise of Union or State executive power be expressed as made by the President or Governor and executed by a person duly authorised by them — non-compliance renders the purported government contract void and unenforceable.
glossary.personal-liability immunity for the Pres: The Article 299(2) rule that neither the President/Governor nor any official executing a government contract on their behalf is personally liable in respect of that contract — liability, if any, attaches to the Government as a juristic entity.
glossary.Government suability under 'Union of Ind: The Article 300(1) rule establishing 'Union of India' and the name of the relevant State as the proper legal names under which the Government of India and State Governments may sue or be sued.
glossary.continuity of suability preserved from p: The Article 300(1) rule preserving the scope of government suability from what applied to the pre-Constitution Dominion of India and the corresponding Provinces/Indian States, subject to any Parliament/State Legislature law made under constitutional powers.
glossary.automatic party-substitution in pending: The Article 300(2) rule automatically substituting the Union of India, or the corresponding State, as a party in any legal proceeding that was pending against the Dominion of India, or a Province/Indian State, at the Constitution's commencement.
glossary.constitutional (statutory, not fundament: The Article 300A guarantee that no person shall be deprived of property save by authority of law — a Part XII 'constitutional right' (added by the 44th Amendment, 1978, replacing the repealed fundamental right to property) rather than a Part III fundamental right, though later Supreme Court jurisprudence has reinforced its substantive content over time.
glossary.nationwide constitutional guarantee of f: The Article 301 guarantee that trade, commerce, and intercourse throughout India's territory shall be free — the foundational Part XIII rule, itself subject to the restrictions Articles 302-305 permit.
glossary.Parliament's public-interest-justified p: The Article 302 power letting Parliament impose, by law, such restrictions on inter-State or intra-territory trade, commerce, or intercourse as the public interest requires — the first qualification on Article 301's general freedom.
glossary.blanket bar on Parliament/State trade-an: The Article 303(1) rule barring both Parliament and State Legislatures from making any law giving preference to one State over another, or discriminating between States, in trade/commerce/intercourse matters arising from any Entry relating to trade/commerce in the Lists.
glossary.Parliament-only scarcity exception, requ: The Article 303(2) exception letting Parliament (not States) make preferential/discriminatory trade laws to deal with a scarcity of goods arising in any part of India's territory, but only if the law itself expressly declares that necessity.
glossary.State's power to tax imported goods on p: The Article 304(a) power letting a State Legislature tax goods imported from other States (or Union territories) the same way it taxes similar goods produced within the State, so long as no discrimination is made between imported and locally-produced goods.
glossary.State's public-interest reasonable-restr: The Article 304(b) power letting a State Legislature impose reasonable restrictions on trade/commerce/intercourse with or within that State in the public interest, but only via a Bill that first receives the President's previous sanction (the proviso further preserves Parliament's power to itself legislate on the same subject).
glossary.general savings of pre-Constitution exis: The Article 305 savings clause protecting laws already in force at the Constitution's commencement from Articles 301 and 303's restrictions, until the President by order otherwise directs — plus separately preserving laws relating to State monopolies referred to in Article 19(6)(ii).
glossary.specific savings protecting State-monopo: The Article 305 proviso specifically shielding laws that create or extend State trade/business monopolies (whether for the State itself or a State-owned/controlled corporation, under Article 19(6)(ii)) from being struck down under Article 301's general trade-freedom guarantee.
glossary.Parliament's power to create an implemen: The Article 307 power letting Parliament by law appoint an authority to carry out the purposes of Articles 301-304, and confer on that authority the powers and duties Parliament considers necessary — a power never actually exercised, paralleling Article 279A(11)'s similarly unimplemented GST Council dispute-resolution mandate.
glossary.Part XIV-specific narrowed definition of: The Article 308 interpretation clause fixing that, throughout Part XIV only, 'State' excludes the State of Jammu and Kashmir — a special-status carve-out distinct from the general Article 12 definition.
glossary.Legislature's primary power to regulate: The Article 309 primary power letting Parliament (Union services) or a State Legislature (State services) enact Acts regulating recruitment and conditions of service of persons in public services/posts.
glossary.President's/Governor's interim rule-maki: The Article 309 proviso letting the President (Union) or Governor (State) make stopgap rules on recruitment/conditions of service until the appropriate Legislature enacts its own law, with such rules yielding to any later Act.
glossary.'doctrine of pleasure' — Union/State civ: The Article 310(1) baseline rule that defence personnel and Union/State civil servants hold their posts 'during the pleasure' of the President or Governor respectively — India's constitutional version of the English at-pleasure doctrine, heavily qualified in practice by Article 311.
glossary.compensation-for-early-termination claus: The Article 310(2) mechanism letting the President/Governor include a compensation clause in a specially-qualified contract appointee's terms, payable if the post is abolished or the person is blamelessly removed before an agreed period ends.
glossary.no-dismissal-by-subordinate-authority ru: The Article 311(1) rule barring a civil servant's dismissal or removal by any authority subordinate in rank to the authority that originally appointed them.
glossary.mandatory inquiry-plus-hearing safeguard: The Article 311(2) core protection requiring a civil servant to be informed of the charges against them and given a reasonable hearing opportunity before dismissal, removal, or reduction in rank.
glossary.penalty-stage representation dispensed w: The Article 311(2) first proviso clarifying that once the disciplinary inquiry is done, the penalty may be imposed on the inquiry evidence without a further separate hearing on the proposed punishment itself.
glossary.criminal-conviction, impracticability, a: The Article 311(2) second proviso's three carve-outs — (a) dismissal following a criminal conviction, (b) the disciplinary authority's recorded finding that an inquiry isn't reasonably practicable, (c) a Presidential/Gubernatorial national-security satisfaction — each of which dispenses with the inquiry requirement altogether.
glossary.Rajya Sabha two-thirds resolution precon: The Article 312(1) federalism safeguard requiring the Council of States (Rajya Sabha) to first pass a resolution, by a two-thirds majority of members present and voting, declaring it nationally necessary or expedient, before Parliament may legislate to create a new all-India service.
glossary.deemed-created status for the pre-existi: The Article 312(2) rule treating the Indian Administrative Service and the Indian Police Service, both already in existence at the Constitution's commencement, as if they had been created by Parliament under Article 312 — no fresh Rajya Sabha resolution needed for them.
glossary.district-judge-or-above floor for any fu: The Article 312(3) restriction that any all-India judicial service Parliament might create under clause (1) cannot include posts inferior to that of a district judge as defined in Article 236 — a service that, despite this authorization, has never actually been created.
