glossary.Parliament's retrospective power to vary: The Article 312A(1) power, inserted by the 28th Amendment (1972), letting Parliament retrospectively or prospectively vary or revoke the remuneration, leave, pension, and disciplinary terms of the last serving or retired pre-Independence 'Secretary of State' civil service appointees.
glossary.protected-office proviso shielding sitti: The Article 312A(1) proviso protecting anyone who holds or has held office as Chief Justice/Judge of the Supreme Court or a High Court, CAG, a Public Service Commission Chairman/member, or the Chief Election Commissioner from having their service conditions in that later office worsened by reason of their earlier Crown-in-India appointment status.
glossary.court-jurisdiction bar over Crown-in-Ind: The Article 312A(3) rule ousting the Supreme Court's and every other court's jurisdiction over disputes arising from pre-Constitution Crown-in-India appointment covenants/letters, and over disputes under Article 314 as originally enacted.
glossary.automatic continuation of pre-Constituti: The Article 313 transitional rule automatically continuing pre-Constitution laws governing still-existing public services/posts in force, until fresh constitutional provision is made and so long as they remain consistent with the Constitution.
glossary.mandatory one-Commission-per-Union/per-S: The Article 315(1) default rule establishing one Public Service Commission for the Union (UPSC) and one for each State, subject to the flexibility mechanisms in the rest of the article.
glossary.opt-in Joint State Public Service Commis: The Article 315(2)-(3) mechanism letting two or more States pool into a single 'Joint Commission', triggered by each participating State Legislature passing a resolution followed by a Parliament law establishing it.
glossary.UPSC-serving-a-State option via Governor: The Article 315(4) mechanism letting a State's Governor request, with the President's approval, that the Union Public Service Commission itself serve all or some of that State's Public Service Commission needs, instead of establishing a separate State Commission.
glossary.President's/Governor's appointment power: The Article 316(1) rule that the President appoints the Chairman and members of the Union Commission or a Joint Commission, while a State's Governor appoints the Chairman and members of that State's own Commission.
glossary.roughly-half-experienced-officers compos: The Article 316(1) proviso requiring that, as nearly as may be, one-half of every Public Service Commission's members have at least ten years' prior government service (Union or State, including pre-Constitution Crown-in-India or Indian-State service) at the time of their appointment.
glossary.acting-Chairman mechanism for vacancy/in: The Article 316(1A) mechanism letting the President (Union/Joint Commission) or Governor (State Commission) appoint another existing member to perform the Chairman's duties when that office is vacant or the Chairman cannot act, until a new Chairman is appointed or the incumbent resumes.
glossary.six-year-term or age-cap (65 UPSC / 62 S: The Article 316(2) tenure rule fixing a Public Service Commission member's term at six years from entering office or a fixed retirement age (65 for the UPSC, 62 for State/Joint Commissions), whichever arrives earlier.
glossary.resignation and Article 317 removal as t: The Article 316(2)-(3) rule that a Commission member may only leave office early by resignation (in writing to the appointing authority) or Article 317 removal, and can never be re-appointed to that same Commission office once their term expires.
glossary.Supreme-Court-inquiry-plus-Presidential-: The Article 317(1) safeguard requiring a Supreme Court Article-145 inquiry and report before the President may remove any Public Service Commission member (Union, Joint, or State) on grounds of misbehaviour.
glossary.Union-exclusive suspension power pending: The Article 317(2) rule that only the President — never a State Governor, even for a State Commission member — may suspend a Commission member from office once a misbehaviour reference has been made to the Supreme Court, pending its report.
glossary.no-inquiry Presidential removal for inso: The Article 317(3) fast-track removal power letting the President remove a Commission member without any Supreme Court inquiry if adjudged insolvent, found engaging in outside paid employment, or considered unfit by reason of infirmity of mind or body.
glossary.deemed-misbehaviour rule for improper go: The Article 317(4) rule automatically treating a Commission member's improper concern or interest in a government contract or agreement (beyond ordinary incorporated-company shareholding) as 'misbehaviour' for Article 317(1) removal purposes.
glossary.President's/Governor's regulation-making: The Article 318 power letting the President (Union/Joint Commission) or Governor (State Commission) fix, by regulation, the number of Commission members and both members' and staff's conditions of service.
glossary.no-disadvantageous-variation guarantee f: The Article 318 proviso guaranteeing that a Public Service Commission member's own conditions of service, once appointed, can never afterward be varied to their disadvantage.
glossary.absolute post-tenure employment bar for: The Article 319(a) rule making a former Union Public Service Commission Chairman permanently ineligible for any further employment under either the Government of India or any State Government.
glossary.cross-Commission-Chairman/membership eli: The Article 319(b)-(d) graduated rules letting former State Commission Chairmen and non-Chairman UPSC/State Commission members move laterally into other specified Public Service Commission roles, while barring them from any other government employment.
glossary.core examination-conducting duty for Uni: The Article 320(1) baseline duty requiring the UPSC and State Public Service Commissions to conduct examinations for appointments to Union and State services respectively.
glossary.UPSC's optional joint-recruitment assist: The Article 320(2) duty requiring the UPSC, if requested by two or more States, to help those States frame and operate joint recruitment schemes for specialist posts.
glossary.mandatory consultation duty on recruitme: The Article 320(3) default consultation duty requiring the appropriate Commission to be consulted on recruitment methods, appointment/promotion/transfer principles and candidate suitability, civil-service disciplinary matters, litigation-cost reimbursement claims, and service-injury pension claims.
glossary.President's/Governor's regulation-making: The Article 320(3) proviso and clause (5) mechanism letting the President or Governor exempt specified matters from the Commission consultation requirement by regulation, provided that regulation is laid before the Legislature for at least 14 days and remains subject to modification or repeal there.
glossary.legislative power to expand Commission f: The Article 321 power letting Parliament or a State Legislature, by Act, extend a Public Service Commission's functions beyond Article 320's baseline to cover local authorities, statutory body corporates, or public institutions.
glossary.charged-expenditure status for Commissio: The Article 322 rule making all Public Service Commission expenses, including members' and staff's salaries, allowances, and pensions, charged expenditure on the Consolidated Fund of India or the relevant State's Consolidated Fund, immune from the annual voting process.
glossary.mandatory annual UPSC report to the Pres: The Article 323(1) accountability mechanism requiring the UPSC to submit an annual work report to the President, who must table it before both Houses of Parliament together with a memorandum explaining any instances of non-acceptance of the Commission's advice.
glossary.mandatory annual State/Joint Commission: The Article 323(2) accountability mechanism requiring a State or Joint Commission to submit an annual work report to the relevant Governor(s), who must table it before the State Legislature together with a non-acceptance memorandum, mirroring the Article 323(1) Union mechanism.
glossary.Parliament-exclusive power to create adm: The Article 323A(1) power, exercisable by Parliament alone, to create administrative tribunals (e.g., the Central Administrative Tribunal) adjudicating recruitment and conditions-of-service disputes for Union, State, local-authority, and government-corporation employees.
glossary.near-total ouster of ordinary-court juri: The Article 323A(2)(d) mechanism letting a tribunal law exclude all court jurisdiction over covered service disputes except the Supreme Court's discretionary Article 136 special-leave power — now read down by L. Chandra Kumar (1997) to preserve High Court Article 226/227 judicial review as well.
glossary.overriding effect notwithstanding any ot: The Article 323A(3) (and Article 323B(4)) clause giving the tribunal-creation power overriding effect over any other provision of the Constitution or any other law for the time being in force.
glossary.appropriate-Legislature (Parliament or S: The Article 323B(1) power letting whichever Legislature (Parliament or a State Legislature) already has ordinary legislative competence over a listed subject also create tribunals to adjudicate disputes, complaints, or offences within that subject.
glossary.taxation, foreign exchange/customs, indu: The Article 323B(2) exhaustive list of ten matter-categories — tax levy/collection, foreign exchange/customs, industrial/labour disputes, land reforms, urban property ceilings, certain elections, essential-goods production/pricing, and rent control, plus incidental/offence matters — within which subject-specific tribunals may be created.
glossary.hierarchy-of-tribunals structure with ne: The Article 323B(3)(a) and (3)(d) mechanism letting a tribunal law establish a multi-tier hierarchy of tribunals for a listed subject, while excluding other courts' jurisdiction except the Supreme Court's Article 136 power (again subject to L. Chandra Kumar's High Court judicial-review carve-back).
glossary.'appropriate Legislature' defined by ord: The Article 323B Explanation defining 'appropriate Legislature', for any given matter, as whichever of Parliament or a State Legislature has ordinary law-making competence over that matter under Part XI's Union/State/Concurrent List scheme.
glossary.Election Commission's plenary superinten: The Article 324(1) grant of complete constitutional authority to the Election Commission of India over preparing electoral rolls and conducting all elections to Parliament, State Legislatures, and the offices of President and Vice-President.
glossary.President's appointment power over the C: The Article 324(2) power letting the President appoint the Chief Election Commissioner and any other Election Commissioners, and fix their number, subject to any law Parliament makes on the subject.
glossary.Judge-of-the-Supreme-Court-equivalent re: The Article 324(5) first proviso giving the Chief Election Commissioner alone the strong removal protection of a Supreme Court Judge (Article 124(4)-style process), plus a guarantee against disadvantageous variation of service conditions after appointment.
glossary.recommendation-gated removal protection: The Article 324(5) second proviso providing that any Election Commissioner other than the CEC, or a Regional Commissioner, can only be removed from office on the Chief Election Commissioner's own recommendation — a weaker protection than the CEC's judge-equivalent safeguard, but still an internal check on government pressure.
glossary.President's/Governor's mandatory staff-p: The Article 324(6) duty requiring the President (for the Election Commission/Regional Commissioners generally) or a State Governor to make available whatever staff the Election Commission requests as necessary to discharge its Article 324(1) functions.
glossary.single general electoral roll per consti: The Article 325 guarantee of one general electoral roll for every constituency, barring exclusion from it or a claim to a separate special roll on grounds only of religion, race, caste, or sex — India's constitutional rejection of colonial-era separate electorates.
glossary.universal adult suffrage guarantee at 18: The Article 326 guarantee that every Indian citizen aged 18 or above is entitled to register as a voter for House of the People and State Legislative Assembly elections, subject only to the four listed disqualification grounds.
glossary.non-residence/unsoundness-of-mind/crime/: The Article 326 exhaustive list of grounds — non-residence, unsoundness of mind, crime, or corrupt/illegal election practice — on which a citizen otherwise eligible under adult suffrage may be disqualified from voter registration.
glossary.Parliament's plenary law-making power ov: The Article 327 power letting Parliament legislate on essentially every matter relating to elections to Parliament and State Legislatures, including electoral rolls and constituency delimitation, subject to the Constitution's own express provisions.
glossary.State Legislature's residual, Parliament: The Article 328 residual power letting a State Legislature legislate on matters relating to elections to its own House(s), but only to the extent Parliament has not already made provision on that matter under Article 327.
glossary.absolute court-jurisdiction bar over del: The Article 329(a) absolute bar preventing any court from questioning the validity of a delimitation-of-constituencies or seat-allotment law made or purporting to be made under Articles 327 or 328.
glossary.election-petition-only route for challen: The Article 329(b) rule that an actual election to Parliament or a State Legislature can only be challenged through a formal election petition presented as prescribed by election law (the Representation of the People Act, 1951), not through ordinary writ petitions or civil suits, per the 'single indivisible process' doctrine of N.P. Ponnuswami v. Returning Officer (1952).
glossary.population-proportionate reservation of: The Article 330(1) guarantee reserving Lok Sabha seats for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in numbers as nearly as practicable proportionate to their population share in each State/Union territory relative to the State/Union territory's total population.
glossary.separate reserved-seat category for Assa: The Article 330(1)(b) carve-out reserving distinct Lok Sabha seats specifically for Scheduled Tribes in the autonomous districts of Assam, separate from the general Scheduled Tribe reservation formula applicable elsewhere.
glossary.frozen-population-figure mechanism ancho: The Article 330 Explanation freezing the population figures used to calculate proportionate SC/ST reservation to the 2001 census (as most recently amended), pending the first census taken after the year 2026 — a mechanism repeatedly extended by constitutional amendment since its original 1971-census anchor.
glossary.President's discretionary power to nomin: The Article 331 power letting the President nominate up to two members of the Anglo-Indian community to the House of the People if of the opinion that the community is not adequately represented — a mechanism discontinued in practical operation by the 104th Amendment Act, 2019, effective 25 January 2020.
glossary.State-Assembly-level population-proporti: The Article 332(1) guarantee reserving seats for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in every State Legislative Assembly in numbers proportionate to their population share, structurally mirroring Article 330's Lok Sabha formula.
glossary.near-total-existing-seats floor for Sche: The Article 332(3) special floor provision guaranteeing Scheduled Tribe seat reservation in Arunachal Pradesh, Meghalaya, Mizoram, and Nagaland Assemblies at levels matching nearly all existing seats, pending the readjustment following the first census after 2026.
glossary.parallel floor-proportion mechanism for: The Article 332 special proviso extending an analogous population-proportion floor guarantee for Scheduled Tribe seat reservation to the Tripura Legislative Assembly.
glossary.Assam autonomous-district-exclusive cons: The Article 332 mechanism restricting certain Assam autonomous-district Assembly seats to autonomous-district residents as candidates, subject to a proviso preserving representation for the Bodoland Territorial Areas District.
glossary.Governor's discretionary power to nomina: The Article 333 power letting a State Governor nominate one member of the Anglo-Indian community to the State Legislative Assembly if of the opinion the community is not adequately represented — likewise discontinued in practical operation by the 104th Amendment Act, 2019.
glossary.80-year sunset clock for SC/ST seat rese: The Article 334 sunset clause, as most recently amended, ceasing SC/ST seat reservation under Articles 330 and 332 upon expiry of 80 years from the Constitution's commencement — extended repeatedly by constitutional amendment (most recently the 104th Amendment, to 2030) from the original 10-year term.
glossary.70-year sunset clock (already expired) f: The Article 334 sunset clause governing Anglo-Indian nomination under Articles 331 and 333, fixed at 70 years from commencement and, unlike the SC/ST reservation clock, not further extended by the 104th Amendment Act, 2019 — reflecting Parliament's 2019 policy judgment to let Anglo-Indian nomination lapse.
glossary.existing-House/Assembly-continuity provi: The Article 334 proviso ensuring that reservation or nomination expiry does not disrupt the composition of a House or Assembly already validly constituted before the sunset date takes effect, preventing mid-term seat vacancies.
glossary.'efficiency of administration' qualifier: The Article 335 main-clause qualifier requiring that SC/ST claims to services and posts be considered consistently with the maintenance of administrative efficiency — historically read as a limiting principle on reservation in public employment.
glossary.express proviso authorizing relaxed qual: The Article 335 proviso (inserted/expanded by subsequent amendments) expressly authorizing relaxed qualifying marks or evaluation standards in examinations, and reservation in matters of promotion, for SC/ST candidates — now the operative, government-favouring gloss enabling Supreme Court jurisprudence upholding promotion-quota schemes.
glossary.two-year step-down reservation of railwa: The Article 336 transitional mechanism reserving a declining share of Union railway, customs, postal, and telegraph service posts for the Anglo-Indian community after Independence, stepping the reservation down 10% every two years and extinguishing it entirely ten years after the Constitution's commencement (by 1960).
glossary.three-year step-down of Anglo-Indian-com: The Article 337 transitional mechanism preserving pre-Independence-level educational grants to Anglo-Indian-community institutions, tapering the special-concession portion by 10% every three years, ending after ten years, and conditioning any grant on at least 40% of admissions being open to other communities.
glossary.National Commission for the Scheduled Ca: The Article 338 body — a five-member Commission (Chairperson, Vice-Chairperson, three Members) appointed by Presidential warrant under hand and seal — created to monitor SC-specific constitutional and statutory safeguards, investigate complaints, and advise on SC socio-economic development.
glossary.civil-court-equivalent investigative pow: The Article 338(8) (and parallel Article 338A(8)/338B(8)) grant of full civil-court powers — summoning witnesses, compelling document production, receiving affidavit evidence, requisitioning public records, and commissioning witness examinations — to the National Commissions for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes, and Backward Classes while investigating safeguard matters or complaints.
glossary.mandatory annual reporting to the Presid: The Article 338(6)-(7) (and parallel provisions in Articles 338A and 338B) duty requiring the Commission's annual reports to be laid before Parliament (and, for State-specific matters, before the relevant State Legislature) together with a memorandum disclosing the government's action taken and reasons for any non-acceptance of recommendations.
glossary.extension of 'Scheduled Castes' referenc: The Article 338(10) clause providing that, for purposes of Article 338 alone, references to 'Scheduled Castes' are construed as including the Anglo-Indian community, a historical carryover distinct from the article's core SC-focused mandate.
glossary.National Commission for Scheduled Tribes: The Article 338A body, inserted by the 89th Amendment (2003), separating Scheduled Tribe oversight from the previously combined National Commission for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes into its own dedicated, structurally identical Commission.
glossary.National Commission for Backward Classes: The Article 338B body, inserted by the 102nd Amendment (2018), elevating the previously statutory National Commission for Backward Classes to full constitutional status matching the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes Commissions, with identical civil-court powers and reporting structure.
glossary.carve-out excusing States from consultin: The Article 338B(9) proviso, inserted by the 105th Amendment (2021), exempting a State's exercise of its own independent Article 342A(3) power to maintain its own backward-classes list from the general Union/State consultation duty otherwise owed to the National Commission for Backward Classes.
glossary.mandatory decennial-trigger Commission o: The Article 339(1) mechanism requiring the President to appoint a Commission to report on Scheduled Area administration and Scheduled Tribe welfare at the ten-year mark from the Constitution's commencement, with discretion to appoint one earlier or again at any time.
glossary.Union executive-direction power over Sta: The Article 339(2) power extending the Union's executive authority to directing States on drawing up and executing schemes the Union considers essential for Scheduled Tribe welfare within that State.
glossary.President's discretionary power to appoi: The Article 340(1) power letting the President appoint a Commission, on terms of his own choosing, to investigate the social and educational conditions of backward classes and recommend steps and grant conditions for their upliftment — the constitutional foundation for the Mandal Commission (1979-1980) and the resulting Indra Sawhney (1992) OBC reservation jurisprudence.
glossary.mandatory laying of the Commission's rep: The Article 340(3) duty requiring the President to ensure the Backward Classes Commission's report, together with a memorandum explaining the government's action taken on it, is laid before each House of Parliament.
glossary.President's Governor-consulted notificat: The Article 341(1) mechanism by which the President, after consulting the relevant State Governor, issues a public notification specifying which castes, races, or tribes (or parts/groups within them) count as Scheduled Castes for a given State or Union territory.
glossary.Parliament-exclusive power to amend a no: The Article 341(2) rule that once a Scheduled Castes notification is issued, only Parliament by law can include or exclude entries from it — no executive order, State law, or court ruling can vary the list, per State of Maharashtra v. Milind (2001).
glossary.President's Governor-consulted notificat: The Article 342(1) mechanism, structurally identical to Article 341, by which the President notifies which tribes or tribal communities (or parts/groups within them) count as Scheduled Tribes for a given State or Union territory.

The Article 342A(1)-(2) mechanism, inserted by the 102nd Amendment (2018), extending the Articles 341/342 notify-and-freeze model to socially and educationally backward classes via a defined 'Central List' used for Central Government purposes.
glossary.express State/Union-territory power to i: The Article 342A(3) non-obstante clause, inserted by the 105th Amendment (2021) to reverse Jaishri Laxmanrao Patil v. State of Maharashtra (2021), guaranteeing every State and Union territory the power to prepare and maintain its own socially-and-educationally-backward-classes list for its own purposes, independent of and potentially differing from the Central List.
glossary.Hindi in Devanagari script as the Union': The Article 343(1) designation of Hindi in Devanagari script as the Union's official language, paired with a requirement to use the international form of Indian numerals for official purposes.
glossary.fifteen-year continuation of English for: The Article 343(2)-(3) mechanism guaranteeing English's continued official Union use for fifteen years after commencement, with clause (3) letting Parliament extend that use indefinitely by ordinary law — exercised via the Official Languages Act, 1963.
glossary.mandatory five-year-then-ten-year Presid: The Article 344(1) requirement that the President constitute an Official Language Commission (representing Eighth Schedule languages) at the five-year mark after commencement and again at the ten-year mark, to recommend on Hindi's progressive official use and English's restriction.
glossary.thirty-member bicameral Parliamentary Co: The Article 344(4)-(5) Committee of thirty members (twenty from the Lok Sabha, ten from the Rajya Sabha, elected by proportional representation) tasked with examining the Official Language Commission's recommendations and reporting its opinion to the President.
glossary.President's power to issue binding direc: The Article 344(6) power letting the President, after considering the Parliamentary Committee's report, issue directions departing from Article 343's default language scheme — the operative mechanism for adjusting the Hindi/English balance over time.
glossary.State Legislature's power to adopt any i: The Article 345 power letting a State Legislature, by ordinary law, choose any language in use within the State (or Hindi) as its own official language for all or any State purposes, subject to Articles 346 and 347.
glossary.default continuation of pre-existing Eng: The Article 345 proviso keeping English as a State's operative official language for pre-existing purposes until the State Legislature actually legislates its own choice under the main clause.
glossary.Union's official language as the default: The Article 346 default rule making the Union's currently authorised official language (Hindi/English) the language for official communication between States, and between a State and the Union.
glossary.bilateral/multilateral State agreement t: The Article 346 proviso letting two or more States agree to use Hindi specifically for their own mutual official communication, even where the Union-level default differs.
glossary.President's demand-triggered power to di: The Article 347 power letting the President, on a demand being made and on being satisfied a substantial proportion of a State's population desires it, direct official recognition of a language throughout that State or a specified part of it.
glossary.default English-only requirement for Sup: The Article 348(1) default rule mandating English for all Supreme Court and High Court proceedings and for the authoritative text of Bills, Acts, Ordinances, and subordinate legislation, subject to change only by Parliament's own law.
glossary.Governor-with-Presidential-consent power: The Article 348(2) power letting a State Governor, with the President's prior consent, authorise Hindi or another State official language for use in that State's principal High Court's proceedings — but never for the actual judgments, decrees, or orders, which must remain in English.
glossary.deemed-authoritative English translation: The Article 348(3) rule that where a State has legislated in a language other than English, the Gazette-published official English translation is deemed the legally authoritative text for Article 348 purposes.
glossary.fifteen-year special procedural safeguar: The Article 349 transitional rule (spent since 1965) requiring Presidential prior sanction, informed by the Article 344 Commission's recommendations and Committee's report, before any Bill altering Article 348(1) court/legal-text language rules could be introduced in Parliament.
glossary.universal citizen entitlement to submit: The Article 350 guarantee letting every person submit a grievance-redress representation to any Union or State officer/authority in any language officially in use in the Union or that State.
glossary.State/local-authority endeavour duty to: The Article 350A best-efforts duty on every State and local authority to provide adequate primary-stage mother-tongue instruction facilities for children of linguistic-minority groups.
glossary.President's supplementary direction-issu: The Article 350A power letting the President issue directions to any State he considers necessary or proper to actually secure the provision of mother-tongue primary-education facilities for linguistic minorities.
glossary.President-appointed Special Officer for: The Article 350B institution — a single Special Officer appointed by the President — charged with investigating linguistic-minority constitutional safeguards nationwide and reporting to the President, Parliament, and the concerned State Governments.
glossary.Union's affirmative duty to promote and: The Article 351 directive-style duty requiring the Union to actively promote the spread and development of Hindi so it can serve as a medium of expression for all elements of India's composite culture.
glossary.enrichment methodology privileging Sansk: The Article 351 prescribed methodology for Hindi's vocabulary enrichment — assimilating Hindustani and other Eighth Schedule languages' forms without disturbing Hindi's own character, and drawing new vocabulary primarily from Sanskrit and secondarily from other languages.
glossary.war/external-aggression/armed-rebellion: The three grounds — war, external aggression, or armed rebellion — on which the President may proclaim a National Emergency under Article 352(1), which may also be invoked before the actual event if imminent danger exists.
glossary.mandatory written Union Cabinet decision: Article 352(3)'s requirement that the President cannot issue or vary an Emergency Proclamation unless the Union Cabinet's decision to do so has been communicated to him in writing.
glossary.one-month provisional window requiring d: The initial one-month period during which an Emergency Proclamation operates under Article 352(4) before it must be approved by both Houses of Parliament to continue.
glossary.six-month renewable Parliamentary approv: The recurring six-month periods for which an approved Emergency Proclamation remains valid under Article 352(5), each renewal requiring a fresh resolution passed by the special majority described in clause (6).
glossary.Lok Sabha's unilateral power to force re: Article 352(7)'s rule that the President must revoke an Emergency Proclamation if the House of the People passes a resolution disapproving it, regardless of the Council of States' position.
glossary.one-tenth-member-notice mechanism compel: Article 352(8)'s procedure allowing not less than one-tenth of the Lok Sabha's members to force a special sitting within fourteen days to consider a resolution disapproving an Emergency Proclamation.
glossary.Union executive-direction power over eve: Article 353(a)'s rule that, during a National Emergency, the Union's executive power extends to directing any State on how to exercise its own executive power, notwithstanding the Constitution's ordinary federal division of powers.
glossary.Parliament's temporary power to legislat: Article 353(b)'s expansion of Parliament's law-making power during a National Emergency to cover matters not enumerated in the Union List, i.e. subjects normally reserved to the States.
glossary.spillover-effect proviso extending both: The proviso to Article 353 extending the Union's executive-direction and legislative powers to States outside a partial Emergency's declared area, where their security is threatened by activities connected to that area.
glossary.President's power to modify the Articles: Article 354's power letting the President, by order, modify how Articles 268 to 279 govern Union-State revenue distribution while a National Emergency is on, with the modification lapsing by the end of the financial year in which the Emergency ends.
glossary.Union's constitutional duty to protect e: Article 355's twin duty imposed on the Union: to protect every State from external aggression and internal disturbance, and to ensure every State's government is carried on in accordance with the Constitution.
glossary.President's Governor-report-or-otherwise: The trigger under Article 356(1) for 'President's Rule' — the President's satisfaction, typically based on a Governor's report, that a State's government cannot be carried on in accordance with the Constitution, empowering assumption of its executive functions and transfer of its legislative powers to Parliament.
glossary.absolute exclusion of High Court powers/: The proviso to Article 356(1) barring the President from assuming any High Court power or suspending any constitutional provision relating to High Courts, even while exercising President's Rule.
glossary.two-month provisional window requiring P: The Article 356(3)-(4) timeline: a President's Rule Proclamation lapses after two months without Parliamentary approval, then runs in renewable six-month blocks up to an overall three-year cap, extended to five years solely for the 11 May 1987 Punjab Proclamation.
glossary.post-one-year extension gateway requirin: Article 356(5)'s rule that extending President's Rule beyond one year requires both an operative Article 352 National Emergency and Election Commission certification that State election difficulties justify the extension.
glossary.Parliament's power to delegate a Preside: Article 357(1)(a)'s mechanism allowing Parliament to confer a President's-Rule State's law-making power on the President, who may further delegate it to another named authority.
glossary.President's power to authorise emergency: Article 357(1)(c)'s power letting the President authorise spending from a President's-Rule State's Consolidated Fund when the Lok Sabha is not sitting, pending that spending's later Parliamentary sanction.
glossary.survival of laws made during President's: Article 357(2)'s rule that laws made under the Article 356/357 mechanism, which Parliament or the President would not otherwise have been competent to make, remain in force after President's Rule ends until a competent Legislature or authority alters, repeals, or amends them.
glossary.automatic suspension of Article 19's res: Article 358(1)'s rule that Article 19's fundamental freedoms automatically cease to restrict State law-making or executive action during a National Emergency proclaimed on the ground of war or external aggression — but not one proclaimed solely on the ground of armed rebellion.
glossary.44th-Amendment-added recital requirement: Article 358(2)'s requirement, added by the 44th Amendment, that the Article 19 suspension applies only to laws containing an explicit recital connecting them to the operative Emergency Proclamation, and to executive action taken under such a law.
glossary.President's discretionary power to suspe: Article 359(1)'s power letting the President, by a specific order, suspend the right to approach courts to enforce named Part III fundamental rights while a National Emergency is in force, with Articles 20 and 21 permanently excluded from any such order.
glossary.consequential State law-making/executive: Article 359(1A)-(1B)'s rule extending to State law-making and executive action, in respect of rights suspended under an Article 359(1) order, the same immunity-with-recital structure that Article 358 applies to Article 19.
glossary.President's satisfaction that India's (o: The trigger under Article 360(1) for a Financial Emergency — the President's satisfaction that the financial stability or credit of India, or any part of it, is threatened.
glossary.two-month provisional window requiring P: Article 360(2)(c)'s rule that a Financial Emergency Proclamation lapses after two months unless approved by both Houses of Parliament, with no overall maximum duration specified once approved, unlike Article 356's three-year cap.
glossary.Union's power to direct States on financ: Article 360(3)-(4)'s powers available during a Financial Emergency: directing States on financial propriety, requiring State employee salary reductions, requiring State Money Bills to be reserved for the President, and even reducing salaries of Union employees including Supreme Court and High Court Judges.
glossary.personal immunity: Protection from being personally hauled before a court, distinct from protection extended to the government or office as an institution.
glossary.official acts immunity: Protection from being made answerable to any court for acts done in the exercise and performance of the powers and duties of an office.
glossary.impeachment review: The one exception to the President's immunity — a Parliamentary body investigating a charge under Article 61 may still review the President's conduct.
glossary.two-month notice: A mandatory waiting period requiring written notice of the proceedings, cause of action, and relief claimed to be delivered before certain civil suits may be instituted against the President or a Governor for personal-capacity acts.
glossary.qualified privilege: A legal defence that shields a substantially true, good-faith report of proceedings from civil or criminal liability, lost only if the publication is shown to have been made with malice.
glossary.substantially true report: A report that captures the essential accuracy of proceedings without requiring word-for-word precision, sufficient to attract qualified privilege under Article 361A.
glossary.malice: An improper motive or ill-will behind a publication; proof of malice defeats the qualified privilege otherwise available for reports of legislative proceedings.
glossary.secret sitting: A closed session of a House of Parliament or a State Legislature, reports of which receive no qualified privilege under Article 361A regardless of truth or good faith.
glossary.remunerative political post: An office under the Government of India, a State Government, or a wholly/partially government-owned body, where the salary or remuneration is paid from public revenue or by that body, excluding merely compensatory payments.
glossary.Tenth Schedule disqualification: Disqualification of a legislator for defection under paragraph 2 of the Tenth Schedule to the Constitution, the trigger condition for the further Article 361B bar on holding remunerative political posts.
glossary.defection: A legislator's act of voluntarily giving up party membership or voting against party direction, attracting disqualification under the Tenth Schedule's anti-defection law.
glossary.ouster of jurisdiction: A constitutional or statutory provision that removes a court's power to hear and decide a particular category of dispute.
glossary.sanad: A formal instrument or grant, historically issued in relation to princely states, recognised as a type of treaty/agreement instrument under Article 363.
glossary.Article 143 reference: A Presidential reference to the Supreme Court for an advisory opinion under Article 143 — the sole route by which disputes otherwise barred under Article 363 can still reach the judiciary.
glossary.accession instruments: Treaties, covenants, agreements, or sanads through which princely states acceded to or integrated with the Dominion/Union of India before the Constitution's commencement.
glossary.privy purse abolition: The Constitution (Twenty-sixth Amendment) Act, 1971's abolition of the guaranteed payments (privy purses) previously made to former Rulers of Indian States, with all associated rights, liabilities, and obligations extinguished.
glossary.de-recognition of Rulers: The withdrawal, by the Twenty-sixth Amendment, 1971, of Presidential recognition previously extended to former princely Rulers and their successors.
glossary.26th Amendment: The Constitution (Twenty-sixth Amendment) Act, 1971, which omitted Article 362, de-recognised former Rulers of Indian States, and abolished privy purses via Article 363A.
glossary.major port: A port declared to be a major port by or under any law made by Parliament or any existing law, including all areas within its limits, as defined in Article 364.
glossary.aerodrome: An aerodrome as defined for the purposes of enactments relating to airways, aircraft, and air navigation, as referenced in Article 364.
glossary.public notification: A notification in the Gazette of India, or the Official Gazette of a State, as defined in Article 366(19) and used as the mechanism for Presidential directions under Article 364.
glossary.Union directions: Directions given to a State in the exercise of the executive power of the Union under various constitutional provisions, non-compliance with which may ground a finding under Article 365 that the State's machinery has broken down.
glossary.deemed breakdown of constitutional machi: The legal fiction under Article 365 by which a State's failure to comply with Union directions may itself be treated as evidence that the State cannot be carried on in accordance with the Constitution, feeding into Article 356.
glossary.constitutional definitions clause: Article 366, the Constitution's master glossary defining nearly thirty terms used throughout the document.
glossary.existing law: Any law, Ordinance, order, bye-law, rule, or regulation passed or made before the Constitution's commencement by any Legislature, authority, or person having power to make it, as defined in Article 366(10).
glossary.Scheduled Castes: Castes, races, or tribes (or parts/groups within them) deemed under Article 341 to be Scheduled Castes for constitutional purposes, as defined in Article 366(24).
glossary.Scheduled Tribes: Tribes or tribal communities (or parts/groups within them) deemed under Article 342 to be Scheduled Tribes for constitutional purposes, as defined in Article 366(25).
glossary.Proclamation of Emergency: A Proclamation issued under Article 352(1), as defined in Article 366(18).
glossary.General Clauses Act: The General Clauses Act, 1897, India's standard statutory-interpretation statute, applied to Constitution interpretation under Article 367(1) subject to adaptations and unless context otherwise requires.
glossary.Ordinance as law reference: The Article 367(2) rule that any constitutional reference to a Parliament-made or State-Legislature-made Act or law also includes a reference to a corresponding Presidential or Gubernatorial Ordinance.
glossary.foreign State: Any State other than India, as defined in Article 367(3), subject to the President's power to declare a State not to be a foreign State for specified purposes.
glossary.constituent power: Parliament's special power under Article 368 to amend the Constitution itself (by addition, variation, or repeal), distinct from its ordinary power to make laws.
glossary.special majority: The procedural requirement under Article 368(2) that a constitutional amendment Bill be passed in each House by a majority of the total membership of that House and by a majority of not less than two-thirds of members present and voting.
glossary.State ratification: The additional requirement, under the proviso to Article 368(2), that certain entrenched categories of constitutional amendment be ratified by the Legislatures of not less than one-half of the States before presidential assent.
glossary.basic structure doctrine: The judicially evolved principle, established in Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973), that Parliament's amending power under Article 368, though wide, cannot be used to damage or destroy the Constitution's basic structure.
glossary.temporary Concurrent List power: A time-limited power given to Parliament under Article 369 to legislate on specified State List subjects (certain essential commodities) as if they were Concurrent List subjects, for five years from the Constitution's commencement.
glossary.five-year sunset clause: A constitutional provision that automatically expires, or causes a law made under it to lose effect, after a fixed five-year period, without needing a separate repeal.
glossary.Instrument of Accession: The legal document by which a princely State's Ruler acceded to the Dominion of India, specifying the subjects (originally defence, external affairs, and communications) on which the Dominion/Union Legislature could make laws for that State.
glossary.asymmetric federalism: A federal arrangement in which different constituent States or regions have different degrees of autonomy or distinct constitutional treatment, rather than all units being governed by identical constitutional rules.
glossary.concurrence of State Government: A requirement that the Union government or President obtain the State Government's agreement before taking a specified constitutional action with respect to that State.
glossary.Presidential notification to cease opera: A formal notification issued by the President under Article 370(3) declaring that Article 370 (or specified parts of it) shall cease to be operative, or shall operate only with specified exceptions and modifications.
glossary.regional development boards: Statutory bodies established under Article 371(2) for sub-regions of Maharashtra (Vidarbha, Marathwada) and Gujarat (Saurashtra, Kutch) to oversee balanced regional development, with annual reporting to the State Legislative Assembly.
glossary.Governor's special responsibility: A constitutionally assigned personal duty placed on a State Governor (distinct from the Governor's ordinary role acting on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers) to attend to a specific matter, such as regional development or law and order, under various Article 371-series provisions.
glossary.Naga customary law: The traditional religious, social, and customary legal practices of the Naga people, which Parliament cannot override by ordinary legislation in Nagaland unless the State's Legislative Assembly resolves to accept the relevant law, under Article 371A(1)(a).
glossary.Governor's individual judgment: A Governor's personal discretion, exercised after consulting (but not bound by) the Council of Ministers, on a matter the Constitution specifically assigns to the Governor individually — made non-justiciable in specified instances such as Article 371A(1)(b).
glossary.regional council: A 35-member body established for the Tuensang district of Nagaland under Article 371A(1)(d), with Governor-made rules on its composition, membership qualifications, terms, and procedure.
glossary.Tuensang district special administration: The ten-year (extendable) transitional regime under Article 371A(2) by which the Governor directly administered Nagaland's Tuensang district, including equitable fund allocation, opt-in application of Nagaland Acts, and a dedicated Minister for Tuensang affairs.
glossary.tribal areas committee: A committee constituted within a State Legislative Assembly, by Presidential order, consisting of members elected from specified Sixth Schedule tribal areas, to give those areas structured representation in the Assembly's procedure (Article 371B, Assam).
glossary.Sixth Schedule tribal areas: Tribal areas in Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, and Mizoram administered under the Sixth Schedule's system of Autonomous District and Regional Councils, distinct from ordinary State administration.
glossary.Hill Areas committee: A committee constituted within the Manipur Legislative Assembly, by Presidential order, consisting of members elected from the State's Hill Areas, to secure representation and proper administration of those areas (Article 371C).
glossary.Governor's annual report to President: A standing constitutional duty on certain State Governors (e.g. Manipur under Article 371C(2)) to report annually, or whenever required, to the President on the administration of specified areas within the State.
glossary.local cadres: Civil service posts organised by Presidential order into region-specific groups within a State, so that recruitment and promotion to those posts are drawn from, and tied to, a specified local area (Article 371D).
glossary.Mulki rules: Residence-based local-preference rules historically applied in the former Hyderabad State and later Andhra Pradesh, restricting certain government posts to local ('Mulki') residents — the subject of the retrospective validation in Article 371D(9).
glossary.Administrative Tribunal: A specialised tribunal constituted by Presidential order under Article 371D(3) to exercise jurisdiction over local-cadre service disputes in Andhra Pradesh and Telangana, with the State High Court's superintending jurisdiction over it expressly ousted.
glossary.equitable opportunities in public employ: The Article 371D(1) mandate requiring the President's order to secure fair access to government jobs and educational admissions for people from different parts of a composite State, through mechanisms such as local cadres and reservation.
glossary.Central University: A university established and funded by the Union, here specifically the University of Hyderabad, set up under Parliament's Article 371E power.
glossary.Parliamentary power to establish a unive: A specific legislative competence given to Parliament by Article 371E to create a university in Andhra Pradesh by ordinary law.
glossary.appointed day: The date of commencement of the Constitution (Thirty-sixth Amendment) Act, 1975, from which Article 371F's Sikkim-integration provisions (deemed Assembly, property vesting, court continuity, etc.) took effect.
glossary.deemed Legislative Assembly: A legal fiction by which an already-existing elected body (here, Sikkim's April 1974-elected Assembly) is treated as if it were duly constituted under the Constitution, without requiring fresh elections.
glossary.Mizo customary law: The traditional religious, social, and customary legal practices of the Mizo people, which Parliament cannot override by ordinary legislation in Mizoram unless the State's Legislative Assembly resolves to accept the relevant law, under Article 371G(a).
glossary.opt-in requirement: A constitutional mechanism under which a Parliamentary law touching specified sensitive subjects (customary law, land ownership, etc.) in certain States applies only if that State's own Legislative Assembly passes a resolution accepting it.
glossary.pre-1986 Central Acts proviso: The proviso to Article 371G(a) preserving the application of Central Acts already in force in the Mizoram Union territory before the Fifty-third Amendment, 1986, regardless of the opt-in requirement for new Parliamentary laws.
glossary.Governor's non-justiciable law-and-order: A Governor's personal, individually-exercised responsibility for law and order (as under Articles 371A(1)(b) and 371H(a)) whose exercise is made final and immune from being questioned in court.
glossary.minimum Assembly strength: A constitutionally fixed floor on the number of members a State's Legislative Assembly must have, as prescribed for several smaller north-eastern and hill States under the Article 371-series provisions.
glossary.continuity of existing law: The principle, embodied in Article 372(1), that all laws in force immediately before the Constitution's commencement remain valid and operative afterward unless altered, repealed, or amended by a competent Legislature or authority.
glossary.law in force: A term defined expansively by Article 372's Explanation I to include any pre-Constitution law not previously repealed, even if dormant or not then operating in particular areas.
glossary.three-year adaptation power: The time-limited power under Article 372(2)-(3) allowing the President to adapt or modify pre-Constitution laws to align them with the Constitution, exercisable only within three years of commencement.
glossary.temporary law expiry: The rule in Article 372's Explanation III that a temporary (time-limited) pre-Constitution law still lapses on its originally fixed expiry date, regardless of the general continuity rule in clause (1).
glossary.Seventh Amendment adaptation power: The Presidential law-adaptation power under Article 372A, specific to aligning existing laws with the sweeping State-reorganisation changes made by the Constitution (Seventh Amendment) Act, 1956, exercisable only before 1 November 1957.
glossary.non-questionable adaptation: A legal immunity attached to certain Presidential adaptation/modification orders (e.g. under Articles 372(2) and 372A(1)) providing that the adaptation itself cannot be challenged or questioned in any court of law.
glossary.preventive detention transitional substi: The temporary textual substitution, under Article 373, of 'President'/'Presidential order' for 'Parliament'/'law made by Parliament' within Article 22(4) and (7), pending Parliament's own preventive detention legislation.
glossary.one-year sunset: A fixed one-year outer time limit from the Constitution's commencement, after which a transitional provision (such as Article 373's preventive-detention substitution) automatically ceases to operate.
glossary.jurisdictional bar on pre-accession trea: A provision (e.g. Article 371F(m), paralleling Article 363) ousting the Supreme Court's and all other courts' jurisdiction over disputes arising from treaties or agreements a State or princely territory entered into with the Government of India before its full merger/accession, while preserving the Supreme Court's special Article 143 advisory jurisdiction.
glossary.Federal Court: The highest court of British India under the Government of India Act, 1935, which the Supreme Court of India succeeded upon the Constitution's commencement in 1950.
glossary.Privy Council: The Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in London, which served as the final court of appeal for British India and many princely States before the Supreme Court of India took over that role.
glossary.His Majesty in Council: The formal constitutional term for the British Crown acting on the advice of the Privy Council, used in the exercise of its judicial appellate functions over Indian courts before 1950.
glossary.transfer of pending proceedings: The automatic removal of cases pending before an old court or authority to its successor court on a specified commencement date, so that litigation already underway is not interrupted by the change in institutions.
glossary.continuity of courts, authorities and of: The Article 375 guarantee that all existing courts, authorities, and officers in India kept functioning after the Constitution's commencement, now subject to the Constitution's provisions.
glossary.transitional continuity of High Court Ju: The Article 376 rule automatically converting sitting Provincial and princely-State High Court Judges into Judges of the corresponding new State's High Court upon the Constitution's commencement.
glossary.non-citizen eligibility exception: A one-time transitional exception under Article 376(1) allowing a sitting High Court Judge to be appointed Chief Justice despite not being an Indian citizen, departing from Article 217's ordinary citizenship requirement.
glossary.transitional continuity of Auditor-Gener: The Article 377 rule automatically converting the sitting pre-Constitution Auditor-General of India into the first Comptroller and Auditor-General of India upon commencement.
glossary.transitional continuity of Public Servic: The Article 378 rule automatically converting sitting Dominion and Provincial Public Service Commission members into members of the corresponding new Union or State Public Service Commissions upon commencement.
glossary.fixed five-year term override: A one-time constitutional override (Article 378A) fixing a specific State Legislative Assembly's term at exactly five years from a specified date, superseding the ordinary Article 172 term rule.
glossary.States Reorganisation Act 1956: The Act of Parliament that reorganised Indian States substantially along linguistic lines in 1956, including constituting the State of Andhra Pradesh, whose first Legislative Assembly's term was fixed by Article 378A.
glossary.difficulty-removal power: A Presidential power (e.g. under Articles 392 and 371F(o)) to make an order removing practical difficulties encountered in implementing a transitional constitutional scheme, usually time-limited and subject to being laid before Parliament.
glossary.adaptation by modification, addition or: The three modes of textual change — modifying, adding to, or omitting from — the Constitution's own provisions that Article 392 uniquely authorised the President to make, within a specified transitional period, to remove difficulties.
glossary.laying before Parliament: A procedural requirement that an executive order or rule be formally placed before Parliament (or a State Legislature) after being made, so that the legislature is informed of, and can scrutinise, the executive action.
glossary.short title: The official, citable name given to a piece of legislation or constitutional text, fixed here by Article 393 as 'the Constitution of India'.
glossary.commencement of this Constitution: The defined term, fixed by Article 394 as 26 January 1950, used throughout the Constitution to mark the date from which its provisions (other than those given immediate effect) took legal effect.
glossary.26 January 1950: The date the Constitution of India came into force, chosen to mark the twentieth anniversary of the 1930 Purna Swaraj (complete independence) declaration.
glossary.immediate-effect articles: The specific set of articles (394 itself plus Articles 5-9, 60, 324, 366, 367, 379, 380, 388, 391, 392, 393) that came into force immediately upon the Constitution's adoption on 26 November 1949, ahead of the general commencement date of 26 January 1950.
glossary.authoritative Hindi text: The Hindi translation of the Constitution and its amendments, published by the President under Article 394A, which is deemed to carry the same legal authority as the original English text.
glossary.Presidential publication duty: The President's constitutional obligation under Article 394A to publish, and where necessary revise, the authoritative Hindi translation of the Constitution and its amendments.
glossary.Constituent-Assembly-signed Hindi transl: The base Hindi translation of the Constitution signed by the members of the Constituent Assembly, which Article 394A(1)(a) requires to be adapted and published as the Constitution's authoritative Hindi text.
glossary.repeal of Indian Independence Act 1947: The complete repeal, by Article 395, of the British statute that created the Dominion of India and ended British paramountcy, once the Constitution of India itself took over as the governing framework.
glossary.repeal of Government of India Act 1935: The complete repeal, by Article 395, of the detailed British framework legislation (and all Acts amending/supplementing it) that had governed India before the Constitution's commencement.
glossary.Abolition of Privy Council Jurisdiction: The specific exclusion, in Article 395's repeal clause, of the Abolition of Privy Council Jurisdiction Act, 1949 from repeal, since that Act's effect (ending Privy Council appeals) remained relevant to the transitional judicial provisions of Article 374.

sections.title: Name and territory of the Union
sections.raw_text: (1) India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States. (2) The States and the territories thereof shall be as specified in the First Schedule. (3) The territory of India shall comprise— (a) the territories of the States; (b) the Union territories specified in the First Schedule; and (c) such other territories as may be acquired.
key_terms: Union of States
First Schedule (Constitution)
Union territory
acquired territory

breakdown.plain_summary: This opening Article fixes the country's two names — India and Bharat — and declares its basic constitutional character: it is a 'Union' of States, not a loose federation that States could choose to leave. Clause (2) points to the First Schedule for the actual list of States and their territorial extent, and clause (3) explains that India's territory is made up of three things: the States themselves, Union territories (areas administered more directly by the Centre, like Delhi or Chandigarh), and any other territory India may acquire in future (by cession, purchase, or other lawful means).
essential_elements: India is declared a 'Union of States', not a federation of independent units with a right to secede
The specific States and their territories are listed in the First Schedule, not spelled out in Article 1 itself
Indian territory comprises State territories, Union territory areas, and any territory acquired afterward
exceptions_and_qualifications: The word 'Union' was deliberately chosen over 'Federation' to signal that no State has a constitutional right to secede from India
Acquisition of new territory under clause (3)(c) does not by itself require a constitutional amendment — see Article 4
breakdown.how_to_read: Treat Article 1 as the Constitution's opening declaration of statehood and territorial identity — read it together with the First Schedule (which lists the States and Union territories by name) and Article 3 (which lets Parliament reorganise those very territories by ordinary law).
breakdown.plain_summary_hi: यह प्रारंभिक अनुच्छेद देश के दो नाम -- भारत और इंडिया -- निश्चित करता है और इसके मूल संवैधानिक स्वरूप की घोषणा करता है: यह राज्यों का एक 'संघ' है, न कि कोई ढीला संघीकरण जिसे राज्य चाहें तो छोड़ सकें। खंड (2) वास्तविक राज्यों और उनके क्षेत्रीय विस्तार की सूची हेतु प्रथम अनुसूची की ओर इंगित करता है, और खंड (3) बताता है कि भारत का राज्यक्षेत्र तीन चीज़ों से मिलकर बना है: स्वयं राज्य, संघ राज्यक्षेत्र (जैसे दिल्ली या चंडीगढ़ जैसे क्षेत्र जो केंद्र द्वारा सीधे प्रशासित होते हैं), और भविष्य में भारत द्वारा अर्जित किया जाने वाला कोई अन्य राज्यक्षेत्र (संक्रमण, क्रय, या अन्य वैध साधनों द्वारा)।
essential_elements_hi: भारत को 'राज्यों का संघ' घोषित किया गया है, न कि पृथक्करण के अधिकार वाली स्वतंत्र इकाइयों का संघीकरण
विशिष्ट राज्य और उनके राज्यक्षेत्र प्रथम अनुसूची में सूचीबद्ध हैं, अनुच्छेद 1 में स्वयं नहीं दिए गए
भारतीय राज्यक्षेत्र में राज्यों के क्षेत्र, संघ राज्यक्षेत्र के क्षेत्र, और बाद में अर्जित कोई भी क्षेत्र शामिल है
exceptions_and_qualifications_hi: 'संघ' शब्द को जानबूझकर 'महासंघ' के स्थान पर चुना गया ताकि यह संकेत मिले कि किसी भी राज्य को भारत से पृथक् होने का संवैधानिक अधिकार नहीं है
खंड (3)(ग) के अंतर्गत नए राज्यक्षेत्र का अर्जन स्वयं में संवैधानिक संशोधन की आवश्यकता नहीं रखता -- अनुच्छेद 4 देखें
breakdown.how_to_read_hi: अनुच्छेद 1 को संविधान की राज्यत्व और क्षेत्रीय पहचान की प्रारंभिक घोषणा मानें -- इसे प्रथम अनुसूची (जो राज्यों और संघ राज्यक्षेत्रों को नाम से सूचीबद्ध करती है) और अनुच्छेद 3 (जो संसद को साधारण विधि द्वारा उन्हीं क्षेत्रों का पुनर्गठन करने देता है) के साथ पढ़ें।

sections.title: Admission or establishment of new States
sections.raw_text: Parliament may by law admit into the Union, or establish, new States on such terms and conditions as it thinks fit.
key_terms: admission of new States
establishment of new States
terms and conditions

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 2 gives Parliament the power to bring entirely new States into India — either by 'admitting' a State that already exists elsewhere (for example, a former princely state or foreign territory that has acceded to India) or by 'establishing' a wholly new State from scratch. Parliament can attach whatever terms and conditions it thinks fit to that admission or establishment, by ordinary legislation.
essential_elements: Power vests exclusively in Parliament, exercised by ordinary law (not necessarily a constitutional amendment)
Covers two distinct situations: admitting an existing external territory, or establishing a new State
Parliament has wide discretion to fix terms and conditions of admission/establishment
exceptions_and_qualifications: Article 2 deals with bringing in territory from outside India's existing boundaries; Article 3 deals with reorganising territory already within India
A law under Article 2 is not treated as a constitutional amendment under Article 368
breakdown.how_to_read: Distinguish Article 2 (admitting/establishing States, typically involving territory not already part of India) from Article 3 (forming new States out of existing Indian territory) — the two are companion powers but operate on different starting points.
breakdown.plain_summary_hi: अनुच्छेद 2 संसद को भारत में बिल्कुल नए राज्य लाने की शक्ति देता है -- या तो 'प्रवेश' द्वारा (उदाहरणार्थ, कोई पूर्व रियासत या विदेशी राज्यक्षेत्र जो भारत में विलय हो गया हो) या 'स्थापना' द्वारा एक बिल्कुल नए राज्य की। संसद साधारण विधायन द्वारा ऐसे प्रवेश या स्थापना पर जो भी निबंधन और शर्तें उचित समझे, लगा सकती है।
essential_elements_hi: शक्ति विशेष रूप से संसद में निहित है, साधारण विधि द्वारा प्रयोग की जाती है (आवश्यक रूप से संवैधानिक संशोधन नहीं)
दो भिन्न स्थितियों को कवर करती है: किसी विद्यमान बाह्य राज्यक्षेत्र का प्रवेश, या नए राज्य की स्थापना
संसद को प्रवेश/स्थापना की शर्तें निश्चित करने का व्यापक विवेकाधिकार प्राप्त है
exceptions_and_qualifications_hi: अनुच्छेद 2 भारत की विद्यमान सीमाओं के बाहर से राज्यक्षेत्र लाने से संबंधित है; अनुच्छेद 3 पहले से भारत के भीतर मौजूद राज्यक्षेत्र के पुनर्गठन से संबंधित है
अनुच्छेद 2 के अंतर्गत विधि अनुच्छेद 368 के अंतर्गत संवैधानिक संशोधन नहीं मानी जाती
breakdown.how_to_read_hi: अनुच्छेद 2 (राज्यों का प्रवेश/स्थापना, जिसमें सामान्यतः वह राज्यक्षेत्र शामिल होता है जो पहले से भारत का भाग नहीं है) को अनुच्छेद 3 (विद्यमान भारतीय राज्यक्षेत्र से नए राज्य बनाना) से अलग करें -- दोनों सहचर शक्तियाँ हैं परन्तु भिन्न प्रारंभिक बिंदुओं पर कार्य करती हैं।

sections.title: [Sikkim to be associated with the Union.] Omitted
sections.raw_text: Omitted by the Constitution (Thirty-sixth Amendment) Act, 1975, s. 5 (w.e.f. 26-4-1975).
key_terms: omitted section

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 2A was inserted in 1975 to associate Sikkim with the Union of India as an 'Associate State' under a Tenth Schedule (the one now dealing with anti-defection is a different, later Tenth Schedule). Barely weeks later, Sikkim became a full State of India, so Article 2A and its associated Schedule were omitted altogether.
essential_elements: This is a numbering-only placeholder in the Constitution's article sequence
exceptions_and_qualifications: Superseded by the Constitution (Thirty-sixth Amendment) Act, 1975, which simultaneously inserted Sikkim as the 22nd State of India in the First Schedule and omitted Article 2A
breakdown.how_to_read: No independent legal content remains — Sikkim's actual constitutional status as a full State is now governed by its entry in the First Schedule read with Article 1, not by this omitted Article.
breakdown.plain_summary_hi: अनुच्छेद 2A को 1975 में सिक्किम को एक दसवीं अनुसूची के अंतर्गत 'सहयुक्त राज्य' के रूप में भारत संघ से जोड़ने हेतु सम्मिलित किया गया था (अब अनुशासनहीनता-विरोधी से संबंधित दसवीं अनुसूची एक भिन्न, बाद की अनुसूची है)। कुछ ही सप्ताहों बाद सिक्किम भारत का पूर्ण राज्य बन गया, इसलिए अनुच्छेद 2A और उससे संबद्ध अनुसूची को पूर्णतः लोप कर दिया गया।
essential_elements_hi: यह संविधान के अनुच्छेद-क्रम में मात्र एक क्रमांकन-धारक है
exceptions_and_qualifications_hi: संविधान (छत्तीसवाँ संशोधन) अधिनियम, 1975 द्वारा अध्यारोहित, जिसने एक साथ सिक्किम को प्रथम अनुसूची में भारत के 22वें राज्य के रूप में सम्मिलित किया और अनुच्छेद 2A को लोप कर दिया
breakdown.how_to_read_hi: अब कोई स्वतंत्र विधिक सामग्री शेष नहीं है -- सिक्किम की पूर्ण राज्य के रूप में वास्तविक संवैधानिक स्थिति अब अनुच्छेद 1 के साथ पठित प्रथम अनुसूची में उसकी प्रविष्टि द्वारा शासित है, न कि इस लोप किए गए अनुच्छेद द्वारा।

sections.title: Formation of new States and alteration of areas, boundaries or names of existing States
sections.raw_text: Parliament may by law— (a) form a new State by separation of territory from any State or by uniting two or more States or parts of States or by uniting any territory to a part of any State; (b) increase the area of any State; (c) diminish the area of any State; (d) alter the boundaries of any State; (e) alter the name of any State: Provided that no Bill for the purpose shall be introduced in either House of Parliament except on the recommendation of the President and unless, where the proposal contained in the Bill affects the area, boundaries or name of any of the States, the Bill has been referred by the President to the Legislature of that State for expressing its views thereon within such period as may be specified in the reference or within such further period as the President may allow and the period so specified or allowed has expired. Explanation I.—In this article, in clauses (a) to (e), 'State' includes a Union territory, but in the proviso, 'State' does not include a Union territory. Explanation II.—The power conferred on Parliament by clause (a) includes the power to form a new State or Union territory by uniting a part of any State or Union territory to any other State or Union territory.
key_terms: State reorganisation
recommendation of the President
reference to State Legislature
alteration of boundaries
alteration of name of a State
Explanation I (Article 3)
Explanation II (Article 3)

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 3 is the engine that lets Parliament redraw India's internal map by ordinary law, without a constitutional amendment — carving new States out of existing ones, merging States, or simply resizing, reshaping, or renaming them. Because this power is so far-reaching, two safeguards apply: a Bill of this kind can only be introduced in Parliament on the President's recommendation, and if it touches a particular State's area, boundaries, or name, that State's own Legislature must first be given a chance to express its views (though Parliament is not bound by what the State says — it only has to consult, not obtain consent). The two Explanations clarify that 'State' in clauses (a)-(e) includes Union territories (so Union territories can also be reorganised this way), but for the consultation proviso specifically, 'State' excludes Union territories (so a Union territory's own 'legislature', where one exists, need not be consulted in the same mandatory way).
essential_elements: Parliament's law-making power covers forming new States, uniting States or parts of States, increasing or diminishing a State's area, altering boundaries, and altering names
A Bill can be introduced only on the President's prior recommendation
Where the Bill affects a specific State's area, boundaries, or name, that State's Legislature must be given an opportunity to express views within a period fixed by the President
'State' includes Union territories for the substantive powers in clauses (a)-(e), but excludes them for the mandatory-reference proviso
exceptions_and_qualifications: The State Legislature's views are only consultative — Parliament need not accept or even follow them
The time period for the State Legislature to respond can be extended by the President, and if the period lapses, Parliament may proceed regardless
Explanation II clarifies clause (a) extends to uniting parts of a State/Union territory with another State/Union territory, not just full States with each other
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the operative power behind every State reorganisation Act in Indian history (e.g., the States Reorganisation Act, 1956, and the bifurcation of Andhra Pradesh in 2014) — always check that a Presidential recommendation preceded introduction and that the affected State's Legislature was given a genuine opportunity to respond, since these are the key procedural safeguards courts have scrutinised.
breakdown.plain_summary_hi: अनुच्छेद 3 वह इंजन है जो संसद को साधारण विधि द्वारा, बिना संवैधानिक संशोधन के, भारत के आंतरिक मानचित्र को पुनः खींचने देता है -- विद्यमान राज्यों में से नए राज्य काटना, राज्यों का विलय करना, या बस उनका आकार, रूप, या नाम बदलना। क्योंकि यह शक्ति इतनी दूरगामी है, दो सुरक्षोपाय लागू होते हैं: इस प्रकार का कोई विधेयक संसद में केवल राष्ट्रपति की सिफारिश पर ही पेश किया जा सकता है, और यदि यह किसी विशेष राज्य के क्षेत्र, सीमाओं, या नाम को छूता है, तो उस राज्य के अपने विधानमंडल को अपने विचार व्यक्त करने का पहले अवसर दिया जाना चाहिए (हालाँकि संसद राज्य जो कहे उससे बाध्य नहीं है -- उसे केवल परामर्श करना है, सहमति प्राप्त नहीं करनी)। दोनों स्पष्टीकरण बताते हैं कि खंड (क)-(ङ) में 'राज्य' में संघ राज्यक्षेत्र शामिल है (इसलिए संघ राज्यक्षेत्रों का भी इस प्रकार पुनर्गठन किया जा सकता है), परन्तु विशेष रूप से परामर्श परंतुक हेतु, 'राज्य' में संघ राज्यक्षेत्र शामिल नहीं है (इसलिए किसी संघ राज्यक्षेत्र के अपने 'विधानमंडल', जहाँ कोई हो, से उसी अनिवार्य रीति में परामर्श करना आवश्यक नहीं है)।
essential_elements_hi: संसद की विधि-निर्माण शक्ति नए राज्य बनाने, राज्यों या राज्यों के भागों को मिलाने, किसी राज्य के क्षेत्र को बढ़ाने या घटाने, सीमाएँ बदलने, और नाम बदलने को कवर करती है
कोई विधेयक केवल राष्ट्रपति की पूर्व सिफारिश पर ही पेश किया जा सकता है
जहाँ विधेयक किसी विशेष राज्य के क्षेत्र, सीमाओं, या नाम को प्रभावित करता है, उस राज्य के विधानमंडल को राष्ट्रपति द्वारा निश्चित अवधि के भीतर अपने विचार व्यक्त करने का अवसर दिया जाना चाहिए
खंड (क)-(ङ) की सारवान शक्तियों हेतु 'राज्य' में संघ राज्यक्षेत्र शामिल है, परन्तु अनिवार्य-निर्देश परंतुक हेतु वे अपवर्जित हैं
exceptions_and_qualifications_hi: राज्य विधानमंडल के विचार केवल परामर्शात्मक हैं -- संसद को उन्हें स्वीकार करना या अनुसरण भी करना आवश्यक नहीं है
राज्य विधानमंडल के उत्तर देने की समय-अवधि राष्ट्रपति द्वारा बढ़ाई जा सकती है, और यदि अवधि समाप्त हो जाए, तो संसद वैसे भी आगे बढ़ सकती है
स्पष्टीकरण II स्पष्ट करता है कि खंड (क) किसी राज्य/संघ राज्यक्षेत्र के भाग को किसी अन्य राज्य/संघ राज्यक्षेत्र से मिलाने तक विस्तारित है, न कि केवल पूर्ण राज्यों को एक-दूसरे से मिलाने तक
breakdown.how_to_read_hi: यह भारतीय इतिहास के हर राज्य पुनर्गठन अधिनियम (जैसे राज्य पुनर्गठन अधिनियम, 1956, और 2014 में आंध्र प्रदेश का विभाजन) के पीछे की संचालक शक्ति है -- हमेशा जाँचें कि परिचय से पहले राष्ट्रपति की सिफारिश थी और प्रभावित राज्य के विधानमंडल को वास्तविक उत्तर देने का अवसर दिया गया था, क्योंकि ये वे प्रमुख प्रक्रियात्मक सुरक्षोपाय हैं जिनकी न्यायालयों ने जाँच की है।

sections.title: Laws made under articles 2 and 3 to provide for the amendment of the First and the Fourth Schedules and supplemental, incidental and consequential matters
sections.raw_text: (1) Any law referred to in article 2 or article 3 shall contain such provisions for the amendment of the First Schedule and the Fourth Schedule as may be necessary to give effect to the provisions of the law and may also contain such supplemental, incidental and consequential provisions (including provisions as to representation in Parliament and in the Legislature or Legislatures of the State or States affected by such law) as Parliament may deem necessary. (2) No such law as aforesaid shall be deemed to be an amendment of this Constitution for the purposes of article 368.
key_terms: Fourth Schedule
supplemental incidental and consequential provisions
representation in Parliament
not an amendment under Article 368

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 4 makes the Article 2/3 process self-contained: a law admitting, establishing, or reorganising States must itself update the First Schedule (list of States/territories) and the Fourth Schedule (allocation of Rajya Sabha seats to States), and may also make any other incidental adjustments Parliament thinks necessary — such as how many seats the affected State(s) get in Parliament or their own Legislature. Clause (2) is the crucial clarification: even though such a law changes parts of the Constitution's own Schedules, it is deliberately not treated as a 'constitutional amendment' requiring the special Article 368 procedure — ordinary legislative majority suffices.
essential_elements: A law under Article 2 or 3 must amend the First Schedule and Fourth Schedule as needed to give effect to it
It may also include supplemental, incidental, and consequential provisions, including on parliamentary/legislative representation
Such a law is expressly deemed NOT to be a constitutional amendment for Article 368 purposes
exceptions_and_qualifications: This exemption from Article 368 is precisely why State reorganisation can be done by simple parliamentary majority rather than the special amendment procedure (special majority, and for some subjects, State ratification)
breakdown.how_to_read: Article 4 is what makes Articles 2 and 3 practically usable as tools of ordinary politics rather than rare constitutional events — remember that any State reorganisation Bill is simultaneously a Schedule-amending Bill, and cite clause (2) whenever someone wrongly argues that a State reorganisation Act needed the Article 368 special procedure.
breakdown.plain_summary_hi: अनुच्छेद 4 अनुच्छेद 2/3 की प्रक्रिया को स्वयं-निहित बनाता है: राज्यों का प्रवेश, स्थापना, या पुनर्गठन करने वाली कोई विधि स्वयं प्रथम अनुसूची (राज्यों/राज्यक्षेत्रों की सूची) और चतुर्थ अनुसूची (राज्यों को राज्य सभा सीटों का आवंटन) को अद्यतन करनी चाहिए, और संसद जो भी अन्य आनुषंगिक समायोजन आवश्यक समझे -- जैसे प्रभावित राज्य(ओं) को संसद में या उनके अपने विधानमंडल में कितनी सीटें मिलती हैं -- वह भी कर सकती है। खंड (2) महत्वपूर्ण स्पष्टीकरण है: भले ही ऐसी विधि संविधान की स्वयं की अनुसूचियों के भागों को बदलती है, इसे जानबूझकर अनुच्छेद 368 की विशेष प्रक्रिया की आवश्यकता वाला 'संवैधानिक संशोधन' नहीं माना जाता -- साधारण विधायी बहुमत पर्याप्त है।
essential_elements_hi: अनुच्छेद 2 या 3 के अंतर्गत कोई विधि आवश्यकतानुसार प्रथम अनुसूची और चतुर्थ अनुसूची में संशोधन करे
इसमें संसदीय/विधायी प्रतिनिधित्व सहित आनुषंगिक, प्रासंगिक, और परिणामिक उपबंध भी शामिल हो सकते हैं
ऐसी विधि को अनुच्छेद 368 के प्रयोजनों हेतु संवैधानिक संशोधन न होना स्पष्ट रूप से माना गया है
exceptions_and_qualifications_hi: अनुच्छेद 368 से यह छूट ठीक इसीलिए है कि राज्य पुनर्गठन विशेष संशोधन प्रक्रिया (विशेष बहुमत, और कुछ विषयों हेतु, राज्य अनुसमर्थन) के बजाय साधारण संसदीय बहुमत से किया जा सकता है
breakdown.how_to_read_hi: अनुच्छेद 4 वह है जो अनुच्छेद 2 और 3 को दुर्लभ संवैधानिक घटनाओं के बजाय साधारण राजनीति के व्यावहारिक रूप से उपयोगी उपकरण बनाता है -- याद रखें कि कोई भी राज्य पुनर्गठन विधेयक एक साथ अनुसूची-संशोधन विधेयक भी है, और जब भी कोई गलत तर्क दे कि राज्य पुनर्गठन अधिनियम को अनुच्छेद 368 की विशेष प्रक्रिया की आवश्यकता थी, तब खंड (2) उद्धृत करें।

sections.title: Citizenship at the commencement of the Constitution
sections.raw_text: At the commencement of this Constitution, every person who has his domicile in the territory of India and— (a) who was born in the territory of India; or (b) either of whose parents was born in the territory of India; or (c) who has been ordinarily resident in the territory of India for not less than five years immediately preceding such commencement, shall be a citizen of India.
key_terms: domicile
commencement of the Constitution
ordinarily resident
citizen of India (Article 5)

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 5 is the Constitution's own 'starting gun' for Indian citizenship — it tells us who automatically became a citizen the moment the Constitution came into force on 26 January 1950.
