Application to multi-State co-operative societies.—The provisions of this Part shall apply to the multi-State co-operative societies subject to the modification that any reference to “Legislature of a State”, “State Act” or “State Government” shall be construed as a reference to “Parliament”, “Central Act” or “the Central Government” respectively.
key_terms: Parliament/Central-Act/Central-Government substitution formula for multi-State co-operative societies

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 243ZR extends every provision of Part IXB to multi-State co-operative societies using a clean substitution formula — wherever the Part refers to 'Legislature of a State,' 'State Act,' or 'State Government,' that reference is read instead as 'Parliament,' 'Central Act,' or 'the Central Government' respectively for a multi-State society.
essential_elements: The substitution is mechanical and complete: every State-oriented reference throughout the Part converts to its Union-level equivalent for multi-State societies.
'Legislature of a State' becomes 'Parliament.'
'State Act' becomes 'Central Act.'
'State Government' becomes 'the Central Government.'
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is the same drafting-economy substitution technique used in Article 243L/243ZB (Governor-to-Administrator for Union territories) — rather than duplicating the entire Part in a Union-legislation version, a single substitution clause converts the whole scheme.

This confirms the Article 243ZH(d)/(f) definitions of 'multi-State co-operative society' and 'Registrar' (Central Registrar) were deliberately drafted to make this substitution formula work seamlessly across the Part.
Because of this Article, Parliament (not any State Legislature) enacts the governing law for multi-State co-operative societies — reflected in the Multi-State Co-operative Societies Act, 2002.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 243ZR as the master key for applying every preceding Part IXB Article to multi-State co-operatives — mentally substitute Parliament/Central Act/Central Government for State Legislature/State Act/State Government whenever a multi-State society is at issue.

sections.title: Application to Union territories (Co-operative Societies)
sections.raw_text: 243ZS. Application to Union territories.—The provisions of this Part shall apply to the Union territories and shall, in their application to a Union territory, having no Legislative Assembly as if the references to the Legislature of a State were a reference to the administrator thereof appointed under article 239 and, in relation to a Union territory having a Legislative Assembly, to that Legislative Assembly: Provided that the President may, by notification in the Official Gazette, direct that the provisions of this Part shall not apply to any Union territory or part thereof as he may specify in the notification.
key_terms: Union-territory extension of Part IXB with administrator/Assembly substitution
Presidential opt-out (rather than opt-in) notification for Part IXB in Union territories

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 243ZS extends Part IXB to Union territories with the familiar administrator/Legislative-Assembly substitution formula, but structures the President's notification power as an opt-out (directing the Part shall NOT apply to a specified territory) rather than the opt-in/modification power Articles 243L, 243ZB, and 240 use elsewhere — a subtle but real drafting difference.
essential_elements: For a Union territory with no Legislative Assembly, 'Legislature of a State' reads as the Article 239 administrator.
For a Union territory with a Legislative Assembly, 'Legislature of a State' reads as that Legislative Assembly.
The proviso lets the President direct, by Official Gazette notification, that this Part shall NOT apply to a specified Union territory or part thereof.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Compare carefully with Article 243L/243ZB's proviso, which lets the President apply the Part 'subject to exceptions and modifications' (an opt-in/tailoring power) — Article 243ZS's proviso instead is framed as a straightforward disapplication (opt-out) power, without the 'exceptions and modifications' tailoring language.

This textual distinction matters for close statutory-construction purposes: under Article 243ZS the default is full application to every Union territory, and the President's power is binary (disapply it entirely for a specified territory/part) rather than a power to tailor specific exceptions within an applying territory.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 243ZS's proviso closely against Article 243L's and Article 243ZB's provisos — the opt-out/binary-disapplication framing here versus the opt-in/exceptions-and-modifications framing there is a genuine textual difference worth flagging in any comparative reading of all three Union-territory-application Articles.

sections.title: Continuance of existing laws (Co-operative Societies)
sections.raw_text: 243ZT. Continuance of existing laws.—Notwithstanding anything in this Part, any provision of any law relating to co-operative societies in force in a State immediately before the commencement of the Constitution (Ninety-seventh Amendment) Act, 2011, which is inconsistent with the provisions of this Part, shall continue to be in force until amended or repealed by a competent Legislature or other competent authority or until the expiration of one year from such commencement, whichever is less.
key_terms: one-year transitional continuance of pre-2012 inconsistent co-operative society laws

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 243ZT closes Part IXB with the same category of transitional savings clause seen in Article 243N and Article 243ZF: pre-existing State co-operative-society laws inconsistent with the new Part IXB scheme continue in force for up to one year after the Ninety-seventh Amendment's commencement (15 February 2012), or until sooner amended or repealed.
essential_elements: Inconsistent pre-commencement co-operative-society laws continue notwithstanding Part IXB, but only until the earlier ('whichever is less') of competent amendment/repeal or one year from commencement.

Unlike Article 243N and Article 243ZF, this Article has no separate proviso protecting already-existing institutions' terms — because co-operative societies have no fixed constitutional 'duration' concept analogous to Article 243E/243U, there is nothing equivalent to protect.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is a now-largely-spent, purely historical transitional provision tied to the 2011-12 commencement, exactly like its Part IX and Part IXA counterparts.
The phrase 'whichever is less' here (versus 'whichever is earlier' in Articles 243N/243ZF) is a minor drafting-style variation with the same practical meaning.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 243ZT as completing the trio of transitional savings clauses (243N for Panchayats, 243ZF for Municipalities, 243ZT for Co-operative Societies) that closes out each of the three self-government Parts — with this Article, Part IXB (and the entire IX/IXA/IXB local-and-associational self-government cluster) is now fully captured.

sections.title: Administration of Scheduled Areas and Tribal Areas
sections.raw_text:
244. Administration of Scheduled Areas and Tribal Areas.—(1) The provisions of the Fifth Schedule shall apply to the administration and control of the Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes in any State other than the States of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram.
(2) The provisions of the Sixth Schedule shall apply to the administration of the tribal areas in the States of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram.
key_terms: Fifth Schedule Scheduled Area administration
Sixth Schedule tribal area administration (Assam/Meghalaya/Tripura/Mizoram)

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 244 opens Part X by dividing India's tribal-area administration between two entirely different constitutional Schedules based on geography: the Fifth Schedule governs Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes in most States, while the Sixth Schedule governs tribal areas specifically in Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, and Mizoram, reflecting the North-East's distinct autonomous-district-council model of tribal self-government.
essential_elements: Clause (1) routes ordinary-State Scheduled Areas/Scheduled Tribes administration to the Fifth Schedule.
Clause (2) routes tribal-area administration in the four named North-Eastern States to the Sixth Schedule instead.
The two Schedules are mutually exclusive by State — a given State's tribal areas are governed by one Schedule or the other, not both.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The four-State list in clause (2) has changed over time through constitutional amendment and reorganisation (originally just Assam, later Meghalaya was separated out, then Tripura and Mizoram were added as they became States) — the current text reflects the post-1987 settled list.

The Fifth Schedule model is Governor-and-Tribes-Advisory-Council-centered (State executive-driven, with the Governor empowered to apply/disapply State and Union laws to Scheduled Areas and to make regulations), whereas the Sixth Schedule model creates elected Autonomous District/Regional Councils with their own legislative, judicial, and executive powers over specified subjects — the two models reflect fundamentally different institutional philosophies for tribal self-government.
Article 244A (added later) carves out a further, third distinct mechanism specifically for certain Sixth Schedule tribal areas within Assam.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 244 as a pure routing provision — its entire substance lies in directing the reader to the Fifth or Sixth Schedule depending on the State in question; the actual administrative machinery is detailed in those Schedules, not in this Article itself.

sections.title: Formation of an autonomous State comprising certain tribal areas in Assam and creation of local Legislature or Council of Ministers or both therefor
sections.raw_text:
244A. Formation of an autonomous State comprising certain tribal areas in Assam and creation of local Legislature or Council of Ministers or both therefor.—(1) Notwithstanding anything in this Constitution, Parliament may, by law, form within the State of Assam an autonomous State comprising (whether wholly or in part) all or any of the tribal areas specified in Part I of the table appended to paragraph 20 of the Sixth Schedule and create therefor—
(a) a body, whether elected or partly nominated and partly elected, to function as a Legislature for the autonomous State, or
(b) a Council of Ministers,
or both with such constitution, powers and functions, in each case, as may be specified in the law.
(2) Any such law as is referred to in clause (1) may, in particular,—
(a) specify the matters enumerated in the State List or the Concurrent List with respect to which the Legislature of the autonomous State shall have power to make laws for the whole or any part thereof, whether to the exclusion of the Legislature of the State of Assam or otherwise;
(b) define the matters with respect to which the executive power of the autonomous State shall extend;
(c) provide that any tax levied by the State of Assam shall be assigned to the autonomous State in so far as the proceeds thereof are attributable to the autonomous State;
(d) provide that any reference to a State in any article of this Constitution shall be construed as including a reference to the autonomous State; and
(e) make such supplemental, incidental and consequential provisions as may be deemed necessary.
(3) An amendment of any such law as aforesaid in so far as such amendment relates to any of the matters specified in sub-clause (a) or sub-clause (b) of clause (2) shall have no effect unless the amendment is passed in each House of Parliament by not less than two-thirds of the members present and voting.
(4) Any such law as is referred to in this article shall not be deemed to be an amendment of this Constitution for the purposes of article 368 notwithstanding that it contains any provision which amends or has the effect of amending this Constitution.
key_terms: Parliament's power to carve an autonomous State out of Assam's Sixth Schedule tribal areas
two-thirds Parliamentary-majority entrenchment for autonomous-State legislative/executive-power amendments
autonomous-State law expressly excluded from Article 368 amendment classification

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 244A (inserted by the Twenty-second Amendment Act, 1969) lets Parliament, by ordinary law, carve an 'autonomous State' out of specified Sixth Schedule tribal areas within Assam and equip it with its own Legislature and/or Council of Ministers, State-List/Concurrent-List law-making power (potentially to the exclusion of Assam's own Legislature), its own executive power, a share of Assam's tax proceeds attributable to it, and deemed-State status for other constitutional-Article purposes — while entrenching any later amendment touching its law-making or executive powers behind a two-thirds Parliamentary majority, yet expressly declaring the whole mechanism outside Article 368's amendment procedure.
essential_elements: Clause (1) is Parliament's power, exercisable 'notwithstanding anything in this Constitution,' to form an autonomous State from all or part of the Sixth Schedule Part I table's specified Assam tribal areas, with a Legislature and/or Council of Ministers as Parliament's law specifies.
Clause (2)(a) lets that law assign State-List/Concurrent-List subjects to the autonomous State's own Legislature, potentially excluding Assam's Legislature from those subjects entirely.
Clause (2)(b)-(c) let the law define the autonomous State's executive-power scope and its share of Assam-levied tax proceeds attributable to it.
Clause (2)(d) lets the law deem the autonomous State a 'State' for other constitutional-Article purposes.

Clause (3) specially entrenches amendments to the law's clause (2)(a)/(b) legislative/executive-power allocations behind a two-thirds-present-and-voting majority in each House of Parliament — stronger than ordinary-law amendment but not full Article 368 procedure.
Clause (4) expressly excludes any such law from being deemed an Article 368 constitutional amendment, even though it may have amendment-like effect.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is a genuinely unusual constitutional design: an ordinary Parliamentary law (not a formal constitutional amendment) that can carve out an autonomous sub-State-level entity with State-like legislative and executive powers within Assam — the clause (3) two-thirds-majority entrenchment is a middle path between fully ordinary legislation and full Article 368 rigidity.

Article 244A has seen limited practical use historically; it was significant in the political context of Northeast India's tribal-autonomy movements of the late 1960s, though most subsequent autonomy arrangements in the region proceeded through full Statehood (e.g., Meghalaya, Mizoram becoming separate States) rather than through the Article 244A autonomous-State mechanism itself.

The Sixth Schedule Part I table's specified tribal areas are the exclusive geographic universe from which such an autonomous State can be formed — Parliament cannot use Article 244A for areas outside that table.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 244A as a specialized, Assam-specific constitutional tool distinct from ordinary Statehood creation under Article 3 — it creates an intermediate entity ('autonomous State') with some but not all attributes of full Statehood, governed by an ordinary Parliamentary law rather than a constitutional amendment, yet partially entrenched by the clause (3) supermajority requirement.

sections.title: Extent of laws made by Parliament and by the Legislatures of States
sections.raw_text:
245. Extent of laws made by Parliament and by the Legislatures of States.—(1) Subject to the provisions of this Constitution, Parliament may make laws for the whole or any part of the territory of India, and the Legislature of a State may make laws for the whole or any part of the State.
(2) No law made by Parliament shall be deemed to be invalid on the ground that it would have extra-territorial operation.
key_terms: territorial extent of Parliamentary law (whole/part of India)
territorial extent of State legislative law (whole/part of State)
extra-territorial operation of Parliamentary law valid

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 245 opens Part XI's Chapter I (Legislative Relations) by fixing the basic territorial reach of law-making power: Parliament may legislate for the whole or any part of India's territory, a State Legislature may legislate for the whole or any part of that State, and — critically — a Parliamentary law is not invalidated merely because it operates extra-territorially (has effects outside India).
essential_elements: Clause (1) grants Parliament India-wide (or part-territory) legislative reach, and each State Legislature State-wide (or part-State) reach, both 'subject to the provisions of this Constitution' (i.e., subject to the distribution-of-powers scheme in Article 246 and beyond).
Clause (2) immunizes Parliamentary laws from an extra-territoriality challenge — a law with effects beyond India's territory is not void merely for that reason.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Clause (2) applies only to Parliament, not State Legislatures — State laws with genuine extra-territorial operation (no real territorial nexus to the State) remain vulnerable to challenge; the constitutional immunity is Union-specific.

'Subject to the provisions of this Constitution' in clause (1) is the textual hook connecting Article 245 to the entire distribution-of-powers scheme (Articles 246 onward) — Article 245 states raw territorial competence, while Article 246 allocates subject-matter competence between Union and States.

Courts have read a 'sufficient territorial nexus' requirement into State legislative competence even for laws with some extra-territorial operation, so long as the nexus to the State is real and not illusory.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 245 as the threshold territorial-competence question (where can this legislature legislate?), distinct from and prior to Article 246's subject-matter-competence question (what can this legislature legislate about?) — both must be satisfied for a law to be valid.

sections.title: Subject-matter of laws made by Parliament and by the Legislatures of States
sections.raw_text:
246. Subject-matter of laws made by Parliament and by the Legislatures of States.—(1) Notwithstanding anything in clauses (2) and (3), Parliament has exclusive power to make laws with respect to any of the matters enumerated in List I in the Seventh Schedule (in this Constitution referred to as the "Union List").
(2) Notwithstanding anything in clause (3), Parliament, and, subject to clause (1), the Legislature of any State also, have power to make laws with respect to any of the matters enumerated in List III in the Seventh Schedule (in this Constitution referred to as the "Concurrent List").
(3) Subject to clauses (1) and (2), the Legislature of any State has exclusive power to make laws for such State or any part thereof with respect to any of the matters enumerated in List II in the Seventh Schedule (in this Constitution referred to as the "State List").
(4) Parliament has power to make laws with respect to any matter for any part of the territory of India not included in a State notwithstanding that such matter is a matter enumerated in the State List.
key_terms: Seventh Schedule three-List distribution of legislative powers
Union List exclusive Parliamentary competence
Concurrent List shared Parliament/State competence
State List exclusive State competence
Parliament's residual power over non-State territory regardless of List

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 246 is the master subject-matter allocation clause: it distributes legislative competence across the Seventh Schedule's three Lists — Union List (Parliament's exclusive domain), State List (State Legislatures' exclusive domain), and Concurrent List (both, with Parliament prevailing per clause (2)'s 'subject to clause (1)' priority) — and clause (4) lets Parliament legislate on any matter, State-List included, for territory not part of any State (Union territories).
essential_elements: Clause (1) gives Parliament exclusive Union List competence, expressly overriding clauses (2) and (3) ('notwithstanding anything in clauses (2) and (3)') — Union List supremacy is textually built in.

Clause (2) gives both Parliament and State Legislatures Concurrent List competence, but itself is 'subject to clause (1)' and overrides clause (3) ('notwithstanding anything in clause (3)') — establishing the three-tier priority Union List > Concurrent List > State List.
Clause (3) gives State Legislatures exclusive State List competence, 'subject to clauses (1) and (2)' — the weakest-priority tier.

Clause (4) is a separate residual grant: Parliament may legislate on any matter (including State List subjects) for territory not included in any State — i.e., Union territories — regardless of the List the matter falls in.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The exclusivity of each List is not always clean in practice — courts apply the 'pith and substance' doctrine to determine which List a law's true subject-matter falls under when a law incidentally touches another List's field, and 'doctrine of colourable legislation' to strike down laws that pretend competence they lack.

Article 246A (inserted by the One Hundred and First Amendment Act, 2016, for GST) is expressly given overriding effect over Article 246 and Article 254 for goods-and-services-tax legislation — a deliberate carve-out from the ordinary three-List scheme.

Clause (4)'s Union-territory residual power exists because Union territories, having no State Legislature of their own by default, would otherwise have no legislative body competent over State List subjects for that territory — Parliament fills that gap.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 246 as the constitutional map key to the Seventh Schedule's three Lists — always ask which List a law's 'pith and substance' falls in, then apply the clause (1)>clause (2)>clause (3) priority ladder if there's overlap; Article 246A is a modern, GST-specific override to keep in mind after 2016.

sections.title: Special provision with respect to goods and services tax
sections.raw_text:
246A. Special provision with respect to goods and services tax.—(1) Notwithstanding anything contained in articles 246 and 254, Parliament, and, subject to clause (2), the Legislature of every State, have power to make laws with respect to goods and services tax imposed by the Union or by such State.
(2) Parliament has exclusive power to make laws with respect to goods and services tax where the supply of goods, or of services, or both takes place in the course of inter-State trade or commerce.
Explanation.—The provisions of this article, shall, in respect of goods and services tax referred to in clause (5) of article 279A, take effect from the date recommended by the Goods and Services Tax Council.
key_terms: GST concurrent Union/State legislative power overriding Articles 246 and 254
Parliament's exclusive GST power over inter-State supply
GST Council-recommended commencement date for petroleum/specified goods

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 246A (inserted by the One Hundred and First Amendment Act, 2016 — the GST Amendment) creates a bespoke, self-contained legislative-competence scheme for goods and services tax, overriding both Article 246's ordinary three-List distribution and Article 254's repugnancy rule: both Parliament and every State Legislature get concurrent GST law-making power for intra-State supply, while Parliament alone has exclusive power over inter-State supply GST (implemented via Article 269A's IGST mechanism).
essential_elements: Clause (1) gives Parliament and every State Legislature concurrent GST power, expressly notwithstanding Articles 246 and 254 — a deliberate carve-out from the ordinary Union/Concurrent/State List scheme and its repugnancy-resolution rule.
Clause (2) reserves inter-State-trade-or-commerce GST exclusively to Parliament — this is the constitutional basis for Integrated GST (IGST) under Article 269A.

The Explanation defers the article's application to specified petroleum products and similar goods referenced in Article 279A(5) until the GST Council recommends a commencement date — a deliberately incomplete rollout mechanism.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This Article is a textbook example of a targeted constitutional carve-out: rather than fitting GST into the existing Union/State/Concurrent List framework, the 2016 Amendment created an entirely separate concurrent-power article specifically for GST, alongside the new Article 279A (GST Council) and Article 269A (inter-State GST apportionment).

Certain goods (petroleum crude, high-speed diesel, motor spirit, natural gas, aviation turbine fuel, alcoholic liquor for human consumption) remain outside GST's practical scope even though Article 246A applies to them in principle — commencement for petroleum products awaits a GST Council recommendation per the Explanation, while alcoholic liquor for human consumption is expressly excluded from GST's definition altogether.

The Union List's Entry 84 and State List's Entry 54 (as amended by the same 101st Amendment) were correspondingly narrowed to exclude GST-covered goods, confirming Article 246A operates as the primary GST competence source rather than the ordinary Lists.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 246A as a freestanding, GST-specific override — do not try to fit GST competence questions into the Article 246 List framework; instead check Article 246A's own concurrent/exclusive split (intra-State vs inter-State) and cross-reference Article 279A for the GST Council's institutional role in recommending rates, exemptions, and commencement dates.

sections.title: Power of Parliament to provide for the establishment of certain additional courts
sections.raw_text: 247. Power of Parliament to provide for the establishment of certain additional courts.—Notwithstanding anything in this Chapter, Parliament may by law provide for the establishment of any additional courts for the better administration of laws made by Parliament or of any existing laws with respect to a matter enumerated in the Union List.
key_terms: Parliament's power to establish additional courts for Union-List law administration

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 247 lets Parliament, by ordinary law, establish additional courts (beyond the regular State judicial hierarchy) specifically to better administer Parliamentary laws or existing laws on Union List matters — an express override of the rest of Chapter I's distribution-of-powers scheme.
essential_elements: The power operates 'notwithstanding anything in this Chapter' — an express override of Articles 245-246A's ordinary competence rules.
The additional courts' purpose is confined to better administering Union List-related laws (Parliamentary laws or pre-existing laws on Union List matters).
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is a rarely-invoked power in practice — most specialized tribunals and courts are instead created under other specific constitutional or statutory heads (e.g., Article 323A/323B for administrative and other tribunals, or ordinary Union List entries on the judiciary).

Article 247 courts are distinct from the ordinary High Court/subordinate-court hierarchy under Part VI (State judiciary) and Part V (Supreme Court) — they are a supplementary, Union-List-focused judicial mechanism.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 247 as a narrow supplementary judicial-establishment power tied specifically to Union List law administration — contrast with the tribunal-creation powers under Articles 323A/323B, which serve a different, broader purpose.

sections.title: Residuary powers of legislation
sections.raw_text:
248. Residuary powers of legislation.—(1) Subject to article 246A, Parliament has exclusive power to make any law with respect to any matter not enumerated in the Concurrent List or State List.
(2) Such power shall include the power of making any law imposing a tax not mentioned in either of those Lists.
key_terms: Parliament's exclusive residuary legislative power
residuary taxation power

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 248 gives Parliament exclusive power over any subject-matter not enumerated in the State List or Concurrent List — the residuary power — including the power to impose any tax not otherwise listed, now expressly made subject to Article 246A's GST scheme.
essential_elements: Clause (1) vests all residuary (non-enumerated) legislative subject-matter exclusively in Parliament, not the States — India's residuary-power allocation favors the Union, unlike some federal constitutions (e.g., the US) that vest residuary power in the constituent states.
Clause (2) confirms the residuary power extends to taxation — Parliament may impose a wholly new tax not mentioned in any of the three Lists.
The 'subject to article 246A' qualifier (added by the 101st Amendment) ensures GST's own concurrent-competence scheme is not overridden by treating GST as a residuary subject.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Union List Entry 97 duplicates this residuary grant textually ('Any other matter not enumerated in List II or List III... residuary power of legislation'), so Article 248 and Entry 97 are read together as confirming the same Union residuary competence.

Because residuary power sits with the Union (not the States), any newly emerging subject-matter not contemplated by the 1950 Lists (e.g., certain aspects of cyberspace regulation, before specific entries or interpretations developed) defaults to Parliament's competence unless found to fall within an existing State or Concurrent List entry through purposive interpretation.

Courts have generally interpreted residuary power narrowly, first exhausting whether a matter fits within an existing State/Concurrent List entry (via pith and substance) before resorting to the residuary clause — the residuary power is a last resort, not a first-choice interpretive shortcut.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 248 as the Union-favoring default rule: whenever a subject-matter cannot be located in the State List or Concurrent List after careful pith-and-substance analysis, competence defaults to Parliament under this residuary clause (and Entry 97) — check Article 246A first for anything GST-adjacent.

sections.title: Power of Parliament to legislate with respect to a matter in the State List in the national interest
sections.raw_text:
249. Power of Parliament to legislate with respect to a matter in the State List in the national interest.—(1) Notwithstanding anything in the foregoing provisions of this Chapter, if the Council of States has declared by resolution supported by not less than two-thirds of the members present and voting that it is necessary or expedient in the national interest that Parliament should make laws with respect to goods and services tax provided under article 246A or any matter enumerated in the State List specified in the resolution, it shall be lawful for Parliament to make laws for the whole or any part of the territory of India with respect to that matter while the resolution remains in force.
(2) A resolution passed under clause (1) shall remain in force for such period not exceeding one year as may be specified therein:
Provided that, if and so often as a resolution approving the continuance in force of any such resolution is passed in the manner provided in clause (1), such resolution shall continue in force for a further period of one year from the date on which under this clause it would otherwise have ceased to be in force.
(3) A law made by Parliament which Parliament would not but for the passing of a resolution under clause (1) have been competent to make shall, to the extent of the incompetency, cease to have effect on the expiration of a period of six months after the resolution has ceased to be in force, except as respects things done or omitted to be done before the expiration of the said period.
key_terms: Rajya Sabha two-thirds national-interest resolution enabling Parliamentary State-List legislation
one-year renewable duration of Article 249 resolution
sunset of Article 249 law six months after resolution lapses

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 249 lets the Council of States (Rajya Sabha) alone — without the Lok Sabha's participation — temporarily authorize Parliament to legislate on a specified State List matter (or GST) by passing a resolution supported by a two-thirds majority of members present and voting, declaring it necessary in the national interest; the resulting Parliamentary competence lasts as long as the resolution (up to one year, renewable), and any law so made survives only six months past the resolution's lapse (preserving past acts/omissions).
essential_elements: Clause (1) requires a Rajya-Sabha-only resolution (the Council of States, representing the States) supported by a two-thirds present-and-voting majority, declaring a specified State List matter (or GST) necessary/expedient for Parliament to legislate on in the national interest — while in force, Parliament may legislate on that matter for all or part of India.
Clause (2) caps each resolution's duration at one year, but allows indefinite renewal via successive approving resolutions passed the same way.

Clause (3) sunsets any law enabled solely by such a resolution: it loses effect (to the extent of the incompetency) six months after the resolution lapses, except as to things already done or omitted under it.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is a Rajya-Sabha-exclusive power — unusual because it lets the Upper House alone (which the States are represented in) authorize an expansion of Union power over State subjects, without requiring Lok Sabha concurrence for the enabling resolution itself (though the resulting law, once Parliament acts on the authorization, must still pass through ordinary bicameral process).

Article 249 is one of three related mechanisms letting Parliament temporarily legislate on State List matters: Article 249 (Rajya Sabha national-interest resolution), Article 250 (national Emergency in operation), and Article 252 (State consent). Each has a different trigger and different States affected.

The GST reference ('goods and services tax provided under article 246A or') was added by the 101st Amendment, extending this national-interest mechanism to GST matters as well, even though GST already has its own Article 246A competence scheme.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 249 as one leg of a three-legged stool of exceptional Parliamentary State-List competence (alongside Articles 250 and 252) — note its distinctive Rajya-Sabha-only trigger, the one-year renewable window, and the six-month grace period for laws once the resolution lapses.

sections.title: Power of Parliament to legislate with respect to any matter in the State List if a Proclamation of Emergency is in operation
sections.raw_text:
250. Power of Parliament to legislate with respect to any matter in the State List if a Proclamation of Emergency is in operation.—(1) Notwithstanding anything in this Chapter, Parliament shall, while a Proclamation of Emergency is in operation, have power to make laws for the whole or any part of the territory of India with respect to goods and services tax provided under article 246A or any of the matters enumerated in the State List.
(2) A law made by Parliament which Parliament would not but for the issue of a Proclamation of Emergency have been competent to make shall, to the extent of the incompetency, cease to have effect on the expiration of a period of six months after the Proclamation has ceased to operate, except as respects things done or omitted to be done before the expiration of the said period.
key_terms: Parliament's full State-List legislative power during a Proclamation of Emergency
six-month sunset of Emergency-enabled law after Proclamation ceases

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 250 gives Parliament complete, automatic power to legislate on any State List matter (or GST) for the whole or any part of India for as long as a Proclamation of Emergency under Article 352 is in operation — no separate resolution is needed, unlike Article 249 — and any such law sunsets six months after the Emergency ends, subject to the same past-acts/omissions savings.
essential_elements: Clause (1) is automatic and total: the mere operation of an Article 352 Emergency Proclamation itself confers full State List (and GST) legislative competence on Parliament, without any additional procedural trigger like Article 249's resolution.
Clause (2) sunsets Emergency-enabled laws six months after the Proclamation ceases to operate, to the extent of the incompetency, with the same things-done-or-omitted savings as Article 249(3).
exceptions_and_qualifications: Unlike Article 249 (which requires an affirmative Rajya Sabha resolution) and Article 252 (which requires State consent), Article 250's trigger is purely the existence of an Emergency Proclamation — the broadest and most automatic of the three exceptional-competence mechanisms.

This dramatically centralizes legislative power during an Emergency, consistent with Part XVIII's broader Emergency-provisions scheme (Articles 352-360) that shifts India's federal balance sharply toward the Union while a Proclamation is in force.

If the Emergency Proclamation is confined to a part of India only, careful reading suggests Parliament's Article 250 power correspondingly should be understood in that context, though the clause's text grants power 'for the whole or any part of the territory of India' — this interacts with the scope of the underlying Proclamation itself.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 250 alongside Articles 352-360 as part of the Emergency-provisions federal-centralization package — its automatic, no-resolution-needed trigger is what most sharply distinguishes it from Article 249's Rajya-Sabha-resolution mechanism.

sections.title: Inconsistency between laws made by Parliament under articles 249 and 250 and laws made by the Legislatures of States
sections.raw_text: 251. Inconsistency between laws made by Parliament under articles 249 and 250 and laws made by the Legislatures of States.—Nothing in articles 249 and 250 shall restrict the power of the Legislature of a State to make any law which under this Constitution it has power to make, but if any provision of a law made by the Legislature of a State is repugnant to any provision of a law made by Parliament which Parliament has under either of the said articles power to make, the law made by Parliament, whether passed before or after the law made by the Legislature of the State, shall prevail, and the law made by the Legislature of the State shall to the extent of the repugnancy, but so long only as the law made by Parliament continues to have effect, be inoperative.
key_terms: State Legislature's law-making power preserved alongside Articles 249/250 Parliamentary power
Parliamentary-law priority on repugnancy under Articles 249/250
State law temporarily (not permanently) inoperative during repugnancy

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 251 resolves conflicts between State laws and Parliamentary laws enacted under the Article 249 (national-interest resolution) or Article 250 (Emergency) exceptional powers: the State Legislature keeps its ordinary law-making power undisturbed, but wherever an actual repugnancy arises, the Parliamentary law prevails and the State law becomes inoperative only to the extent of, and only for as long as, that repugnancy persists — not permanently void.
essential_elements: The State Legislature's ordinary competence is expressly preserved — Articles 249/250 do not strip States of their own law-making power on those same subjects.
On actual repugnancy (not mere overlap — a genuine, direct conflict), the Parliamentary Article 249/250 law prevails regardless of which law was enacted first.

The State law is only inoperative 'to the extent of the repugnancy' and 'so long only as the law made by Parliament continues to have effect' — a temporary, partial eclipse, not a permanent repeal; once the Parliamentary law lapses (e.g., the Article 249 resolution expires or the Emergency ends, subject to the respective six-month sunset), the State law revives to full operation.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This 'temporary eclipse' doctrine mirrors the general Indian constitutional-law principle applied to repugnant State laws generally (the 'doctrine of eclipse') — the State law is not erased from the books, merely rendered dormant while the overriding Union law persists.

Article 251 is structurally parallel to Article 254's general Union/State law-repugnancy rule for ordinary Concurrent List legislation, but is specifically scoped to the Article 249/250 exceptional-competence context rather than ordinary Concurrent List overlap.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 251 as confirming the temporary, self-correcting nature of Article 249/250 Parliamentary intrusion into State List territory — State legislative power is suspended only where and while actually repugnant, and automatically springs back once the Parliamentary authority lapses.

sections.title: Power of Parliament to legislate for two or more States by consent and adoption of such legislation by any other State
sections.raw_text:
252. Power of Parliament to legislate for two or more States by consent and adoption of such legislation by any other State.—(1) If it appears to the Legislatures of two or more States to be desirable that any of the matters with respect to which Parliament has no power to make laws for the States except as provided in articles 249 and 250 should be regulated in such States by Parliament by law, and if resolutions to that effect are passed by all the Houses of the Legislatures of those States, it shall be lawful for Parliament to pass an act for regulating that matter accordingly, and any Act so passed shall apply to such States and to any other State by which it is adopted afterwards by resolution passed in that behalf by the House or, where there are two Houses, by each of the Houses of the Legislature of that State.
(2) Any Act so passed by Parliament may be amended or repealed by an Act of Parliament passed or adopted in like manner but shall not, as respects any State to which it applies, be amended or repealed by an Act of the Legislature of that State.
key_terms: State-consent mechanism for Parliamentary legislation on State List matters
later adoption by other States via resolution
State Legislatures barred from amending/repealing an adopted Parliamentary Article 252 Act

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 252 lets two or more States voluntarily cede State List legislative authority on a specified matter to Parliament by passing consenting resolutions in all Houses of their Legislatures; Parliament then enacts a single uniform law applying to those consenting States, which any other State may later opt into by its own resolution — and crucially, once adopted, that Act can only be amended or repealed by Parliament, never by the adopting State's own Legislature.
essential_elements: Clause (1) requires resolutions passed by all Houses of the Legislatures of two or more States requesting Parliament to legislate on a matter otherwise outside Parliament's ordinary competence (except via Articles 249/250) — Parliament may then enact a uniform law applying to those States, and any further State can adopt it later by its own resolution.
Clause (2) locks in Parliamentary control: once passed/adopted, only Parliament (not the adopting State's own Legislature) can amend or repeal that Act as applied to that State.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is a voluntary, State-initiated mechanism — contrast with Articles 249 (Rajya Sabha-triggered) and 250 (Emergency-triggered), both of which operate without any individual State's consent.

The clause (2) bar on State-level amendment/repeal is a significant and permanent-feeling consequence of adoption — a State that opts in surrenders ongoing legislative control over that subject to Parliament indefinitely (unless Parliament itself later repeals the Act for that State), making the consent decision practically significant and not easily reversible unilaterally.

Historical examples of Article 252 legislation include the Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976 (later repealed) and the Prize Competitions Act, 1955 — illustrating its real but limited practical use for matters States found more efficiently regulated uniformly (e.g., certain economic/regulatory subjects).
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 252 as the voluntary, opt-in counterpart to Articles 249/250's non-consensual mechanisms — a State considering adoption should weigh clause (2)'s practical irreversibility (only Parliament, not the State itself, can later undo it) before passing the adopting resolution.

sections.title: Legislation for giving effect to international agreements
sections.raw_text: 253. Legislation for giving effect to international agreements.—Notwithstanding anything in the foregoing provisions of this Chapter, Parliament has power to make any law for the whole or any part of the territory of India for implementing any treaty, agreement or convention with any other country or countries or any decision made at any international conference, association or other body.
key_terms: Parliament's treaty-implementation legislative power overriding ordinary List distribution

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 253 gives Parliament a sweeping, override power to legislate on any subject-matter — including State List matters — for the purpose of implementing a treaty, agreement, or convention with another country, or any decision of an international conference, association, or body, regardless of the ordinary Article 246 distribution of powers.
essential_elements: The power operates 'notwithstanding anything in the foregoing provisions of this Chapter' — an express override of the entire Article 245-252 competence scheme, including State List exclusivity.

The power is limited by purpose (implementing a treaty/agreement/convention/international decision), not by subject-matter — any subject can be regulated by Parliament under this Article as long as the law genuinely implements such an international instrument.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is one of the most significant sources of Union legislative power over State List matters in the Constitution, since India is a dualist state (international treaties do not automatically become domestic law — Article 253 legislation is typically how they are domesticated) and treaty subject-matter frequently touches State List areas (e.g., environment, agriculture, forests).

Landmark environmental legislation (e.g., laws implementing the Stockholm Declaration, Ramsar Convention-related wetlands protections, and various environmental treaties) has been enacted under Article 253's authority even where the subject-matter would otherwise fall in the State List (e.g., Entry 17 water, Entry 14 agriculture).

Courts have generally read Article 253 broadly (a genuine international-implementation purpose is usually sufficient), though the law must have a real and direct connection to implementing the underlying international instrument — a purely pretextual invocation of a treaty to reach unrelated State List subjects would not be sustained.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 253 as India's principal treaty-implementation gateway — when a Parliamentary law is challenged as trenching on State List territory, check whether it can be justified as implementing a genuine treaty/convention/international decision under this Article, which overrides the ordinary distribution of powers entirely for that purpose.

sections.title: Inconsistency between laws made by Parliament and laws made by the Legislatures of States
sections.raw_text:
254. Inconsistency between laws made by Parliament and laws made by the Legislatures of States.—(1) If any provision of a law made by the Legislature of a State is repugnant to any provision of a law made by Parliament which Parliament is competent to enact, or to any provision of an existing law with respect to one of the matters enumerated in the Concurrent List, then, subject to the provisions of clause (2), the law made by Parliament, whether passed before or after the law made by the Legislature of such State, or, as the case may be, the existing law, shall prevail and the law made by the Legislature of the State shall, to the extent of the repugnancy, be void.
(2) Where a law made by the Legislature of a State with respect to one of the matters enumerated in the Concurrent List contains any provision repugnant to the provisions of an earlier law made by Parliament or an existing law with respect to that matter, then, the law so made by the Legislature of such State shall, if it has been reserved for the consideration of the President and has received his assent, prevail in that State:
Provided that nothing in this clause shall prevent Parliament from enacting at any time any law with respect to the same matter including a law adding to, amending, varying or repealing the law so made by the Legislature of the State.
key_terms: general Concurrent List repugnancy rule — Parliamentary law prevails
Presidential-assent exception letting reserved State law prevail in that State
Parliament's continuing power to override even a Presidential-assent-protected State law

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 254 is the Constitution's central Concurrent List repugnancy rule: as a default, whenever a State law conflicts with a Parliamentary law (or pre-existing law) on a Concurrent List matter, the Parliamentary/existing law prevails and the State law is void to the extent of the conflict — but clause (2) carves out an important exception letting a State law prevail within that State specifically if it was reserved for Presidential consideration and received the President's assent, though even then Parliament retains an unrestricted continuing power to override it later by fresh legislation.
essential_elements: Clause (1) states the default rule: on genuine repugnancy over a Concurrent List matter, the Parliamentary law (whether enacted before or after the State law) or existing law prevails, and the State law is void to the extent of the repugnancy — a permanent voidness (contrast Article 251's temporary inoperability for the Article 249/250 context specifically).

Clause (2)'s proviso-exception: if the State law was reserved for the President's consideration (under Article 200) and received Presidential assent, it prevails in that State despite conflicting with an earlier Parliamentary/existing law.

The clause (2) proviso immediately qualifies that exception: Parliament remains free at any time to enact a fresh law on the same matter, including one that adds to, amends, varies, or repeals the President-assented State law — so the clause (2) exception is never final or immune from subsequent Parliamentary override.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The key practical distinction from clause (1) 'void' language versus Article 251's 'inoperative... so long only as' language: ordinary Article 254(1) repugnancy renders the State law void outright (not merely dormant), a more severe result than the temporary Article 251 eclipse used for the special Article 249/250 context.

Clause (2)'s Presidential-assent route is a meaningful practical tool for States to secure a locally tailored Concurrent List law that would otherwise be repugnant to an existing Parliamentary law — but its protection is contingent and always subject to a later Parliamentary override, making it a delaying/localizing mechanism rather than a permanent shield.

This repugnancy framework has generated extensive Supreme Court jurisprudence on what counts as genuine 'repugnancy' (requiring a direct, irreconcilable conflict — mere overlap or difference in degree is insufficient) versus fields that are merely 'occupied' by Parliamentary legislation without literal conflict.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 254 as the general-purpose Concurrent List conflict-resolution rule (contrast with Article 251's narrower Article 249/250-specific version) — always check first whether a State law was reserved and received Presidential assent under clause (2) before assuming automatic voidness under clause (1), but remember clause (2)'s protection is never absolute against a later Parliamentary law.

sections.title: Requirements as to recommendations and previous sanctions to be regarded as matters of procedure only
key_terms: procedural (not fatal) treatment of missing recommendation/previous-sanction requirements
curative effect of subsequent assent

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 255 closes Chapter I with a curative rule: an Act of Parliament or a State Legislature is not invalidated merely because a constitutionally required prior recommendation or previous sanction (e.g., a Governor's or President's recommendation before introducing certain Bills) was missing, so long as the relevant authority's assent was ultimately given to the Act — treating such recommendation/sanction requirements as procedural rather than as conditions precedent whose breach is fatal.
essential_elements: The curative rule applies where the required recommendation was that of the Governor — cured by either the Governor's or the President's assent.

It applies where the required recommendation was that of a Rajpramukh (a now-obsolete title for the head of certain former princely-state unions) — cured by either the Rajpramukh's or the President's assent.
It applies where the required recommendation or previous sanction was that of the President — cured by the President's own assent.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The 'Rajpramukh' reference is now a historical relic — Rajpramukhs (heads of unions of former princely states like Patiala and East Punjab States Union, Saurashtra, etc.) ceased to exist after the States Reorganisation Act, 1956 restructured India's internal boundaries; this provision remains in the text unamended but has no ongoing practical application.

This Article prevents what would otherwise be a very technical, easily-overlooked procedural defect (e.g., forgetting to obtain a Governor's prior recommendation before introducing a Money Bill in a State Legislature under Article 207) from retroactively invalidating an entire Act — as long as assent was eventually given by the appropriate constitutional authority.

This is a pragmatic, government-continuity-preserving rule, conceptually similar to 'directory vs mandatory' statutory-interpretation distinctions — recommendation/sanction requirements are treated as directory procedural safeguards, not mandatory jurisdictional prerequisites, once the ultimate assent has cured the omission.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 255 as a technical validity-preserving safety net closing out Chapter I — it prevents recommendation/sanction procedural lapses from being weaponized to strike down otherwise properly assented Acts, while the Rajpramukh reference is best understood as inert constitutional-history text rather than living law.

sections.title: Obligation of States and the Union
sections.raw_text: 256. Obligation of States and the Union.—The executive power of every State shall be so exercised as to ensure compliance with the laws made by Parliament and any existing laws which apply in that State, and the executive power of the Union shall extend to the giving of such directions to a State as may appear to the Government of India to be necessary for that purpose.
key_terms: State's obligation to ensure compliance with Parliamentary/existing laws
Union's directive power to secure that compliance

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 256 opens Chapter II (Administrative Relations) by imposing a basic obligation on every State: exercise its executive power so as to ensure compliance with Parliamentary laws and other laws applicable in that State, backed by a corresponding Union power to issue directions to the State as necessary to secure that compliance.
essential_elements: States must exercise their executive power consistently with ensuring compliance with Parliamentary laws and existing laws applicable within the State.
The Union's executive power correspondingly extends to giving directions to a State wherever the Government of India considers it necessary to secure such compliance.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Article 256 is the general obligation-and-directive-power provision; its more specific application to particular subjects (communications, railways) is spelled out in Article 257 immediately following.

Failure or refusal by a State Government to comply with Union directions under this Article (and Article 257) can, under Article 365, be treated as a situation where the government of the State cannot be carried on in accordance with the Constitution — potentially triggering President's Rule under Article 356.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 256 as the general administrative-compliance and Union-oversight backbone of Chapter II — pair it with Article 365's consequence (President's Rule exposure) to appreciate the real force behind an otherwise simple-sounding 'compliance' obligation.

sections.title: Control of the Union over States in certain cases
sections.raw_text:
257. Control of the Union over States in certain cases.—(1) The executive power of every State shall be so exercised as not to impede or prejudice the exercise of the executive power of the Union, and the executive power of the Union shall extend to the giving of such directions to a State as may appear to the Government of India to be necessary for that purpose.
(2) The executive power of the Union shall also extend to the giving of directions to a State as to the construction and maintenance of means of communication declared in the direction to be of national or military importance:
Provided that nothing in this clause shall be taken as restricting the power of Parliament to declare highways or waterways to be national highways or national waterways or the power of the Union with respect to the highways or waterways so declared or the power of the Union to construct and maintain means of communication as part of its functions with respect to naval, military and air force works.
(3) The executive power of the Union shall also extend to the giving of directions to a State as to the measures to be taken for the protection of the railways within the State.
(4) Where in carrying out any direction given to a State under clause (2) as to the construction or maintenance of any means of communication or under clause (3) as to the measures to be taken for the protection of any railway, costs have been incurred in excess of those which would have been incurred in the discharge of the normal duties of the State if such direction had not been given, there shall be paid by the Government of India to the State such sum as may be agreed, or, in default of agreement, as may be determined by an arbitrator appointed by the Chief Justice of India, in respect of the extra costs so incurred by the State.
key_terms: State obligation not to impede Union executive power
Union directions on nationally/militarily important communications
Union directions on railway protection measures
Union's obligation to reimburse States' excess compliance costs

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 257 strengthens Article 256's general principle into specific Union directive powers: States must not impede the Union's executive power, and the Union may direct States on construction/maintenance of communications declared nationally or militarily important and on measures to protect railways within the State — with a built-in cost-sharing guarantee reimbursing States for any excess costs incurred in complying with such directions.
essential_elements: Clause (1) states the negative obligation (States must not impede/prejudice Union executive power) and the corresponding Union directive power to secure that.

Clause (2) empowers Union directions specifically on construction/maintenance of communications the Union itself declares to be of national or military importance, with a proviso preserving Parliament's separate national-highway/waterway declaration powers and the Union's own defence-related construction powers.
Clause (3) empowers Union directions on railway-protection measures within a State.

Clause (4) guarantees Union reimbursement to the State for costs incurred in excess of the State's normal-duty costs when complying with clause (2)/(3) directions — by agreement, or failing agreement, by a Chief-Justice-of-India-appointed arbitrator.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Clause (4)'s arbitration mechanism (Chief Justice of India appointing an arbitrator on cost disagreements) is a distinctive federal-cost-sharing dispute-resolution feature not found in most other Union-direction provisions.

Article 257A (which once dealt with deployment of Union armed/other forces to assist States) was inserted by the 42nd Amendment (1976) and later omitted by the 44th Amendment (1978) — now a spent, omitted provision with no current legal effect, reflecting the post-Emergency (1975-77) rollback of centralizing amendments.

This Article's directions are backed by the same Article 365 consequence as Article 256 — non-compliance with a lawful Union direction can expose a State Government to a claim that its governance is not being carried on in accordance with the Constitution.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 257 as the specific-subject elaboration of Article 256's general compliance obligation — pay attention to clause (4)'s cost-reimbursement guarantee, which tempers what would otherwise be an unfunded-mandate-style burden on States, and note that Article 257A is now an inert historical relic.

sections.title: Power of the Union to confer powers, etc., on States in certain cases
sections.raw_text:
258. Power of the Union to confer powers, etc., on States in certain cases.—(1) Notwithstanding anything in this Constitution, the President may, with the consent of the Government of a State, entrust either conditionally or unconditionally to that Government or to its officers functions in relation to any matter to which the executive power of the Union extends.
(2) A law made by Parliament which applies in any State may, notwithstanding that it relates to a matter with respect to which the Legislature of the State has no power to make laws, confer powers and impose duties, or authorise the conferring of powers and the imposition of duties, upon the State or officers and authorities thereof.
(3) Where by virtue of this article powers and duties have been conferred or imposed upon a State or officers or authorities thereof, there shall be paid by the Government of India to the State such sum as may be agreed, or, in default of agreement, as may be determined by an arbitrator appointed by the Chief Justice of India, in respect of any extra costs of administration incurred by the State in connection with the exercise of those powers and duties.
key_terms: Presidential entrustment of Union executive functions to a consenting State
Parliament's power to confer State-implementation duties even on non-State-List matters
Union's reimbursement obligation for extra administrative costs under Article 258

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 258 lets the Union delegate downward: the President may, with a State's consent, entrust Union executive functions to that State's Government or officers (clause (1)), and Parliament may, by law, confer powers/duties on a State or its officers to help implement Union laws even on matters outside the State Legislature's own competence (clause (2)) — again backed by a Union reimbursement guarantee for extra administrative costs, using the same Chief-Justice-arbitrator mechanism as Article 257(4).
essential_elements: Clause (1) is a President-to-State-Government entrustment power, requiring the State's consent, and covering any matter within the Union's executive power — conditional or unconditional.

Clause (2) is a Parliament-to-State-Government/officers conferral power via ordinary legislation, notably not requiring State consent (unlike clause (1)) and applicable even to matters where the State Legislature itself has no law-making competence.
Clause (3) mirrors Article 257(4)'s cost-reimbursement guarantee and Chief-Justice-of-India arbitration mechanism for extra administrative costs incurred under either clause (1) or clause (2).
exceptions_and_qualifications: Clause (1)'s consent requirement versus clause (2)'s absence of an explicit consent requirement is a meaningful textual distinction — clause (2) operates through ordinary Parliamentary legislation applicable in the State, which itself supplies the legal authority without needing separate State Government consent for each instance.

Article 258A (inserted by the 7th Amendment, 1956) is the mirror-image power for a State to entrust its own executive functions to the Union (with the Governor entrusting, subject to Union Government consent) — together, Articles 258 and 258A create a genuinely bidirectional executive-function-sharing mechanism between Union and States.

This is a practical, commonly used delegation mechanism (Union schemes and programmes are frequently implemented through State machinery under Article 258 entrustment) that avoids the Union needing to build entirely separate administrative infrastructure in every State.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 258 (and its mirror, Article 258A) as the Constitution's administrative-delegation toolkit — Union-to-State under Article 258, State-to-Union under Article 258A — both cost-reimbursed via the same Chief-Justice-arbitrator mechanism used in Article 257(4).

sections.title: Power of the States to entrust functions to the Union
sections.raw_text: 258A. Power of the States to entrust functions to the Union.—Notwithstanding anything in this Constitution, the Governor of a State may, with the consent of the Government of India, entrust either conditionally or unconditionally to that Government or to its officers functions in relation to any matter to which the executive power of the State extends.
key_terms: Gubernatorial entrustment of State executive functions to the Union

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 258A (inserted by the Constitution (Seventh Amendment) Act, 1956) is the precise mirror-image of Article 258(1): it lets a State's Governor, with the consent of the Government of India, entrust State executive functions to the Union Government or its officers, conditionally or unconditionally.
essential_elements: The entrusting authority is the State's Governor (not the State Government or Legislature directly, though the Governor acts on the State Council of Ministers' aid and advice per ordinary constitutional practice).
Union consent is required — the reciprocal requirement to Article 258(1)'s State-consent requirement.
The functions entrusted must be ones to which the State's own executive power extends.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This Article completes the bidirectional entrustment scheme with Article 258 — Union-to-State entrustment needs State consent (Article 258(1)); State-to-Union entrustment needs Union consent (Article 258A) — a symmetric federal cooperation design.

Unlike Article 258, Article 258A has no separate cost-reimbursement clause of its own; in practice, cost arrangements for State-to-Union entrustments would need to be separately negotiated or provided for, since Article 258(3)'s reimbursement mechanism is textually tied to 'this article' (Article 258), not Article 258A.
This provision was added relatively early (1956) alongside the broader post-States-Reorganisation-Act constitutional adjustments of that period.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 258A immediately alongside Article 258(1) as a matched pair — same conditional/unconditional entrustment structure, opposite direction, and note the absence of an explicit Article 258A cost-reimbursement clause as a genuine asymmetry between the two provisions.

sections.title: Jurisdiction of the Union in relation to territories outside India
sections.raw_text: 260. Jurisdiction of the Union in relation to territories outside India.—The Government of India may by agreement with the Government of any territory not being part of the territory of India undertake any executive, legislative or judicial functions vested in the Government of such territory, but every such agreement shall be subject to, and governed by, any law relating to the exercise of foreign jurisdiction for the time being in force.
key_terms: Union's power to undertake executive/legislative/judicial functions in foreign territory by agreement

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 260 lets the Government of India, by agreement with the government of a foreign territory (not part of India), undertake executive, legislative, or judicial functions otherwise vested in that foreign territory's government — subject always to any law on the exercise of foreign jurisdiction then in force.
essential_elements: The mechanism requires an agreement with the foreign territory's government — it is consensual, not unilateral.
The functions that may be undertaken span all three branches (executive, legislative, judicial) of the foreign territory's governance.
Any such agreement operates subject to, and is governed by, existing foreign-jurisdiction law (historically, legislation like the Foreign Jurisdiction Act, 1947).
exceptions_and_qualifications: This Article has had limited but real historical application — for instance, arrangements involving Sikkim before its 1975 accession as a full State, or certain protectorate/agency-style historical arrangements with neighbouring territories.

Article 260 is functionally distinct from Article 1's definition of India's own territory and from Article 2/3's admission/formation of new States — it deals with the Union exercising governmental functions in territory that remains outside India, rather than incorporating new territory into India.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 260 as a specialized, agreement-based extension of Indian governmental functions into foreign territory — distinct from and narrower than actual territorial incorporation, and always bounded by prevailing foreign-jurisdiction law.

sections.title: Public acts, records and judicial proceedings
sections.raw_text:
261. Public acts, records and judicial proceedings.—(1) Full faith and credit shall be given throughout the territory of India to public acts, records and judicial proceedings of the Union and of every State.
(2) The manner in which and the conditions under which the acts, records and proceedings referred to in clause (1) shall be proved and the effect thereof determined shall be as provided by law made by Parliament.
(3) Final judgments or orders delivered or passed by civil courts in any part of the territory of India shall be capable of execution anywhere within that territory according to law.
key_terms: full faith and credit for public acts/records/judicial proceedings across India
Parliament's power to prescribe proof/effect procedure
pan-India executability of civil court final judgments

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 261 guarantees that public acts, records, and judicial proceedings of the Union and every State are given full faith and credit throughout India's territory — so a document or judgment valid in one State is recognized throughout the country — with Parliament empowered to legislate on how such acts/records/proceedings are proved and their legal effect, and with a specific guarantee that final civil-court judgments/orders are executable anywhere in India according to law.
essential_elements: Clause (1) is the core full-faith-and-credit guarantee, borrowed conceptually from the analogous US constitutional clause, ensuring inter-State/Union legal recognition rather than treating each State as a separate legal universe.
Clause (2) delegates the proof-and-effect mechanics (how such acts/records/proceedings are established in evidence and what legal weight they carry) to Parliamentary legislation.

Clause (3) specifically guarantees pan-India executability of final civil judgments/orders — a litigant who wins a civil decree in one State's courts can enforce it anywhere in India, subject to applicable procedural law (principally the Code of Civil Procedure's provisions on execution of decrees, including transfer of decrees for execution in another court).
exceptions_and_qualifications: This Article underpins the practical operation of India's unified judicial system despite its federal political structure — unlike the US, where full faith and credit was historically more contested for certain matters, India's single integrated judiciary (with the Supreme Court at its apex over all State High Courts) gives this guarantee a comparatively smoother practical application.

Clause (3)'s execution guarantee is what makes decree-transfer provisions under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (e.g., Section 39, execution of decrees by courts which passed them or by transferee courts) constitutionally grounded and mandatory in their pan-India reach.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 261 as the constitutional foundation for treating India's legal landscape as a single, mutually-recognizing system — clause (3) in particular is the direct constitutional root of the CPC's decree-execution-transfer machinery familiar from civil procedure practice.

sections.title: Adjudication of disputes relating to waters of inter-State rivers or river valleys
sections.raw_text:
262. Adjudication of disputes relating to waters of inter-State rivers or river valleys.—(1) Parliament may by law provide for the adjudication of any dispute or complaint with respect to the use, distribution or control of the waters of, or in, any inter-State river or river valley.
(2) Notwithstanding anything in this Constitution, Parliament may by law provide that neither the Supreme Court nor any other court shall exercise jurisdiction in respect of any such dispute or complaint as is referred to in clause (1).
key_terms: Parliament's power to legislate inter-State river water dispute adjudication mechanisms
Parliament's power to oust Supreme Court/all-court jurisdiction over such disputes

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 262 gives Parliament exclusive power to create special adjudication mechanisms for inter-State river/river-valley water disputes, and — remarkably — lets Parliament by law bar even the Supreme Court (and all other courts) from exercising jurisdiction over such disputes, channeling them instead into the specialized tribunal mechanisms Parliament creates (principally under the Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956).
essential_elements: Clause (1) empowers Parliament to legislate on adjudicating disputes over the use, distribution, or control of inter-State river/river-valley waters.

Clause (2) is the unusual ouster clause: 'notwithstanding anything in this Constitution,' Parliament may exclude both the Supreme Court's and every other court's jurisdiction over such disputes — a rare express constitutional authorization to oust even Supreme Court jurisdiction, which otherwise enjoys broad original jurisdiction under Article 131 over Centre-State/inter-State disputes.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is one of the very few provisions in the Constitution expressly permitting exclusion of the Supreme Court's jurisdiction — a significant departure from the Court's ordinarily entrenched role, reflecting the framers' judgment that river-water disputes (often highly technical, politically sensitive, and multi-State) are better resolved through specialized tribunals than ordinary adversarial litigation.

The Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956 (enacted under Article 262) establishes the tribunal mechanism actually used for major disputes (e.g., Cauvery, Krishna, Narmada water disputes) — tribunal awards under that Act have historically been treated as having the same practical force as a Supreme Court decree once notified, though litigation over the scope of the jurisdictional bar and the tribunals' functioning has repeatedly reached the Supreme Court on related/collateral questions.

Whether Article 262(2)'s ouster is absolute in practice has been contested — courts have entertained certain collateral challenges (e.g., procedural fairness, tribunal composition) even while broadly respecting the jurisdictional bar on the merits of water allocation itself.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 262 as a deliberately specialized federal-dispute carve-out — its clause (2) ouster power is exceptional constitutional text, and should be read alongside the Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956's tribunal mechanism to understand how the power has actually been exercised.

sections.title: Provisions with respect to an inter-State Council
sections.raw_text:
263. Provisions with respect to an inter-State Council.—If at any time it appears to the President that the public interests would be served by the establishment of a Council charged with the duty of—
(a) inquiring into and advising upon disputes which may have arisen between States;
(b) investigating and discussing subjects in which some or all of the States, or the Union and one or more of the States, have a common interest; or
(c) making recommendations upon any such subject and, in particular, recommendations for the better co-ordination of policy and action with respect to that subject,
it shall be lawful for the President by order to establish such a Council, and to define the nature of the duties to be performed by it and its organisation and procedure.
key_terms: Presidential power to establish an Inter-State Council
Inter-State Council's three-fold advisory/investigative/recommendatory functions

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 263 closes Part XI by empowering the President, whenever the public interest would be served, to establish an Inter-State Council by order — a cooperative-federalism body charged with inquiring into and advising on inter-State disputes, investigating/discussing matters of common Union-State or inter-State interest, and making policy-coordination recommendations, with its organisation and procedure defined by the same Presidential order.
essential_elements: The power is discretionary and conditional on the President's assessment that public interest would be served — there is no mandatory obligation to establish such a Council.
Clause (a) empowers the Council to inquire into and advise on inter-State disputes.
Clause (b) empowers it to investigate and discuss subjects of common interest among States, or between the Union and States.
Clause (c) empowers it to make recommendations, particularly for better policy/action coordination, on such subjects.
The President's order also fixes the Council's organisation and procedure — Article 263 itself does not prescribe a fixed composition.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The actual Inter-State Council was established by Presidential Order in 1990 (following the Sarkaria Commission's recommendation), decades after the Constitution's commencement — illustrating that this is a genuinely discretionary, not self-executing, power.
