exceptions_and_qualifications: This is a frequently litigated Article — questions about whether a particular levy (e.g., a municipal property tax, service charge, or 'fee' dressed as a tax) actually falls within 'taxes imposed by a State or by any authority within a State' on 'property of the Union' have generated substantial case law distinguishing genuine taxes from regulatory fees/service charges (which are typically not barred by Article 285).

Because only Parliament (not the Union executive) can waive the clause (1) exemption, a State cannot unilaterally tax Union property no matter how compelling its local fiscal need — the exemption is constitutionally entrenched against State action specifically.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 285 as the mirror image of Article 289 — together they establish a general, mutual Union-State property-tax immunity, each overridable only by the taxing level's own Parliament/Legislature counterpart (here, only Parliament can waive Article 285; per Article 289(2)-(3), only Parliament can authorize Union taxation of State trade/business property).

sections.title: Restrictions as to imposition of tax on the supply of goods or services or both
sections.raw_text:
286. Restrictions as to imposition of tax on the sale or purchase of goods.—(1) No law of a State shall impose, or authorise the imposition of, a tax on the supply of goods or of services or both, where such supply takes place—
(a) outside the State; or
(b) in the course of the import of the goods or services or both into, or export of the goods or services or both out of, the territory of India.
(2) Parliament may by law formulate principles for determining when a supply of goods or of services or both in any of the ways mentioned in clause (1).
key_terms: State GST/sales-tax barred on extra-territorial, import, and export supplies
Parliament's power to formulate situs principles for Article 286 purposes

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 286 bars any State law from taxing a supply of goods or services that takes place outside that State, or in the course of import into or export out of India's territory — protecting inter-State/international trade from being multiply or extraterritorially taxed by individual States — while letting Parliament formulate the principles for determining exactly when a supply falls into one of those excluded categories.
essential_elements: Clause (1)(a) bars a State from taxing supplies occurring 'outside the State' — an extraterritoriality bar preventing States from taxing transactions with no genuine territorial nexus to them.

Clause (1)(b) bars State taxation of import-into-India and export-out-of-India supplies — reserving that field for Union taxation (customs duties under the Union List, and now IGST under Article 269A's deeming rule for imports).

Clause (2) delegates to Parliament the power to formulate the 'situs' principles determining when a supply falls into the outside-the-State/import/export categories — the GST-era successor, in near-identical language, to Article 269(3)'s older inter-State-sale-situs-principles power.

Post-101st-Amendment, the Article's language was updated from 'sale or purchase of goods' to 'supply of goods or of services or both' to match the GST regime's supply-based (rather than sale-based) tax trigger.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Article 286 works as the negative/restrictive counterpart to Article 269A's positive IGST-apportionment mechanism — 286 tells States what they cannot tax, while 269A tells the Union how it collects and apportions IGST on exactly those inter-State/import supplies.

Pre-GST, Article 286 (alongside the Central Sales Tax Act, 1956 enacted under the old Article 269(3)) was the primary constitutional battleground for disputes over when a sale was genuinely 'inter-State' versus a local sale artificially structured to look inter-State (or vice versa) — extensive Supreme Court jurisprudence (e.g., the 'Bengal Immunity' and later cases) developed the situs tests Parliament's CST Act then codified.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 286 as the negative-restriction mirror of Article 269A — always pair a 'can State X tax this supply' question with both Article 286's territorial/import/export bars and Article 269A's IGST mechanism to see the complete picture of who taxes what in an inter-State or international transaction.

sections.title: Exemption from taxes on electricity
sections.raw_text:
287. Exemption from taxes on electricity.—Save in so far as Parliament may by law otherwise provide, no law of a State shall impose, or authorise the imposition of, a tax on the consumption or sale of electricity (whether produced by a Government or other persons) which is—
(a) consumed by the Government of India, or sold to the Government of India for consumption by that Government; or
(b) consumed in the construction, maintenance or operation of any railway by the Government of India or a railway company operating that railway, or sold to that Government or any such railway company for consumption in the construction, maintenance or operation of any railway,
and any such law imposing, or authorising the imposition of, a tax on the sale of electricity shall secure that the price of electricity sold to the Government of India for consumption by that Government, or to any such railway company as aforesaid for consumption in the construction, maintenance or operation of any railway, shall be less by the amount of the tax than the price charged to other consumers of a substantial quantity of electricity.
key_terms: State electricity-tax exemption for Union-consumed and railway-consumed electricity
pass-through price-reduction guarantee equal to the tax amount

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 287 exempts electricity consumed by the Government of India, and electricity consumed in constructing/maintaining/operating any railway, from State taxation — and where a State does tax electricity sales generally, it must ensure the Union/railway-company purchaser's price is reduced by exactly the tax amount compared to what ordinary large consumers pay, effectively guaranteeing the exemption reaches the Union in substance, not just in form.
essential_elements: The exemption covers two specific categories: electricity consumed directly by the Government of India, and electricity consumed in railway construction/maintenance/operation (by the Government of India or a railway company operating that railway).
The exemption applies 'whether produced by a Government or other persons' — the source of the electricity generation doesn't matter, only who consumes it.
Parliament may override this exemption by law — the same 'default exemption, Parliament can waive' pattern as Article 285.

The price-guarantee clause is a substantive anti-evasion mechanism: even if a State taxes the seller (not directly the Union buyer), the seller must still pass on a price reduction equal to the tax, preventing States from circumventing the exemption via indirect seller-side taxation.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This Article reflects the historical importance of Indian Railways (a Union subject) as a massive electricity consumer, and ensures State electricity taxation cannot be used to indirectly burden railway operations or general Union governmental functions.

The price-reduction mechanism in the final clause is a notable drafting technique — rather than simply barring the tax, the Constitution ensures the tax's economic incidence cannot be shifted onto the exempted consumer through pricing structure, a more robust protection than a bare exemption would provide.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 287 alongside Article 285 as another sector-specific instance of the general Union-property/consumption tax-immunity theme — note its distinctive anti-evasion price-guarantee mechanism, which goes further than Article 285's simple exemption by regulating how the tax's economic burden must be allocated even where a State does tax the underlying electricity sale.

sections.title: Exemption from taxation by States in respect of water or electricity in certain cases
sections.raw_text:
288. Exemption from taxation by States in respect of water or electricity in certain cases.—(1) Save in so far as the President may by order otherwise provide, no law of a State in force immediately before the commencement of this Constitution shall impose, or authorise the imposition of, a tax in respect of any water or electricity stored, generated, consumed, distributed or sold by any authority established by any existing law or any law made by Parliament for regulating or developing any inter-State river or river-valley.
Explanation.—The expression "law of a State in force" in this clause shall include a law of a State passed or made before the commencement of this Constitution and not previously repealed, notwithstanding that it or parts of it may not be then in operation either at all or in particular areas.
(2) The Legislature of a State may by law impose, or authorise the imposition of, any such tax as is mentioned in clause (1), but no such law shall have any effect unless it has, after having been reserved for the consideration of the President, received his assent; and if any such law provides for the fixation of the rates and other incidents of such tax by means of rules or orders to be made under the law by any authority, the law shall provide for the previous consent of the President being obtained to the making of any such rule or order.
key_terms: default exemption of inter-State river/river-valley authority water-and-electricity operations from pre-existing State tax laws
State Legislature's power to newly impose such taxes, but only with Presidential assent (reservation mechanism)

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 288 protects inter-State river/river-valley regulatory authorities (bodies established under existing law or Parliamentary law to regulate/develop an inter-State river or river-valley) from pre-Constitution State tax laws touching their water/electricity operations — the default is exemption unless the President orders otherwise — while still letting a State Legislature impose a fresh tax on such operations going forward, but only through a law reserved for and receiving the President's assent (and any rate-fixing rules under that law also need the President's prior consent).
essential_elements: Clause (1) is a default exemption specifically for pre-existing (pre-26 January 1950) State tax laws as applied to inter-State river/river-valley authorities' water/electricity activities — the President can lift this default exemption by order.

The Explanation broadly defines 'law of a State in force' to include dormant/unrepealed pre-Constitution laws even if not currently operative in all areas — closing a potential loophole where a technically-unrepealed-but-inactive law might otherwise escape the exemption's scope.

Clause (2) is forward-looking: a State Legislature may impose a fresh tax on such authorities' water/electricity operations, but such a law only takes effect after Presidential reservation-and-assent (the Article 200 reservation mechanism, applied here as a mandatory precondition rather than the Governor's discretion) — and even subordinate rate-fixing rules/orders under that law need the President's prior consent.

This Article specifically concerns inter-State river/river-valley regulatory authorities (like the kind Article 262 and the Inter-State River Water Disputes Act contemplate) — not electricity/water generally, which is covered by the more general State List/Concurrent List taxing powers.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Article 288 directly connects back to Article 262 (Part XI, already committed) and the broader inter-State river-water-dispute framework — protecting the fiscal viability of bodies like river-valley development authorities from being taxed into dysfunction by individual riparian States, a recurring source of Centre-State and inter-State friction over projects spanning multiple States.

The double-layered Presidential-assent requirement (both for the taxing law itself and for any subordinate rate-fixing rules/orders under it) is unusually strict compared to ordinary Article 200 reservation — reflecting the sensitivity of taxing bodies whose operations span multiple States' interests.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 288 as a specialized fiscal-protection provision for inter-State river/river-valley authorities — connect it back to Article 262's dispute-adjudication framework in Part XI, and note its unusually strict double Presidential-consent requirement (for both the taxing law and any subordinate rate-fixing rules).

sections.title: Exemption of property and income of a State from Union taxation
sections.raw_text:
289. Exemption of property and income of a State from Union taxation.—(1) The property and income of a State shall be exempt from Union taxation.
(2) Nothing in clause (1) shall prevent the Union from imposing, or authorising the imposition of, any tax to such extent, if any, as Parliament may by law provide in respect of a trade or business of any kind carried on by, or on behalf of, the Government of a State, or any operations connected therewith, or any property used or occupied for the purposes of such trade or business, or any income accruing or arising in connection therewith.
(3) Nothing in clause (2) shall apply to any trade or business, or to any class of trade or business, which Parliament may by law declare to be incidental to the ordinary functions of Government.
key_terms: general State-property/income exemption from Union taxation
Parliament's power to tax State government trade/business activity
'ordinary functions of Government' carve-out excluding incidental trade/business from Union taxation

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 289 is the mirror image of Article 285: a State's property and income are generally exempt from Union taxation, but Parliament may by law tax a State Government's trade or business activities (and related property/income) specifically — unless Parliament itself declares that particular trade or business to be an 'ordinary function of Government,' in which case even that carve-out taxing power doesn't apply.
essential_elements: Clause (1) sets the general rule: State property and income are immune from Union taxation.

Clause (2) carves out an exception letting Parliament tax a State Government's trade/business operations (and connected property/income) — but only 'to such extent, if any, as Parliament may by law provide,' meaning the exception requires affirmative Parliamentary legislation to activate, not automatic.

Clause (3) is a further carve-back on the carve-out: even trade/business activity would otherwise be taxable under clause (2), Parliament can declare specific trades/businesses (or classes of them) to be 'incidental to the ordinary functions of Government,' removing them from clause (2)'s taxing scope entirely.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This three-layer structure (general exemption → trade/business exception → 'ordinary government function' exception-to-the-exception) generated significant Supreme Court litigation over where to draw the line between genuine sovereign/governmental functions and quasi-commercial State trading activity — e.g., cases addressing whether State-run transport undertakings, lotteries, or similar commercial-flavored State activities fall inside or outside the taxable trade/business category.

The Article works in tandem with Article 285 to create full reciprocal tax immunity between the two levels of government for genuinely governmental (non-commercial) property/income/activity, while leaving room for both levels' Parliament/Legislature to reach the other's genuinely commercial activity if they choose to legislate for it.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 289 as Article 285's mirror — property/income immunity is the default at both levels, but note Article 289's extra two-tier structure (trade/business exception, then 'ordinary government function' exception-to-the-exception) has no exact parallel in Article 285's simpler single-exception structure.

sections.title: Adjustment in respect of certain expenses and pensions
sections.raw_text:
290. Adjustment in respect of certain expenses and pensions.—Where under the provisions of this Constitution the expenses of any court or Commission, or the pension payable to or in respect of a person who has served before the commencement of this Constitution under the Crown in India or after such commencement in connection with the affairs of the Union or of a State, are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India or the Consolidated Fund of a State, then, if—
(a) in the case of a charge on the Consolidated Fund of India, the court or Commission serves any of the separate needs of a State, or the person has served wholly or in part in connection with the affairs of a State; or
(b) in the case of a charge on the Consolidated Fund of a State, the court or Commission serves any of the separate needs of the Union or another State, or the person has served wholly or in part in connection with the affairs of the Union or another State,
there shall be charged on and paid out of the Consolidated Fund of the State or, as the case may be, the Consolidated Fund of India or the Consolidated Fund of the other State, such contribution in respect of the expenses or pension as may be agreed, or as may in default of agreement be determined by an arbitrator to be appointed by the Chief Justice of India.
key_terms: cross-reimbursement of shared court/Commission expenses and pensions between Union and States
agreement-or-Chief-Justice-appointed-arbitrator mechanism

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 290 ensures fair cost-sharing where a court's, Commission's, or pensioner's service benefits more than one government: if a body/person's expenses or pension are charged on one government's Consolidated Fund but that body/person actually serves (or served) another government's separate needs too, the benefiting government must contribute its fair share — by agreement, or, failing agreement, as determined by an arbitrator appointed by the Chief Justice of India (the same dispute-resolution mechanism used elsewhere in Articles 257(4) and 258(3)).
essential_elements: Covers two distinct categories: expenses of a court/Commission serving multiple governments' needs, and pensions of persons who served under the Crown pre-Constitution or the Union/States post-Constitution across more than one government.

Clause (a) handles the Union-Fund-charged, State-benefiting scenario; clause (b) handles the State-Fund-charged, Union-or-other-State-benefiting scenario — a fully reciprocal cross-charging structure.
The contribution amount is primarily consensual ('as may be agreed'), with Chief-Justice-of-India-appointed arbitration as the default dispute-resolution mechanism only if agreement fails.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This Article reuses the identical 'agreement, or Chief Justice of India appoints an arbitrator' dispute-resolution formula seen in Articles 257(4) and 258(3) (Part XI, already committed) — a recurring pattern for Union-State cost-sharing disputes throughout the Constitution, reflecting a deliberate preference for judicial-branch-appointed neutral arbitration over political/executive dispute resolution in these fiscal contexts.

In practice this Article most commonly applies to shared judicial infrastructure (e.g., a High Court serving a Union Territory alongside a State) and pension liabilities for officials who transferred between Union and State service, or who served under the pre-Constitution Crown administration.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 290 as the general cross-reimbursement rule for shared court/Commission/pension costs — recognize its 'agreement, or CJI-appointed arbitrator' formula as the same recurring dispute-resolution pattern already seen in Articles 257(4) and 258(3), rather than a new or unique mechanism.

sections.title: Annual payment to certain Devaswom Funds
sections.raw_text: 290A. Annual payment to certain Devaswom Funds.—A sum of forty-six lakhs and fifty thousand rupees shall be charged on, and paid out of, the Consolidated Fund of the State of Kerala every year to the Travancore Devaswom Fund; and a sum of thirteen lakhs and fifty thousand rupees shall be charged on, and paid out of, the Consolidated Fund of the State of Tamil Nadu every year to the Devaswom Fund established in that State for the maintenance of Hindu temples and shrines in the territories transferred to that State on the 1st day of November, 1956, from the State of Travancore-Cochin.
key_terms: fixed annual Devaswom Fund payments charged on Kerala's and Tamil Nadu's Consolidated Funds

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 290A (added by the Seventh Amendment, 1956) is a highly specific, fixed-sum provision mandating annual charged payments from the Consolidated Funds of Kerala (₹46.5 lakhs) and Tamil Nadu (₹13.5 lakhs) to Devaswom Funds — bodies responsible for maintaining Hindu temples and shrines in territories that were part of the former princely State of Travancore-Cochin before its territory was reorganized between Kerala and Tamil Nadu in 1956.
essential_elements: Both payments are charged expenditure — automatically payable each year without needing a fresh annual appropriation vote, like other 'charged on the Consolidated Fund' items throughout the Constitution.

The specific rupee amounts (₹46,50,000 to Kerala's Travancore Devaswom Fund; ₹13,50,000 to Tamil Nadu's corresponding Devaswom Fund) are fixed directly in the constitutional text itself, not left to ordinary legislation.

The historical trigger is the 1 November 1956 States Reorganisation transfer of certain Travancore-Cochin territories to the then-Madras State (now Tamil Nadu) — the provision ensures temple-maintenance funding continuity across that territorial reorganization.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is one of the Constitution's most narrowly tailored, region-and-institution-specific provisions — comparable in character to Article 273's now-spent jute-export-duty grants, but unlike Article 273, Article 290A remains fully live and operative today with no sunset clause.

It illustrates that the Constitution occasionally embeds highly particular, non-generalizable historical settlements (here, protecting specific religious-endowment funding arrangements disrupted by the 1956 States Reorganisation) directly into constitutional text rather than leaving them to ordinary State legislation — making amendment (not mere repeal by State law) the only way to alter these figures.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 290A as a narrow but permanently operative historical-settlement provision protecting specific Devaswom (temple) fund payments across the Kerala/Tamil Nadu post-1956-reorganization boundary — contrast with Article 273's similar-flavored but now-expired jute-export-duty grants to see how some such settlements were designed as permanent while others were designed as transitional.

sections.title: Borrowing by the Government of India
sections.raw_text: 292. Borrowing by the Government of India.—The executive power of the Union extends to borrowing upon the security of the Consolidated Fund of India within such limits, if any, as may from time to time be fixed by Parliament by law and to the giving of guarantees within such limits, if any, as may be so fixed.
key_terms: Union executive borrowing power secured on the Consolidated Fund of India
Parliament's power to fix borrowing/guarantee limits by law

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 292 grants the Union executive the power to borrow money on the security of the Consolidated Fund of India, and to give guarantees, but both powers are subject to whatever limits Parliament chooses to fix by law — meaning borrowing itself is an executive act, but Parliament retains ultimate control over how much debt/guarantee exposure the Union can take on.
essential_elements: The borrowing power is an executive power (exercised in the President's name per Article 53), not requiring a fresh Parliamentary vote for each loan — but it operates 'within such limits, if any, as may... be fixed by Parliament by law.'
The security for Union borrowing is the Consolidated Fund of India itself.
The same Article also covers the Union giving guarantees (e.g., guaranteeing a loan taken by another entity), again subject to Parliament-fixed limits.

If Parliament has fixed no limit ('if any'), the executive borrowing/guarantee power is, on the bare text, unlimited — though in practice fiscal responsibility legislation (like the FRBM Act) now constrains this.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management (FRBM) Act, 2003 is the modern Parliamentary law exercising this Article 292 limit-fixing power, setting fiscal deficit and debt targets that constrain how much the Union actually borrows in practice, even though Article 292 itself does not mandate any specific limit.

Because borrowing is executive (not requiring a fresh appropriation-style vote per loan), Article 292 illustrates a deliberate design choice: unlike expenditure (which needs the Article 114 Appropriation Act process), taking on debt is treated as an ordinary executive financial-management function, subject only to whatever ceiling Parliament chooses to legislate.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 292 as granting executive borrowing autonomy subject to a Parliament-settable ceiling — pair it with the FRBM Act, 2003 to see how that theoretical ceiling-setting power has actually been exercised in modern fiscal practice.

sections.title: Borrowing by States
sections.raw_text:
293. Borrowing by States.—(1) Subject to the provisions of this article, the executive power of a State extends to borrowing within the territory of India upon the security of the Consolidated Fund of the State within such limits, if any, as may from time to time be fixed by the Legislature of such State by law and to the giving of guarantees within such limits, if any, as may be so fixed.
(2) The Government of India may, subject to such conditions as may be laid down by or under any law made by Parliament, make loans to any State or, so long as any limits fixed under article 292 are not exceeded, give guarantees in respect of loans raised by any State, and any sums required for the purpose of making such loans shall be charged on the Consolidated Fund of India.
(3) A State may not without the consent of the Government of India raise any loan if there is still outstanding any part of a loan which has been made to the State by the Government of India or by its predecessor Government, or in respect of which a guarantee has been given by the Government of India or by its predecessor Government.
(4) A consent under clause (3) may be granted subject to such conditions, if any, as the Government of India may think fit to impose.
key_terms: State executive borrowing power secured on its own Consolidated Fund, capped by State Legislature
Union's power to lend to States or guarantee State loans
State's borrowing restricted (Union consent needed) while any Union loan/guarantee remains outstanding

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 293 is the State-level mirror of Article 292 (a State may borrow on the security of its own Consolidated Fund, within limits its own Legislature fixes) but adds a crucial extra layer: the Union may itself lend money to States or guarantee their loans, and — critically — once a State has any outstanding Union loan or Union-guaranteed loan, it cannot raise any further loan at all without the Union Government's consent, giving the Union a powerful practical lever over heavily-indebted-to-the-Centre States' fiscal autonomy.
essential_elements: Clause (1) is the State-level borrowing power itself, mirroring Article 292 but capped by the State's own Legislature rather than Parliament.

Clause (2) lets the Union make loans to States or guarantee State-raised loans (subject to Parliament-made conditions and the Article 292 limits), with loan funds charged on the Consolidated Fund of India.

Clause (3) is the significant restriction: a State cannot raise any new loan (not just from the Union, but from any source) without Union consent, if any part of a prior Union loan or Union-guaranteed loan to that State remains outstanding.
Clause (4) lets the Union attach conditions to any consent it gives under clause (3) — giving it substantial negotiating leverage.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Clause (3)'s consent requirement is enormously significant in practice: because most States have had outstanding Union loans/guarantees for decades, nearly every State effectively needs continuous Union Government consent (formalized via annual/periodic 'Consent under Article 293(3)' letters) to access open-market borrowing at all — a major, structurally embedded Union lever over State fiscal policy that goes well beyond what a casual reading of the Article's borrowing-power framing might suggest.

This consent mechanism has been a recurring point of Centre-State fiscal-federalism friction, since the Union can (and has, in various periods) attach policy conditions unrelated to debt sustainability as a precondition for Article 293(3) consent, effectively giving the Union informal policy leverage over States via their borrowing needs.

Following FRBM-style fiscal legislation at both Union and State levels, this Article's consent mechanism increasingly operates alongside statutory fiscal-deficit ceilings, layering a second (constitutional) control on top of a first (statutory) one.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 293 as granting States formal borrowing autonomy in clause (1), then immediately note how clauses (2)-(4) practically subordinate that autonomy to Union consent wherever any Union loan/guarantee is outstanding — this consent mechanism is one of the more consequential, under-appreciated levers of Union fiscal control over the States.

sections.title: Succession to property, assets, rights, liabilities and obligations in certain cases
sections.raw_text:
294. Succession to property, assets, rights, liabilities and obligations in certain cases.—As from the commencement of this Constitution—
(a) all property and assets which immediately before such commencement were vested in His Majesty for the purposes of the Government of the Dominion of India and all property and assets which immediately before such commencement were vested in His Majesty for the purposes of the Government of each Governor's Province shall vest respectively in the Union and the corresponding State, and
(b) all rights, liabilities and obligations of the Government of the Dominion of India and of the Government of each Governor's Province, whether arising out of any contract or otherwise, shall be the rights, liabilities and obligations respectively of the Government of India and the Government of each corresponding State,
subject to any adjustment made or to be made by reason of the creation before the commencement of this Constitution of the Dominion of Pakistan or of the Provinces of West Bengal, East Bengal, West Punjab and East Punjab.
key_terms: automatic Crown-to-Union/State succession of property, assets, rights, liabilities, obligations at commencement
adjustments carved out for Partition-related territorial creation

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 294 is a foundational transitional provision ensuring legal continuity at independence's constitutional culmination: all property/assets that were vested in the British Crown (His Majesty) for the Dominion of India Government's or a Governor's Province's purposes automatically vest in the Union or the corresponding State respectively from 26 January 1950, and all of the old Dominion/Provincial Governments' contractual and other rights/liabilities/obligations likewise automatically become the new Union's/State's rights/liabilities/obligations — subject to adjustments needed because of Partition (the creation of Pakistan and the split of Bengal/Punjab).
essential_elements: Clause (a) transfers property/assets: Dominion-of-India-level Crown property vests in the Union; Governor's-Province-level Crown property vests in the corresponding State.

Clause (b) transfers rights/liabilities/obligations (contractual or otherwise) on the same Dominion-to-Union, Province-to-State mapping — ensuring no legal vacuum in existing contracts, debts, or obligations at the constitutional transition.

The whole succession is expressly 'subject to any adjustment made or to be made' because of Partition — recognizing that some pre-Constitution property/rights/liabilities needed special handling given the division into India and Pakistan and the splitting of Bengal and Punjab.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This Article (along with Article 295, 296) forms a trio of 'succession' provisions handling different categories of pre-Constitution property/rights transfer — 294 handles the core Dominion-of-India/Governor's-Province succession, while 295 separately handles former princely-State (Part B States) succession, reflecting India's more complex post-independence integration of both directly-British-ruled and princely-State territories.

These provisions have overwhelmingly exhausted their operative significance today (three-quarters of a century after 1950) but remain occasionally relevant in long-running litigation over historical property titles or pre-Constitution contractual obligations where lineage of legal succession must be traced.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 294 as the general Crown-to-Union/State succession rule for the directly-British-administered parts of pre-independence India — contrast it with Article 295's separate, differently-structured succession rule for former princely States (Part B States) covered next.

sections.title: Succession to property, assets, rights, liabilities and obligations in other cases
sections.raw_text:
295. Succession to property, assets, rights, liabilities and obligations in other cases.—(1) As from the commencement of this Constitution—
(a) all property and assets which immediately before such commencement were vested in any Indian State corresponding to a State specified in Part B of the First Schedule shall vest in the Union, if the purposes for which such property and assets were held immediately before such commencement will thereafter be purposes of the Union relating to any of the matters enumerated in the Union List, and
(b) all rights, liabilities and obligations of the Government of any Indian State corresponding to a State specified in Part B of the First Schedule, whether arising out of any contract or otherwise, shall be the rights, liabilities and obligations of the Government of India, if the purposes for which such rights were acquired or liabilities or obligations were incurred before such commencement will thereafter be purposes of the Government of India relating to any of the matters enumerated in the Union List,
subject to any agreement entered into in that behalf by the Government of India with the Government of that State.
(2) Subject as aforesaid, the Government of each State specified in Part B of the First Schedule shall, as from the commencement of this Constitution, be the successor of the Government of the corresponding Indian State as regards all property and assets and all rights, liabilities and obligations, whether arising out of any contract or otherwise, other than those referred to in clause (1).
key_terms: purpose-based Union-vs-Part-B-State succession test for former princely-State property/rights
residual/default succession to the corresponding Part B State for everything else

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 295 handles the succession of property, assets, rights, liabilities, and obligations from the former princely (Indian) States that became Part B States — using a purpose-based test: if the property/right's purpose would thereafter serve a Union List matter, it vests in/becomes the Union's; everything else defaults to the corresponding Part B State as the former princely State's general successor.
essential_elements: Clause (1) is the Union-vesting test: former princely-State property/assets/rights/liabilities vest in the Union specifically where their purpose will thereafter relate to a Union List matter — a purpose-based, not blanket, transfer rule, also subject to any specific Government-of-India/former-princely-State agreement.

Clause (2) is the residual default: for everything not caught by clause (1), the corresponding Part B State is the general successor of the former princely State's government as regards all property/assets/rights/liabilities/obligations.

This differs structurally from Article 294's simpler Dominion-to-Union/Province-to-State mapping — here, a single former princely State's legal position gets split between the Union (Union-List-purpose items) and the corresponding new State (everything else).
exceptions_and_qualifications: 'Part B of the First Schedule' States refers to the former princely-State-based units under the original 1950 constitutional classification (States were classified Part A/B/C) — this classification itself was abolished by the States Reorganisation Act, 1956, making this Article now purely historical/transitional in current application, relevant chiefly to legacy litigation over princely-era property or obligations.

The purpose-based split test in clause (1) reflects the practical complexity of princely-State integration compared to directly-British-administered territory — princely states often held assets/rights serving what would become both Union-level functions (defense, foreign relations related infrastructure) and ordinary State-level functions, requiring this more nuanced allocation rule.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 295 alongside Article 294 as the second half of the succession-provision pair — 294 covers directly-British-administered Dominion/Province succession, while 295 covers the more complex former-princely-State (Part B State) succession using a purpose-based Union/State split test, now of primarily historical relevance following the 1956 States Reorganisation.

sections.title: Property accruing by escheat or lapse or as bona vacantia
sections.raw_text:
296. Property accruing by escheat or lapse or as bona vacantia.—Subject as hereinafter provided, any property in the territory of India which, if this Constitution had not come into operation, would have accrued to His Majesty or, as the case may be, to the Ruler of an Indian State by escheat or lapse, or as bona vacantia for want of a rightful owner, shall, if it is property situate in a State, vest in such State, and shall, in any other case, vest in the Union:
Provided that any property which at the date when it would have so accrued to His Majesty or to the Ruler of an Indian State was in the possession or under the control of the Government of India or the Government of a State shall, according as the purposes for which it was then used or held were purposes of the Union or of a State, vest in the Union or in that State.
Explanation.—In this article, the expressions "Ruler" and "Indian State" have the same meanings as in article 363.
key_terms: escheat/lapse/bona vacantia property vesting in the State (if State-situated) or Union (otherwise)
possession-and-purpose-based proviso overriding the general situs rule

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 296 modernizes the ancient doctrine of escheat (property reverting to the sovereign when an owner dies without heirs or a valid will) and bona vacantia (ownerless property) for the constitutional era: property that would have gone to the Crown or a princely Ruler under the old law now vests in the State where it's located, or in the Union if not located within any State — subject to a proviso that property already in a government's possession for a specific Union or State purpose instead follows that purpose, not mere geography.
essential_elements: The general rule is situs-based: escheat/lapse/bona-vacantia property vests in the State where it is physically situated, or in the Union if it's not situated in any State (e.g., in a Union Territory).

The proviso overrides the general situs rule where the property was already in a government's possession/control for a specific purpose at the relevant date — there, purpose (Union vs. State) controls over mere location.

The Explanation cross-references Article 363's definitions of 'Ruler' and 'Indian State,' tying this Article into the broader constitutional framework governing former princely rulers' rights (also relevant to the now-repealed privy purse provisions).
exceptions_and_qualifications: This Article remains fully live and practically significant today — it is the constitutional basis for the modern law of escheat/bona vacantia in India, governing what happens to a deceased person's property when they die intestate with no legal heirs (a recurring, non-merely-historical property-law scenario), with State Governments (or the Union, for Union Territory property) as the ultimate successor-in-title.

Unlike Articles 294-295 (which are largely spent, historical transitional provisions), Article 296 continues to operate as an ordinary, ongoing rule of property devolution, illustrating that not everything in this Chapter III cluster is purely transitional.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 296 as a still-live, ongoing rule of Indian property law (not a spent historical transitional provision like Articles 294-295) — it directly answers who inherits genuinely ownerless property today: the State by default, the Union if not State-situated, or whichever government already held it for a specific purpose per the proviso.

sections.title: Things of value within territorial waters or continental shelf and resources of the exclusive economic zone to vest in the Union
sections.raw_text:
297. Things of value within territorial waters or continental shelf and resources of the exclusive economic zone to vest in the Union.—(1) All lands, minerals and other things of value underlying the ocean within the territorial waters, or the continental shelf, or the exclusive economic zone, of India shall vest in the Union and be held for the purposes of the Union.
(2) All other resources of the exclusive economic zone of India shall also vest in the Union and be held for the purposes of the Union.
(3) The limits of the territorial waters, the continental shelf, the exclusive economic zone, and other maritime zones, of India shall be such as may be specified, from time to time, by or under any law made by Parliament.
key_terms: Union ownership of undersea lands/minerals/resources in territorial waters, continental shelf, EEZ
Parliament's power to specify maritime-zone limits

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 297 (substituted by the 40th Amendment, 1976) vests all undersea lands, minerals, and other things of value within India's territorial waters, continental shelf, and exclusive economic zone (EEZ), along with all other EEZ resources, exclusively in the Union — reflecting that maritime/offshore resources are a national, not State, asset — with Parliament empowered to define the precise geographic limits of these maritime zones by law.
essential_elements: Clause (1) covers physical undersea resources — lands, minerals, and other things of value — underlying the ocean within territorial waters, continental shelf, or the EEZ, all vesting in the Union.

Clause (2) is a catch-all extending Union vesting to 'all other resources' of the EEZ beyond the physical undersea items covered by clause (1) — e.g., fisheries and other living/non-mineral resources.

Clause (3) delegates to Parliament the power to specify (and revise) the actual geographic limits of territorial waters, continental shelf, EEZ, and other maritime zones — implemented via the Territorial Waters, Continental Shelf, Exclusive Economic Zone and other Maritime Zones Act, 1976.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is the constitutional foundation for India's offshore oil/gas exploration and production regime (e.g., ONGC's offshore operations) and its maritime fisheries/EEZ resource management — since these are exclusively Union assets, no coastal State can claim ownership of or royalty rights over offshore mineral/hydrocarbon resources merely because they lie geographically closer to that State's coast.

The Article was substituted (not merely amended) by the 40th Amendment in 1976, the same year Parliament enacted the Maritime Zones Act giving concrete effect to India's EEZ claims under international law (consistent with the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea framework then developing) — a deliberate, coordinated constitutional-and-statutory assertion of India's offshore sovereign rights.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 297 as the constitutional anchor for India's entire offshore-resource sovereignty regime — remember it vests both physical undersea resources (clause 1) and other EEZ resources like fisheries (clause 2) exclusively in the Union, with Parliament's Maritime Zones Act, 1976 giving the geographic limits concrete definition under clause (3).

sections.title: Power to carry on trade, etc.
sections.raw_text:
298. Power to carry on trade, etc.—The executive power of the Union and of each State shall extend to the carrying on of any trade or business and to the acquisition, holding and disposal of property and the making of contracts for any purpose:
Provided that—
(a) the said executive power of the Union shall, in so far as such trade or business or such purpose is not one with respect to which Parliament may make laws, be subject in each State to legislation by the State; and
(b) the said executive power of each State shall, in so far as such trade or business or such purpose is not one with respect to which the State Legislature may make laws, be subject to legislation by Parliament.
key_terms: executive power to trade, acquire/hold/dispose property, and contract, held by both Union and States
reciprocal subjection to the other level's legislation where the underlying purpose is outside the actor's own legislative competence

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 298 (substituted by the Seventh Amendment, 1956) confirms both the Union and every State's executive power extends to carrying on trade/business and to acquiring, holding, and disposing of property and making contracts for any purpose — but where that trade/business/purpose falls outside the acting government's own legislative competence, its executive action in that field remains subject to the other level's legislative override (State legislation can constrain Union executive action within that State on non-Union-List matters, and Parliament can constrain State executive action on non-State-List matters).
essential_elements: The main body grants a broad, general executive power to both Union and States to trade, hold property, and contract for any purpose — deliberately not confined to matters within their respective legislative competence.

Proviso (a) limits the Union's exercise of this power within a State: where the Union's trade/business/purpose is not a Parliament-legislatable (Union List) matter, that State's own legislation can regulate/constrain the Union's executive action there.

Proviso (b) is the mirror: where a State's trade/business/purpose is not a State-Legislature-legislatable (State List) matter, Parliament's legislation can regulate/constrain that State's executive action.

This creates the same asymmetry as Article 298's sibling Article 289 (State trade/business taxable by Parliament) — executive trading power is broad, but the other level of government retains an overriding legislative check wherever the activity strays outside the actor's own legislative field.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This Article is the constitutional basis for governments (Union and State) running public-sector trading/commercial enterprises, holding property, and entering into ordinary commercial contracts even in fields beyond their strict legislative competence — explaining, for instance, how a State Government can operate a State Trading Corporation-style enterprise in a nominally Union List-adjacent field, subject to Parliament's overriding legislative check.

Read together with Article 299 (contract execution formalities) and Article 289 (State trade/business Union-taxability), this Article completes the practical toolkit for how governments function as commercial/property-holding/contracting actors, not merely as legislative/regulatory bodies.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 298 as the general executive trade/property/contract power for both Union and States, and always check its two provisos when a government trades or contracts in a field outside its own legislative competence — that's exactly when the other level's overriding legislative check under proviso (a) or (b) becomes relevant.

sections.title: Contracts
sections.raw_text:
299. Contracts.—(1) All contracts made in the exercise of the executive power of the Union or of a State shall be expressed to be made by the President, or by the Governor of the State, as the case may be, and all such contracts and all assurances of property made in the exercise of that power shall be executed on behalf of the President or the Governor by such persons and in such manner as he may direct or authorise.
(2) Neither the President nor the Governor shall be personally liable in respect of any contract or assurance made or executed for the purposes of this Constitution, or for the purposes of any enactment relating to the Government of India heretofore in force, nor shall any person making or executing any such contract or assurance on behalf of any of them be personally liable in respect thereof.
key_terms: mandatory 'expressed to be made by the President/Governor' formality for government contracts
personal-liability immunity for the President/Governor and contract-executing officials

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 299 lays down the mandatory formalities for government contracts: every contract made in exercise of Union or State executive power must be expressed as made by the President or Governor (as the nominal contracting party, reflecting that all executive action is formally the Head of State's/Head of the State's act) and executed by whichever person the President/Governor authorizes — and, importantly, neither the President/Governor personally, nor any official who executes such a contract on their behalf, bears personal liability for it.
essential_elements: Clause (1) has two distinct formal requirements: the contract must be 'expressed to be made by' the President/Governor, and it must be 'executed... by such persons and in such manner as he may direct or authorise' — both are treated by courts as conditions for a valid, enforceable government contract, not mere drafting formalities.

Clause (2) grants blanket personal-liability immunity: the President/Governor is never personally liable on a government contract, and neither is any official who executes a contract on their behalf — liability, if any, attaches to the Government (Union or State) as a juristic entity, not to the individual signatories.

The formality requirement in clause (1) exists precisely because clause (2) removes personal liability from individual officials — the strict formalities ensure there's always a clearly identifiable, accountable government (not merely an individual official) bound by the contract.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Supreme Court jurisprudence (e.g., a long line of cases starting with early post-independence decisions) has firmly held that non-compliance with Article 299(1)'s formalities renders a purported government contract void and unenforceable against the Government — even where all parties otherwise intended to be bound — making this one of the most practically consequential formality requirements a contract-drafting practitioner dealing with government contracts must observe, since informal assurances or contracts not properly 'expressed' and 'executed' as required create serious enforceability risk.

Courts have carved out limited equitable relief (e.g., under Section 70 of the Indian Contract Act, for quasi-contractual restitution) for parties who performed under a defectively-formalized government contract, but this is a narrower, less certain remedy than a properly formed and enforceable contract would provide — reinforcing why strict compliance with Article 299(1) matters practically, not just formally.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 299 as imposing strict, court-enforced formalities on government contracting — as a drafting practitioner, always verify a government contract is expressed as made by the President/Governor and executed by a duly authorized person, since defective compliance risks total unenforceability against the Government, with only narrow quasi-contractual remedies as a fallback.

sections.title: Suits and proceedings
sections.raw_text:
300. Suits and proceedings.—(1) The Government of India may sue or be sued by the name of the Union of India and the Government of a State may sue or be sued by the name of the State and may, subject to any provisions which may be made by Act of Parliament or of the Legislature of such State enacted by virtue of powers conferred by this Constitution, sue or be sued in relation to their respective affairs in the like cases as the Dominion of India and the corresponding Provinces or the corresponding Indian States might have sued or been sued if this Constitution had not been enacted.
(2) If at the commencement of this Constitution—
(a) any legal proceedings are pending to which the Dominion of India is a party, the Union of India shall be deemed to be substituted for the Dominion in those proceedings; and
(b) any legal proceedings are pending to which a Province or an Indian State is a party, the corresponding State shall be deemed to be substituted for the Province or the Indian State in those proceedings.
key_terms: Government suability under 'Union of India'/State name
continuity of suability preserved from pre-Constitution Dominion/Province/Indian-State litigation practice
automatic party-substitution in pending pre-Constitution proceedings

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 300 establishes that governments can sue and be sued like ordinary legal persons — the Union of India and each State Government are suable under those specific names — and largely preserves pre-Constitution suability practice (i.e., governments remain suable in the same kinds of cases the old Dominion/Provincial/princely-State governments were), while clause (2) automatically substitutes the new Union/State as a party in any legal proceeding that was already pending against the old Dominion/Province/Indian State when the Constitution commenced.
essential_elements: Clause (1) is the core suability rule: 'Union of India' and 'State of [X]' are the proper legal names for suing or being sued, subject to whatever specific provisions Parliament or a State Legislature enacts under constitutional powers.

Clause (1) also carries forward historical continuity: the scope of suability mirrors what applied to the Dominion of India and the corresponding Provinces/Indian States before the Constitution — meaning this Article did not create suability from scratch but preserved and continued a pre-existing legal capacity.

Clause (2)(a)-(b) is a procedural continuity mechanism: pending legal proceedings against the old Dominion of India, or against a Province/Indian State, automatically continue with the new Union of India or corresponding State substituted as the party — no fresh suit or re-filing needed.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This Article is the constitutional root of the near-universal Indian litigation practice of naming 'Union of India' as a respondent/defendant in writ petitions and civil suits against the Central Government — any CPC practitioner drafting a plaint or petition against the Central Government cites this Article (implicitly, via the practice it establishes) when naming the Union of India as the proper party.

Government suability under Article 300 is not unlimited — it operates 'subject to' sovereign-immunity-type principles historically recognized at common law for genuinely sovereign/governmental functions (a doctrine substantially narrowed but not entirely eliminated by later Supreme Court jurisprudence on State tortious liability), so the availability of a suit against the Government still depends on the nature of the underlying claim.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 300 as the constitutional basis for naming 'Union of India' or a specific State as a litigant — directly relevant background for any civil-procedure practitioner (recall the CPC's own party-naming and substitution rules) drafting proceedings against government entities, and note clause (2)'s automatic party-substitution mechanism for any proceeding that predates the Constitution itself.

sections.title: Persons not to be deprived of property save by authority of law
sections.raw_text: 300A. Persons not to be deprived of property save by authority of law.—No person shall be deprived of his property save by authority of law.
key_terms: constitutional (statutory, not fundamental-right) property-deprivation protection requiring legal authority

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 300A (inserted by the 44th Amendment, 1978, forming a new Chapter IV — Right to Property) provides that no person can be deprived of their property except by authority of law — a deliberately downgraded successor to the original fundamental right to property (formerly Articles 19(1)(f) and 31, both repealed by the same 44th Amendment), now a mere 'constitutional right' rather than a fundamental right, meaning it can be enforced but is not subject to the same heightened judicial-review standard or direct Article 32 Supreme Court writ remedy that fundamental rights enjoy.
essential_elements: The right protected is narrow and purely procedural on its face: deprivation must be 'by authority of law' — i.e., there must be a valid law authorizing it, but the Article itself does not require 'just compensation' or substantive fairness in the way the pre-1978 fundamental right to property did.

This Article sits in its own standalone Chapter IV of Part XII (added specifically for this single Article), reflecting the deliberate, self-conscious constitutional demotion of property rights from Part III fundamental-rights status to this weaker Part XII/Article 300A form.

Because it is not a fundamental right, a person alleging Article 300A violation generally cannot invoke the Article 32 direct-Supreme-Court-writ remedy (though Article 226 High Court writ jurisdiction remains available, and ordinary civil suits are also available).
exceptions_and_qualifications: Despite being merely a 'constitutional' (not 'fundamental') right, the Supreme Court has in more recent jurisprudence (e.g., cases from the 2010s-2020s) meaningfully strengthened Article 300A's substantive content, holding that 'authority of law' must be a valid, non-arbitrary law, and in various cases treating uncompensated or unreasonably delayed government acquisition of property as an Article 300A violation — softening (though not eliminating) the original 1978 downgrade's practical effect over time.

This Article must always be read alongside Article 31A/31B/31C (Part III, if committed — the Ninth Schedule/land-reform-protective provisions) and the land acquisition statutory framework (now the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013) to fully understand contemporary property-deprivation law in India, since Article 300A alone states only the bare 'authority of law' requirement without prescribing compensation standards.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 300A as the constitutional right to property's much-diminished modern form — remember it was deliberately demoted from a Part III fundamental right (formerly Articles 19(1)(f)/31, both repealed in 1978) to this narrower Part XII provision, though later Supreme Court jurisprudence has partially reinforced its substantive teeth over time.

sections.title: Freedom of trade, commerce and intercourse
sections.raw_text: 301. Freedom of trade, commerce and intercourse.—Subject to the other provisions of this Part, trade, commerce and intercourse throughout the territory of India shall be free.
key_terms: nationwide constitutional guarantee of free trade, commerce, and intercourse, subject to Part XIII's own qualifications

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 301 lays down India's constitutional 'common market' guarantee: trade, commerce, and intercourse throughout Indian territory shall be free — meaning neither internal customs barriers nor unreasonable State/Union restrictions can fragment India's economy into isolated trading zones — but this freedom is expressly made 'subject to the other provisions of this Part,' meaning Articles 302-307's specific restriction-permitting powers qualify rather than override this general guarantee.
essential_elements: The freedom guaranteed spans three overlapping concepts: 'trade,' 'commerce,' and 'intercourse' — broadly interpreted by courts to cover the movement of goods, persons, and economic activity throughout Indian territory, not merely formal commercial transactions.
The freedom is nationwide/inter-territorial in character — its central target is barriers between States/regions, not (primarily) purely local regulation with no inter-State dimension.

The opening qualifier 'subject to the other provisions of this Part' is critical: Article 301 does not stand alone as an absolute guarantee — it must always be read together with Articles 302-307, which authorize various restrictions.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The landmark Atiabari Tea Co. v. State of Assam (1961) and Automobile Transport (Rajasthan) v. State of Rajasthan (1962) decisions established that Article 301 targets only restrictions that directly and immediately impede the free movement of trade (not every tax or regulation that merely touches trade incidentally) — a 'direct and immediate effect' test that has shaped decades of subsequent litigation over State taxation and regulatory measures.

The Supreme Court's 9-judge bench in Jindal Stainless Ltd. v. State of Haryana (2016) significantly refined this doctrine, holding that non-discriminatory compensatory taxes do not violate Article 301 at all, and that only discriminatory or protectionist barriers (not mere revenue-raising taxes with no protectionist intent) genuinely offend the freedom of trade guarantee — considerably narrowing the earlier 'direct and immediate effect' test's practical reach.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 301 as the opening, general-principle provision of a five-Article interlocking scheme (301-305, plus the enforcement Article 307) — never analyze Article 301 in isolation from Articles 302-305's restriction-permitting powers, and apply the Jindal Stainless (2016) discriminatory/protectionist-barrier test as the modern operative standard rather than the older, broader Atiabari 'direct and immediate effect' formulation.

sections.title: Power of Parliament to impose restrictions on trade, commerce and intercourse
sections.raw_text: 302. Power of Parliament to impose restrictions on trade, commerce and intercourse.—Parliament may by law impose such restrictions on the freedom of trade, commerce or intercourse between one State and another or within any part of the territory of India as may be required in the public interest.
key_terms: Parliament's public-interest-justified power to restrict inter-State/intra-territory trade freedom

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 302 lets Parliament impose restrictions on the Article 301 freedom of trade, commerce, and intercourse — both between States and within any part of India's territory — wherever required in the public interest, giving the Union legislature the primary, general power to qualify the trade-freedom guarantee for the whole country.
essential_elements: The restricting power belongs to Parliament alone under this specific Article (State Legislatures get their own, narrower restricting power under Article 304).
The restriction must be justified as 'required in the public interest' — a substantive, judicially reviewable standard, not an unlimited discretion.

The power covers both inter-State trade restrictions and restrictions 'within any part of the territory of India' — meaning Parliament's Article 302 power is not limited to cross-border/inter-State measures alone.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Article 302's 'public interest' restriction power is itself subject to Article 303's non-discrimination bar (discussed next) — Parliament cannot use Article 302 to give one State a preference over another or discriminate between States, except in the narrow scarcity-related circumstance Article 303(2) allows.

In practice, Article 302 restrictions are relatively rare compared to State-level Article 304 restrictions, since most day-to-day trade regulation affecting inter-State commerce (like State-level entry taxes, mandi/APMC regulations, or check-post requirements) has historically arisen at the State level, testing Article 304 rather than Article 302.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 302 as Parliament's general trade-restriction power, but always cross-check any purported Article 302 restriction against Article 303(1)'s discrimination bar — a 'public interest' restriction under 302 cannot itself become a preference/discrimination device between States except under Article 303(2)'s narrow scarcity exception.

sections.title: Restrictions on the legislative powers of the Union and of the States with regard to trade and commerce
sections.raw_text:
303. Restrictions on the legislative powers of the Union and of the States with regard to trade and commerce.—(1) Notwithstanding anything in article 302, neither Parliament nor the Legislature of a State shall have power to make any law giving, or authorising the giving of, any preference to one State over another, or making, or authorising the making of, any discrimination between one State and another, by virtue of any entry relating to trade and commerce in any of the Lists in the Seventh Schedule.
(2) Nothing in clause (1) shall prevent Parliament from making any law giving, or authorising the giving of, any preference or making, or authorising the making of, any discrimination if it is declared by such law that it is necessary to do so for the purpose of dealing with a situation arising from scarcity of goods in any part of the territory of India.
key_terms: blanket bar on Parliament/State trade-and-commerce laws that prefer or discriminate between States
Parliament-only scarcity exception, requiring express legislative declaration of necessity

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 303 imposes a strict non-discrimination/non-preference rule on both Parliament and every State Legislature: neither may use any Seventh Schedule trade-and-commerce entry to make a law that prefers one State over another or discriminates between States — even Parliament's own Article 302 public-interest restriction power is expressly overridden by this bar — with a single, narrow exception letting Parliament (not States) legislate preference/discrimination specifically to address goods scarcity in part of India's territory, provided the law itself expressly declares that necessity.
essential_elements: Clause (1)'s bar operates 'notwithstanding anything in article 302' — meaning it overrides even Parliament's general public-interest restriction power, making non-discrimination a stronger, near-absolute constitutional principle within its scope.
The bar applies to both Parliament and State Legislatures equally — no level of government may prefer or discriminate between States via trade-and-commerce legislative entries.

Clause (2)'s exception is deliberately narrow and Parliament-only (States get no equivalent scarcity exception): it applies solely to addressing goods scarcity, and the law itself must expressly declare that the preference/discrimination is necessary for that purpose — a mandatory, judicially checkable self-declaration requirement, not an implied or inferred justification.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This Article reflects the Constituent Assembly's deliberate design choice to make India an economically unified 'common market' where the Centre cannot play favorites among States through ordinary trade legislation — a foundational commitment to inter-State economic equality distinct from (and stronger than) the general Article 301 freedom-of-trade guarantee.

The scarcity exception in clause (2) has historically been invoked in the context of essential-commodities legislation (like the Essential Commodities Act framework) permitting geographically differentiated distribution/rationing measures during shortages — but any such law must carry the express necessity declaration or risk being struck down under clause (1)'s general bar.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 303 as a stronger, near-absolute non-discrimination principle sitting above even Article 302's public-interest restriction power — remember the scarcity exception in clause (2) is available to Parliament only (never States) and requires an express statutory declaration of necessity, not merely a de facto scarcity-response effect.

sections.title: Restrictions on trade, commerce and intercourse among States
sections.raw_text:
304. Restrictions on trade, commerce and intercourse among States.—Notwithstanding anything in article 301 or article 303, the Legislature of a State may by law—
(a) impose on goods imported from other States or the Union territories any tax to which similar goods manufactured or produced in that State are subject, so, however, as not to discriminate between goods so imported and goods so manufactured or produced; and
(b) impose such reasonable restrictions on the freedom of trade, commerce or intercourse with or within that State as may be required in the public interest:
Provided that no Bill or amendment for the purposes of clause (b) shall be introduced or moved in the Legislature of a State without the previous sanction of the President.
key_terms: State's power to tax imported goods on par with local goods, non-discriminatorily
State's public-interest reasonable-restriction power, subject to mandatory Presidential prior sanction

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 304 grants State Legislatures two specific powers, notwithstanding Articles 301 and 303: first, to tax goods imported from other States/Union territories at the same rate as similar locally-produced goods (a non-discriminatory equalization tax, not a protectionist import tax), and second, to impose reasonable public-interest restrictions on trade/commerce/intercourse with or within that State — but any Bill for the second power requires the President's prior sanction before it can even be introduced in the State Legislature.
essential_elements: Clause (a) permits a State to tax imported goods, but strictly on a non-discriminatory, equal-treatment basis — the imported-goods tax rate cannot exceed what similar locally-manufactured/produced goods already bear; this is an anti-protectionism safeguard built directly into the taxing power itself.

Clause (b) is a general reasonable-restriction power for trade/commerce/intercourse 'with or within' the State, justified by public interest — narrower in formal scope than Parliament's Article 302 power (State-specific rather than nationwide) but requiring an extra procedural safeguard.

The proviso is a mandatory prior-sanction requirement specifically for clause (b) Bills (not clause (a) taxing Bills) — the President's sanction must be obtained before the Bill is even introduced or moved, not merely before it takes effect, making this a stronger procedural check than an assent-stage requirement.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Clause (a)'s 'discriminate' bar has generated extensive litigation testing whether a State tax scheme genuinely equalizes imported and local goods or covertly favors local production through exemptions, rebates, or differential administrative treatment — courts scrutinize the practical/economic effect, not just the formal tax rate, to detect disguised protectionism.

The Presidential-prior-sanction requirement for clause (b) Bills exists precisely because such restrictions could otherwise be used by a State to erect protectionist barriers against other States' trade — requiring Union-level vetting before the Bill even enters the legislative process, a stronger safeguard than the ordinary Article 200 assent-stage reservation mechanism used elsewhere.

Post-GST (101st Amendment), clause (a)'s practical significance for goods taxation has substantially diminished since State-level differential goods taxation is now largely subsumed into the unified GST framework — but the Article remains textually intact and potentially relevant to non-GST-covered goods or other trade-restriction contexts.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 304 as the States' counterpart to Parliament's Article 302 power — note its two distinct sub-powers have different safeguards: clause (a)'s built-in non-discrimination requirement versus clause (b)'s external Presidential-prior-sanction requirement, and recognize clause (a)'s practical significance has shrunk considerably in the post-GST goods-taxation landscape.

sections.title: Saving of existing laws and laws providing for State monopolies
sections.raw_text: 305. Saving of existing laws and laws providing for State monopolies.—Nothing in articles 301 and 303 shall affect the provisions of any existing law except in so far as the President may by order otherwise direct; and nothing in article 301 shall affect the operation of any law made before the commencement of the Constitution (Fourth Amendment) Act, 1955, in so far as it relates to, or prevent Parliament or the Legislature of a State from making any law relating to, any such matter as is referred to in sub-clause (ii) of clause (6) of article 19.
key_terms: general savings of pre-Constitution existing laws from Articles 301/303, Presidential-order-overridable
specific savings protecting State-monopoly legislation from Article 301

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 305 (substituted by the Fourth Amendment, 1955) is a savings clause with two limbs: first, it generally protects any 'existing law' (pre-Constitution law) from being struck down under Articles 301 or 303's trade-freedom/non-discrimination principles, unless the President specifically orders otherwise; second, it specifically protects laws (whenever made, before or after the Fourth Amendment for the Article 19(6)(ii) category) establishing State monopolies in any trade/business/industry/service from Article 301 challenge, reflecting the Constitution's accommodation of State-run monopoly enterprises.
essential_elements: The first limb's general 'existing law' savings applies to both Articles 301 and 303, but the President retains power to lift the savings by order for any specific existing law — a case-by-case override mechanism.

The second limb specifically cross-references Article 19(6)(ii) — the fundamental-rights provision (Part III) permitting the State to carry on any trade/business/industry/service to the partial or complete exclusion of citizens (i.e., State monopolies) — and ensures Article 301's trade-freedom guarantee cannot be used to challenge legislation creating or continuing such State monopolies.

This second limb's protection extends beyond merely pre-1955 laws: it also 'prevent[s]... Parliament or the Legislature of a State from making any law relating to' such State-monopoly matters, meaning future State-monopoly legislation is also protected from Article 301 challenge, not just historical laws.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This Article explains the constitutional coexistence of India's historically extensive public-sector monopolies/near-monopolies (e.g., railways, and formerly banking, insurance, and various other sectors before liberalization) with the Article 301 free-trade guarantee — State monopoly creation is a deliberate carve-out, not an accidental gap, in the free-trade scheme.

The Article 19(6)(ii) cross-reference means this Article must be read together with Part III's fundamental-rights framework (specifically the reasonable-restrictions-on-trade provision) to fully understand its scope — it is one of relatively few Part XIII provisions that explicitly interlocks with a Part III fundamental right provision.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 305 as protecting two distinct categories from Article 301/303 challenge — general pre-Constitution existing laws (Presidential-order-overridable) and State-monopoly legislation specifically (protected via the Article 19(6)(ii) cross-reference, extending to future as well as past legislation) — and always trace the second limb back to Part III's Article 19(6)(ii) to fully understand this Article's scope.

sections.title: Appointment of authority for carrying out the purposes of articles 301 to 304
sections.raw_text: 307. Appointment of authority for carrying out the purposes of articles 301 to 304.—Parliament may by law appoint such authority as it considers appropriate for carrying out the purposes of articles 301, 302, 303 and 304, and confer on the authority so appointed such powers and such duties as it thinks necessary.
key_terms: Parliament's power to create an implementing/enforcement authority for the Part XIII trade-freedom scheme

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 307 lets Parliament establish, by law, a dedicated authority to carry out the purposes of Articles 301-304 (the core trade-freedom, restriction, and non-discrimination scheme), and to confer on that authority whatever powers and duties Parliament considers necessary — envisioning an institutional enforcement/oversight mechanism for India's internal common-market guarantee, though this power has famously never been exercised.
essential_elements: The authority-creation power is entirely discretionary ('Parliament may') — there is no constitutional mandate that such an authority actually be created.

The authority's purposes are tied specifically to Articles 301-304 (not 305-306) — i.e., enforcing/implementing the freedom-of-trade guarantee, the Parliament/State restriction powers, and the non-discrimination principle.
Parliament has full discretion over what powers/duties to confer on any such authority — the Article itself specifies no minimum institutional design.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Despite being in the Constitution since 1950, Parliament has never actually exercised this Article 307 power to create a dedicated trade-freedom-enforcement authority — meaning Part XIII's Article 301 guarantee has been enforced entirely through ordinary judicial review (the Atiabari/Automobile Transport/Jindal Stainless line of cases) rather than through any specialized administrative body, a notable and long-standing implementation gap.

This mirrors the similar non-implementation of the GST Council's Article 279A(11) dispute-mechanism mandate — both are examples of constitutionally-authorized-but-never-created institutional mechanisms in the fiscal/trade-federalism space, with courts filling the resulting gap through ordinary litigation instead.
