(3) Notwithstanding anything contained in clause (2), the number of seats reserved in the House of the People for the Scheduled Tribes in the autonomous districts of Assam shall bear to the total number of seats allotted to that State a proportion not less than the population of the Scheduled Tribes in the said autonomous districts bears to the total population of the State. Explanation.—In this article and in article 332, the expression "population" means the population as ascertained at the last preceding census of which the relevant figures have been published: Provided that the reference in this Explanation to the last preceding census of which the relevant figures have been published shall, until the relevant figures for the first census taken after the year 2026 have been published, be construed as a reference to the 2001 census.
key_terms: population-proportionate reservation of Lok Sabha seats for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes
separate reserved-seat category for Assam autonomous-district Scheduled Tribes
frozen-population-figure mechanism anchored to the 2001 census pending the first post-2026 census

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 330 mandates reserved Lok Sabha seats for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, with the number of reserved seats in each State/Union territory set roughly proportionate to that group's share of the population — Assam's autonomous-district Scheduled Tribes get their own separate reservation category. Crucially, for calculating these proportions, 'population' is frozen to the 2001 census figures until the first census after 2026 is published, deliberately decoupling reservation math from more recent (post-1971) population growth patterns across States.
essential_elements: Three reserved categories: (a) Scheduled Castes generally, (b) Scheduled Tribes excluding Assam's autonomous districts, (c) Scheduled Tribes within Assam's autonomous districts
Proportionality formula: reserved seats in a State/UT bear the same proportion to total seats as the relevant population bears to total population
Assam autonomous-district Scheduled Tribes get a clause (3) floor proportion, overriding the ordinary clause (2) formula
The population figure used is frozen to the 2001 census (via a chain of amendments) until the first census after 2026 is published
exceptions_and_qualifications: This population freeze — originally tied to the 1971 census and repeatedly extended (42nd, 84th, and later amendments) — was designed to avoid penalizing States that successfully controlled population growth with reduced political representation, and remains a live, actively-extended policy choice rather than a one-time historical figure
breakdown.how_to_read: Always check which census year is 'frozen' as the applicable population base at the time of the dispute — this Explanation has been amended multiple times to keep extending the freeze, so the operative reference point shifts with each constitutional amendment (currently 2001, pending the first census after 2026).

sections.title: Representation of the Anglo-Indian Community in the House of the People
sections.raw_text: Notwithstanding anything in article 81, the President may, if he is of opinion that the Anglo-Indian community is not adequately represented in the House of the People, nominate not more than two members of that community to the House of the People.
key_terms: President's discretionary power to nominate up to two Anglo-Indian members to the Lok Sabha

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 331 let the President nominate up to two members of the Anglo-Indian community to the House of the People whenever he judged that community inadequately represented through ordinary elections — an override of Article 81's normal composition rules for the Lok Sabha.
essential_elements: Nomination power is discretionary ('if he is of opinion'), not mandatory
Capped at a maximum of two nominated members
Overrides Article 81's ordinary House-of-the-People composition scheme ('notwithstanding anything in article 81')
exceptions_and_qualifications: This nomination mechanism, along with the parallel Article 333 State-level mechanism, was allowed to lapse: the 104th Amendment Act, 2019 discontinued Anglo-Indian nominations to the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies with effect from 25 January 2020, even though the underlying Article 331 text itself was not repealed outright — read together with Article 334's sunset clause
breakdown.how_to_read: A now-lapsed nomination power — confirm the 104th Amendment's 2020 cutoff before assuming Anglo-Indian nominations remain operative; the constitutional text persists but the practical nomination mechanism has ended.

sections.title: Reservation of seats for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in the Legislative Assemblies of the States
sections.raw_text: (1) Seats shall be reserved for the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes, except the Scheduled Tribes in the autonomous districts of Assam, in the Legislative Assembly of every State. (2) Seats shall be reserved also for the autonomous districts in the Legislative Assembly of the State of Assam. (3) The number of seats reserved for the Scheduled Castes or the Scheduled Tribes in the Legislative Assembly of any State under clause (1) shall bear, as nearly as may be, the same proportion to the total number of seats in the Assembly as the population of the Scheduled Castes in the State or of the Scheduled Tribes in the State or part of the State, as the case may be, in respect of which seats are so reserved, bears to the total population of the State. (3A) Notwithstanding anything contained in clause (3), until the taking effect, under article 170, of the re-adjustment, on the basis of the first census after the year 2026, of the number of seats in the Legislative Assemblies of the States of Arunachal Pradesh, Meghalaya, Mizoram and Nagaland, the seats which shall be reserved for the Scheduled Tribes in the Legislative Assembly of any such State shall be,— (a) if all the seats in the Legislative Assembly of such State in existence on the date of coming into force of the Constitution (Fifty-seventh Amendment) Act, 1987 (hereafter in this clause referred to as the existing Assembly) are held by members of the Scheduled Tribes, all the seats except one; (b) in any other case, such number of seats as bears to the total number of seats, a proportion not less than the number (as on the said date) of members belonging to the Scheduled Tribes in the existing Assembly bears to the total number of seats in the existing Assembly. (3B) Notwithstanding anything contained in clause (3), until the re-adjustment, under article 170, takes effect on the basis of the first census after the year 2026, of the number of seats in the Legislative Assembly of the State of Tripura, the seats which shall be reserved for the Scheduled Tribes in the Legislative Assembly shall be, such number of seats as bears to the total number of seats, a proportion not less than the number, as on the date of coming into force of the Constitution (Seventy-second Amendment) Act, 1992, of members belonging to the Scheduled Tribes in the Legislative Assembly in existence on the said date bears to the total number of seats in that Assembly. (4) The number of seats reserved for an autonomous district in the Legislative Assembly of the State of Assam shall bear to the total number of seats in that Assembly a proportion not less than the population of the district bears to the total population of the State. (5) The constituencies for the seats reserved for any autonomous district of Assam shall not comprise any area outside that district. (6) No person who is not a member of a Scheduled Tribe of any autonomous district of the State of Assam shall be eligible for election to the Legislative Assembly of the State from any constituency of that district: Provided that for elections to the Legislative Assembly of the State of Assam, the representation of the Scheduled Tribes and non-Scheduled Tribes in the constituencies included in the Bodoland Territorial Areas District, so notified, and existing prior to the constitution of Bodoland Territorial Areas District, shall be maintained.
key_terms: State-Assembly-level population-proportionate reservation mirroring Article 330's Lok Sabha scheme
near-total-existing-seats floor for Scheduled Tribe reservation in Arunachal Pradesh, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland pending post-2026 re-adjustment
parallel floor-proportion mechanism for Tripura's Legislative Assembly
Assam autonomous-district-exclusive constituency and candidacy restrictions, with a Bodoland Territorial Areas District representation-preservation proviso

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 332 replicates Article 330's population-proportionate reservation scheme at the State Legislative Assembly level for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, with several special mechanisms: Assam's autonomous districts get their own reserved seats restricted to that district's territory and open only to that district's Scheduled Tribe members; four North-Eastern States (Arunachal Pradesh, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland) and Tripura have special frozen floor-proportion formulas protecting near-total or high Scheduled Tribe representation until a future re-adjustment; and the Bodoland Territorial Areas District has its own proviso preserving pre-existing Scheduled Tribe/non-Scheduled Tribe seat representation patterns.
essential_elements: Clause (1)-(3): baseline population-proportionate SC/ST reservation formula, mirroring Article 330
Clause (3A): near-total (or high-floor) Scheduled Tribe seat protection for Arunachal Pradesh, Meghalaya, Mizoram, and Nagaland, frozen pending post-2026-census Article 170 re-adjustment
Clause (3B): a similar high-floor protection specifically for Tripura

Clauses (4)-(6): Assam autonomous-district-specific rules — proportionate reservation, geographically confined constituencies, and Scheduled-Tribe-only candidacy eligibility, with the Bodoland proviso preserving pre-existing representation patterns
exceptions_and_qualifications: The Bodoland Territorial Areas District proviso (inserted by the 90th Amendment, 2003) is a narrow exception preserving specific historical constituency representation patterns that predate the Bodoland district's own creation — it does not extend to other autonomous districts
breakdown.how_to_read: A dense article full of State-specific carve-outs — when analysing a specific State's Assembly reservation, first check whether that State falls under the general clause (3) formula or one of the special frozen-floor regimes (clause 3A for the four named North-Eastern States, clause 3B for Tripura, or clauses 4-6 for Assam's autonomous districts).

sections.title: Representation of the Anglo-Indian community in the Legislative Assemblies of the States
sections.raw_text: Notwithstanding anything in article 170, the Governor of a State may, if he is of opinion that the Anglo-Indian community needs representation in the Legislative Assembly of the State and is not adequately represented therein, nominate one member of that community to the Assembly.
key_terms: Governor's discretionary power to nominate one Anglo-Indian member to a State Legislative Assembly

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 333 mirrored Article 331 at the State level, letting a Governor nominate one Anglo-Indian community member to that State's Legislative Assembly whenever the Governor judged the community inadequately represented — overriding Article 170's normal Assembly composition rules.
essential_elements: Nomination power is discretionary ('if he is of opinion'), not mandatory
Capped at a single nominated member per State Assembly
Overrides Article 170's ordinary Legislative Assembly composition scheme
exceptions_and_qualifications: Like Article 331, this nomination mechanism was discontinued by the 104th Amendment Act, 2019 with effect from 25 January 2020, subject to Article 334's sunset/continuity proviso for sitting members
breakdown.how_to_read: Read together with Article 331 as the State-level twin of the Lok Sabha Anglo-Indian nomination power — both are now lapsed in practical operation following the 104th Amendment.

sections.title: Reservation of seats and special representation to cease after certain period
sections.raw_text: Notwithstanding anything in the foregoing provisions of this Part, the provisions of this Constitution relating to— (a) the reservation of seats for the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes in the House of the People and in the Legislative Assemblies of the States; and (b) the representation of the Anglo-Indian community in the House of the People and in the Legislative Assemblies of the States by nomination, shall cease to have effect on the expiration of a period of eighty years in respect of clause (a) and seventy years in respect of clause (b) from the commencement of this Constitution: Provided that nothing in this article shall affect any representation in the House of the People or in the Legislative Assembly of a State until the dissolution of the then existing House or Assembly, as the case may be.
key_terms: 80-year sunset clock for SC/ST seat reservation (Lok Sabha and State Assemblies)
70-year sunset clock (already expired) for Anglo-Indian nomination
existing-House/Assembly-continuity proviso preventing mid-term disruption

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 334 is the constitutional sunset clause for Part XVI's political-representation mechanisms: SC/ST seat reservation was originally meant to be temporary and is now set to expire after 80 years from the Constitution's 1950 commencement (repeatedly extended by amendment, most recently via the 104th Amendment, 2019, to 2030), while Anglo-Indian nomination's shorter 70-year clock has already run out (2020) and was not further extended. Either way, sitting reserved-seat or nominated members keep their seats until their current House/Assembly is dissolved — the cessation only bites at the next election/nomination cycle.
essential_elements: Clause (a)'s SC/ST reservation sunset: 80 years from commencement (i.e., 2030, per the 104th Amendment's extension)
Clause (b)'s Anglo-Indian nomination sunset: 70 years from commencement (i.e., 2020) — this clock was allowed to expire, discontinuing nominations
Proviso: cessation doesn't unseat sitting members mid-term; it only takes effect from the next dissolution of the House/Assembly onward
exceptions_and_qualifications: The differential treatment — SC/ST reservation repeatedly extended while Anglo-Indian nomination was allowed to lapse — reflects Parliament's 2019 policy judgment (via the 104th Amendment) that the Anglo-Indian community no longer needed a dedicated nomination mechanism, while SC/ST political reservation remained necessary
breakdown.how_to_read: Always check the current sunset date against the latest amendment before assuming reservation continues — the 80-year SC/ST figure has been extended multiple times since 1950 (originally 10 years, extended repeatedly to the present 80-year/2030 figure) and could in principle be extended again before it lapses.

sections.title: Claims of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes to services and posts
sections.raw_text: The claims of the members of the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes shall be taken into consideration, consistently with the maintenance of efficiency of administration, in the making of appointments to services and posts in connection with the affairs of the Union or of a State: Provided that nothing in this article shall prevent in making of any provision in favour of the members of the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes for relaxation in qualifying marks in any examination or lowering the standards of evaluation, for reservation in matters or promotion to any class or classes of services or posts in connection with the affairs of the Union or of a State.
key_terms: 'efficiency of administration' qualifier on SC/ST service-appointment consideration
express proviso authorizing relaxed qualifying marks/evaluation standards and promotion reservation for SC/ST candidates

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 335 requires that Scheduled Caste and Scheduled Tribe claims be taken into account in Union/State public service appointments, but frames this 'consistently with the maintenance of efficiency of administration' — historically read as a limiting principle on reservation policy. The proviso, added later, expressly clarifies that relaxed qualifying marks, lowered evaluation standards, and promotion-stage reservation for SC/ST candidates are not barred by that efficiency qualifier.
essential_elements: The main clause's efficiency-of-administration language qualifies, but does not eliminate, the duty to consider SC/ST claims in appointments
The proviso expressly protects examination-mark relaxation, evaluation-standard lowering, and promotion reservation from being challenged as inconsistent with the efficiency principle
exceptions_and_qualifications: Article 320(4) (Part XIV) already exempts Article 16(4) reservation-implementation matters and Article 335 matters from mandatory Public Service Commission consultation

The Supreme Court has read 'efficiency of administration' narrowly in later jurisprudence, treating it as compatible with substantial reservation rather than as an independent ceiling — most notably in the context of upholding promotion-quota schemes after the proviso's insertion
breakdown.how_to_read: Read the proviso as the operative, government-favouring gloss on an otherwise limiting main clause — post-amendment, Article 335 is now primarily cited to defend (not restrict) SC/ST reservation and relaxation measures in appointments and promotions, despite its efficiency-qualifier framing.

sections.title: Special provision for Anglo-Indian community in certain services
sections.raw_text: (1) During the first two years after the commencement of this Constitution, appointments of members of the Anglo-Indian community to posts in the railway, customs, postal and telegraph services of the Union shall be made on the same basis as immediately before the fifteenth day of August, 1947. During every succeeding period of two years, the number of posts reserved for the members of the said community in the said services shall, as nearly as possible, be less by ten per cent. than the numbers so reserved during the immediately preceding period of two years: Provided that at the end of ten years from the commencement of this Constitution all such reservations shall cease. (2) Nothing in clause (1) shall bar the appointment of members of the Anglo-Indian community to posts other than, or in addition to, those reserved for the community under that clause if such members are found qualified for appointment on merit as compared with the members of other communities.
key_terms: two-year step-down reservation of railway/customs/postal/telegraph posts for the Anglo-Indian community, capped at a ten-year total sunset

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 336 reserved a declining share of Union railway, customs, postal, and telegraph service posts for the Anglo-Indian community after Independence, tapering the reservation by ten percentage points every two years and extinguishing it entirely ten years after the Constitution's commencement (i.e., by 1960). The provision is now historically spent — its operative reservation window closed decades ago — but the constitutional text itself was never repealed.
essential_elements: Applied only to four specifically named Union services: railway, customs, postal, and telegraph
Reservation percentage stepped down by 10% every two-year period from the 1947 baseline
Absolute ten-year outer limit from the Constitution's commencement, after which all such reservations ceased regardless of the step-down math
exceptions_and_qualifications: Clause (2) preserved merit-based appointment of Anglo-Indians to non-reserved posts or in addition to reserved posts throughout, so the sunset only ended preferential reservation, not eligibility
breakdown.how_to_read: Read as a spent transitional provision, structurally similar to Article 306 and Article 314 in effect (though textually unrepealed) — useful chiefly as historical context for why Articles 331, 333, and 334 later needed their own separate, longer sunset clocks for Anglo-Indian political (rather than service) representation.

sections.title: Special provision with respect to educational grants for the benefit of Anglo-Indian community
sections.raw_text: During the first three financial years after the commencement of this Constitution, the same grants, if any, shall be made by the Union and by each State for the benefit of the Anglo-Indian community in respect of education as were made in the financial year ending on the thirty-first day of March, 1948. During every succeeding period of three years the grants may be less by ten per cent. than those for the immediately preceding period of three years: Provided that at the end of ten years from the commencement of this Constitution such grants, to the extent to which they are a special concession to the Anglo-Indian community, shall cease: Provided further that no educational institution shall be entitled to receive any grant under this article unless at least forty per cent. of the annual admissions therein are made available to members of communities other than the Anglo-Indian community.
key_terms: three-year step-down of Anglo-Indian-community educational grants, capped at a ten-year sunset, with a forty-percent other-community admission condition

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 337 preserved, for a limited transitional window, the pre-Independence level of Union and State educational grants specifically benefiting Anglo-Indian-community schools, tapering the special-concession portion by ten percent every three years and ending it entirely after ten years — while conditioning any such grant on at least 40% of admissions being open to non-Anglo-Indian students, ensuring the funding never created fully exclusive institutions.
essential_elements: Grant baseline anchored to the financial year ending 31 March 1948
Step-down of 10% every three-year period
Absolute ten-year outer limit mirroring Article 336's sunset
Forty-percent other-community admission floor as a precondition for receiving any grant under the article
exceptions_and_qualifications: The sunset only extinguishes the grant 'to the extent to which they are a special concession' to the Anglo-Indian community — ordinary, non-preferential educational funding to the same institutions is unaffected
breakdown.how_to_read: Read alongside Article 336 as a paired, now-spent transitional safeguard for the Anglo-Indian community — one covering government service employment, the other covering educational funding — both deliberately time-boxed to a single decade of post-Independence adjustment.

sections.title: National Commission for Scheduled Castes
sections.raw_text: (1) There shall be a Commission for the Scheduled Castes to be known as the National Commission for the Scheduled Castes. (2) Subject to the provisions of any law made in this behalf by Parliament, the Commission shall consist of a Chairperson, Vice-Chairperson and three other Members and the conditions of service and tenure of office of the Chairperson, Vice-Chairperson and other Members so appointed shall be such as the President may by rule determine. (3) The Chairperson, Vice-Chairperson and other Members of the Commission shall be appointed by the President by warrant under his hand and seal. (4) The Commission shall have the power to regulate its own procedure. (5) It shall be the duty of the Commission— (a) to investigate and monitor all matters relating to the safeguards provided for the Scheduled Castes under this Constitution or under any other law for the time being in force or under any order of the Government and to evaluate the working of such safeguards; (b) to inquire into specific complaints with respect to the deprivation of rights and safeguards of the Scheduled Castes; (c) to participate and advise on the planning process of socio-economic development of the Scheduled Castes and to evaluate the progress of their development under the Union and any State; (d) to present to the President, annually and at such other times as the Commission may deem fit, reports upon the working of those safeguards; (e) to make in such reports recommendations as to the measures that should be taken by the Union or any State for the effective implementation of those safeguards and other measures for the protection, welfare and socio-economic development of the Scheduled Castes; and (f) to discharge such other functions in relation to the protection, welfare and development and advancement of the Scheduled Castes as the President may, subject to the provisions of any law made by Parliament, by rule specify. (6) The President shall cause all such reports to be laid before each House of Parliament along with a memorandum explaining the action taken or proposed to be taken on the recommendations relating to the Union and the reasons for the non-acceptance, if any, of any of such recommendations. (7) Where any such report, or any part thereof, relates to any matter with which any State Government is concerned, a copy of such report shall be forwarded to the Governor of the State who shall cause it to be laid before the Legislature of the State along with a memorandum explaining the action taken or proposed to be taken on the recommendations relating to the State and the reasons for the non-acceptance, if any, of any of such recommendations. (8) The Commission shall, while investigating any matter referred to in sub-clause (a) or inquiring into any complaint referred to in sub-clause (b) of clause (5), have all the powers of a civil court trying a suit and in particular in respect of the following matters, namely:— (a) summoning and enforcing the attendance of any person from any part of India and examining him on oath; (b) requiring the discovery and production of any document; (c) receiving evidence on affidavits; (d) requisitioning any public record or copy thereof from any court or office; (e) issuing commissions for the examination of witnesses and documents; (f) any other matter which the President may, by rule, determine. (9) The Union and every State Government shall consult the Commission on all major policy matters affecting Scheduled Castes. (10) In this article, references to the Scheduled Castes shall be construed as including references to the Anglo-Indian community.
key_terms: National Commission for the Scheduled Castes with President-appointed Chairperson/Vice-Chairperson/three Members
civil-court-equivalent investigative powers for safeguard-monitoring and complaint inquiry
mandatory annual reporting to the President with a non-acceptance-reason disclosure duty
extension of 'Scheduled Castes' references in this article to the Anglo-Indian community

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 338, substantially rewritten by the 65th (1990) and 89th (2003) Amendments, establishes a permanent National Commission for the Scheduled Castes with the same investigative, civil-court-equivalent powers and mandatory reporting-with-reasons structure the Constitution already uses for the Public Service Commissions and the Election Commission — a five-member body (Chairperson, Vice-Chairperson, three Members) appointed by Presidential warrant, tasked with monitoring SC-specific constitutional and statutory safeguards, investigating complaints, advising on SC socio-economic development, and reporting annually to Parliament and to State Legislatures where State matters are implicated.
essential_elements: Originally a combined SC+ST Commission until the 89th Amendment (2003) split off a separate National Commission for Scheduled Tribes under new Article 338A
Clause (8) grants full civil-court powers — summoning witnesses, compelling document production, receiving affidavit evidence, requisitioning records, commissioning witness examinations
Clause (9) imposes a mandatory Union/State consultation duty on all major SC-affecting policy matters
Clause (10) folds the Anglo-Indian community into 'Scheduled Castes' for this article's purposes
exceptions_and_qualifications: The Commission's recommendations remain advisory — clause (6)'s disclosure-of-non-acceptance-reasons duty creates political and reporting accountability, not a binding veto over government policy, mirroring the Article 320/323 pattern for Public Service Commissions
breakdown.how_to_read: Read as the SC-specific counterpart to Article 338A's ST Commission and Article 338B's Backward Classes Commission — the three now share near-identical nine-clause structures (membership, appointment, procedure, duties, reporting, civil-court powers, consultation duty), a deliberate constitutional design choice giving all three bodies equal institutional standing.

sections.title: National Commission for Scheduled Tribes
sections.raw_text: (1) There shall be a Commission for the Scheduled Tribes to be known as the National Commission for the Scheduled Tribes. (2) Subject to the provisions of any law made in this behalf by Parliament, the Commission shall consist of a Chairperson, Vice-Chairperson and three other Members and the conditions of service and tenure of office of the Chairperson, Vice-Chairperson and other Members so appointed shall be such as the President may by rule determine. (3) The Chairperson, Vice-Chairperson and other Members of the Commission shall be appointed by the President by warrant under his hand and seal. (4) The Commission shall have the power to regulate its own procedure. (5) It shall be the duty of the Commission— (a) to investigate and monitor all matters relating to the safeguards provided for the Scheduled Tribes under this Constitution or under any other law for the time being in force or under any order of the Government and to evaluate the working of such safeguards; (b) to inquire into specific complaints with respect to the deprivation of rights and safeguards of the Scheduled Tribes; (c) to participate and advise on the planning process of socio-economic development of the Scheduled Tribes and to evaluate the progress of their development under the Union and any State; (d) to present to the President, annually and at such other times as the Commission may deem fit, reports upon the working of those safeguards; (e) to make in such reports recommendations as to the measures that should be taken by the Union or any State for the effective implementation of those safeguards and other measures for the protection, welfare and socio-economic development of the Scheduled Tribes; and (f) to discharge such other functions in relation to the protection, welfare and development and advancement of the Scheduled Tribes as the President may, subject to the provisions of any law made by Parliament, by rule specify. (6) The President shall cause all such reports to be laid before each House of Parliament along with a memorandum explaining the action taken or proposed to be taken on the recommendations relating to the Union and the reasons for the non-acceptance, if any, of any such recommendations. (7) Where any such report, or any part thereof, relates to any matter with which any State Government is concerned, a copy of such report shall be forwarded to the Governor of the State who shall cause it to be laid before the Legislature of the State along with a memorandum explaining the action taken or proposed to be taken on the recommendations relating to the State and the reasons for the non-acceptance, if any, of any such recommendations. (8) The Commission shall, while investigating any matter referred to in sub-clause (a) or inquiring into any complaint referred to in sub-clause (b) of clause (5), have all the powers of a civil court trying a suit and in particular in respect of the following matters, namely:— (a) summoning and enforcing the attendance of any person from any part of India and examining him on oath; (b) requiring the discovery and production of any document; (c) receiving evidence on affidavits; (d) requisitioning any public record or copy thereof from any court or office; (e) issuing commissions for the examination of witnesses and documents; (f) any other matter which the President may, by rule, determine. (9) The Union and every State Government shall consult the Commission on all major policy matters affecting Scheduled Tribes.
key_terms: National Commission for Scheduled Tribes as a standalone body split off from the former combined SC/ST Commission by the 89th Amendment (2003)

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 338A, inserted by the 89th Amendment (2003), gave the Scheduled Tribes their own dedicated National Commission — structurally and functionally identical to Article 338's Scheduled Castes Commission (same five-member composition, same civil-court powers, same annual reporting and Union/State consultation duties) — recognising that ST-specific issues (tribal land alienation, forest rights, autonomous-area administration) merited a body no longer sharing attention and resources with SC matters.
essential_elements: Five-member Commission (Chairperson, Vice-Chairperson, three Members) appointed by Presidential warrant
Full civil-court investigative powers identical to Article 338(8)
Mandatory annual reporting to Parliament, with State-matter reports routed through the Governor to the State Legislature
Mandatory Union/State consultation duty on major ST-affecting policy matters
exceptions_and_qualifications: Unlike Article 338, Article 338A carries no clause extending its scope to the Anglo-Indian community — that extension is unique to the Scheduled Castes Commission under Article 338(10)
breakdown.how_to_read: Read as the direct institutional twin of Article 338, created specifically to give Scheduled Tribes an undivided, dedicated national oversight body — the split itself (from one combined SC+ST Commission into two separate ones) is a significant institutional history point distinguishing pre-2003 and post-2003 practice.

sections.title: National Commission for Backward Classes
sections.raw_text: (1) There shall be a Commission for the socially and educationally backward classes to be known as the National Commission for Backward Classes. (2) Subject to the provisions of any law made in this behalf by Parliament, the Commission shall consist of a Chairperson, Vice-Chairperson and three other Members and the conditions of service and tenure of office of the Chairperson, Vice-Chairperson and other Members so appointed shall be such as the President may by rule determine. (3) The Chairperson, Vice-Chairperson and other Members of the Commission shall be appointed by the President by warrant under his hand and seal. (4) The Commission shall have the power to regulate its own procedure. (5) It shall be the duty of the Commission— (a) to investigate and monitor all matters relating to the safeguards provided for the socially and educationally backward classes under this Constitution or under any other law for the time being in force or under any order of the Government and to evaluate the working of such safeguards; (b) to inquire into specific complaints with respect to the deprivation of rights and safeguards of the socially and educationally backward classes; (c) to participate and advise on the socio-economic development of the socially and educationally backward classes and to evaluate the progress of their development under the Union and any State; (d) to present to the President, annually and at such other times as the Commission may deem fit, reports upon the working of those safeguards; (e) to make in such reports the recommendations as to the measures that should be taken by the Union or any State for the effective implementation of those safeguards and other measures for the protection, welfare and socio-economic development of the socially and educationally backward classes; and (f) to discharge such other functions in relation to the protection, welfare and development and advancement of the socially and educationally backward classes as the President may, subject to the provisions of any law made by Parliament, by rule specify. (6) The President shall cause all such reports to be laid before each House of Parliament along with a memorandum explaining the action taken or proposed to be taken on the recommendations relating to the Union and the reasons for the non-acceptance, if any, of any such recommendations. (7) Where any such report, or any part thereof, relates to any matter with which any State Government is concerned, a copy of such report shall be forwarded to the State Government which shall cause it to be laid before the Legislature of the State along with a memorandum explaining the action taken or proposed to be taken on the recommendations relating to the State and the reasons for the non-acceptance, if any, of any of such recommendations. (8) The Commission shall, while investigating any matter referred to in sub-clause (a) or inquiring into any complaint referred to in sub-clause (b) of clause (5), have all the powers of a civil court trying a suit and in particular in respect of the following matters, namely:— (a) summoning and enforcing the attendance of any person from any part of India and examining him on oath; (b) requiring the discovery and production of any document; (c) receiving evidence on affidavits; (d) requisitioning any public record or copy thereof from any court or office; (e) issuing commissions for the examination of witnesses and documents; (f) any other matter which the President may by rule, determine. (9) The Union and every State Government shall consult the Commission on all major policy matters affecting the socially and educationally backward classes: Provided that nothing in this clause shall apply for the purposes of clause (3) of article 342A.
key_terms: National Commission for Backward Classes given constitutional (rather than merely statutory) status by the 102nd Amendment (2018)
carve-out excusing States from consulting the Commission when exercising their own independent Article 342A(3) backward-classes-list power

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 338B, inserted by the 102nd Amendment (2018), elevated the previously statutory National Commission for Backward Classes to full constitutional status, matching the institutional standing the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes Commissions already had — giving India's third major reservation-beneficiary category (socially and educationally backward classes, OBCs) the same civil-court investigative powers and mandatory annual-reporting structure.
essential_elements: Same five-member composition, civil-court powers, and annual-reporting mechanics as Articles 338 and 338A
Clause (9)'s general Union/State consultation duty is expressly carved out from applying to a State's own independent Article 342A(3) list-maintenance power
exceptions_and_qualifications: The proviso to clause (9) was itself inserted by the 105th Amendment (2021) specifically to correct the fallout from Jaishri Laxmanrao Patil v. State of Maharashtra (2021) — the Supreme Court's Maratha reservation ruling that had read the 102nd Amendment as stripping States of the power to maintain their own SEBC lists, a reading Parliament reversed by simultaneously adding Article 342A(3) and this consultation carve-out
breakdown.how_to_read: Read together with Article 342A: Article 338B is the OBC-specific oversight-Commission counterpart to Articles 338/338A, but its practical significance is inseparable from the 2021 constitutional correction restoring State autonomy over local backward-classes lists after the Maratha reservation litigation.

sections.title: Control of the Union over the administration of Scheduled Areas and the welfare of Scheduled Tribes
sections.raw_text: (1) The President may at any time and shall, at the expiration of ten years from the commencement of this Constitution by order appoint a Commission to report on the administration of the Scheduled Areas and the welfare of the Scheduled Tribes in the States. The order may define the composition, powers and procedure of the Commission and may contain such incidental or ancillary provisions as the President may consider necessary or desirable. (2) The executive power of the Union shall extend to the giving of directions to a State as to the drawing up and execution of schemes specified in the direction to be essential for the welfare of the Scheduled Tribes in the State.
key_terms: mandatory decennial-trigger Commission on Scheduled Area administration and Scheduled Tribe welfare
Union executive-direction power over State Scheduled-Tribe-welfare schemes

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 339 combines a one-time-mandatory, otherwise-discretionary review mechanism — the President must appoint a Commission to report on Scheduled Area administration and Scheduled Tribe welfare at the ten-year mark (and may appoint one earlier or again at will) — with an ongoing Union executive power under clause (2) to directly direct States on drawing up and executing Scheduled-Tribe-welfare schemes, reinforcing the Union's Article 339(2)-anchored oversight role over how States actually implement tribal welfare on the ground.
essential_elements: Clause (1)'s Commission appointment is mandatory at the ten-year mark but otherwise fully discretionary in timing, composition, and procedure, all left to Presidential order
Clause (2) is a freestanding, continuing Union executive-direction power independent of whether any Commission has been appointed
Directions under clause (2) are limited to schemes the Union considers 'essential' for Scheduled Tribe welfare in a State
exceptions_and_qualifications: This article's Union-direction power under clause (2) operates alongside, not instead of, the Fifth and Sixth Schedules' own Scheduled Area/tribal-area administrative frameworks — it supplements rather than displaces those specialised regimes
breakdown.how_to_read: Read alongside the Fifth Schedule (Scheduled Areas/Scheduled Tribes administration in non-tribal-council States) and Sixth Schedule (tribal areas of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, Mizoram) as part of the Constitution's layered tribal-welfare architecture — Article 339 supplies Union oversight and directive power that cuts across both Schedule regimes.

sections.title: Appointment of a Commission to investigate the conditions of backward classes
sections.raw_text: (1) The President may by order appoint a Commission consisting of such persons as he thinks fit to investigate the conditions of socially and educationally backward classes within the territory of India and the difficulties under which they labour and to make recommendations as to the steps that should be taken by the Union or any State to remove such difficulties and to improve their condition and as to the grants that should be made for the purpose by the Union or any State and the conditions subject to which such grants should be made, and the order appointing such Commission shall define the procedure to be followed by the Commission. (2) A Commission so appointed shall investigate the matters referred to them and present to the President a report setting out the facts as found by them and making such recommendations as they think proper. (3) The President shall cause a copy of the report so presented together with a memorandum explaining the action taken thereon to be laid before each House of Parliament.
key_terms: President's discretionary power to appoint a Backward Classes Commission to investigate conditions and recommend remedial measures
mandatory laying of the Commission's report and an action-taken memorandum before Parliament

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 340 is the constitutional foundation for every major backward-classes investigation India has conducted — most famously the Mandal Commission (Second Backward Classes Commission, appointed 1979, reported 1980) — letting the President appoint a Commission of his choosing to investigate the actual social and educational conditions of backward classes nationwide and recommend concrete steps and grant conditions for their upliftment, with the report and the government's response mandatorily placed before Parliament.
essential_elements: Commission composition, procedure, and terms of reference are entirely at the President's discretion via the appointing order
Clause (2) requires the Commission to report both its factual findings and its recommendations

Clause (3) makes public parliamentary disclosure of the report and the government's action-taken response mandatory, mirroring the transparency mechanism used for Articles 338/338A/338B and the Finance Commission
exceptions_and_qualifications: The article does not itself define who qualifies as a 'socially and educationally backward class' — that determination is left to the Commission's own investigation and to subsequent Supreme Court jurisprudence, most notably Indra Sawhney's creamy-layer exclusion and 50% overall reservation ceiling

The Commission's recommendations, like those of the Article 338/338A/338B Commissions, remain advisory — Parliament and State Legislatures are not bound to accept them, only to disclose reasons for non-acceptance
breakdown.how_to_read: Read as the historical trigger for the Mandal Commission report and the Supreme Court's landmark nine-judge decision in Indra Sawhney v. Union of India (1992), which upheld 27% OBC reservation in Union public employment (subject to the exclusion of the 'creamy layer') while capping total reservation at 50% — Article 340 is thus the constitutional starting point for virtually all subsequent OBC reservation jurisprudence and legislation.

sections.title: Scheduled Castes
sections.raw_text: (1) The President may with respect to any State or Union territory, and where it is a State, after consultation with the Governor thereof, by public notification, specify the castes, races or tribes or parts of or groups within castes, races or tribes which shall for the purposes of this Constitution be deemed to be Scheduled Castes in relation to that State or Union territory, as the case may be. (2) Parliament may by law include in or exclude from the list of Scheduled Castes specified in a notification issued under clause (1) any caste, race or tribe or part of or group within any caste, race or tribe, but save as aforesaid a notification issued under the said clause shall not be varied by any subsequent notification.
key_terms: President's Governor-consulted notification power specifying Scheduled Castes State-by-State/Union-territory-by-Union-territory
Parliament-exclusive power to amend a notified Scheduled Castes list, with all other variation barred

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 341 is the sole constitutional gateway for a caste, race, or tribe (or part/group within one) to acquire legal 'Scheduled Caste' status: the President, after consulting the State Governor, issues a public notification specifying the list for that State or Union territory, and once issued, that list is frozen — only Parliament, by ordinary legislation, can add to or remove from it. No executive order, State law, or court judgment can vary the list once notified.
essential_elements: Notification is State/Union-territory-specific — the same caste name can be a Scheduled Caste in one State and not in another
Governor consultation is mandatory before notification for a State (not required for a Union territory, which has no Governor)
Once notified, the list is rigid — clause (2)'s 'save as aforesaid' language makes Parliament's law-making power the exclusive variation route
exceptions_and_qualifications: A person or sub-group not expressly named in the notified list cannot claim Scheduled Caste status merely by showing factual or social similarity to a listed entry — inclusion requires either an express notification or a Parliamentary amendment under clause (2), not judicial extension
breakdown.how_to_read: Read together with the Supreme Court's ruling in State of Maharashtra v. Milind (2001), which held that courts cannot expand or reinterpret a notified Scheduled Castes/Tribes list to include castes or sub-groups not expressly named in it — reinforcing that Article 341's rigidity is deliberate and that any correction must go through Parliament, not litigation.

sections.title: Scheduled Tribes
sections.raw_text: (1) The President may with respect to any State or Union territory, and where it is a State, after consultation with the Governor thereof, by public notification, specify the tribes or tribal communities or parts of or groups within tribes or tribal communities which shall for the purposes of this Constitution be deemed to be Scheduled Tribes in relation to that State or Union territory, as the case may be. (2) Parliament may by law include in or exclude from the list of Scheduled Tribes specified in a notification issued under clause (1) any tribe or tribal community or part of or group within any tribe or tribal community, but save as aforesaid a notification issued under the said clause shall not be varied by any subsequent notification.
key_terms: President's Governor-consulted notification power specifying Scheduled Tribes State-by-State/Union-territory-by-Union-territory, mirroring Article 341's Scheduled Castes mechanism

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 342 is the Scheduled Tribes mirror of Article 341's Scheduled Castes mechanism: the President, after State Governor consultation, notifies which tribes or tribal communities (or parts/groups within them) count as Scheduled Tribes for a given State or Union territory, with the resulting list rigid and amendable only by Parliament, not by executive order, State law, or judicial reinterpretation.
essential_elements: Structurally identical to Article 341 — State/Union-territory-specific notification, mandatory Governor consultation for States, Parliament-exclusive amendment power

Tribal status determination has historically relied on criteria like primitive traits, geographical isolation, distinctive culture, and shyness of contact with the community at large, though these criteria appear in policy practice rather than the article's text itself
exceptions_and_qualifications: A tribe recognised as a Scheduled Tribe in one State does not automatically carry that status into another State upon migration — a separate notification specific to the new State or Union territory is required before Scheduled Tribe status applies there
breakdown.how_to_read: Read as Article 341's direct structural twin — apply the same State of Maharashtra v. Milind (2001) rigidity principle: courts cannot judicially expand a notified Scheduled Tribes list beyond its literal terms, and any correction requires Parliament to legislate under clause (2).

sections.title: Socially and educationally backward classes
sections.raw_text: (1) The President may with respect to any State or Union territory, and where it is a State, after consultation with the Governor thereof, by public notification, specify the socially and educationally backward classes in the Central List which shall for the purposes of the Central Government be deemed to be socially and educationally backward classes in relation to that State or Union territory, as the case may be. (2) Parliament may by law include in or exclude from the Central List of socially and educationally backward classes specified in a notification issued under clause (1) any socially and educationally backward class, but save as aforesaid a notification issued under the said clause shall not be varied by any subsequent notification. Explanation.—For the purposes of clauses (1) and (2), the expression "Central List" means the list of socially and educationally backward classes prepared and maintained by and for the Central Government. (3) Notwithstanding any contained in clauses (1) and (2), every State or Union territory may, by law, prepare and maintain, for its own purposes, a list of socially and educationally backward classes, entries in which may be different from the Central List.
key_terms: President's Governor-consulted notification power creating a Central List of socially and educationally backward classes for Central Government purposes, mirroring Articles 341/342
express State/Union-territory power to independently prepare and maintain its own backward-classes list, distinct from and possibly different from the Central List

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 342A, inserted by the 102nd Amendment (2018) and significantly clarified by the 105th Amendment (2021), extends the Articles 341/342 notification-and-freeze model to socially and educationally backward classes (OBCs) for Central Government purposes via a 'Central List' — while clause (3), added in 2021, expressly preserves every State and Union territory's independent power to prepare and maintain its own backward-classes list for its own purposes, which may differ from the Central List.
essential_elements: Clauses (1)-(2) mirror Articles 341/342's structure but are expressly scoped to 'the purposes of the Central Government' via a defined 'Central List'
Clause (3) is a non-obstante override ('Notwithstanding any[thing] contained in clauses (1) and (2)') guaranteeing State/Union-territory list-making autonomy for their own purposes
exceptions_and_qualifications: Clause (3) and the accompanying Article 338B(9) proviso were both inserted by the 105th Amendment specifically to reverse the Supreme Court's reading in Jaishri Laxmanrao Patil v. State of Maharashtra (2021), which had held the 102nd Amendment stripped States of independent OBC-list-making power — without this fix, the Maratha reservation collapse would have applied to every State's OBC list nationwide
breakdown.how_to_read: Read as the most recently and most directly amended provision in Part XVI — the 2018-to-2021 sequence (102nd Amendment creating the Central List regime, Jaishri Patil reading it as centralising all OBC-list power, then the 105th Amendment's clause (3) restoring State autonomy) is essential context for understanding why this article looks the way it does today.

sections.title: Official language of the Union
sections.raw_text: (1) The official language of the Union shall be Hindi in Devanagari script. The form of numerals to be used for the official purposes of the Union shall be the international form of Indian numerals. (2) Notwithstanding anything in clause (1), for a period of fifteen years from the commencement of this Constitution, the English language shall continue to be used for all the official purposes of the Union for which it was being used immediately before such commencement: Provided that the President may, during the said period, by order authorise the use of the Hindi language in addition to the English language and of the Devanagari form of numerals in addition to the international form of Indian numerals for any of the official purposes of the Union. (3) Notwithstanding anything in this article, Parliament may by law provide for the use, after the said period of fifteen years, of— (a) the English language, or (b) the Devanagari form of numerals, for such purposes as may be specified in the law.
key_terms: Hindi in Devanagari script as the Union's official language, with international-form Indian numerals
fifteen-year continuation of English for pre-existing official purposes, extendable indefinitely by Parliament under clause (3)

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 343 formally designates Hindi in Devanagari script as the Union's official language, but simultaneously guaranteed English's continued use for a full fifteen years after the Constitution's commencement (until 1965) for whatever official purposes it was already being used — and, critically, clause (3) let Parliament extend English's official use by ordinary law beyond that fifteen-year window, which Parliament did via the Official Languages Act, 1963, preserving English as a co-official language indefinitely alongside Hindi.
essential_elements: Hindi in Devanagari script is the constitutionally designated official language of the Union
Clause (2)'s fifteen-year English continuation was a transitional guarantee, not a sunset on English's use as such
Clause (3) gives Parliament an open-ended, ordinary-legislation power to keep English (or Devanagari numerals) in official use beyond 1965
exceptions_and_qualifications: 'Official language' governs government business and does not restrict the languages citizens may use in their private, commercial, or educational life

The article does not by itself make Hindi the sole or National language — India has no constitutionally declared 'National Language'; Article 343 only fixes the Union's administrative/official language
breakdown.how_to_read: Read alongside the Official Languages Act, 1963 (enacted under clause (3)) as the operative instrument that made English's continued official Union use permanent rather than merely a fifteen-year transitional measure — a frequent point of confusion, since the constitutional text alone might suggest English's official status expired in 1965.

sections.title: Commission and Committee of Parliament on official language
sections.raw_text: (1) The President shall, at the expiration of five years from the commencement of this Constitution and thereafter at the expiration of ten years from such commencement, by order constitute a Commission which shall consist of a Chairman and such other members representing the different languages specified in the Eighth Schedule as the President may appoint, and the order shall define the procedure to be followed by the Commission. (2) It shall be the duty of the Commission to make recommendations to the President as to— (a) the progressive use of the Hindi language for the official purposes of the Union; (b) restrictions on the use of the English language for all or any of the official purposes of the Union; (c) the language to be used for all or any of the purposes mentioned in article 348; (d) the form of numerals to be used for any one or more specified purposes of the Union; (e) any other matter referred to the Commission by the President as regards the official language of the Union and the language for communication between the Union and a State or between one State and another and their use. (3) In making their recommendations under clause (2), the Commission shall have due regard to the industrial, cultural and scientific advancement of India, and the just claims and the interests of persons belonging to the non-Hindi speaking areas in regard to the public services. (4) There shall be constituted a Committee consisting of thirty members, of whom twenty shall be members of the House of the People and ten shall be members of the Council of States to be elected respectively by the members of the House of the People and the members of the Council of States in accordance with the system of proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote. (5) It shall be the duty of the Committee to examine the recommendations of the Commission constituted under clause (1) and to report to the President their opinion thereon. (6) Notwithstanding anything in article 343, the President may, after consideration of the report referred to in clause (5), issue directions in accordance with the whole or any part of that report.
key_terms: mandatory five-year-then-ten-year Presidential Official Language Commission
thirty-member bicameral Parliamentary Committee reviewing the Commission's recommendations
President's power to issue binding directions notwithstanding Article 343, based on the Committee's report

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 344 built a two-stage review mechanism into the Constitution's language policy: a Presidentially-appointed Commission (first at the five-year mark, again at ten years) representing the Eighth Schedule's languages recommends how far Hindi's official use should progress and English's should recede, a thirty-member Parliamentary Committee (twenty Lok Sabha, ten Rajya Sabha members, elected by proportional representation) reviews those recommendations, and the President may then issue directions departing from Article 343's default scheme based on that Committee's report — giving Parliament, through its Committee, real influence over how the Hindi/English balance actually evolves.
essential_elements: Clause (1)'s Commission is mandatory at the five-year and ten-year marks (unlike Article 340's fully discretionary Backward Classes Commission)
Clause (3) requires the Commission to weigh non-Hindi-speaking-area interests in public-service access, not just linguistic policy in the abstract

Clause (6)'s Presidential directions expressly override Article 343 ('Notwithstanding anything in article 343'), making this the operative mechanism for adjusting the default language scheme over time
exceptions_and_qualifications: The Parliamentary Committee's report and the Commission's recommendations are advisory inputs feeding the President's clause (6) directive power — Parliament as a whole does not itself vote to ratify the resulting directions, so influence is channelled through the Committee's members rather than a floor vote
breakdown.how_to_read: Read as the procedural machinery behind Article 343's substantive language designation — Article 343 sets the default rule, but Article 344's Commission-then-Committee-then-Presidential-direction sequence is how that default has actually been adjusted in practice since 1955 and 1960 (the first two Commissions).

sections.title: Official language or languages of a State
sections.raw_text: Subject to the provisions of articles 346 and 347, the Legislature of a State may by law adopt any one or more of the languages in use in the State or Hindi as the language or languages to be used for all or any of the official purposes of that State: Provided that, until the Legislature of the State otherwise provides by law, the English language shall continue to be used for those official purposes within the State for which it was being used immediately before the commencement of this Constitution.
key_terms: State Legislature's power to adopt any in-use State language or Hindi as its own official language(s)
default continuation of pre-existing English official use pending a State law

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 345 gives every State Legislature the autonomy to choose its own official language(s) by ordinary law — any language actually in use within the State, or Hindi — while ensuring administrative continuity through a default proviso keeping English as the operative official language for whatever purposes it already served until the State Legislature actually legislates otherwise.
essential_elements: State choice is subject to Articles 346 (inter-State/State-Union communication) and 347 (linguistic-minority special recognition)
The State may adopt multiple languages simultaneously for different official purposes, not just a single exclusive language
The English-continuation proviso operates only as a default, displaced automatically once the State Legislature legislates its own choice
exceptions_and_qualifications: A State's language choice under this article governs only its own official purposes — it cannot dictate the language used by Union offices situated within that State, which remains governed by Articles 343 and 348
breakdown.how_to_read: Read as the State-level mirror of Article 343 — just as the Union chose Hindi (with a transitional and then Parliament-extendable English guarantee), each State independently chooses its own official language(s) subject only to the inter-State communication rule (Article 346) and the linguistic-minority safeguard (Article 347).

sections.title: Official language for communication between one State and another or between a State and the Union
sections.raw_text: The language for the time being authorised for use in the Union for official purposes shall be the official language for communication between one State and another State and between a State and the Union: Provided that if two or more States agree that the Hindi language should be the official language for communication between such States, that language may be used for such communication.
key_terms: Union's official language as the default language for inter-State and State-Union official communication
bilateral/multilateral State agreement to use Hindi instead for communication between themselves

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 346 fixes the default rule for official correspondence crossing State or Union-State lines: whatever language is currently authorised for Union official purposes (Hindi, with English continuing per Article 343) governs that inter-governmental communication by default, but any two or more States are free to agree among themselves to use Hindi specifically for their own mutual communication even if the Union-level default at that time is different.
essential_elements: The default tracks whatever the Union's currently authorised official language is at any given time — an automatically updating cross-reference to Article 343's regime, not a fixed rule
The proviso's Hindi-by-agreement option applies only to State-to-State communication, not to State-Union communication
exceptions_and_qualifications: The proviso is not a unilateral entitlement for any single State — it requires an actual mutual agreement among the States concerned before Hindi can be substituted for the default Union-language rule between them
breakdown.how_to_read: Read as a coordination rule preventing linguistic fragmentation in inter-governmental correspondence — it anchors to Article 343's Union language by default while leaving a narrow, consensual Hindi-specific carve-out for States that prefer it among themselves.

sections.title: Special provision relating to language spoken by a section of the population of a State
sections.raw_text: On a demand being made in that behalf the President may, if he is satisfied that a substantial proportion of the population of a State desire the use of any language spoken by them to be recognised by that State, direct that such language shall also be officially recognised throughout that State or any part thereof for such purpose as he may specify.
key_terms: President's demand-triggered power to direct official recognition of a substantial-population-share language within a State

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 347 protects significant linguistic minorities within a State from being administratively invisible: on a demand being made, if the President is satisfied a substantial proportion of the State's population desires a language they speak to be officially recognised, the President may direct that language's official recognition throughout the State or a specified part of it, for purposes the President specifies.
essential_elements: Triggered only by a demand, not automatically
Requires Presidential satisfaction that the population share is 'substantial' — an undefined, discretionary threshold
Recognition can be geographically limited (to part of the State) and purpose-limited (to specified official purposes only), not necessarily comprehensive
exceptions_and_qualifications: A Presidential direction under this article need not extend to the entire State or to every official purpose — the scope actually granted can be narrower than the language's real geographic spread or the community's full range of administrative needs
breakdown.how_to_read: Read alongside Article 350A/350B's linguistic-minority protections as part of the Constitution's layered response to India's linguistic diversity — Article 345 lets a State choose its own official language, Article 347 is the safety-valve letting the President compel recognition of an under-represented but substantial linguistic group within that same State.

sections.title: Language to be used in the Supreme Court and in the High Courts and for Acts, Bills, etc.
sections.raw_text: (1) Notwithstanding anything in the foregoing provisions of this Part, until Parliament by law otherwise provides— (a) all proceedings in the Supreme Court and in every High Court, (b) the authoritative texts— (i) of all Bills to be introduced or amendments thereto to be moved in either House of Parliament or in the House or either House of the Legislature of a State, (ii) of all Acts passed by Parliament or the Legislature of a State and of all Ordinances promulgated by the President or the Governor of a State, and (iii) of all orders, rules, regulations and bye-laws issued under this Constitution or under any law made by Parliament or the Legislature of a State, shall be in the English language. (2) Notwithstanding anything in sub-clause (a) of clause (1), the Governor of a State may, with the previous consent of the President, authorise the use of the Hindi language, or any other language used for any official purposes of the State, in proceedings in the High Court having its principal seat in that State: Provided that nothing in this clause shall apply to any judgment, decree or order passed or made by such High Court. (3) Notwithstanding anything in sub-clause (b) of clause (1), where the Legislature of a State has prescribed any language other than the English language for use in Bills introduced in, or Acts passed by, the Legislature of the State or in Ordinances promulgated by the Governor of the State or in any order, rule, regulation or bye-law referred to in paragraph (iii) of that sub-clause, a translation of the same in the English language published under the authority of the Governor of the State in the Official Gazette of that State shall be deemed to be the authoritative text thereof in the English language under this article.
key_terms: default English-only requirement for Supreme Court/High Court proceedings and for authoritative legislative/executive-instrument texts, overridable only by Parliament
Governor-with-Presidential-consent power to authorise Hindi/State-language use in a High Court's proceedings, excluding judgments/decrees/orders
deemed-authoritative English translation of State-language Bills/Acts/Ordinances/subordinate legislation published in the State's Official Gazette

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 348 locks in English as the default, Parliament-overridable language for the highest courts' proceedings and for the legally authoritative text of all legislative and executive instruments — while carving out a narrow, Presidentially-supervised exception letting a State's High Court use Hindi or another State language in its day-to-day proceedings (though never in its actual judgments, decrees, or orders, which must remain in English), and ensuring that if a State legislates in another language, an official English translation still counts as the authoritative legal text.
essential_elements: Clause (1)'s English requirement is itself expressly subject to Parliament changing it by law — it is a 'until Parliament by law otherwise provides' default, not an entrenched permanent rule
Clause (2)'s Governor-authorised Hindi/State-language use requires the President's prior consent and excludes judgments/decrees/orders entirely
Clause (3) treats the Gazette-published English translation as legally authoritative regardless of which language the original State enactment was drafted in
exceptions_and_qualifications: The English-only default for judgments/decrees/orders under clause (2)'s proviso remains firm even where a High Court has been authorised to conduct its general proceedings in Hindi or another State language — the final legal instrument itself stays in English
breakdown.how_to_read: Read as the practical language rule actually governing Indian courtroom and legislative-drafting practice — distinguish clause (1)'s general English default (for courts and authoritative legal texts) from clause (2)'s narrow, President-consented High Court proceedings exception, which several States (e.g., Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh) have in fact invoked to use Hindi in High Court proceedings while keeping judgments in English.

sections.title: Special procedure for enactment of certain laws relating to language
sections.raw_text: During the period of fifteen years from the commencement of this Constitution, no Bill or amendment making provision for the language to be used for any of the purposes mentioned in clause (1) of article 348 shall be introduced or moved in either House of Parliament without the previous sanction of the President, and the President shall not give his sanction to the introduction of any such Bill or the moving of any such amendment except after he has taken into consideration the recommendations of the Commission constituted under clause (1) of article 344 and the report of the Committee constituted under clause (4) of that article.
key_terms: fifteen-year special procedural safeguard requiring Presidential prior sanction, informed by the Article 344 Commission/Committee, before any Article 348(1)-language-altering Bill could even be introduced in Parliament

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 349 was a transitional procedural safeguard preventing Parliament from hastily changing the Article 348(1) language rules (for courts and authoritative legal texts) during the Constitution's first fifteen years, by requiring any such Bill to first get the President's sanction — sanction the President could only give after actually considering the Article 344 Commission's recommendations and the Parliamentary Committee's report, ensuring deliberate, expert-informed decision-making rather than snap legislative changes on a sensitive issue.
essential_elements: Applied only to Bills/amendments touching Article 348(1) purposes (court proceedings and authoritative legal texts), not language policy generally
Fifteen-year window tied to the Constitution's commencement (i.e., until 1965), like Article 343(2)'s parallel English-continuation window
Presidential sanction was itself conditioned on having considered the Article 344 Commission and Committee outputs, not a free-standing discretionary check
exceptions_and_qualifications: The special procedure's fifteen-year window has long closed (1965), so any present-day Bill altering Article 348(1) language rules now follows Parliament's ordinary legislative procedure without needing prior Presidential sanction under this article
breakdown.how_to_read: Read as a now historically spent procedural safeguard (its fifteen-year window closed in 1965) whose purpose was to ensure any early post-Independence changes to court/legal-text language rules went through the deliberative Article 344 Commission-Committee process rather than ordinary snap legislation.

sections.title: Language to be used in representations for redress of grievances
sections.raw_text: Every person shall be entitled to submit a representation for the redress of any grievance to any officer or authority of the Union or a State in any of the languages used in the Union or in the State, as the case may be.
key_terms: universal citizen entitlement to submit grievance representations in any language in official use in the Union or the relevant State

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 350 guarantees every person the right to petition any Union or State officer or authority for grievance redress in any language that is in official use in the Union or that State, ensuring language is never a barrier to a citizen's basic right to seek administrative redress.
essential_elements: Entitlement runs to 'every person', not just citizens, making it one of the Constitution's broader beneficiary classes
Covers any officer or authority of the Union or a State, not merely designated language-officers
exceptions_and_qualifications: The guarantee covers only the language in which the representation may be submitted — it does not itself guarantee a response in that same language or any substantive right to have the underlying grievance actually resolved
breakdown.how_to_read: Read as a practical, access-to-administration guarantee distinct from the official-language-designation articles (343-348) — those articles set what language government uses; Article 350 ensures citizens are never forced to use an unfamiliar language just to file a grievance.

sections.title: Facilities for instruction in mother-tongue at primary stage
sections.raw_text: It shall be the endeavour of every State and of every local authority within the State to provide adequate facilities for instruction in the mother-tongue at the primary stage of education to children belonging to linguistic minority groups; and the President may issue such directions to any State as he considers necessary or proper for securing the provision of such facilities.
key_terms: State/local-authority endeavour duty to provide mother-tongue primary-education instruction for linguistic-minority children
President's supplementary direction-issuing power to secure that endeavour

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 350A, inserted by the Seventh Amendment (1956), places an 'endeavour' (best-efforts, non-absolute) duty on every State and local authority to provide adequate primary-stage instruction in a linguistic-minority child's mother tongue, backed by the President's power to issue directions to any State he considers necessary to actually secure that provision.
essential_elements: The duty is framed as an 'endeavour', a softer standard than an absolute mandatory obligation, though still a real constitutional directive
Limited to the primary stage of education specifically, not secondary or higher education
The President's direction power is a backstop mechanism, exercisable when a State's own endeavour proves inadequate
exceptions_and_qualifications: As a best-efforts 'endeavour' rather than an absolute command, the provision is generally treated as directory rather than independently enforceable in the same manner as a fundamental right, though courts have drawn on it when interpreting related linguistic-minority education claims
breakdown.how_to_read: Read alongside Article 29(1)'s cultural/linguistic-minority right to conserve a distinct language, script, or culture — Article 350A operationalises that broader cultural-conservation value specifically in the primary-education context, while Article 350B's Special Officer (below) monitors compliance.

sections.title: Special Officer for linguistic minorities
sections.raw_text: (1) There shall be a Special Officer for linguistic minorities to be appointed by the President. (2) It shall be the duty of the Special Officer to investigate all matters relating to the safeguards provided for linguistic minorities under this Constitution and report to the President upon those matters at such intervals as the President may direct, and the President shall cause all such reports to be laid before each House of Parliament, and sent to the Governments of the States concerned.
key_terms: President-appointed Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities with a nationwide safeguard-investigation and reporting mandate
