breakdown.plain_summary: Article 350B, also inserted by the Seventh Amendment (1956), creates a single-officer institution — the Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities, appointed by the President — dedicated to investigating how well the Constitution's linguistic-minority safeguards are actually being implemented, reporting to the President at Presidentially-set intervals, with those reports mandatorily laid before Parliament and sent to the relevant State Governments.
essential_elements: A single Special Officer, not a multi-member Commission like Articles 338/338A/338B/340's bodies
Reporting interval is left to Presidential direction, not fixed by the article itself
Reports go both to Parliament (via mandatory laying) and directly to the concerned State Governments
exceptions_and_qualifications: The Special Officer's reports are purely informational — identifying safeguard failures does not itself compel any remedial action; follow-through still depends on subsequent government or parliamentary response
breakdown.how_to_read: Read as the institutional monitoring counterpart to Article 350A's substantive mother-tongue-instruction duty and to Article 29(1)'s cultural-conservation right — the Special Officer is the Constitution's dedicated watchdog ensuring these linguistic-minority protections are not merely paper guarantees.

sections.title: Directive for development of the Hindi language
sections.raw_text: It shall be the duty of the Union to promote the spread of the Hindi language, to develop it so that it may serve as a medium of expression for all the elements of the composite culture of India and to secure its enrichment by assimilating without interfering with its genius, the forms, style and expressions used in Hindustani and in the other languages of India specified in the Eighth Schedule, and by drawing, wherever necessary or desirable, for its vocabulary, primarily on Sanskrit and secondarily on other languages.
key_terms: Union's affirmative duty to promote and develop Hindi as a composite-culture medium of expression
enrichment methodology privileging Sanskrit primarily and other Indian languages secondarily, while preserving Hindi's own genius

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 351 is a directive-style provision (structurally similar to the Part IV Directive Principles) imposing on the Union an affirmative duty to actively promote the spread and development of Hindi as a language capable of expressing India's composite culture, specifying a deliberate enrichment methodology: assimilate Hindustani and other Eighth Schedule languages' forms and expressions without disturbing Hindi's own character, and draw new vocabulary primarily from Sanskrit and secondarily from other languages.
essential_elements: Framed as a 'duty of the Union', giving it directive force even though it sits outside Part IV's formal Directive Principles chapter
The enrichment methodology is specific and ordered — Sanskrit first, other languages second — rather than an open-ended borrowing instruction
Requires assimilation 'without interfering with its genius', a built-in limit against changes that would fundamentally alter Hindi's character
exceptions_and_qualifications: Being a directive rather than a fundamental right, Article 351 is not independently enforceable by a citizen in court, and it has been read as complementary to rather than in tension with Article 29(1)'s minority-language conservation right
breakdown.how_to_read: Read as Part XVII's closing directive, setting the aspirational policy goal underlying the entire language scheme (Articles 343-351) — while Articles 343-350B establish the legal/administrative rules for official language use, Article 351 supplies the underlying cultural-development rationale and methodology for Hindi's promotion specifically.

sections.title: Proclamation of Emergency.
sections.raw_text:
(1) If the President is satisfied that a grave emergency exists whereby the security of India or of any part of the territory thereof is threatened, whether by war or external aggression or armed rebellion, he may, by Proclamation, make a declaration to that effect in respect of the whole of India or of such part of the territory thereof as may be specified in the Proclamation.

Explanation.—A Proclamation of Emergency declaring that the security of India or any part of the territory thereof is threatened by war or by external aggression or by armed rebellion may be made before the actual occurrence of war or of any such aggression or rebellion, if the President is satisfied that there is imminent danger thereof.

(2) A Proclamation issued under clause (1) may be varied or revoked by a subsequent Proclamation.

(3) The President shall not issue a Proclamation under clause (1) or a Proclamation varying such Proclamation unless the decision of the Union Cabinet (that is to say, the Council consisting of the Prime Minister and other Ministers of Cabinet rank appointed under article 75) that such a Proclamation may be issued has been communicated to him in writing.

(4) Every Proclamation issued under this article shall be laid before each House of Parliament and shall, except where it is a Proclamation revoking a previous Proclamation, cease to operate at the expiration of one month unless before the expiration of that period it has been approved by resolutions of both Houses of Parliament:
Provided that if any such Proclamation (not being a Proclamation revoking a previous Proclamation) is issued at a time when the House of the People has been dissolved, or the dissolution of the House of the People takes place during the period of one month referred to in this clause, and if a resolution approving the Proclamation has been passed by the Council of States, but no resolution with respect to such Proclamation has been passed by the House of the People before the expiration of that period, the Proclamation shall cease to operate at the expiration of thirty days from the date on which the House of the People first sits after its reconstitution, unless before the expiration of the said period of thirty days a resolution approving the Proclamation has been also passed by the House of the People.

(5) A Proclamation so approved shall, unless revoked, cease to operate on the expiration of a period of six months from the date of the passing of the second of the resolutions approving the Proclamation under clause (4):
Provided that if and so often as a resolution approving the continuance in force of such a Proclamation is passed by both Houses of Parliament, the Proclamation shall, unless revoked, continue in force for a further period of six months from the date on which it would otherwise have ceased to operate under this clause:
Provided further that if the dissolution of the House of the People takes place during any such period of six months and a resolution approving the continuance in force of such Proclamation has been passed by the Council of States but no resolution with respect to the continuance in force of such Proclamation has been passed by the House of the People during the said period, the Proclamation shall cease to operate at the expiration of thirty days from the date on which the House of the People first sits after its reconstitution unless before the expiration of the said period of thirty days, a resolution approving the continuance in force of the Proclamation has been also passed by the House of the People.

(6) For the purposes of clauses (4) and (5), a resolution may be passed by either House of Parliament only by a majority of the total membership of that House and by a majority of not less than two-thirds of the Members of that House present and voting.

(7) Notwithstanding anything contained in the foregoing clauses, the President shall revoke a Proclamation issued under clause (1) or a Proclamation varying such Proclamation if the House of the People passes a resolution disapproving, or, as the case may be, disapproving the continuance in force of, such Proclamation.

(8) Where a notice in writing signed by not less than one-tenth of the total number of members of the House of the People has been given, of their intention to move a resolution for disapproving, or, as the case may be, for disapproving the continuance in force of, a Proclamation issued under clause (1) or a Proclamation varying such Proclamation,—
(a) to the Speaker, if the House is in session; or
(b) to the President, if the House is not in session,
a special sitting of the House shall be held within fourteen days from the date on which such notice is received by the Speaker, or, as the case may be, by the President, for the purpose of considering such resolution.

(9) The power conferred on the President by this article shall include the power to issue different Proclamations on different grounds, being war or external aggression or armed rebellion or imminent danger of war or external aggression or armed rebellion, whether or not there is a Proclamation already issued by the President under clause (1) and such Proclamation is in operation.
key_terms: war/external-aggression/armed-rebellion grounds for a National Emergency Proclamation, with an imminent-danger anticipatory trigger
mandatory written Union Cabinet decision as a precondition to issuing or varying the Proclamation
one-month provisional window requiring double-majority Parliamentary approval to continue in force
six-month renewable Parliamentary approval cycles by special majority
Lok Sabha's unilateral power to force revocation via a disapproval resolution
one-tenth-member-notice mechanism compelling a special sitting to consider disapproval

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 352 lets the President declare a 'National Emergency' when India's security is gravely threatened by war, external aggression, or armed rebellion — the President can even act in anticipation if the danger is imminent. But this is not a unilateral power: the President must first have a written Cabinet decision in hand, and the Proclamation lapses after one month unless both Houses of Parliament approve it by a special double majority (majority of total membership plus two-thirds of those present and voting). Once approved, it must be renewed every six months the same way, and the Lok Sabha alone can force an end to it at any time by passing a disapproval resolution — a check Parliament can trigger even against the government's wishes.
essential_elements: Grave emergency threatening India's (or part of its) security by war, external aggression, or armed rebellion
Written Union Cabinet decision communicated to the President before issuance or variation
One-month provisional operation, extendable only by both Houses' approval
Six-month renewable cycles once approved, by special (total-membership-plus-two-thirds) majority
Lok Sabha disapproval resolution compels revocation regardless of Council of States' view
One-tenth-member written notice compels a special sitting within fourteen days to consider disapproval
exceptions_and_qualifications: Clause (9) allows multiple, independently-grounded Proclamations to coexist or be layered — a fresh Proclamation on one ground does not require revoking an existing one on another ground

The original 1950 text used the vaguer ground 'internal disturbance'; the 44th Amendment Act, 1978 replaced it with the narrower 'armed rebellion' and shortened the provisional window from two months to one month, both direct responses to the perceived misuse of this article during the 1975-77 Emergency

House-of-the-People-dissolution provisos protect against an emergency lapsing or being force-approved merely because the Lok Sabha happens to be dissolved at the critical moment — the Council of States' approval keeps it alive until the reconstituted Lok Sabha can act
breakdown.how_to_read: Read clause (1) for the three grounds and the anticipatory trigger, then clause (3) for the Cabinet-decision precondition that constrains the President's discretion. Clauses (4)-(6) form the Parliamentary-control timeline: one month, then renewable six-month blocks, both requiring the special majority. Clauses (7)-(8) are the built-in off-switch — the Lok Sabha can end an Emergency unilaterally, and even a minority of members can force the question onto the floor.

sections.title: Effect of Proclamation of Emergency.
sections.raw_text:
While a Proclamation of Emergency is in operation, then—

(a) notwithstanding anything in this Constitution, the executive power of the Union shall extend to the giving of directions to any State as to the manner in which the executive power thereof is to be exercised;

(b) the power of Parliament to make laws with respect to any matter shall include power to make laws conferring powers and imposing duties, or authorising the conferring of powers and the imposition of duties, upon the Union or officers and authorities of the Union as respects that matter, notwithstanding that it is one which is not enumerated in the Union List:

Provided that where a Proclamation of Emergency is in operation only in any part of the territory of India,—
(i) the executive power of the Union to give directions under clause (a), and
(ii) the power of Parliament to make laws under clause (b),
shall also extend to any State other than a State in which or in any part of which the Proclamation of Emergency is in operation if and in so far as the security of India or any part of the territory thereof is threatened by activities in or in relation to the part of the territory of India in which the Proclamation of Emergency is in operation.
key_terms: Union executive-direction power over every State's executive functioning during a National Emergency, overriding the Constitution's normal federal division
Parliament's temporary power to legislate on any matter whatsoever, including matters outside the Union List, during a National Emergency
spillover-effect proviso extending both powers to unaffected States where their security is threatened by activities linked to the emergency-affected area

breakdown.plain_summary: Once a National Emergency under Article 352 is in force, India's normally federal structure temporarily tilts heavily toward the Union: the Union executive can directly instruct any State on how to use its executive powers, and Parliament's law-making power expands to cover subjects that would otherwise belong exclusively to the States under the State List. This is the practical mechanism by which 'Emergency' converts India's federal system into something close to a unitary one for the duration.
essential_elements: Union executive directions override the normal Centre-State executive division, applicable to every State regardless of which party governs it
Parliament's expanded legislative competence reaches subjects not enumerated in the Union List, i.e. effectively State List and Concurrent List subjects
Both powers are available even over States where the Emergency Proclamation itself is not in operation, if cross-border security threats originating from the affected area justify it
exceptions_and_qualifications: The proviso's spillover extension is itself conditional — it only reaches an unaffected State 'in so far as' that State's security is threatened by activities connected to the Proclamation's area, not as a general extension of Union control nationwide

The expanded powers under this article exist only 'while a Proclamation of Emergency is in operation' — they automatically lapse the moment the Proclamation under Article 352 ceases to operate, with no separate revocation needed for Article 353's effects specifically
breakdown.how_to_read: Read clause (a) and (b) as the twin pillars of Emergency centralisation — executive control plus legislative reach — then read the proviso as a geographic extension clause for partial (not whole-of-India) Proclamations, not as an independent trigger.

sections.title: Application of provisions relating to distribution of revenues while a Proclamation of Emergency is in operation.
sections.raw_text:
(1) The President may, while a Proclamation of Emergency is in operation, by order direct that all or any of the provisions of articles 268 to 279 shall for such period, not extending in any case beyond the expiration of the financial year in which such Proclamation ceases to operate, as may be specified in the order, have effect subject to such exceptions or modifications as he thinks fit.

(2) Every order made under clause (1) shall, as soon as may be after it is made, be laid before each House of Parliament.
key_terms: President's power to modify the Articles 268-279 Union-State revenue distribution scheme during a National Emergency, capped at the end of the financial year in which the Emergency ceases

breakdown.plain_summary: Articles 268 to 279 normally govern how tax revenue is divided and distributed between the Union and the States. Article 354 lets the President temporarily alter or override that distribution scheme by order while a National Emergency is on — recognising that an emergency (war, external aggression, armed rebellion) may demand the Union redirect financial resources differently than the peacetime scheme allows. The modification cannot outlast the financial year in which the Emergency itself ends, and every such order must be laid before Parliament.
essential_elements: Power is exercisable only 'while a Proclamation of Emergency is in operation' under Article 352
Any modification of articles 268-279 automatically expires at the end of the financial year in which the Proclamation ceases to operate, even if the order purported to run longer
The order must be laid before both Houses of Parliament as soon as may be after it is made
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is a time-boxed, Emergency-dependent power only — it does not give the President any standing authority to alter Centre-State revenue sharing outside an Article 352 Emergency

Laying before Parliament is a transparency/oversight requirement, not itself a precondition to the order's validity — unlike Article 352's clauses which require active Parliamentary approval to continue in force
breakdown.how_to_read: Treat this as a financial-federalism companion to Article 353's executive/legislative centralisation — Article 353 covers governance and law-making, Article 354 covers who gets how much tax revenue, both time-limited to the Emergency's own duration.

sections.title: Duty of the Union to protect States against external aggression and internal disturbance
sections.raw_text: It shall be the duty of the Union to protect every State against external aggression and internal disturbance and to ensure that the Government of every State is carried on in accordance with the provisions of this Constitution.
key_terms: Union's constitutional duty to protect every State from external aggression and internal disturbance, and to ensure State governance stays constitutionally compliant

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 355 imposes a dual duty on the Union: first, to defend every State from external aggression and internal disturbance (a protective/security duty), and second, to ensure that every State's government actually functions in accordance with the Constitution (a compliance-monitoring duty). This second limb is the textual hook that the Union has historically invoked to justify stepping in under Article 356 when a State's constitutional machinery is said to have broken down — the duty to 'ensure' constitutional governance is read as implicitly authorising corrective Union action.
essential_elements: Twin duties: protection from external aggression/internal disturbance, and ensuring constitutionally compliant State governance
Owed to 'every State' — a general, standing Union obligation, not an emergency-triggered one
exceptions_and_qualifications: Article 355 is a duty-conferring provision, not itself a power-conferring one — the actual power to act on a breakdown of constitutional machinery comes from Article 356, with Article 355 supplying the constitutional justification/rationale

In S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994), the Supreme Court used Article 355 together with Article 356 to insist that Union intervention be read narrowly and remain judicially reviewable, rather than treating Article 355 as a blank cheque for unlimited Central interference in State affairs
breakdown.how_to_read: Read this article as the 'why' that explains Article 356's 'how' — Article 355 states the Union's underlying constitutional obligation, and Article 356 is the specific mechanism Parliament gave the President to discharge that obligation when a State's machinery fails.

sections.title: Provisions in case of failure of constitutional machinery in States
sections.raw_text:
(1) If the President, on receipt of a report from the Governor of a State or otherwise, is satisfied that a situation has arisen in which the Government of the State cannot be carried on in accordance with the provisions of this Constitution, the President may by Proclamation—
(a) assume to himself all or any of the functions of the Government of the State and all or any of the powers vested in or exercisable by the Governor or any body or authority in the State other than the Legislature of the State;
(b) declare that the powers of the Legislature of the State shall be exercisable by or under the authority of Parliament;
(c) make such incidental and consequential provisions as appear to the President to be necessary or desirable for giving effect to the objects of the Proclamation, including provisions for suspending in whole or in part the operation of any provisions of this Constitution relating to any body or authority in the State:
Provided that nothing in this clause shall authorise the President to assume to himself any of the powers vested in or exercisable by a High Court, or to suspend in whole or in part the operation of any provision of this Constitution relating to High Courts.

(2) Any such Proclamation may be revoked or varied by a subsequent Proclamation.

(3) Every Proclamation under this article shall be laid before each House of Parliament and shall, except where it is a Proclamation revoking a previous Proclamation, cease to operate at the expiration of two months unless before the expiration of that period it has been approved by resolutions of both Houses of Parliament:
Provided that if any such Proclamation (not being a Proclamation revoking a previous Proclamation) is issued at a time when the House of the People is dissolved or the dissolution of the House of the People takes place during the period of two months referred to in this clause, and if a resolution approving the Proclamation has been passed by the Council of States, but no resolution with respect to such Proclamation has been passed by the House of the People before the expiration of that period, the Proclamation shall cease to operate at the expiration of thirty days from the date on which the House of the People first sits after its reconstitution unless before the expiration of the said period of thirty days a resolution approving the Proclamation has been also passed by the House of the People.

(4) A Proclamation so approved shall, unless revoked, cease to operate on the expiration of a period of six months from the date of issue of the Proclamation:
Provided that if and so often as a resolution approving the continuance in force of such a Proclamation is passed by both Houses of Parliament, the Proclamation shall, unless revoked, continue in force for a further period of six months from the date on which under this clause it would otherwise have ceased to operate, but no such Proclamation shall in any case remain in force for more than three years:
Provided further that if the dissolution of the House of the People takes place during any such period of six months and a resolution approving the continuance in force of such Proclamation has been passed by the Council of States, but no resolution with respect to the continuance in force of such Proclamation has been passed by the House of the People during the said period, the Proclamation shall cease to operate at the expiration of thirty days from the date on which the House of the People first sits after its reconstitution unless before the expiration of the said period of thirty days a resolution approving the continuance in force of the Proclamation has been also passed by the House of the People:
Provided also that in the case of the Proclamation issued under clause (1) on the 11th day of May, 1987 with respect to the State of Punjab, the reference in the first proviso to this clause to “three years” shall be construed as a reference to five years.

(5) Notwithstanding anything contained in clause (4), a resolution with respect to the continuance in force of a Proclamation approved under clause (3) for any period beyond the expiration of one year from the date of issue of such Proclamation shall not be passed by either House of Parliament unless—
(a) a Proclamation of Emergency is in operation, in the whole of India or, as the case may be, in the whole or any part of the State, at the time of the passing of such resolution, and
(b) the Election Commission certifies that the continuance in force of the Proclamation approved under clause (3) during the period specified in such resolution is necessary on account of difficulties in holding general elections to the Legislative Assembly of the State concerned:
Provided that nothing in this clause shall apply to the Proclamation issued under clause (1) on the 11th day of May, 1987 with respect to the State of Punjab.
key_terms: President's Governor-report-or-otherwise-triggered satisfaction that a State's constitutional machinery has failed, empowering assumption of State executive/legislative functions ('President's Rule')
absolute exclusion of High Court powers/provisions from any Article 356 assumption or suspension
two-month provisional window requiring Parliamentary approval, then six-month renewable cycles capped at a three-year outer limit (five years for the 1987 Punjab Proclamation)
post-one-year extension gateway requiring a concurrent National Emergency plus Election Commission certification of election-holding difficulties

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 356 — commonly called 'President's Rule' — lets the President take over a State's executive and legislative functions when satisfied, typically on the Governor's report, that the State's government can no longer function constitutionally. The President can assume the Governor's and other State authorities' powers (but never the High Court's), and hand the State Legislature's law-making power to Parliament. Like a National Emergency, it needs Parliamentary approval within two months to survive, then renewal every six months, but — unlike Article 352 — there is a hard three-year ceiling (one historical exception: Punjab's 1987 Proclamation got five years), and extending it past one year requires both a live National Emergency and an Election Commission certification that elections genuinely cannot be held yet.
essential_elements: President's satisfaction, on a Governor's report or otherwise, that the State's government cannot be carried on in accordance with the Constitution

Scope of assumption: executive functions of the State Government, powers of the Governor or any State body/authority other than the Legislature, plus a declaration transferring the Legislature's law-making power to Parliament
Power to make incidental and consequential provisions, including suspending constitutional provisions relating to State bodies/authorities, to give effect to the Proclamation
Two-month provisional window followed by renewable six-month Parliamentary-approval cycles, capped at an overall three-year limit
exceptions_and_qualifications: High Courts and their constitutional provisions can never be touched by an Article 356 Proclamation — the proviso to clause (1) is an absolute carve-out
Three-year outer limit on total duration, with the sole historical exception being the Punjab Proclamation of 11 May 1987 extended to five years by a specific proviso
Extension beyond one year requires BOTH a concurrent Article 352 National Emergency AND Election Commission certification of election difficulties — not either alone
The Punjab 1987 Proclamation is also expressly exempted from the one-year extension gateway's conditions by the final proviso to clause (5)

S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994) (nine-judge bench) held that the President's 'satisfaction' under clause (1) is not immune from judicial review — courts can strike down a Proclamation issued mala fide, on irrelevant grounds, or as a fraud on the Constitution, and mandated that a floor test on the floor of the Assembly is the only conclusive way to demonstrate loss of majority, not the Governor's subjective assessment
breakdown.how_to_read: Read clause (1) for the trigger and scope (noting the High Court carve-out), then clauses (3)-(4) for the Parliamentary-approval timeline culminating in the three-year cap, and clause (5) as the narrow post-one-year exception. Keep Bommai in mind throughout: the textual 'satisfaction' language reads as subjective and unreviewable, but constitutional practice since 1994 is that it is objectively reviewable.

sections.title: Exercise of legislative powers under Proclamation issued under article 356
key_terms: Parliament's power to delegate a President's-Rule State's legislative function to the President, who may further sub-delegate it
President's power to authorise emergency State expenditure from the Consolidated Fund of the State pending Parliamentary sanction when the Lok Sabha is not in session
survival of laws made during President's Rule beyond the Proclamation's own cessation, until altered by a competent Legislature

breakdown.plain_summary: Once Article 356 has transferred a State's law-making power to Parliament, Article 357 works out the mechanics: Parliament can either make the State's laws itself, or hand that job to the President, who can further sub-delegate it to someone else he names. The President also gets a practical fiscal tool — authorising emergency spending from the State's own Consolidated Fund when the Lok Sabha isn't sitting to approve it formally. Crucially, any law validly made this way doesn't automatically die when President's Rule ends — it stays in force until a normal, competent State Legislature actively changes or repeals it.
essential_elements: Delegation chain: Parliament may delegate to the President, who may further sub-delegate to another named authority — a two-tier delegation structure
Clause (1)(c)'s emergency-expenditure authorisation power is available only 'when the House of the People is not in session', and remains subject to Parliament's later sanction

Clause (2)'s survival rule applies only to laws that Parliament/President/delegate would NOT otherwise have been competent to make but for the Article 356 Proclamation — i.e., laws trenching on the State's own exclusive domain
exceptions_and_qualifications: Clause (2) is a stability safeguard, not a loophole for permanent Central legislation — the surviving law remains fully subject to being altered, repealed, or amended by the State's own competent Legislature once normal governance resumes
breakdown.how_to_read: Read clause (1)'s three sub-clauses as parallel tools unlocked the moment Article 356's clause (1)(b) kicks in — delegation of law-making, further sub-delegation, and emergency spending authority — then read clause (2) as the answer to 'what happens to these laws once President's Rule ends.'

sections.title: Suspension of provisions of article 19 during emergencies
sections.raw_text:
(1) While a Proclamation of Emergency declaring that the security of India or any part of the territory thereof is threatened by war or by external aggression is in operation, nothing in article 19 shall restrict the power of the State as defined in Part III to make any law or to take any executive action which the State would but for the provisions contained in that Part be competent to make or to take, but any law so made shall, to the extent of the incompetency, cease to have effect as soon as the Proclamation ceases to operate, except as respects things done or omitted to be done before the law so ceases to have effect:
Provided that where such Proclamation of Emergency is in operation only in any part of the territory of India, any such law may be made, or any such executive action may be taken, under this article in relation to or in any State or Union territory in which or in any part of which the Proclamation of Emergency is not in operation, if and in so far as the security of India or any part of the territory thereof is threatened by activities in or in relation to the part of the territory of India in which the Proclamation of Emergency is in operation.

(2) Nothing in clause (1) shall apply —
(a) to any law which does not contain a recital to the effect that such law is in relation to the Proclamation of Emergency in operation when it is made; or
(b) to any executive action taken otherwise than under a law containing such a recital.
key_terms: automatic suspension of Article 19's restrictions on State law-making/executive action, but only during a war/external-aggression National Emergency (not an armed-rebellion-only Emergency)
44th-Amendment-added recital requirement confining the suspension to laws/actions that expressly declare their connection to the Proclamation

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 358 automatically frees the State from Article 19's six freedoms (speech, assembly, movement, etc.) the moment a National Emergency is declared on the ground of war or external aggression — but, after the 44th Amendment, pointedly NOT when the Emergency's only ground is armed rebellion. This is narrower than it sounds, though: any law or executive action relying on this suspension must say so explicitly (a 'recital') connecting it to the Emergency, and the suspension's effect automatically ends when the Proclamation ends (except for things already done under it).
essential_elements: Applies only to war/external-aggression Emergencies, not armed-rebellion-only Emergencies — a deliberate narrowing introduced by the 44th Amendment, 1978
Suspension is automatic (no separate Presidential order needed, unlike Article 359), but only covers Article 19, not the whole of Part III
Any law relying on this suspension must carry an explicit recital declaring its connection to the Emergency Proclamation, or clause (2) excludes it from protection entirely
The incompetent part of any such law automatically lapses once the Proclamation ends, except as to things already done or omitted under it
exceptions_and_qualifications: Before the 44th Amendment, Article 358 suspended Article 19 for any Emergency regardless of ground, and had no recital requirement — both the ground-restriction and the recital safeguard were added specifically to prevent a repeat of the broad Article 19 suspensions used during the 1975-77 Emergency
breakdown.how_to_read: Contrast this immediately with Article 359 next door: Article 358 is automatic but narrow (only Article 19, only war/aggression grounds), while Article 359 is discretionary (needs a separate Presidential order) but can reach any Part III right except Articles 20 and 21, for any Emergency ground.

sections.title: Suspension of the enforcement of the rights conferred by Part III during emergencies
sections.raw_text:
(1) Where a Proclamation of Emergency is in operation, the President may by order declare that the right to move any court for the enforcement of such of the rights conferred by Part III (except articles 20 and 21) as may be mentioned in the order and all proceedings pending in any court for the enforcement of the rights so mentioned shall remain suspended for the period during which the Proclamation is in force or for such shorter period as may be specified in the order.

(1A) While an order made under clause (1) mentioning any of the rights conferred by Part III (except articles 20 and 21) is in operation, nothing in that Part conferring those rights shall restrict the power of the State as defined in the said Part to make any law or to take any executive action which the State would but for the provisions contained in that Part be competent to make or to take, but any law so made shall, to the extent of the incompetency, cease to have effect as soon as the order aforesaid ceases to operate, except as respects things done or omitted to be done before the law so ceases to have effect:
Provided that where a Proclamation of Emergency is in operation only in any part of the territory of India, any such law may be made, or any such executive action may be taken, under this article in relation to or in any State or Union territory in which or in any part of which the Proclamation of Emergency is not in operation, if and in so far as the security of India or any part of the territory thereof is threatened by activities in or in relation to the part of the territory of India in which the Proclamation of Emergency is in operation.

(1B) Nothing in clause (1A) shall apply—
(a) to any law which does not contain a recital to the effect that such law is in relation to the Proclamation of Emergency in operation when it is made; or
(b) to any executive action taken otherwise than under a law containing such a recital.

(2) An order made as aforesaid may extend to the whole or any part of the territory of India:
Provided that where a Proclamation of Emergency is in operation only in a part of the territory of India, any such order shall not extend to any other part of the territory of India unless the President, being satisfied that the security of India or any part of the territory thereof is threatened by activities in or in relation to the part of the territory of India in which the Proclamation of Emergency is in operation, considers such extension to be necessary.

(3) Every order made under clause (1) shall, as soon as may be after it is made, be laid before each House of Parliament.
key_terms: President's discretionary power to suspend the right to move any court to enforce specified Part III rights during any National Emergency, expressly excluding Articles 20 and 21
consequential State law-making/executive-action immunity mirroring Article 358's mechanism, again subject to the 44th-Amendment recital requirement

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 359 lets the President, by a separate order (unlike Article 358's automatic trigger), suspend people's ability to go to court to enforce specific Part III fundamental rights while any National Emergency is on — but Articles 20 (protection in respect of conviction for offences) and 21 (protection of life and personal liberty) can never be touched, a permanent safeguard added by the 44th Amendment after the ADM Jabalpur controversy. Once such an order is made for particular rights, the State also gets the same law-making/executive-action immunity structure as Article 358, again requiring an explicit recital connecting any such law to the Emergency.
essential_elements: Requires a separate, discretionary Presidential order (not automatic like Article 358) specifying exactly which rights are suspended
Articles 20 and 21 are permanently and absolutely excluded from any suspension order — this cannot be overridden by any future order
Available during any National Emergency (war, external aggression, or armed rebellion), unlike Article 358's narrower war/external-aggression-only trigger
The order itself, and any law relying on clause (1A)'s immunity, must still be laid before Parliament and carry the recital required by clause (1B)
exceptions_and_qualifications: Before the 44th Amendment, Article 359 permitted suspension of the right to approach courts for ALL Part III rights with no permanent exclusion — it was this unrestricted version that the Supreme Court controversially upheld as covering even Article 21 in ADM Jabalpur v. Shivkant Shukla (1976), allowing habeas corpus petitions to be barred during the 1975-77 Emergency

The 44th Amendment's addition of the Articles 20/21 carve-out was a direct legislative reversal of ADM Jabalpur, and ADM Jabalpur itself was later expressly overruled by the Supreme Court in K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) on the right to privacy, which held the majority's reasoning in ADM Jabalpur to have been wrong even for its own time
breakdown.how_to_read: Compare directly against Article 358: here the President must act by a specific order naming the rights, the trigger can be any Emergency ground, and Articles 20/21 are permanently off-limits — read clause (1) for the court-access suspension, then (1A)-(1B) for the mirrored State-immunity mechanism, keeping the ADM Jabalpur history in mind as the reason the Article 20/21 exclusion exists at all.

sections.title: Provisions as to financial emergency
key_terms: President's satisfaction that India's (or any part's) financial stability or credit is threatened, triggering a Financial Emergency Proclamation
two-month provisional window requiring Parliamentary approval, with no fixed outer time cap (unlike Article 356's three-year limit)

Union's power to direct States on financial-propriety canons and, via clause (4), to compel salary reductions for State employees, State Money Bill reservation for Presidential consideration, and even Union employee/judicial salary reductions

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 360 is the Constitution's third and least-used emergency mechanism: a Financial Emergency, triggered when the President is satisfied India's (or part of its) financial stability or credit is under threat. Once proclaimed, it needs Parliamentary approval within two months (no renewal-cycle cap is specified, unlike Articles 352 and 356). While in force, the Union can direct States to follow specified standards of financial discipline, require State salary cuts, force State Money Bills to be reserved for Presidential consideration — and, remarkably, even direct salary reductions for Union employees, including Supreme Court and High Court judges.
essential_elements: Trigger is financial stability/credit threat to India or any part, assessed solely on the President's satisfaction
Two-month provisional window before requiring Parliamentary approval by ordinary resolution (not the special majority Article 352 requires)
Clause (4)(b)'s judicial-salary-reduction power is a notable, express exception to judicial independence/security-of-tenure norms, applicable 'notwithstanding anything in this Constitution'
exceptions_and_qualifications: Unlike Articles 352 and 356, Article 360 specifies no outer time limit or mandatory six-month renewal cycle for a Financial Emergency's continuance beyond the initial two-month approval — this is a structural gap, not an oversight the text otherwise addresses

As of this record, Article 360 has never been invoked in India's constitutional history — it is the Constitution's one entirely dormant emergency power, in contrast to Articles 352 (invoked three times) and 356 (invoked over 100 times)
breakdown.how_to_read: Read clause (1) for the trigger, clause (2) for the two-month Parliamentary-approval gate, and clauses (3)-(4) for the Union's financial-discipline toolkit — pay particular attention to clause (4)(b) as the one place the Constitution expressly permits touching judicial salaries by executive direction, a sharp contrast to the otherwise strong protections for judicial independence elsewhere.

sections.title: Protection of President and Governors and Rajpramukhs
sections.raw_text:
(1) The President, or the Governor or Rajpramukh of a State, shall not be answerable to any court for the exercise and performance of the powers and duties of his office or for any act done or purporting to be done by him in the exercise and performance of those powers and duties:
Provided that the conduct of the President may be brought under review by any court, tribunal or body appointed or designated by either House of Parliament for the investigation of a charge under article 61:
Provided further that nothing in this clause shall be construed as restricting the right of any person to bring appropriate proceedings against the Government of India or the Government of a State.
(2) No criminal proceedings whatsoever shall be instituted or continued against the President, or the Governor of a State, in any court during his term of office.
(3) No process for the arrest or imprisonment of the President, or the Governor of a State, shall issue from any court during his term of office.
(4) No civil proceedings in which relief is claimed against the President, or the Governor of a State, shall be instituted during his term of office in any court in respect of any act done or purporting to be done by him in his personal capacity, whether before or after he entered upon his office as President, or as Governor of such State, until the expiration of two months next after notice in writing has been delivered to the President or the Governor, as the case may be, or left at his office stating the nature of the proceedings, the cause of action therefor, the name, description and place of residence of the party by whom such proceedings are to be instituted and the relief which he claims.
key_terms: personal immunity
official acts immunity
impeachment review
two-month notice

breakdown.plain_summary: The President and State Governors enjoy sweeping personal immunity while in office: they cannot be hauled before any court to answer for how they exercised their official powers, cannot face criminal proceedings or arrest/imprisonment at all during their term, and civil suits over personal-capacity acts can only be filed after two months' prior written notice. The one carve-out is that Parliament's own impeachment process under Article 61 can still scrutinise the President's conduct, and ordinary suits against the Government of India or a State Government (as opposed to against the individual officeholder) remain unaffected.
essential_elements: Clause (1): blanket non-answerability before any court for acts done in the exercise and performance of the powers and duties of the office
Clause (2): total bar on instituting or continuing criminal proceedings against the President or a Governor during the term of office
Clause (3): total bar on any court issuing process for arrest or imprisonment during the term of office

Clause (4): civil proceedings for personal-capacity acts (whether arising before or after entering office) require two months' prior written notice specifying the proceedings, cause of action, party details, and relief claimed
exceptions_and_qualifications: The President's conduct can still be reviewed by a Parliamentary body investigating an Article 61 impeachment charge
The immunity does not restrict any person's right to bring appropriate proceedings against the Government of India or the Government of a State as such (as opposed to the individual officeholder)
The criminal and arrest immunities under clauses (2) and (3) are time-limited to the term of office only — proceedings can be instituted after the term ends
Civil immunity under clause (4) is not absolute, only deferred — it merely imposes a two-month notice precondition, after which the suit may proceed

The reference to 'Rajpramukh' is a vestige of the original 1950 text (Part B States, abolished by the Seventh Amendment, 1956) and has no operative application today; only 'President' and 'Governor' remain live in clauses (2)-(4)
breakdown.how_to_read: Read this as the structural counterpart to the President's and Governors' lack of real discretionary power — the Constitution trades their relative powerlessness for near-total legal insulation. When pleading against the Union or a State, always frame the proceedings against the 'Government of India'/'Government of a State' rather than naming the President or Governor personally, both to respect this immunity and because that is the constitutionally correct party under Article 300 in any event.

sections.title: Protection of publication of proceedings of Parliament and State Legislatures
sections.raw_text:
(1) No person shall be liable to any proceedings, civil or criminal, in any court in respect of the publication in a newspaper of a substantially true report of any proceedings of either House of Parliament or the Legislative Assembly, or, as the case may be, either House of the Legislature, of a State, unless the publication is proved to have been made with malice:
Provided that nothing in this clause shall apply to the publication of any report of the proceedings of a secret sitting of either House of Parliament or the Legislative Assembly, or, as the case may be, either House of the Legislature, of a State.
(2) Clause (1) shall apply in relation to reports or matters broadcast by means of wireless telegraphy as part of any programme or service provided by means of a broadcasting station as it applies in relation to reports or matters published in a newspaper.
Explanation.—In this article, “newspaper” includes a news agency report containing material for publication in a newspaper.
key_terms: qualified privilege
substantially true report
malice
secret sitting

breakdown.plain_summary: The press and broadcasters get qualified legal protection for reporting on Parliament and State Legislature proceedings: if a newspaper or broadcast report is substantially true, no civil or criminal liability attaches to it, even if the underlying statements reported were defamatory or otherwise actionable. This protection evaporates if the publication was made with malice, and it never extends to reports of secret sittings.
essential_elements: The report must be of proceedings of either House of Parliament, or the Legislative Assembly, or either House of a State Legislature
The report must be substantially true, not necessarily word-perfect
Immunity is lost if the publication is proved to have been made with malice
Clause (2) extends the same protection to wireless/broadcast reports of such proceedings, treated on par with newspaper publication
The Explanation widens 'newspaper' to include a news agency report prepared for newspaper publication, even before it is actually printed
exceptions_and_qualifications: The proviso carves out reports of secret sittings of either House — no privilege attaches to publishing those regardless of truth or good faith
Malice destroys the privilege entirely — a substantially true but maliciously published report is not protected

This Article was not part of the original 1950 Constitution; it was inserted by the Constitution (Forty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1978, restoring press protections that had been removed during the Emergency era
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the constitutional source of 'qualified privilege' that journalists and editors rely on when covering legislative debates — plead it as a complete defence to a defamation claim arising purely from fair legislative reportage, but be ready to prove 'substantial truth' and absence of malice, since both are factual questions a plaintiff can contest.

sections.title: Disqualification for appointment on remunerative political post
sections.raw_text:
A member of a House belonging to any political party who is disqualified for being a member of the House under paragraph 2 of the Tenth Schedule shall also be disqualified to hold any remunerative political post for duration of the period commencing from the date of his disqualification till the date on which the term of his office as such member would expire or till the date on which he contests an election to a House and is declared elected, whichever is earlier.
Explanation.—For the purposes of this article,—
(a) the expression “House” has the meaning assigned to it in clause (a) of paragraph 1 of the Tenth Schedule;
(b) the expression “remunerative political post” means any office—
(i) under the Government of India or the Government of a State where the salary or remuneration for such office is paid out of the public revenue of the Government of India or the Government of the State, as the case may be; or
(ii) under a body, whether incorporated or not, which is wholly or partially owned by the Government of India or the Government of State, and the salary or remuneration for such office is paid by such body,
except where such salary or remuneration paid is compensatory in nature.
key_terms: remunerative political post
Tenth Schedule disqualification
defection

breakdown.plain_summary: This Article closes an anti-defection loophole: a legislator who gets disqualified under the Tenth Schedule for defection cannot simply be rewarded with a paid government post (minister, chairman of a public corporation, etc.) to soften the blow. The post-ban runs from the date of disqualification until either the original term would have ended or the member gets re-elected, whichever comes first.
essential_elements: Applies only to a member already disqualified for being a member of a House under paragraph 2 of the Tenth Schedule (the anti-defection provision)

Bars holding any 'remunerative political post' as defined in the Explanation — government offices or offices under wholly/partially government-owned bodies that pay salary or remuneration from public revenue

The disqualification period runs from the date of disqualification to the earlier of (a) the date the original term of office would have expired, or (b) the date the person contests and is declared elected to a House
exceptions_and_qualifications: The bar does not apply to remuneration that is merely 'compensatory in nature' (e.g. genuine reimbursement of expenses) rather than a salary

This provision was not part of the Constitution of India, 1950 — it was inserted by the Constitution (Ninety-first Amendment) Act, 2003, alongside the tightening of anti-defection law and the cap on council of ministers' size
breakdown.how_to_read: Use this alongside the Tenth Schedule when arguing that a defector's subsequent ministerial or corporation-chairmanship appointment is unconstitutional — the disqualification under the Tenth Schedule and the post-ban under Article 361B operate as a single continuous sanction, not two independent inquiries.

sections.title: Bar to interference by courts in disputes arising out of certain treaties, agreements, etc.
sections.raw_text:
(1) Notwithstanding anything in this Constitution but subject to the provisions of article 143, neither the Supreme Court nor any other court shall have jurisdiction in any dispute arising out of any provision of a treaty, agreement, covenant, engagement, sanad or other similar instrument which was entered into or executed before the commencement of this Constitution by any Ruler of an Indian State and to which the Government of the Dominion of India or any of its predecessor Governments was a party and which has or has been continued in operation after such commencement, or in any dispute in respect of any right accruing under or any liability or obligation arising out of any of the provisions of this Constitution relating to any such treaty, agreement, covenant, engagement, sanad or other similar instrument.
(2) In this article—
(a) “Indian State” means any territory recognised before the commencement of this Constitution by His Majesty or the Government of the Dominion of India as being such a State; and
(b) “Ruler” includes the Prince, Chief or other person recognised before such commencement by His Majesty or the Government of the Dominion of India as the Ruler of any Indian State.
key_terms: ouster of jurisdiction
sanad
Article 143 reference
accession instruments

breakdown.plain_summary: No court — not even the Supreme Court — can hear a dispute about the treaties, covenants, or 'sanads' (royal grants/instruments) through which the princely states acceded to or integrated with India before the Constitution began, or about rights and obligations the Constitution itself creates in relation to those instruments. The only route by which such questions can still reach the judiciary is a Presidential reference to the Supreme Court for an advisory opinion under Article 143.
essential_elements: The ouster is total: 'neither the Supreme Court nor any other court shall have jurisdiction'

It covers disputes arising out of any treaty, agreement, covenant, engagement, sanad, or similar instrument entered into or executed before the Constitution's commencement by a Ruler of an Indian State
The Government of the Dominion of India (or a predecessor Government) must have been a party, and the instrument must have continued in operation after the Constitution commenced
It also covers disputes about rights, liabilities, or obligations arising under constitutional provisions relating to such instruments
Clause (2) defines 'Indian State' and 'Ruler' by reference to pre-commencement recognition by His Majesty or the Dominion Government
exceptions_and_qualifications: The entire bar operates 'subject to the provisions of article 143' — a Presidential reference for the Supreme Court's advisory opinion remains available even though ordinary litigation does not
The bar is specifically about pre-commencement instruments between Rulers and the Dominion/predecessor Governments — it does not oust jurisdiction over unrelated post-Constitution disputes
breakdown.how_to_read: This is a classic jurisdictional-bar provision to check first in any litigation touching former princely-state accession instruments or privy-purse-era arrangements — raise it at the threshold (even via Order VII Rule 11 analogy) to seek outright dismissal for want of jurisdiction, since no amount of pleading skill on the merits can cure an Article 363 bar.

sections.title: Recognition granted to Rulers of Indian States to cease and privy purses to be abolished
key_terms: privy purse abolition
de-recognition of Rulers
26th Amendment

breakdown.plain_summary: This is the operative provision that actually ended the special constitutional status of former princely rulers: from the moment the Twenty-sixth Amendment, 1971 took effect, every person previously recognised by the President as a Ruler (or as a Ruler's successor) stopped being so recognised, and the privy purse payments guaranteed to them at the time of accession were abolished outright, wiping out all associated rights, liabilities, and obligations.
essential_elements: Operates notwithstanding anything else in the Constitution or any other law currently in force — an overriding non-obstante provision
Clause (a): de-recognises, with effect from the 26th Amendment's commencement, every person who had been recognised as a Ruler or a Ruler's successor before that date
Clause (b): abolishes the privy purse entirely from the same commencement date and extinguishes all rights, liabilities, and obligations connected to it
exceptions_and_qualifications: No exceptions are carved out within the Article itself — it is a clean, total abolition applying to every former Ruler/successor without distinction
breakdown.how_to_read: Article 363A must be read together with Article 363's jurisdictional bar and Article 362's omission (clause guaranteeing Rulers' personal rights/privileges/dignities) to see the complete picture: the 26th Amendment first struck out the guarantee clause (Article 362), then separately enacted this provision to affirmatively abolish the privy purse — plead both together when a historical privy-purse claim resurfaces, since Article 363A forecloses it on the merits while Article 363 forecloses it on jurisdiction.

sections.title: Special provisions as to major ports and aerodromes
sections.raw_text:
(1) Notwithstanding anything in this Constitution, the President may by public notification direct that as from such date as may be specified in the notification—
(a) any law made by Parliament or by the Legislature of a State shall not apply to any major port or aerodrome or shall apply thereto subject to such exceptions or modifications as may be specified in the notification, or
(b) any existing law shall cease to have effect in any major port or aerodrome except as respects things done or omitted to be done before the said date, or shall in its application to such port or aerodrome have effect subject to such exceptions or modifications as may be specified in the notification.
(2) In this article—
(a) “major port” means a port declared to be a major port by or under any law made by Parliament or any existing law and includes all areas for the time being included within the limits of such port;
(b) “aerodrome” means aerodrome as defined for the purposes of the enactments relating to airways, aircraft and air navigation.
key_terms: major port
aerodrome
public notification

breakdown.plain_summary: The President can carve out major ports and aerodromes from the ordinary application of central or state laws by issuing a public notification — either disapplying a law to that port/aerodrome entirely, applying it with modifications, or switching off an existing law there (without disturbing things already done under it) from a date the notification specifies. This gives the Union a direct, notification-based tool to apply specialised port/airport regulatory regimes.
essential_elements: Operates notwithstanding anything else in the Constitution
Exercised by the President through a public notification specifying an effective date
Clause (1)(a): can disapply, or apply with exceptions/modifications, a Parliament-made or State-Legislature-made law to a major port or aerodrome

Clause (1)(b): can switch off an existing (pre-Constitution) law's effect in a major port or aerodrome, or apply it with exceptions/modifications, while preserving the validity of things already done or omitted before the specified date
Clause (2) defines 'major port' (by reference to any law declaring it such, including all areas within its limits) and 'aerodrome' (by reference to aviation-law definitions)
exceptions_and_qualifications: The power only operates prospectively from the date specified in the notification — things done or omitted before that date under a disapplied existing law remain valid and unaffected
breakdown.how_to_read: A narrow, specialised Union power — relevant mainly in administrative-law disputes over whether a particular State enactment (e.g. local taxation or labour law) validly applies within the territorial limits of a notified major port or aerodrome; always check the Gazette for an Article 364 notification before assuming ordinary State law governs activity physically located inside port/airport limits.

sections.title: Effect of failure to comply with, or to give effect to, directions given by the Union
sections.raw_text: Where any State has failed to comply with, or to give effect to, any directions given in the exercise of the executive power of the Union under any of the provisions of this Constitution, it shall be lawful for the President to hold that a situation has arisen in which the Government of the State cannot be carried on in accordance with the provisions of this Constitution.
key_terms: Union directions
deemed breakdown of constitutional machinery

breakdown.plain_summary: If a State government ignores or fails to carry out lawful directions issued to it by the Union in exercise of executive power, the President is entitled to treat that failure itself as proof that the State's constitutional machinery has broken down — which is the exact trigger condition for invoking President's Rule under Article 356.
essential_elements: Applies where a State fails to comply with, or give effect to, directions given in the exercise of the executive power of the Union under any constitutional provision
On such failure, it becomes lawful for the President to hold that a situation has arisen in which the State's government cannot be carried on in accordance with the Constitution
exceptions_and_qualifications: Article 365 does not itself impose President's Rule — it only supplies a deeming basis the President may rely on when forming the satisfaction required under Article 355/356

Not every instance of non-compliance with a Union direction automatically triggers this Article; it is 'lawful' for the President to so hold, not mandatory, and the resulting Article 356 Proclamation remains subject to the same judicial-review safeguards established in S.R. Bommai v. Union of India
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the textual bridge connecting the many scattered Union-direction powers throughout the Constitution (e.g. over railways, communications, or Article 256/257 directions) to the Article 356 President's Rule machinery — when a State is accused of defying a specific Union direction, plead Article 365 as the link that elevates ordinary non-compliance into constitutional-breakdown territory, but remember Bommai's floor-test and judicial-review safeguards still constrain how far that can be taken.

sections.title: Definitions
key_terms: constitutional definitions clause
existing law
Scheduled Castes
Scheduled Tribes
Proclamation of Emergency

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 366 is the Constitution's master glossary — a single list of nearly thirty defined terms (from 'agricultural income' to 'Union territory') that fix the precise legal meaning of expressions used throughout the document, so that every other Article can be read against a stable, shared vocabulary instead of being interpreted word-by-word in isolation.
essential_elements: Applies 'unless the context otherwise requires' — a rebuttable default, not an absolute override of context-specific meaning elsewhere in the Constitution
Defines foundational structural terms: 'article', 'clause', 'sub-clause', 'Part', 'Schedule', 'existing law', 'public notification'

Defines key substantive terms load-bearing for other Parts: 'Scheduled Castes' and 'Scheduled Tribes' (tied to Articles 341-342), 'Proclamation of Emergency' (tied to Article 352(1)), 'High Court', 'Indian State'
Defines fiscal/financial terms central to Part XII: 'agricultural income', 'corporation tax', 'estate duty', 'debt', 'tax on the sale or purchase of goods', 'taxation'
Defines 'Anglo-Indian' and 'Union territory', each tied to specific representational or territorial provisions elsewhere in the Constitution
exceptions_and_qualifications: The currently-shown text omits the original 1950 definitions of 'Rajpramukh', 'Ruler', and 'Uparajpramukh' (clauses 21, 22, 30 of the 1950 text) — these were definitionally tied to Part B States and princely-state integration and became redundant after the States Reorganisation and the 26th Amendment's abolition of Ruler recognition
Clause numbering has gaps (21-22 absent, 29A inserted) reflecting successive amendments rather than a clean sequential renumbering
breakdown.how_to_read: Treat Article 366 as the first port of call whenever a word used elsewhere in the Constitution seems ambiguous — before reaching for external dictionaries or the General Clauses Act (Article 367(1)), check whether the term is specifically defined here, since a specific constitutional definition always displaces a general one.

sections.title: Interpretation
sections.raw_text:
(1) Unless the context otherwise requires, the General Clauses Act, 1897, shall, subject to any adaptations and modifications that may be made therein under article 372, apply for the interpretation of this Constitution as it applies for the interpretation of an Act of the Legislature of the Dominion of India.
(2) Any reference in this Constitution to Acts or laws of, or made by, Parliament, or to Acts or laws of, or made by, the Legislature of a State, shall be construed as including a reference to an Ordinance made by the President or, to an Ordinance made by a Governor, as the case may be.
(3) For the purposes of this Constitution “foreign State” means any State other than India:
Provided that, subject to the provisions of any law made by Parliament, the President may by order declare any State not to be a foreign State for such purposes as may be specified in the order.
key_terms: General Clauses Act
Ordinance as law reference
foreign State

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 367 supplies the Constitution's general interpretive toolkit: it imports the General Clauses Act, 1897 (the standard statutory-interpretation statute) to fill gaps Article 366's specific glossary doesn't cover; it clarifies that wherever the Constitution refers to a Parliamentary or State Legislature 'Act' or 'law', that reference also covers an Ordinance made by the President or a Governor; and it defines 'foreign State' as any State other than India, while letting the President carve out exceptions by order.
essential_elements: Clause (1): applies the General Clauses Act, 1897 to Constitution interpretation (subject to adaptations made under Article 372), unless context otherwise requires
Clause (2): deems references to Parliament-made or State-Legislature-made Acts/laws to include Ordinances made by the President or a Governor
Clause (3): defines 'foreign State' as any State other than India for constitutional purposes
exceptions_and_qualifications: All three clauses are themselves qualified — clause (1) by 'unless the context otherwise requires' and by Article 372 adaptations, clause (3) by the President's order-making proviso (itself subject to any Parliamentary law on the subject)
The 'foreign State' default rule can be displaced for specified purposes by Presidential order, without amending the Constitution itself
breakdown.how_to_read: Cite Article 367(1) to justify borrowing General Clauses Act definitions (e.g. of 'person', 'shall'/'may', or rules for computing time) whenever the Constitution itself is silent and Article 366 does not independently define the term in question — this is the default fallback, not the first stop.

sections.title: Power of Parliament to amend the Constitution and procedure therefor
sections.raw_text:
(1) Notwithstanding anything in this Constitution, Parliament may in exercise of its constituent power amend by way of addition, variation or repeal any provision of this Constitution in accordance with the procedure laid down in this article.
(2) An amendment of this Constitution may be initiated only by the introduction of a Bill for the purpose in either House of Parliament, and when the Bill is passed in each House by a majority of the total membership of that House and by a majority of not less than two-thirds of the members of that House present and voting, it shall be presented to the President who shall give his assent to the Bill and thereupon the Constitution shall stand amended in accordance with the terms of the Bill:
Provided that if such amendment seeks to make any change in—
(a) article 54, article 55, article 73, article 162, article 241 or article 279A; or
(b) Chapter IV of Part V, Chapter V of Part VI, or Chapter I of Part XI; or
(c) any of the Lists in the Seventh Schedule; or
(d) the representation of States in Parliament; or
(e) the provisions of this article,
the amendment shall also require to be ratified by the Legislatures of not less than one-half of the States by resolutions to that effect passed by those Legislatures before the Bill making provision for such amendment is presented to the President for assent.
(3) Nothing in article 13 shall apply to any amendment made under this article.
(4) No amendment of this Constitution (including the provisions of Part III) made or purporting to have been made under this article whether before or after the commencement of section 55 of the Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Act, 1976 shall be called in question in any court on any ground.
(5) For the removal of doubts, it is hereby declared that there shall be no limitation whatever on the constituent power of Parliament to amend by way of addition, variation or repeal the provisions of this Constitution under this article.
key_terms: constituent power
special majority
State ratification
basic structure doctrine

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 368 is the Constitution's own amendment manual: Parliament can add to, vary, or repeal any constitutional provision, but only by a Bill passed in each House with a 'special majority' (majority of total membership, and two-thirds of members present and voting), followed by Presidential assent. A defined list of entrenched provisions — the President's/Governors'/Vice-President's election mechanics, Centre-State legislative relations, the Seventh Schedule Lists, State representation in Parliament, and Article 368 itself — additionally needs ratification by at least half the State Legislatures before presidential assent. Clauses (4) and (5), inserted by the 42nd Amendment to declare the amending power limitless and non-justiciable, were themselves struck down by the Supreme Court as unconstitutional.
essential_elements: Clause (1): vests Parliament with 'constituent power' (as distinct from ordinary legislative power) to amend by addition, variation, or repeal, notwithstanding anything else in the Constitution

Clause (2): prescribes the universal procedure — a Bill introduced in either House, passed by special majority in each House (majority of total membership AND two-thirds of those present and voting), then Presidential assent, which is mandatory once validly passed

The proviso to clause (2): identifies the entrenched category of amendments additionally requiring ratification by not less than one-half of State Legislatures before presidential assent — covering Presidential/Vice-Presidential election provisions, Centre-State executive/legislative relations chapters, the Seventh Schedule Lists, States' Parliamentary representation, and the amending procedure itself
Clause (3): expressly excludes Article 13 (which voids ordinary laws inconsistent with Part III) from applying to constitutional amendments made under Article 368
exceptions_and_qualifications: Clauses (4) and (5), inserted by the Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Act, 1976 to place constitutional amendments beyond all judicial review and declare the amending power unlimited, were struck down as unconstitutional by the Supreme Court in Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India, (1980) 3 SCC 625 — they remain in the printed text but have no legal effect, since limited government and judicial review are themselves part of the basic structure the amending power cannot touch

Clause (3)'s exclusion of Article 13 does not mean amendments are wholly unreviewable — Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala, (1973) 4 SCC 225 (13-judge bench) held that while Parliament's amending power is wide enough to amend any Part of the Constitution including Part III fundamental rights, it cannot be used to damage or destroy the Constitution's 'basic structure'

There is no exhaustive list of 'basic structure' features — subsequent decisions have recognised judicial review, free and fair elections, federalism, secularism, separation of powers, and the rule of law (among others) as part of it, developed case-by-case rather than exhaustively codified
breakdown.how_to_read: Kesavananda Bharati is the ratio to plead whenever a constitutional amendment is challenged: Parliament's amending power under Article 368 is wide but not unlimited, and any amendment that damages or destroys the Constitution's basic structure is liable to be struck down by courts — despite the text of clauses (4) and (5) purporting to say otherwise. Always check whether a challenged amendment falls within the special-majority-only category or the additional State-ratification category under the proviso, since a procedural defect (wrong majority, missing ratification) is an independent, easier ground than a substantive basic-structure challenge.

sections.title: Temporary power to Parliament to make laws with respect to certain matters in the State List as if they were matters in the Concurrent List
sections.raw_text:
Notwithstanding anything in this Constitution, Parliament shall, during a period of five years from the commencement of this Constitution, have power to make laws with respect to the following matters as if they were enumerated in the Concurrent List, namely:—
(a) trade and commerce within a State in, and the production, supply and distribution of, cotton and woollen textiles, raw cotton (including ginned cotton and unginned cotton or kapas), cotton seed, paper (including newsprint), food-stuffs (including edible oilseeds and oil), cattle fodder (including oil-cakes and other concentrates), coal (including coke and derivatives of coal), iron, steel and mica;
(b) offences against laws with respect to any of the matters mentioned in clause (a), jurisdiction and powers of all courts except the Supreme Court with respect to any of those matters, and fees in respect of any of those matters but not including fees taken in any court,
but any law made by Parliament, which Parliament would not but for the provisions of this article have been competent to make, shall, to the extent of the incompetency, cease to have effect on the expiration of the said period, except as respects things done or omitted to be done before the expiration thereof.
key_terms: temporary Concurrent List power
five-year sunset clause

breakdown.plain_summary: For exactly five years from the Constitution's commencement (i.e. until 26 January 1955), Parliament got a time-limited power to legislate on certain essential-commodities matters — textiles, foodstuffs, coal, iron, steel, mica, and related offences/court jurisdiction/fees — that would otherwise sit exclusively in the State List. Any law Parliament passed using only this borrowed power automatically lost effect once the five years ran out, though things already done under it before expiry stayed valid.
essential_elements: Operates notwithstanding anything else in the Constitution, for a fixed five-year window from commencement
Covers trade/commerce/production/supply/distribution within a State of specified essential commodities (textiles, raw cotton, paper, foodstuffs, cattle fodder, coal, iron, steel, mica)
Also covers offences against laws on those matters, court jurisdiction and powers (except the Supreme Court) over those matters, and related fees (excluding court fees)
Any law relying solely on this temporary competence automatically ceases to have effect, to the extent of the incompetency, once the five-year period expires
exceptions_and_qualifications: Things done or omitted to be done before the expiry of the five-year period remain unaffected even after the temporary power lapses
This Article is now spent/historical — its operative five-year window closed in 1955, and it survives in the text only as a record of that transitional arrangement
breakdown.how_to_read: A purely historical provision today — useful mainly to explain why certain mid-1950s Parliamentary enactments on textiles/foodstuffs/coal were valid despite touching State List subjects, and as an example of a self-executing sunset clause embedded directly in constitutional text rather than left to ordinary legislative repeal.

sections.title: Temporary provisions with respect to the State of Jammu and Kashmir
sections.raw_text:
(1) Notwithstanding anything in this Constitution,—
(a) the provisions of article 238 shall not apply in relation to the State of Jammu and Kashmir;
(b) the power of Parliament to make laws for the said State shall be limited to—
