(i) those matters in the Union List and the Concurrent List which, in consultation with the Government of the State, are declared by the President to correspond to matters specified in the Instrument of Accession governing the accession of the State to the Dominion of India as the matters with respect to which the Dominion Legislature may make laws for that State; and
(ii) such other matters in the said Lists as, with the concurrence of the Government of the State, the President may by order specify.
Explanation.—For the purposes of this article, the Government of the State means the person for the time being recognised by the President as the Maharaja of Jammu and Kashmir acting on the advice of the Council of Ministers for the time being in office under the Maharaja's Proclamation dated the fifth day of March, 1948;
(c) the provisions of article 1 and of this article shall apply in relation to that State;
(d) such of the other provisions of this Constitution shall apply in relation to that State subject to such exceptions and modifications as the President may by order specify:
Provided that no such order which relates to the matters specified in the Instrument of Accession of the State referred to in paragraph (i) of sub-clause (b) shall be issued except in consultation with the Government of the State:
Provided further that no such order which relates to matters other than those referred to in the last preceding proviso shall be issued except with the concurrence of that Government.
(2) If the concurrence of the Government of the State referred to in paragraph (ii) of sub-clause (b) of clause (1) or in the second proviso to sub-clause (d) of that clause be given before the Constituent Assembly for the purpose of framing the Constitution of the State is convened, it shall be placed before such Assembly for such decision as it may take thereon.
(3) Notwithstanding anything in the foregoing provisions of this article, the President may, by public notification, declare that this article shall cease to be operative or shall be operative only with such exceptions and modifications and from such date as he may specify:
Provided that the recommendation of the Constituent Assembly of the State referred to in clause (2) shall be necessary before the President issues such a notification.
key_terms: Instrument of Accession
asymmetric federalism
concurrence of State Government
Presidential notification to cease operation

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 370 was the constitutional vehicle for Jammu and Kashmir's distinctive relationship with the Union: Parliament's law-making power over the State was limited to subjects tied to the original Instrument of Accession (defence, foreign affairs, communications) unless the State Government concurred to extend it further, and other constitutional provisions applied to the State only as the President specified by order, generally needing the State Government's consultation or concurrence. Clause (3) always contained a built-in mechanism for the President to declare the Article inoperative — the very route used in August 2019 to effectively end its operation.
essential_elements: Clause (1)(a): disapplies Article 238 (the now-repealed Part B States provision) to Jammu and Kashmir
Clause (1)(b): caps Parliament's law-making power over the State to Instrument-of-Accession-linked Union/Concurrent List matters, extendable only with the State Government's concurrence
Clause (1)(c): keeps Article 1 (the Union and its territory) and Article 370 itself applicable to the State

Clause (1)(d): makes other constitutional provisions apply to the State only as the President specifies by order, subject to consultation (for Instrument-of-Accession matters) or concurrence (for all other matters)
Clause (2): any concurrence given before the State's own Constituent Assembly convened had to be placed before that Assembly for its decision
Clause (3): empowers the President to notify that the Article ceases to be operative, or operates only with specified exceptions/modifications, from a specified date
exceptions_and_qualifications: The proviso to clause (3) required the recommendation of the State's Constituent Assembly before such a notification — the State's Constituent Assembly, however, dissolved in 1957 after completing its work without making any such recommendation, a fact later central to the legal debate over whether clause (3) could still be validly exercised

In August 2019, the President issued C.O. 272 (using clause (1) to apply the entire Constitution to Jammu and Kashmir) followed by a notification under clause (3) (relying on the concurrence of Parliament acting in place of the State's Legislative Assembly, which was under President's Rule at the time) declaring Article 370 to have ceased to be operative except for clause (1) — effectively abrogating the State's special status and enabling its reorganisation into two Union territories

The Supreme Court in In Re: Article 370 of the Constitution, (2023) upheld the validity of this 2019 abrogation, holding that Article 370 was always intended as a temporary provision and that the President's power under clause (3) could be exercised without the State's Constituent Assembly's recommendation once that body had ceased to exist
breakdown.how_to_read: Treat Article 370 as now a largely historical provision given its 2019 abrogation and the Supreme Court's 2023 affirmance — but it remains essential to understand pre-2019 Jammu and Kashmir jurisprudence (e.g. the non-application of most fundamental rights and central laws to the State during that period) and as the leading case study on how a textually 'temporary' asymmetric-federalism provision can be terminated through its own internal mechanism rather than the ordinary Article 368 amendment process.

sections.title: Special provision with respect to the States of Maharashtra and Gujarat
sections.raw_text:
(2) Notwithstanding anything in this Constitution, the President may by order made with respect to the State of Maharashtra or Gujarat, provide for any special responsibility of the Governor for—
(a) the establishment of separate development boards for Vidarbha, Marathwada, and the rest of Maharashtra or, as the case may be, Saurashtra, Kutch and the rest of Gujarat with the provision that a report on the working of each of these boards will be placed each year before the State Legislative Assembly;
(b) the equitable allocation of funds for developmental expenditure over the said areas, subject to the requirements of the State as a whole; and
(c) an equitable arrangement providing adequate facilities for technical education and vocational training, and adequate opportunities for employment in services under the control of the State Government, in respect of all the said areas, subject to the requirements of the State as a whole.
key_terms: regional development boards
Governor's special responsibility

breakdown.plain_summary: The President can, by order, give the Governors of Maharashtra and Gujarat a special responsibility to ensure balanced regional development — setting up separate development boards for historically under-developed sub-regions (Vidarbha and Marathwada within Maharashtra; Saurashtra and Kutch within Gujarat), fairly distributing development funds across those regions, and ensuring equitable access to technical education, vocational training, and State government jobs across all the State's regions.
essential_elements: Exercised by Presidential order with respect to either Maharashtra or Gujarat specifically
Covers establishment of regional development boards with mandatory annual reporting to the State Legislative Assembly
Covers equitable fund allocation for developmental expenditure across the named sub-regions, subject to overall State requirements
Covers equitable technical education, vocational training, and State-service employment opportunities across the named sub-regions, subject to overall State requirements
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is the current operative text (clause (2)); the original 1950 Article 371 (which placed all Part B States under general Presidential control for ten years) was substituted by subsequent constitutional amendments (1956 and 1973) and is no longer in force in that form
breakdown.how_to_read: Cite this Article when a regional-imbalance grievance arises within Maharashtra or Gujarat (e.g. a Vidarbha separate-statehood or development-funding dispute) — it is the constitutional hook for demanding a development board or equitable-allocation order, though the provision only empowers the President to act, it does not itself guarantee any particular outcome.

sections.title: Special provision with respect to the State of Nagaland
key_terms: Naga customary law
Governor's individual judgment
regional council
Tuensang district special administration

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 371A gives Nagaland the deepest customary-law protection of any State: Parliament cannot apply any law touching Naga religious/social practices, customary law, customary civil/criminal justice, or land ownership unless Nagaland's own Legislative Assembly opts in by resolution. It also gave the Governor an unusually powerful personal 'individual judgment' role over law and order (immune from being questioned in court) and set up a transitional special-administration regime for the Tuensang district, including its own regional council and a dedicated Minister for Tuensang affairs.
essential_elements: Clause (1)(a): opt-in requirement — Parliamentary Acts on Naga religious/social practices, customary law/procedure, customary justice administration, or land/resource ownership apply only if Nagaland's Assembly resolves to accept them

Clause (1)(b): Governor's special, individually-exercised responsibility for law and order tied to continuing Naga Hills-Tuensang Area disturbances, exercisable after consulting (not being bound by) the Council of Ministers
Clause (1)(c): ring-fencing of Union grants for specific services within Nagaland's budget demands
Clause (1)(d): establishment of a 35-member Tuensang regional council with Governor-made rules on its composition, qualifications, terms, procedure, and staff

Clause (2): a ten-year (extendable) special administration regime for Tuensang district — Governor-run administration, equitable fund allocation, opt-in application of Nagaland Acts, Governor's regulation-making power (even with retrospective effect), a dedicated Tuensang Minister, and Governor's final discretion on Tuensang matters
Clause (2)(g)-(h): special representation adjustments for Tuensang in Presidential/Vice-Presidential elections and the composition of Nagaland's own Legislative Assembly
Clause (3): a time-limited (three-year) Presidential difficulty-removal power
exceptions_and_qualifications: The Governor's 'individual judgment' determination on whether a matter requires his discretion is made final and non-justiciable by the first proviso to clause (1)(b) — a rare express ouster of judicial review over a specific gubernatorial discretion
The President can terminate the Governor's special law-and-order responsibility once satisfied it is no longer necessary, under the second proviso to clause (1)(b)

The entire Tuensang special-administration regime under clause (2) was designed as temporary (ten years, extendable only by Governor's notification on the regional council's recommendation), reflecting its transitional character rather than a permanent constitutional feature
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the paradigm example of 'asymmetric federalism' protecting indigenous customary law — when a Nagaland-specific dispute touches land ownership or customary justice, check first whether the Nagaland Legislative Assembly has actually passed a resolution accepting the relevant Parliamentary Act, since without it the Act simply does not apply in the State regardless of its general applicability elsewhere in India.

sections.title: Special provision with respect to the State of Assam
sections.raw_text: Notwithstanding anything in this Constitution, the President may, by order made with respect to the State of Assam, provide for the constitution and functions of a committee of the Legislative Assembly of the State consisting of members of that Assembly elected from the tribal areas specified in Part 1 of the table appended to paragraph 20 of the Sixth Schedule and such number of other members of that Assembly as may be specified in the order and for the modifications to be made in the rules of procedure of that Assembly for the constitution and proper functioning of such committee.
key_terms: tribal areas committee
Sixth Schedule tribal areas

breakdown.plain_summary: The President can, by order, set up a special committee within Assam's own Legislative Assembly made up of members elected from the State's Sixth Schedule tribal areas (plus other specified members), giving those tribal constituencies a structured, dedicated voice within the Assembly's internal procedure.
essential_elements: Exercised by Presidential order specific to the State of Assam
The committee's core membership is drawn from Assembly members elected from the tribal areas specified in Part 1 of the table appended to paragraph 20 of the Sixth Schedule
The order may add other specified Assembly members and must provide for corresponding modifications to the Assembly's rules of procedure to constitute and operate the committee
exceptions_and_qualifications: This Article was not part of the original 1950 Constitution — it was inserted by the Constitution (Twenty-second Amendment) Act, 1969
breakdown.how_to_read: A narrow, institution-design provision relevant mainly to Assam's internal legislative procedure and tribal-area representation — check any Assam Assembly rules dispute touching Sixth Schedule tribal-area members against the specific Presidential order issued under this Article, since the committee's structure is order-defined rather than fixed by the constitutional text itself.

sections.title: Special provision with respect to the State of Manipur
sections.raw_text:
(1) Notwithstanding anything in this Constitution, the President may, by order made with respect to the State of Manipur, provide for the constitution and functions of a committee of the Legislative Assembly of the State consisting of members of that Assembly elected from the Hill Areas of that State, for the modifications to be made in the rules of business of the Government and in the rules of procedure of the Legislative Assembly of the State and for any special responsibility of the Governor in order to secure the proper functioning of such committee.
(2) The Governor shall annually, or whenever so required by the President, make a report to the President regarding the administration of the Hill Areas in the State of Manipur and the executive power of the Union shall extend to the giving of directions to the State as to the administration of the said areas.
Explanation.—In this article, the expression “Hill Areas” means such areas as the President may, by order, declare to be Hill areas.
key_terms: Hill Areas committee
Governor's annual report to President

breakdown.plain_summary: Parallel to Assam's tribal-areas committee, Manipur gets a Presidentially-constituted Legislative Assembly committee for its Hill Areas (as declared by Presidential order), with the Governor carrying a special responsibility to ensure the committee functions properly and a standing duty to report annually (or on demand) to the President on Hill Areas administration — with the Union executive empowered to directly give administrative directions on those areas.
essential_elements: Clause (1): Presidential order establishes a Hill-Areas-elected committee within Manipur's Legislative Assembly, with corresponding modifications to government business rules and Assembly procedure, plus a special Governor responsibility for the committee's proper functioning

Clause (2): mandatory annual (or on-demand) Gubernatorial reporting to the President on Hill Areas administration, coupled with a Union executive power to issue administration directions for those areas
The Explanation defines 'Hill Areas' entirely by reference to Presidential declaration — there is no independent textual definition
exceptions_and_qualifications: This Article was not part of the original 1950 Constitution — it was inserted by the Constitution (Twenty-seventh Amendment) Act, 1971, following Manipur's formation as a full State
breakdown.how_to_read: Always check the specific Presidential order under clause (1) before assuming any Manipur Hill Areas committee has a particular composition or power — like Article 371B, the operative detail lives in the order, not the constitutional text, and 'Hill Areas' itself is a creature of Presidential declaration rather than a fixed geography.

sections.title: Special provisions with respect to the State of Andhra Pradesh or the State of Telangana
sections.raw_text:
(1) The President may by order made with respect to the State of Andhra Pradesh or the State of Telangana, provide, having regard to the requirement of each State, for equitable opportunities and facilities for the people belonging to different parts of such State, in the matter of public employment and in the matter of education, and different provisions may be made for various parts of the States.
(2) An order made under clause (1) may, in particular,—
(a) require the State Government to organise any class or classes of posts in a civil service of, or any class or classes of civil posts under, the State into different local cadres for different parts of the State and allot in accordance with such principles and procedure as may be specified in the order the persons holding such posts to the local cadres so organised;
(b) specify any part or parts of the State which shall be regarded as the local area—
(i) for direct recruitment to posts in any local cadre (whether organised in pursuance of an order under this article or constituted otherwise) under the State Government;
(ii) for direct recruitment to posts in any cadre under any local authority within the State; and
(iii) for the purposes of admission to any University within the State or to any other educational institution which is subject to the control of the State Government;
(c) specify the extent to which, the manner in which and the conditions subject to which, preference or reservation shall be given or made—
(i) in the matter of direct recruitment to posts in any such cadre referred to in sub-clause (b) as may be specified in this behalf in the order;
(ii) in the matter of admission to any such University or other educational institution referred to in sub-clause (b) as may be specified in this behalf in the order, to or in favour of candidates who have resided or studied for any period specified in the order in the local area in respect of such cadre, University or other educational institution, as the case may be.
(3) The President may, by order, provide for the constitution of an Administrative Tribunal for the State of Andhra Pradesh and for the State of Telangana to exercise such jurisdiction, powers and authority, including any jurisdiction, power and authority which immediately before the commencement of the Constitution (Thirty-second Amendment) Act, 1973, was exercisable by any court (other than the Supreme Court) or by any tribunal or other authority, as may be specified in the order with respect to the following matters, namely:—
(a) appointment, allotment or promotion to such class or classes of posts in any civil service of the State, or to such class or classes of civil posts under the State, or to such class or classes of posts under the control of any local authority within the State, as may be specified in the order;
(b) seniority of persons appointed, allotted or promoted to such class or classes of posts in any civil service of the State, or to such class or classes of civil posts under the State, or to such class or classes of posts under the control of any local authority within the State, as may be specified in the order;
(c) such other conditions of service of persons appointed, allotted or promoted to such class or classes of posts in any civil service of the State or to such class or classes of civil posts under the State or to such class or classes of posts under the control of any local authority within the State, as may be specified in the order.
(4) An order made under clause (3) may—
(a) authorise the Administrative Tribunal to receive representations for the redress of grievances relating to any matter within its jurisdiction as the President may specify in the order and to make such orders thereon as the Administrative Tribunal deems fit;
(b) contain such provisions with respect to the powers and authorities and procedure of the Administrative Tribunal (including provisions with respect to the powers of the Administrative Tribunal to punish for contempt of itself) as the President may deem necessary;
(c) provide for the transfer to the Administrative Tribunal of such classes of proceedings, being proceedings relating to matters within its jurisdiction and pending before any court (other than the Supreme Court) or tribunal or other authority immediately before the commencement of such order, as may be specified in the order;
(d) contain such supplemental, incidental and consequential provisions (including provisions as to fees and as to limitation, evidence or for the application of any law for the time being in force subject to any exceptions or modifications) as the President may deem necessary.
(5) The Order of the Administrative Tribunal finally disposing of any case shall become effective upon its confirmation by the State Government or on the expiry of three months from the date on which the order is made, whichever is earlier:
Provided that the State Government may, by special order made in writing and for reasons to be specified therein, modify or annul any order of the Administrative Tribunal before it becomes effective and in such a case, the order of the Administrative Tribunal shall have effect only in such modified form or be of no effect, as the case may be.
(6) Every special order made by the State Government under the proviso to clause (5) shall be laid, as soon as may be after it is made, before both Houses of the State Legislature.
(7) The High Court for the State shall not have any powers of superintendence over the Administrative Tribunal and no court (other than the Supreme Court) or tribunal shall exercise any jurisdiction, power or authority in respect of any matter subject to the jurisdiction, power or authority of, or in relation to, the Administrative Tribunal.
(8) If the President is satisfied that the continued existence of the Administrative Tribunal is not necessary, the President may by order abolish the Administrative Tribunal and make such provisions in such order as he may deem fit for the transfer and disposal of cases pending before the Tribunal immediately before such abolition.
(9) Notwithstanding any judgment, decree or order of any court, tribunal or other authority,—
(a) no appointment, posting, promotion or transfer of any person—
(i) made before the 1st day of November, 1956, to any post under the Government of, or any local authority within, the State of Hyderabad as it existed before that date; or
(ii) made before the commencement of the Constitution (Thirty-second Amendment) Act, 1973, to any post under the Government of, or any local or other authority within, the State of Andhra Pradesh; and
(b) no action taken or thing done by or before any person referred to in sub-clause (a),
shall be deemed to be illegal or void or ever to have become illegal or void merely on the ground that the appointment, posting, promotion or transfer of such person was not made in accordance with any law, then in force, providing for any requirement as to residence within the State of Hyderabad or, as the case may be, within any part of the State of Andhra Pradesh, in respect of such appointment, posting, promotion or transfer.
(10) The provisions of this article and of any order made by the President thereunder shall have effect notwithstanding anything in any other provision of this Constitution or in any other law for the time being in force.
key_terms: local cadres
Mulki rules
Administrative Tribunal
equitable opportunities in public employment and education

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 371D is the constitutional 'local cadre' / local-preference machinery for Andhra Pradesh and Telangana: the President can, by order, organise State civil service posts into region-specific cadres and reserve local-area preference in both public employment and university admissions, to ensure historically less-developed parts of the composite State get equitable opportunity. It also authorised a special Administrative Tribunal to handle service disputes arising from this local-cadre scheme, deliberately keeping such disputes out of the ordinary High Court's superintending jurisdiction, and it retroactively validated pre-1973 'Mulki rules'-era appointments against residence-requirement challenges.
essential_elements: Clause (1)-(2): Presidential order power to organise local cadres, designate local areas for recruitment/admission purposes, and fix preference/reservation terms for residence or study within the local area

Clause (3)-(4): power to constitute a State Administrative Tribunal with jurisdiction over local-cadre service matters (appointment, seniority, conditions of service), including powers to receive grievance representations, punish for contempt, and absorb pending proceedings from other courts/tribunals

Clause (5)-(6): Tribunal orders become effective only on State Government confirmation or after three months, subject to the State Government's power to modify/annul with recorded reasons, which must then be laid before the State Legislature
Clause (7): ousts the High Court's superintendence over the Tribunal and excludes other courts'/tribunals' jurisdiction over matters within the Tribunal's domain
Clause (8): Presidential power to abolish the Tribunal once satisfied it is no longer necessary, with transitional case-transfer provisions

Clause (9): retrospective validation clause protecting pre-1 November 1956 Hyderabad-era and pre-1973 Andhra Pradesh-era appointments from being invalidated solely for non-compliance with residence requirements
Clause (10): a non-obstante clause giving the entire Article and any order under it overriding effect over other constitutional provisions and other laws
exceptions_and_qualifications: The Tribunal's finality under clause (5) is itself qualified by the State Government's pre-effectiveness modification/annulment power — Tribunal orders are not automatically final the way ordinary court judgments are

This Article was not part of the original 1950 Constitution — it was inserted by the Constitution (Thirty-second Amendment) Act, 1973, and later extended in application to the newly carved-out State of Telangana after Andhra Pradesh's 2014 bifurcation
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the key provision to plead in any Telangana or Andhra Pradesh local-cadre or 'Mulki rules'-style residence-requirement service dispute — but remember the jurisdictional ouster in clause (7) means such disputes may need to go first to the Administrative Tribunal (where still constituted) rather than directly to the High Court, and clause (9)'s retrospective validation forecloses residence-requirement challenges to pre-1973 appointments entirely.

sections.title: Establishment of Central University in Andhra Pradesh
sections.raw_text: Parliament may by law provide for the establishment of a University in the State of Andhra Pradesh.
key_terms: Central University
Parliamentary power to establish a university

breakdown.plain_summary: A short, enabling provision that simply authorises Parliament to pass a law setting up a university in Andhra Pradesh — nothing more. It was the constitutional basis for creating the University of Hyderabad in 1974.
essential_elements: Confers a specific legislative power on Parliament to establish a University in the State of Andhra Pradesh by ordinary law
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is a permissive, not mandatory, power — Parliament 'may' legislate, it is not required to

This Article was not part of the original 1950 Constitution — it was inserted by the Constitution (Thirty-second Amendment) Act, 1973, following which the University of Hyderabad was established in 1974
breakdown.how_to_read: A narrow, single-purpose enabling clause — relevant mainly as a historical/structural curiosity showing how a specific institution's creation was sometimes given its own dedicated constitutional peg rather than being left to Parliament's general Entry 63/64 List I legislative powers over institutions of national importance.

sections.title: Special provisions with respect to the State of Sikkim
key_terms: appointed day
deemed Legislative Assembly
Governor's special responsibility
jurisdictional bar on pre-accession treaties

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 371F is the comprehensive constitutional integration clause for Sikkim, which became a full Indian State in 1975. It deems Sikkim's own 1974-elected Assembly to be its first constitutional Legislative Assembly (with a shortened four-year term), guarantees it minimum representation, gives the Governor a discretionary special responsibility for peace and equitable social/economic advancement, continues pre-merger property, courts, laws and officers into the new constitutional order, and — mirroring Article 363 — bars courts from entertaining disputes over Sikkim's pre-merger treaties with India, while expressly preserving the Supreme Court's special Article 143 advisory jurisdiction.
essential_elements: Clause (a): minimum 30-member Legislative Assembly for Sikkim

Clauses (b)-(c): the April 1974-elected 32-member Sikkim Assembly is deemed the State's first duly-constituted constitutional Legislative Assembly, with its term treated as four years (not the usual five) from the 'appointed day'

Clauses (d)-(f): one Lok Sabha seat/constituency for Sikkim (until Parliament legislates otherwise), indirect election of that MP by the State Assembly, and a Parliamentary power to reserve Assembly seats for specific population sections
Clause (g): the Governor's discretionary special responsibility for peace and equitable social/economic advancement of Sikkim's different population sections, subject to Presidential directions
Clauses (h)-(k): continuity of pre-merger Sikkim Government property/assets, the High Court, all courts/authorities/officers, and all laws in force, into the post-merger constitutional framework
Clause (l): a two-year Presidential law-adaptation power over continued Sikkim laws, non-questionable in any court

Clause (m): ouster of Supreme Court and all other courts' jurisdiction over disputes arising from pre-merger Sikkim treaties/agreements with the Government of India, expressly without derogating from Article 143's Presidential-reference advisory jurisdiction
Clause (n): Presidential power to extend other States' enactments to Sikkim by public notification
Clause (o): a two-year Presidential difficulty-removal power
Clause (p): validates all things done in or for Sikkim between the appointed day and the Thirty-sixth Amendment's Presidential assent, so long as they conform to the Constitution as so amended
exceptions_and_qualifications: The jurisdictional bar in clause (m) parallels Article 363's bar on princely-State-accession disputes, but is specific to Sikkim's distinct 1975 merger (not the general 1947-50 integration of princely States) and expressly carves out Article 143 advisory references rather than leaving that ambiguous

The Governor's special responsibility under clause (g) is exercised in the Governor's own discretion, but remains subject to Presidential directions — unlike Article 371A's law-and-order discretion for Nagaland, it is not insulated from Presidential control
This Article was not part of the original 1950 Constitution — it was inserted by the Constitution (Thirty-sixth Amendment) Act, 1975, the same amendment that made Sikkim a full State of the Union
breakdown.how_to_read: The master reference for any Sikkim constitutional-status or pre-merger-treaty dispute — note that clause (m)'s court-jurisdiction bar is narrower than it first appears, since it only reaches disputes about the treaties/agreements themselves and explicitly leaves Article 143 advisory jurisdiction untouched.

sections.title: Special provision with respect to the State of Mizoram
sections.raw_text:
Notwithstanding anything in this Constitution,—
(a) no Act of Parliament in respect of—
(i) religious or social practices of the Mizos,
(ii) Mizo customary law and procedure,
(iii) administration of civil and criminal justice involving decisions according to Mizo customary law,
(iv) ownership and transfer of land,
shall apply to the State of Mizoram unless the Legislative Assembly of the State of Mizoram by a resolution so decides:
Provided that nothing in this clause shall apply to any Central Act in force in the Union territory of Mizoram immediately before the commencement of the Constitution (Fifty-third Amendment) Act, 1986;
(b) the Legislative Assembly of the State of Mizoram shall consist of not less than forty members.
key_terms: Mizo customary law
opt-in requirement
pre-1986 Central Acts proviso

breakdown.plain_summary: Mirroring Article 371A's Nagaland model, Mizoram gets the same opt-in protection for Mizo religious/social practices, customary law, customary civil/criminal justice, and land ownership — Parliament's laws on these subjects apply only if Mizoram's own Legislative Assembly resolves to accept them. Unlike Nagaland's provision, Mizoram's version carries an express carve-out preserving Central Acts that were already in force in the Mizoram Union territory before full statehood in 1986.
essential_elements: Opt-in requirement: Parliamentary Acts on Mizo religious/social practices, customary law/procedure, customary justice administration, or land ownership/transfer apply only if Mizoram's Assembly resolves to accept them
Proviso: Central Acts already in force in the Mizoram Union territory immediately before the Fifty-third Amendment's commencement are unaffected by the opt-in requirement and continue to apply
Clause (b): minimum 40-member Legislative Assembly for Mizoram
exceptions_and_qualifications: The proviso to clause (a) is the key structural difference from Article 371A(1)(a) (Nagaland), which has no equivalent carve-out for pre-existing Central Acts
This Article was not part of the original 1950 Constitution — it was inserted by the Constitution (Fifty-third Amendment) Act, 1986, following the creation of the State of Mizoram
breakdown.how_to_read: When arguing a Mizoram customary-law or land-ownership dispute, always check first whether the challenged Central Act was already in force in the Mizoram Union territory before 1986 — if so, the opt-in protection does not help, since the proviso preserves such pre-existing Central Acts regardless of any State Assembly resolution.

sections.title: Special provision with respect to the State of Arunachal Pradesh
sections.raw_text:
Notwithstanding anything in this Constitution,—
(a) the Governor of Arunachal Pradesh shall have special responsibility with respect to law and order in the State of Arunachal Pradesh and in the discharge of his functions in relation thereto, the Governor shall, after consulting the Council of Ministers, exercise his individual judgment as to the action to be taken:
Provided that if any question arises whether any matter is or is not a matter as respects which the Governor is under this clause required to act in the exercise of his individual judgment, the decision of the Governor in his discretion shall be final, and the validity of anything done by the Governor shall not be called in question on the ground that he ought or ought not to have acted in the exercise of his individual judgment:
Provided further that if the President on receipt of a report from the Governor or otherwise is satisfied that it is no longer necessary for the Governor to have special responsibility with respect to law and order in the State of Arunachal Pradesh, he may by order direct that the Governor shall cease to have such responsibility with effect from such date as may be specified in the order;
(b) the Legislative Assembly of the State of Arunachal Pradesh shall consist of not less than thirty members.
key_terms: Governor's non-justiciable law-and-order discretion
minimum Assembly strength

breakdown.plain_summary: Arunachal Pradesh gets the same structure of Governor's personal, non-justiciable law-and-order discretion as Nagaland's Article 371A(1)(b) — the Governor must consult the Council of Ministers but then exercises individual judgment, with that judgment call itself immune from being questioned in court, subject to the President's power to withdraw the special responsibility once satisfied it is no longer needed. It also fixes a minimum 30-member Legislative Assembly.
essential_elements: Clause (a): Governor's special responsibility for law and order, exercised in individual judgment after (not necessarily in accordance with) consulting the Council of Ministers
First proviso: the Governor's own decision on whether a matter calls for individual judgment is final and non-justiciable
Second proviso: the President may terminate this special responsibility by order once satisfied it is no longer necessary
Clause (b): minimum 30-member Legislative Assembly for Arunachal Pradesh
exceptions_and_qualifications: This Article was not part of the original 1950 Constitution — it was inserted by the Constitution (Fifty-fifth Amendment) Act, 1986, following the creation of the State of Arunachal Pradesh
breakdown.how_to_read: Structurally identical to Article 371A(1)(b)'s Nagaland law-and-order discretion — treat the two as a matched pair when researching the limits of judicial review over a Governor's 'individual judgment' power, since both share the same non-justiciability proviso and Presidential-withdrawal mechanism.

sections.title: Continuance in force of existing laws and their adaptation
sections.raw_text:
(1) Notwithstanding the repeal by this Constitution of the enactments referred to in article 395 but subject to the other provisions of this Constitution, all the law in force in the territory of India immediately before the commencement of this Constitution shall continue in force therein until altered or repealed or amended by a competent Legislature or other competent authority.
(2) For the purpose of bringing the provisions of any law in force in the territory of India into accord with the provisions of this Constitution, the President may by order make such adaptations and modifications of such law, whether by way of repeal or amendment, as may be necessary or expedient, and provide that the law shall, as from such date as may be specified in the order, have effect subject to the adaptations and modifications so made, and any such adaptation or modification shall not be questioned in any court of law.
(3) Nothing in clause (2) shall be deemed—
(a) to empower the President to make any adaptation or modification of any law after the expiration of three years from the commencement of this Constitution; or
(b) to prevent any competent Legislature or other competent authority from repealing or amending any law adapted or modified by the President under the said clause.
Explanation I.—The expression “law in force” in this article shall include a law passed or made by a Legislature or other competent authority in the territory of India before the commencement of this Constitution and not previously repealed, notwithstanding that it or parts of it may not be then in operation either at all or in particular areas.
Explanation II.—Any law passed or made by a Legislature or other competent authority in the territory of India which immediately before the commencement of this Constitution had extra-territorial effect as well as effect in the territory of India shall, subject to any such adaptations and modifications as aforesaid, continue to have such extra-territorial effect.
Explanation III.—Nothing in this article shall be construed as continuing any temporary law in force beyond the date fixed for its expiration or the date on which it would have expired if this Constitution had not come into force.
Explanation IV.—An Ordinance promulgated by the Governor of a Province under section 88 of the Government of India Act, 1935, and in force immediately before the commencement of this Constitution shall, unless withdrawn by the Governor of the corresponding State earlier, cease to operate at the expiration of six weeks from the first meeting after such commencement of the Legislative Assembly of that State functioning under clause (1) of article 382, and nothing in this article shall be construed as continuing any such Ordinance in force beyond the said period.
key_terms: continuity of existing law
law in force
three-year adaptation power
temporary law expiry

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 372 is the master continuity clause that kept the entire pre-Constitution legal system running on 26 January 1950 instead of leaving a legal vacuum — all laws in force at that moment stayed valid until some competent Legislature or authority changed them. To smooth over inconsistencies with the new Constitution, the President got a three-year window to adapt or modify any such law by order (immune from court challenge), after which only ordinary legislatures could make further changes. Four Explanations clarify technical edge cases: dormant laws still count as 'in force,' extra-territorial laws keep that effect, temporary laws still expire on schedule, and specific pre-Constitution Provincial Ordinances get a fixed cut-off after the new State Assembly first meets.
essential_elements: Clause (1): all pre-commencement law continues in force (despite Article 395's repeal of the Government of India Act 1935 and Indian Independence Act 1947), subject to the rest of the Constitution, until altered by a competent Legislature or authority
Clause (2): Presidential order power to adapt/modify existing law to align it with the Constitution, with such adaptations not questionable in any court
Clause (3)(a): the Presidential adaptation power is time-limited to three years from commencement
Clause (3)(b): competent Legislatures/authorities remain free to further repeal or amend even President-adapted laws
Explanation I: 'law in force' includes dormant/unenforced pre-Constitution laws not yet repealed
Explanation II: pre-existing extra-territorial effect of a law continues (subject to adaptation)
Explanation III: temporary laws still lapse on their original expiry date — this Article does not extend them
Explanation IV: Governor's Ordinances under the 1935 Act cease six weeks after the new State Assembly's first meeting, unless earlier withdrawn
exceptions_and_qualifications: The three-year adaptation window under clause (3)(a) has long since lapsed — this is now a historical limitation with no ongoing operative effect, though the laws it was used to adapt during 1950-1953 remain in force as adapted
Clause (2)'s immunity from court challenge covers only the adaptation/modification itself, not the underlying law's substantive validity, which remains open to ordinary constitutional challenge
breakdown.how_to_read: The conceptual starting point for understanding why colonial-era statutes (IPC 1860, CrPC, Evidence Act, General Clauses Act, etc.) remained valid Indian law after 1950 — cite Article 372(1) whenever a pre-Constitution enactment's continued validity is questioned, and remember any claimed Presidential 'adaptation' of such a law must trace back to an order made within the three-year window that closed in 1953.

sections.title: Power of the President to adapt laws
sections.raw_text:
(1) For the purposes of bringing the provisions of any law in force in India or in any part thereof, immediately before the commencement of the Constitution (Seventh Amendment) Act, 1956, into accord with the provisions of this Constitution as amended by that Act, the President may by order made before the first day of November, 1957, make such adaptations and modifications of the law, whether by way of repeal or amendment, as may be necessary or expedient, and provide that the law shall, as from such date as may be specified in the order, have effect subject to the adaptations and modifications so made, and any such adaptation or modification shall not be questioned in any court of law.
(2) Nothing in clause (1) shall be deemed to prevent a competent Legislature or other competent authority from repealing or amending any law adapted or modified by the President under the said clause.
key_terms: Seventh Amendment adaptation power
non-questionable adaptation

breakdown.plain_summary: A second, narrower version of Article 372's adaptation power, created specifically to help existing laws catch up with the sweeping State-reorganisation changes made by the Seventh Amendment, 1956 (which abolished the Part A/B/C/D State classification and redrew State boundaries on linguistic lines). The President got until 1 November 1957 to make the necessary adaptations, again immune from court challenge, with ordinary legislatures free to override such adaptations afterward.
essential_elements: Clause (1): Presidential order power, exercisable only before 1 November 1957, to adapt/modify any law to align it with the Constitution as amended by the Seventh Amendment Act, 1956; such adaptations not questionable in any court
Clause (2): competent Legislatures/authorities remain free to repeal or amend any law so adapted by the President
exceptions_and_qualifications: This power is entirely spent — its exercise window (up to 1 November 1957) closed decades ago, and it survives in the text only to explain the legal basis for laws adapted during that specific post-reorganisation period

This Article was not part of the original 1950 Constitution — it was inserted by the Constitution (Seventh Amendment) Act, 1956, as a companion provision to that amendment's major State-reorganisation changes
breakdown.how_to_read: Use this Article only when tracing the historical pedigree of a law that was adapted specifically to reflect the 1956 States Reorganisation — it is functionally a one-time, amendment-specific twin of Article 372(2)'s general adaptation power, not an independent ongoing source of Presidential authority.

sections.title: Power of President to make order in respect of persons under preventive detention in certain cases
sections.raw_text: Until provision is made by Parliament under clause (7) of article 22, or until the expiration of one year from the commencement of this Constitution, whichever is earlier, the said article shall have effect as if for any reference to Parliament in clauses (4) and (7) thereof there were substituted a reference to the President and for any reference to any law made by Parliament in those clauses there were substituted a reference to an order made by the President.
key_terms: preventive detention transitional substitution
one-year sunset

breakdown.plain_summary: A short-lived bridging provision: until Parliament actually legislated under Article 22(7) on preventive detention, or for at most one year after the Constitution commenced (whichever came first), Article 22's references to 'Parliament' and 'law made by Parliament' in clauses (4) and (7) were instead read as references to the President and a Presidential order — letting the President temporarily exercise what would normally be Parliament's preventive-detention law-making role while Parliament got organised.
essential_elements: Operates only until Parliament makes provision under Article 22(7), or for one year from the Constitution's commencement, whichever happens first
During that window, Article 22(4) and (7) are read with 'President'/'Presidential order' substituted for 'Parliament'/'law made by Parliament'
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is a purely transitional, now long-spent provision — its one-year outer limit expired in January 1951, and Parliament had in any event since legislated on preventive detention under Article 22(7)
breakdown.how_to_read: A historical footnote relevant only to understanding how preventive detention orders made in India's first year under the Constitution derived their legal authority, before Parliament's own Preventive Detention Act, 1950 and successor legislation took over the field.

sections.title: Provisions as to Judges of the Federal Court and proceedings pending in the Federal Court or before His Majesty in Council
sections.raw_text:
(1) The Judges of the Federal Court holding office immediately before the commencement of this Constitution shall, unless they have elected otherwise, become on such commencement the Judges of the Supreme Court and shall thereupon be entitled to such salaries and allowances and to such rights in respect of leave of absence and pension as are provided for under article 125 in respect of the Judges of the Supreme Court.
(2) All suits, appeals and proceedings, civil or criminal, pending in the Federal Court at the commencement of this Constitution shall stand removed to the Supreme Court, and the Supreme Court shall have jurisdiction to hear and determine the same, and the judgments and orders of the Federal Court delivered or made before the commencement of this Constitution shall have the same force and effect as if they had been delivered or made by the Supreme Court.
(3) Nothing in this Constitution shall operate to invalidate the exercise of jurisdiction by His Majesty in Council to dispose of appeals and petitions from, or in respect of, any judgment, decree or order of any court within the territory of India in so far as the exercise of such jurisdiction is authorised by law, and any order of His Majesty in Council made on any such appeal or petition after the commencement of this Constitution shall for all purposes have effect as if it were an order or decree made by the Supreme Court in the exercise of the jurisdiction conferred on such Court by this Constitution.
(4) On and from the commencement of this Constitution the jurisdiction of the authority functioning as the Privy Council in a State specified in Part B of the First Schedule to entertain and dispose of appeals and petitions from or in respect of any judgment, decree or order of any court within that State shall cease, and all appeals and other proceedings pending before the said authority at such commencement shall be transferred to, and disposed of by, the Supreme Court.
(5) Further provision may be made by Parliament by law to give effect to the provisions of this article.
key_terms: Federal Court
Privy Council
His Majesty in Council
transfer of pending proceedings

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 374 handled the judicial handover from the colonial-era court system to the new Supreme Court: sitting Federal Court Judges automatically became Supreme Court Judges, every pending Federal Court case transferred straight to the Supreme Court with the Federal Court's past judgments treated as if the Supreme Court itself had made them, pre-existing Privy Council appellate jurisdiction over already-authorised appeals was preserved (with any such post-commencement Privy Council order treated as a Supreme Court order), and the separate Privy-Council-equivalent jurisdiction that Part B (princely) States had maintained ceased entirely, with their pending matters moving to the Supreme Court.
essential_elements: Clause (1): automatic conversion of sitting Federal Court Judges into Supreme Court Judges (unless they elect otherwise), carrying equivalent salary/allowance/leave/pension rights
Clause (2): automatic transfer of all pending Federal Court suits/appeals/proceedings to the Supreme Court, with past Federal Court judgments given Supreme Court force and effect

Clause (3): preserves already-authorised Privy Council jurisdiction to dispose of pending appeals/petitions even after commencement, deeming such post-commencement Privy Council orders to be Supreme Court orders
Clause (4): terminates Part B States' own Privy-Council-equivalent appellate jurisdiction, transferring their pending appeals to the Supreme Court
Clause (5): Parliament may make further law to implement this Article
exceptions_and_qualifications: This Article is now entirely of historical interest — the transitional judicial handover it describes was completed in the early 1950s and has no ongoing operative effect
breakdown.how_to_read: Useful only as background when researching the institutional lineage of the Supreme Court of India or tracing a specific pre-1950 Federal Court or Privy Council decision's binding status — cite it to explain why such colonial-era judgments still carry Supreme Court-level authority today.

sections.title: Courts, authorities and officers to continue to function subject to the provisions of the Constitution
sections.raw_text: All courts of civil, criminal and revenue jurisdiction, all authorities and all officers, judicial, executive and ministerial, throughout the territory of India, shall continue to exercise their respective functions subject to the provisions of this Constitution.
key_terms: continuity of courts, authorities and officers

breakdown.plain_summary: A single-sentence continuity guarantee: every existing court (civil, criminal, revenue), authority, and officer — judicial, executive, or ministerial — kept functioning after the Constitution came into force, just now operating subject to the Constitution's provisions rather than the earlier colonial framework.
essential_elements: Covers all courts of civil, criminal, and revenue jurisdiction throughout the territory of India
Covers all authorities and all officers, whether judicial, executive, or ministerial
Continuity is expressly made subject to the provisions of the Constitution
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is a blanket continuity clause with no time limit or sunset, unlike several of the other transitional Part XXI provisions
breakdown.how_to_read: A foundational continuity clause ensuring there was no administrative or judicial vacuum on 26 January 1950 — pair it with Article 372 (continuity of laws) when explaining why the entire pre-Constitution apparatus of courts and officials carried over seamlessly into the new constitutional order.

sections.title: Provisions as to Judges of High Courts
sections.raw_text:
(1) Notwithstanding anything in clause (2) of article 217, the Judges of a High Court in any Province holding office immediately before the commencement of this Constitution shall, unless they have elected otherwise, become on such commencement the Judges of the High Court in the corresponding State, and shall thereupon be entitled to such salaries and allowances and to such rights in respect of leave of absence and pension as are provided for under article 221 in respect of the Judges of such High Court. Any such Judge shall, notwithstanding that he is not a citizen of India, be eligible for appointment as Chief Justice of such High Court, or as Chief Justice or other Judge of any other High Court.
(2) The Judges of a High Court in any Indian State corresponding to any State specified in Part B of the First Schedule holding office immediately before the commencement of this Constitution shall, unless they have elected otherwise, become on such commencement the Judges of the High Court in the State so specified and shall, notwithstanding anything in clauses (1) and (2) of article 217 but subject to the proviso to clause (1) of that article, continue to hold office until the expiration of such period as the President may by order determine.
(3) In this article, the expression “Judge” does not include an acting Judge or an additional Judge.
key_terms: transitional continuity of High Court Judges
non-citizen eligibility exception

breakdown.plain_summary: Mirroring Article 374's treatment of Federal Court Judges, Article 376 carried over sitting Provincial High Court Judges into the new State High Courts automatically, with equivalent salary/allowance/leave/pension rights, and — notably — allowed such a Judge to be appointed Chief Justice despite not being an Indian citizen (an express exception to Article 217's usual citizenship requirement). Judges of former princely-State High Courts (Part B States) got the same continuity, but only for a period the President would separately determine by order.
essential_elements: Clause (1): automatic conversion of sitting Provincial High Court Judges into Judges of the corresponding State's High Court, with equivalent service/pension rights, and eligibility for Chief Justice appointment even without Indian citizenship
Clause (2): similar continuity for Judges of Part B (princely) State High Courts, but time-limited to a period fixed by Presidential order rather than open-ended
Clause (3): expressly excludes acting and additional Judges from the protective meaning of 'Judge' in this Article
exceptions_and_qualifications: The non-citizen Chief Justice eligibility in clause (1) was a one-time transitional accommodation for Judges already in office at commencement, not a standing exception to Article 217's ordinary citizenship requirement
Part B State Judges' continuity under clause (2) was always conditional on a Presidential time-limit order, unlike the open-ended continuity given to Provincial High Court Judges under clause (1)
breakdown.how_to_read: Cite this Article only when researching the transitional judicial history of a specific State High Court formed from a former Province or princely State — it has no bearing on current High Court Judge appointments, which are governed entirely by Articles 217 and 224 today.

sections.title: Provisions as to Comptroller and Auditor-General of India
sections.raw_text: The Auditor-General of India holding office immediately before the commencement of this Constitution shall, unless he has elected otherwise, become on such commencement the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India and shall thereupon be entitled to such salaries and to such rights in respect of leave of absence and pension as are provided for under clause (3) of article 148 in respect of the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India and be entitled to continue to hold office until the expiration of his term of office as determined under the provisions which were applicable to him immediately before such commencement.
key_terms: transitional continuity of Auditor-General

breakdown.plain_summary: The pre-Constitution Auditor-General of India automatically became independent India's first Comptroller and Auditor-General, keeping the salary, leave, and pension terms set out for that office under Article 148(3), and remaining in post for whatever term had already been fixed under the rules that applied to him before the Constitution commenced.
essential_elements: Automatic conversion of the sitting Auditor-General of India into the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India, unless he elected otherwise
Entitlement to salary, leave, and pension rights as provided under Article 148(3)
Continuation in office for the remainder of the term fixed under his pre-Constitution terms of appointment
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is a one-time transitional provision tied to the specific individual in office at commencement — it has no bearing on how the Comptroller and Auditor-General is appointed or how long they serve today, which is governed by Article 148
breakdown.how_to_read: A historical bridging clause only — useful for explaining the institutional continuity of the CAG's office from the colonial Auditor-General, but of no operative relevance to any current CAG appointment or tenure dispute.

sections.title: Provisions as to Public Service Commissions
sections.raw_text:
(1) The members of the Public Service Commission for the Dominion of India holding office immediately before the commencement of this Constitution shall, unless they have elected otherwise, become on such commencement the members of the Public Service Commission for the Union and shall, notwithstanding anything in clauses (1) and (2) of article 316 but subject to the proviso to clause (2) of that article, continue to hold office until the expiration of their term of office as determined under the rules which were applicable immediately before such commencement to such members.
(2) The Members of a Public Service Commission of a Province or of a Public Service Commission serving the needs of a group of Provinces holding office immediately before the commencement of this Constitution shall, unless they have elected otherwise, become on such commencement the members of the Public Service Commission for the corresponding State or the members of the Joint State Public Service Commission serving the needs of the corresponding States, as the case may be, and shall, notwithstanding anything in clauses (1) and (2) of article 316 but subject to the proviso to clause (2) of that article, continue to hold office until the expiration of their term of office as determined under the rules which were applicable immediately before such commencement to such members.
key_terms: transitional continuity of Public Service Commission members

breakdown.plain_summary: Members of the pre-Constitution Public Service Commission for the Dominion of India automatically became members of the new Union Public Service Commission, and members of Provincial (or multi-Province joint) Public Service Commissions automatically became members of the corresponding State (or Joint State) Public Service Commission — each continuing to serve out their existing term under their pre-Constitution appointment rules, despite Article 316's ordinarily different tenure provisions.
essential_elements: Clause (1): automatic conversion of Dominion Public Service Commission members into Union Public Service Commission members, continuing their existing term under pre-Constitution rules

Clause (2): automatic conversion of Provincial or joint-Province Public Service Commission members into the corresponding State or Joint State Public Service Commission, on the same continuing-term basis
Both clauses operate notwithstanding Article 316(1)-(2)'s ordinary tenure rules, but remain subject to the proviso to Article 316(2)
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is a one-time transitional provision for individuals already in office at commencement — current Public Service Commission appointments and terms are governed entirely by Article 316
breakdown.how_to_read: Relevant only to the institutional history of the Union and State Public Service Commissions — not a source of any live entitlement or obligation today.

sections.title: Special provision as to duration of Andhra Pradesh Legislative Assembly
sections.raw_text: Notwithstanding anything contained in article 172, the Legislative Assembly of the State of Andhra Pradesh as constituted under the provisions of sections 28 and 29 of the States Reorganisation Act, 1956, shall, unless sooner dissolved, continue for a period of five years from the date referred to in the said section 29 and no longer and the expiration of the said period shall operate as a dissolution of that Legislative Assembly.
key_terms: fixed five-year term override
States Reorganisation Act 1956

breakdown.plain_summary: A one-time override of Article 172's ordinary State Assembly term rule, fixing the newly-formed (1956) Andhra Pradesh Legislative Assembly's term at exactly five years from the date specified in the States Reorganisation Act, 1956 — with automatic dissolution the moment that period expired, unless the Assembly was dissolved even sooner.
essential_elements: Operates notwithstanding Article 172's general State Assembly term provision
Applies specifically to the Andhra Pradesh Legislative Assembly as constituted under sections 28-29 of the States Reorganisation Act, 1956
Fixes the term at five years from the section 29 date, with automatic dissolution on expiry unless already sooner dissolved
exceptions_and_qualifications: This Article was inserted by the Constitution (Seventh Amendment) Act, 1956, as a companion provision to the broader 1956 State reorganisation
It is now entirely spent — that specific five-year term expired decades ago, and subsequent Andhra Pradesh Assemblies have been governed by the ordinary Article 172 rule ever since
breakdown.how_to_read: A narrow, one-time transitional provision relevant only to the institutional history of Andhra Pradesh's first post-reorganisation Legislative Assembly — no bearing on any current Assembly term question, which is governed by Article 172.

sections.title: Power of the President to remove difficulties
sections.raw_text:
(1) The President may, for the purpose of removing any difficulties, particularly in relation to the transition from the provisions of the Government of India Act, 1935, to the provisions of this Constitution, by order direct that this Constitution shall, during such period as may be specified in the order, have effect subject to such adaptations, whether by way of modification, addition or omission, as he may deem to be necessary or expedient:
Provided that no such order shall be made after the first meeting of Parliament duly constituted under Chapter II of Part V.
(2) Every order made under clause (1) shall be laid before Parliament.
(3) The powers conferred on the President by this article, by article 324, by clause (3) of article 367 and by article 391 shall, before the commencement of this Constitution, be exercisable by the Governor-General of the Dominion of India.
key_terms: difficulty-removal power
adaptation by modification, addition or omission
laying before Parliament

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 392 gave the President a broad, one-time power to patch the Constitution's own text — by modification, addition, or omission — wherever genuine transition difficulties arose in moving from the Government of India Act, 1935 to the new constitutional order, but only up until Parliament's first proper meeting under Part V, and every such order had to be placed before Parliament. Before the Constitution actually commenced, this power (along with the Election Commission power under Article 324, the foreign-State-recognition power under Article 367(3), and the now-omitted Article 391) was exercised instead by the Governor-General of the Dominion of India.
essential_elements: Clause (1): Presidential order power to adapt the Constitution itself (by modification, addition, or omission) for a specified period, to remove transition difficulties, especially from the Government of India Act, 1935
Proviso to clause (1): this power could not be exercised after Parliament's first meeting under Part V, Chapter II
Clause (2): every such order had to be laid before Parliament

Clause (3): before the Constitution's commencement, this power (plus the powers under Articles 324, 367(3), and 391) was exercised by the Governor-General of the Dominion of India rather than the President
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is a time-boxed, now-spent power — its window closed once the first post-Constitution Parliament met in 1952, and it cannot be revived or exercised today

Unlike the adaptation powers in Articles 372, 372A, and 371F(l) (which adapt ordinary laws), Article 392 uniquely empowered adaptation of the Constitution's own text itself, making it one of the most extraordinary (if narrowly time-limited) powers in the transitional scheme
breakdown.how_to_read: A historical curiosity illustrating just how much transitional flexibility the framers built in — useful to explain why a handful of early Presidential orders appear to have modified constitutional text outside the ordinary Article 368 amendment process, but with zero contemporary operative relevance given its permanent lapse after Parliament's first 1952 meeting.

sections.title: Short title
sections.raw_text: This Constitution may be called the Constitution of India.
key_terms: short title

breakdown.plain_summary: A one-line naming provision: the document the Constituent Assembly adopted is officially called the Constitution of India — the formal legal name used in every citation, enactment, and court reference to it.
essential_elements: Fixes the official short title of the entire document as 'the Constitution of India'
exceptions_and_qualifications: A short title provision of this kind is standard legislative drafting practice, giving a document its citable name without affecting its substantive content
breakdown.how_to_read: The simplest possible provision in the Constitution — cite it only if a pedantic question ever arises about the document's correct formal name, which is otherwise universally assumed.

sections.title: Commencement
sections.raw_text: This article and articles 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 60, 324, 366, 367, 379, 380, 388, 391, 392 and 393 shall come into force at once, and the remaining provisions of this Constitution shall come into force on the twenty-sixth day of January, 1950, which day is referred to in this Constitution as the commencement of this Constitution.
key_terms: commencement of this Constitution
26 January 1950
immediate-effect articles

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 394 is the Constitution's own 'switch-on' clause: a short list of articles — mostly dealing with citizenship (Articles 5-9), the President's oath (Article 60), the Election Commission (Article 324), definitions (Articles 366-367), transitional Parliament/President provisions (Articles 379, 380, 388), the President's difficulty-removal powers (Articles 391-392), and the short title itself (Article 393) — took effect the moment the Constitution was adopted (26 November 1949), while every other provision waited until 26 January 1950, the date the Constitution itself defines as its 'commencement.'
essential_elements: Lists the specific articles (this Article plus 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 60, 324, 366, 367, 379, 380, 388, 391, 392, 393) that came into force immediately upon adoption, ahead of the rest of the Constitution
Fixes 26 January 1950 as the date on which all remaining provisions came into force
Defines 26 January 1950 as 'the commencement of this Constitution' — the reference date used throughout the rest of the constitutional text
exceptions_and_qualifications: 26 January was deliberately chosen to mark the anniversary of the 1930 Purna Swaraj (complete independence) declaration, not for any purely administrative reason

The early-effect articles were specifically those needed to get citizenship, the Presidency, the Election Commission, and the transitional provisional Parliament machinery running before the full Constitution took hold, so India would not have a governance gap between adoption and formal commencement
breakdown.how_to_read: The definitional anchor for the phrase 'commencement of this Constitution' used throughout the entire document — whenever another Article refers to that phrase, it means 26 January 1950, with the narrow list of Article 394's named exceptions having already applied from 26 November 1949.

sections.title: Authoritative text in the Hindi language
sections.raw_text:
(1) The President shall cause to be published under his authority,—
(a) the translation of this Constitution in the Hindi language, signed by the members of the Constituent Assembly, with such modifications as may be necessary to bring it in conformity with the language, style and terminology adopted in the authoritative texts of Central Acts in the Hindi language, and incorporating therein all the amendments of this Constitution made before such publication; and
(b) the translation in the Hindi language of every amendment of this Constitution made in the English language.
(2) The translation of this Constitution and of every amendment thereof published under clause (1) shall be construed to have the same meaning as the original thereof and if any difficulty arises in so construing any part of such translation, the President shall cause the same to be revised suitably.
(3) The translation of this Constitution and of every amendment thereof published under this article shall be deemed to be, for all purposes, the authoritative text thereof in the Hindi language.
key_terms: authoritative Hindi text
Presidential publication duty
Constituent-Assembly-signed Hindi translation

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 394A makes the official Hindi translation of the Constitution just as legally authoritative as the original English text — not merely a convenience translation. The President must publish a Hindi version based on the translation the Constituent Assembly members themselves signed, updated with proper Central-Acts Hindi legal terminology and all amendments made before publication, plus a Hindi translation of every future English-language amendment; any construction difficulty in the Hindi text triggers a Presidential revision duty, and once published, the Hindi text is deemed authoritative for all purposes.
essential_elements: Clause (1)(a): Presidential duty to publish a Hindi translation based on the Constituent-Assembly-signed version, adapted to standard Central Acts Hindi terminology, incorporating all pre-publication amendments
Clause (1)(b): ongoing Presidential duty to publish a Hindi translation of every subsequent English-language constitutional amendment
Clause (2): the Hindi translation must be construed to carry the same meaning as the original; any construction difficulty obliges the President to revise the translation
Clause (3): once published under this Article, the Hindi translation is deemed the authoritative Hindi text for all purposes — not merely persuasive or explanatory
exceptions_and_qualifications: This Article was not part of the original 1950 Constitution — it was inserted by the Constitution (Fifty-eighth Amendment) Act, 1987, decades after the Constitution's commencement

The deeming of 'authoritative' status under clause (3) applies only to translations actually published under this Article's procedure — an unofficial or uncertified Hindi translation carries no such status
breakdown.how_to_read: The key provision to invoke whenever a case turns on interpreting the Hindi text of the Constitution or an amendment — remember that Article 394A gives the properly published Hindi version equal authoritative status with the English text, not merely explanatory value, and that the President bears an ongoing duty to resolve any interpretive mismatch between the two.

sections.title: Repeals
sections.raw_text: The Indian Independence Act, 1947, and the Government of India Act, 1935, together with all enactments amending or supplementing the latter Act, but not including the Abolition of Privy Council Jurisdiction Act, 1949, are hereby repealed.
key_terms: repeal of Indian Independence Act 1947
repeal of Government of India Act 1935
Abolition of Privy Council Jurisdiction Act 1949 preserved

breakdown.plain_summary: The Constitution's final article is a clean-break repeal clause: it formally ends the legal life of the two British framework statutes that had governed India — the Indian Independence Act, 1947 (which created the Dominion of India) and the Government of India Act, 1935 (the detailed governance framework, along with everything that amended or supplemented it) — while specifically sparing the Abolition of Privy Council Jurisdiction Act, 1949, from this repeal, since that Act's own job (ending Privy Council appeals) remained relevant to the transitional judicial provisions (Article 374) still operating under the new Constitution.
essential_elements: Repeals the Indian Independence Act, 1947 in its entirety
Repeals the Government of India Act, 1935 together with all enactments amending or supplementing it
Expressly excludes the Abolition of Privy Council Jurisdiction Act, 1949 from this repeal, leaving it in force
exceptions_and_qualifications: Article 372(1) is the necessary counterpart to this repeal — it is what kept ordinary laws made under the repealed 1935 Act (as opposed to the framework Act itself) continuing in force, so the repeal here does not create a legal vacuum for subordinate legislation

The specific preservation of the Abolition of Privy Council Jurisdiction Act, 1949 reflects that its substantive work (terminating Privy Council appellate jurisdiction) was itself still being given transitional effect through Article 374, making its continuation useful rather than redundant
breakdown.how_to_read: The Constitution's formal 'clean slate' provision — cite it together with Article 372 whenever explaining why colonial-era subordinate legislation survived 1950 even though the two overarching framework Acts that had once authorised it were expressly repealed by this Article.
